blocks.label: OT
blocks.meaning: 1-out-of-\( N \) oblivious transfer of \( \tau \)-bit strings: the sender inputs \( N \) strings and the receiver learns the one it chooses, as in PRTY20's \( \mathcal{F}^{\tau}_{N\text{-OT}} \).

params.meaning: Strings the receiver chooses from
params.name: N

params.meaning: String length in bits, where the paper states it
params.name: \tau

blocks.label: ROT
blocks.meaning: Random OT: as OT, but the sender inputs nothing and receives random strings, as in PRTY20's \( \mathcal{F}^{\tau}_{N\text{-ROT}} \).

params.meaning: Strings the receiver chooses from
params.name: N

params.meaning: String length in bits, where the paper states it
params.name: \tau

blocks.label: C-OT
blocks.meaning: Correlated OT of \( \tau \)-bit strings: the sender fixes a correlation \( f \) and gets a random \( m_0 \) with \( m_1 = f(m_0) \), and the receiver learns \( m_b \) for its choice bit \( b \), as KRSSW19 takes it from ALSZ13.

params.meaning: String length in bits
params.name: \tau

blocks.label: OOS
blocks.meaning: The OT extension of Orrù, Orsini and Scholl as PRTY20 defines it: for the sender's \( s \) and the receiver's choices \( d_1, \ldots, d_m \), the sender gets \( q_i \) and the receiver \( r_i = q_i \oplus s \wedge C(d_i) \), for a binary linear code \( C \) of length \( n_C \), dimension \( \tau \) and distance at least \( \kappa \); the outputs are XOR-homomorphic across instances.

params.meaning: Dimension: the number of instances, all with one sender string \( s \)
params.name: m

params.meaning: Length of the linear code: the width of the OT-extension matrix
params.name: n_C

params.meaning: Dimension of the code: the length in bits of each choice string, so \( N = 2^{\tau} \)
params.name: \tau

blocks.label: OLE
blocks.meaning: Oblivious linear function evaluation over \( \mathbb{F} \): the sender inputs \( a, b \), the receiver \( x \), and the receiver learns \( ax + b \), as GS19's \( \mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{OLE}} \).

params.meaning: The field: named (\( \mathbb{F}_{2^{\kappa}} \)), or given by the size of its elements in bits, \( |\mathbb{F}| \), as everywhere in the table
params.name: \mathbb{F}

blocks.label: VOLE
blocks.meaning: Vector OLE of dimension \( m \) over a field \( \mathbb{F} \): the sender gets \( \Delta \) and \( \vec{B} \), the receiver \( \vec{A} \) and \( \vec{C} = \vec{A}\Delta + \vec{B} \); random, as in RS21's \( \mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{vole}} \), or with the receiver's vector chosen, as in GPRTY21's vOLE.

params.meaning: Dimension: the number of correlations, all with one \( \Delta \)
params.name: m

params.meaning: The field: named (\( \mathbb{F}_{2^{\kappa}} \)), or given by the size of its elements in bits, \( |\mathbb{F}| \), as everywhere in the table
params.name: \mathbb{F}

blocks.label: sub-VOLE
blocks.meaning: Subfield VOLE: \( \vec{A} \) over a base field \( \mathbb{B} \), and \( \Delta \), \( \vec{B} \), \( \vec{C} \) over its extension \( \mathbb{F} \), as in RR22's \( \mathcal{F}_{\textsf{sub-vole}} \).

params.meaning: Dimension: the number of correlations
params.name: m

params.meaning: The base field: named, or given by the size of its elements in bits, \( |\mathbb{B}| \)
params.name: \mathbb{B}

params.meaning: The extension field: named, or given by the size of its elements in bits, \( |\mathbb{F}| \)
params.name: \mathbb{F}

blocks.label: OPRF
blocks.meaning: Oblivious PRF: the receiver inputs queries \( q_1, \ldots, q_c \) and learns \( F(k, q_i) \), the sender inputs or gets the key \( k \), as PSTY19 defines it; its one-time \( \mathcal{F}_{\mathsf{OPRF}} \) has \( c = 1 \).

blocks.label: OPPRF

conventions.rule: Where the paper assumes every set has the same size, formulas use \( n = n_X = n_Y \); where the sizes may differ, \( n_X \) (sender) and \( n_Y \) (receiver).
Two-party tables count messages (one flow in one direction is one message); multiparty tables count rounds (every party may send in a round).
Phases run one after another and are listed apart. Within a phase, steps that need nothing from each other run at the same time, so the count is the longest chain of dependent steps.
Every cost is counted from the protocol: each message and who sends it, each operation and who performs it. Communication is the bits a role sends. A paper's own figures only check the count.
Computation counts only the costly operations. XORs, additions (in a field too), code encodings, lookups, comparisons and permutations are not counted.
Each evaluation of a hash function is one sym op, hashing items into bins included.
OTs and circuit AND gates count invocations of a building block; only a closed row shows them.

A building block is what a protocol uses and its paper neither builds nor costs: a functionality of its hybrid model (VOLE, OT, OPRF, 2PC) or a garbled circuit. \( k\,\mathsf{Func}[\ldots] \) is \( k \) independent invocations.
An open row costs a block from the protocol its paper names for it, counted like the protocol itself with the instance's parameters.

Where the roles invoke a block a different number of times (a leader paired with every client), its arrow gives each role's count; its one-time setup runs once per pairing, so each role's setup figures count its own pairings.

A block used without a protocol named for it is not counted: its line reads "not instantiated by" the paper that leaves it abstract. Messages leave such a block inside an implementation out and name it after "excl.", so that count is no bound.
Hashing and OKVS expansion constants are written as the paper prints them; a parameter the paper fixes as a function of the set sizes or security parameters is substituted.

constructions.security_model: standalone, static passive adversary; Theorem 3 in the (F_△, F_vec-leq)-hybrid model and Theorem 4 in the F_pict-hybrid model (pp. 9-10); correctness except with probability \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (Theorem 3, p. 9)
constructions.security_notion: two-party threshold PSI
constructions.summary: Two-party threshold PSI that hashes both sets into \( t \) buckets under \( \lambda \) functions and runs the Ghosh-Simkin cardinality test at a logarithmic threshold on every bucket, combining the secret-shared results. If some partition shows a small symmetric difference, the intersection is then computed.

edges.evidenceLocator: HEK12 §7.3 with footnotes 3-4 (p. 12), Figure 11 and Table 2 (p. 13), NDSS 2012 PDF dated 2011-11-28

The leaky malicious-sender protocol uses labeled PSI with hash-valued labels as its only output channel and drops the intersection polynomial.

edges.evidenceLocator: CMGD21 §3 (p. 6) and §3.1 (p. 7), IACR ePrint 2021/1116, PDF dated 2021-11-14
edges.note: Prime-field slots are safe only because CMGD21 makes the CHLR18 OPRF step mandatory: partial matches of OPRF outputs reveal nothing about the sender's items.

PSTY19 adapts the polynomial OPPRF of KMPRT17 to a one-query definition that allows correlated targets and batches the hints of all bins into one polynomial of total size linear in the programmed points.

edges.evidenceLocator: PRTY20 §1.1 (pp. 2-3); Table 1 (p. 21); Table 2 (p. 24); Appendix D (pp. 34-35), IACR ePrint 2020/193, PDF dated 2020-02-16
edges.note: PaXoS-PSI improves on the communication of Rindal-Rosulek dual-execution malicious PSI from \( O(\kappa n \log n) \) to \( O(\kappa n) \), replacing hashing into small bins with a PaXoS encoding over OOS; for \( 2^{20} \) items it reports 202.04 MB against 22,183 MB for the dual-execution variant with 64-bit items and 1,322 MB for the encode-commit variant.

edges.evidenceLocator: RT21 abstract (p. 1), §1 (p. 2), §1.2 (pp. 5-6), IACR ePrint 2021/1159, version of October 17, 2021
edges.note: RT21 present their malicious protocol as an improvement of the classic Diffie-Hellman protocol of Huberman, Franklin, and Hogg: \( n + 1 \) group elements plus n hashes against \( 2n \) group elements plus n hashes, while security rises from semi-honest to malicious.
PSTY19 reduces the \( \omega(n) \) comparisons of the PSWW18 construction, \( s \cdot n \) of which serve a stash of size \( \omega(1) \), to \( O(n) \) comparisons and linear communication.
CMGD21 builds its labeled mode on the CHLR18 approach of encrypting labels under part of the OPRF output and interpolating the encrypted labels, adapting it to prime-field chunks.

edges.evidenceLocator: FNP04 §4.2 (pp. 6-8), EUROCRYPT 2004, LNCS 3027, printed pages
edges.note: Balanced-allocation hashing splits the client's polynomial into low-degree bin polynomials, reducing the server's exponentiations from \( O(k_C k_S) \) to \( O(k_C + k_S \ln \ln k_C) \).

edges.evidenceLocator: PSTY19 abstract (p. 1), Table 3 (p. 25), and Table 5 (p. 27), IACR ePrint 2019/241, PDF dated 2019-02-28
edges.note: The stash-less OPPRF protocol communicates 2.6 to 12.8 times less and runs 2.8 to 5.8 times faster than the 2D cuckoo-hashing protocol, the previous best circuit-based PSI.

edges.evidenceLocator: GS23 §1.3, paper outline paragraph, and footnote 5 (p. 4), IACR ePrint 2023/919, PDF dated 2023-06-12

edges.evidenceLocator: RR22 §1 (p. 3); §5.1 and Table 1 (pp. 23-25), IACR ePrint 2022/320, PDF dated 2022-11-02

edges.evidenceLocator: RT21 Appendix A.1 (pp. 23-24) and A.2 (p. 26), IACR ePrint 2021/1159, version of October 17, 2021

edges.evidenceLocator: FNP04 §5 (pp. 9-13), EUROCRYPT 2004, LNCS 3027, printed pages
edges.note: The malicious-client and malicious-server protocols modify PM-Semi-Honest, with balanced-allocation hashing, by cut-and-choose and by random-oracle derandomization.

edges.evidenceLocator: GS23 abstract (p. 1), §1 (p. 1), §1.2 (p. 2), and Corollary 6 (p. 16), IACR ePrint 2023/919, PDF dated 2023-06-12

CHLR18 applies an OPRF to both sets before the CLR17 homomorphic intersection, which removes noise flooding, bin padding, and polynomial randomization and raises security from semi-honest to a malicious receiver (with privacy against a malicious sender).

edges.evidenceLocator: GS23 §1 (pp. 1-2), IACR ePrint 2023/919, PDF dated 2023-06-12
edges.note: GS23 note that the BMRR \( \tilde O(\lambda \ell t) \) protocol without FHE is equivalent to two-party threshold PSI for \( \ell = 2 \) but for \( \ell > 2 \) requires fewer than t distinct elements outside the intersection among all sets, a condition GS23's large-intersection protocol does not impose.

edges.evidenceLocator: NTY §5.1 and Tables 3-4 (pp. 11-12), IACR ePrint 2021/1221, PDF dated 2021-09-17

Raghuraman and Rindal extend the VOLE-PSI protocol to subfield VOLE, so that the OKVS lives in a base field of about \( \lambda + \log(n_x n_y) \) bits; for \( 2^{20} \) items they report \( 180n \) bits against \( 426n \).

CMGD21 lowers the number of encrypted query powers from \( O(\log B) \), as with CLR17 windowing, to \( O(1) \) using depth-free Frobenius operations, reducing communication from \( \tilde O(2^{C} C^{2}) \) to \( \tilde O(C^{2}) \) with \( C = \log \log |X| \).

edges.note: VCE count tk OPPRFs at the leader and k per assistant for the ZeroXOR step of NTY, 3.5tk OTs in total, and describe it as outperforming the protocols of Kolesnikov et al., Ben-Efraim et al., and Chandran et al.

CHLR18 restricts what a malicious sender can do in FHE-based unbalanced PSI from forcing the intersection to be the receiver's full set, as in CLR17, to X ∩ Y ∩ leakage(Y), under an H-limited FHE assumption.
KMPRT build every OPPRF from the KKRT batched OPRF, one OPRF instance per bin plus a sender hint, and inherit its related-key and leakage relaxations.

VOLE-PSI's circuit-PSI keeps the PSTY19 protocol and replaces its polynomial-based OPPRF with one built from the VOLE OPRF and XoPaXoS; for \( 2^{20} \) items it runs in 23.3 s against 72.0 s at 5 Gbps with IKNP-based GMW.

edges.evidenceLocator: CHLR18 §1.3 (p. 3) and §5.1 (pp. 11-12), IACR ePrint 2018/787, PDF dated 2018-08-27
edges.note: CHLR18 extends the CLR17 protocol to labeled PSI: the sender additionally evaluates a label-interpolation polynomial per bin, keeping communication sublinear in the sender's set.

GS23 follows the GS19 split into a cardinality test and an intersection step, and instantiates the inner two-party test of its compiler with the GS19 cardinality test, adapted to secret-shared output and run at logarithmic thresholds.

edges.evidenceLocator: NTY §2 (pp. 4-5), Protocol 4.2 (p. 10), §5 (p. 11), IACR ePrint 2021/1221, PDF dated 2021-09-17
edges.note: NTY take the OPPRF definitions almost verbatim from KMPRT and run an OPPRF from each of t parties to P_n inside ZeroXOR.

edges.evidenceLocator: PSWW18 abstract (p. 1), §1.4 (p. 5), and §6.2 (pp. 21-22), IACR ePrint 2018/120, PDF dated 2019-01-24
edges.note: Mirror cuckoo hashing reduces the comparisons of circuit-based PSI from the \( O(n \log n) \) of the sort-compare-shuffle circuit to \( \omega(n) \).
The OKVS definition generalizes PaXoS from binary to linear and other key-value encodings and makes obliviousness explicit; a binary OKVS is a PaXoS.

edges.evidenceLocator: BMRR §1.1 (p. 2) and §2.3 (p. 6), IACR ePrint 2020/600, PDF dated 2021-02-25
edges.note: BMRR generalize the two-party threshold PSI functionality of GS19 to two multiparty functionalities that coincide for two parties.

edges.evidenceLocator: CMGD21 §1.2 (p. 3) and §3.1 (pp. 7-8), IACR ePrint 2021/1116, PDF dated 2021-11-14
edges.note: CMGD21 replaces computing all powers up to the partition size, as in the CLR17 framework retained by CHLR18, with Paterson-Stockmeyer evaluation, reducing non-scalar multiplications per bin from linear to \( O(\sqrt{B}) \).

edges.evidenceLocator: NTY §2.0.4 (p. 5), Protocol 4.4 (p. 10), §5 (p. 11), IACR ePrint 2021/1221, PDF dated 2021-09-17
edges.note: Each client sends the pivot a single OKVS encoding its items instead of running pairwise OPPRFs, using the OKVS definition of Garimella et al. and PaXoS as the instance they prove oblivious.
Used as the binary OKVS of PaXoS-PSI, the three-hash table reduces the malicious protocol's communication 1.61 times for \( 2^{20} \) items, because \( 1.3n \) OTs replace \( 2.4n \).

edges.evidenceLocator: RT21 §1 (p. 2), §1.2 (pp. 5-6), Table 1 (p. 4), IACR ePrint 2021/1159, version of October 17, 2021
edges.note: RT21's semi-honest variants send one key-agreement message, one field element per receiver item, and one short key per sender item, against the classic Diffie-Hellman protocol's group element per item in both directions, which RT21 names as the protocol it improves.

edges.evidenceLocator: Ion et al. §3.1 (p. 5) and §4.2 (p. 8), IACR ePrint 2019/723, PDF dated 2020-09-05
edges.note: Ion et al. extend the shuffled commutative-exponentiation intersection-cardinality protocol of Huberman, Franklin, and Hogg with additively homomorphic tags so that one party also learns the sum of values over the intersection.

edges.evidenceLocator: PSTY19 §6 (pp. 21-22), IACR ePrint 2019/241, PDF dated 2019-02-28
edges.note: Payloads are injected with a second batched OPPRF whose targets differ per item, XORing the bin mask with each item's payload.

edges.evidenceLocator: GS19 §1 (p. 2), IACR ePrint 2019/175, PDF dated 2020-05-27
edges.note: GS19 lists PSWW18 among threshold PSI solutions whose communication scales at least linearly in the smaller set, and gives protocols whose communication depends mainly on t.

edges.evidenceLocator: RS21 §2, Eq. (1) and Conjecture 2.1 (pp. 11-12); Lemma 3.3 (p. 18), IACR ePrint 2021/266, PDF dated 2024-08-08
edges.note: The malicious-receiver proof of the VOLE-based OPRF uses the PaXoS bound to limit the receiver's effective set to \( O(n) \), and conjectures a tighter bound of m.

sections.content: Unbalanced PSI from leveled FV: the receiver sends its cuckoo table batched and encrypted, and the sender homomorphically evaluates, slot by slot, the polynomial whose roots are its items in the matching bin. Windowing, partitioning and modulus switching keep the depth and the reply small, so communication is \( O(n_Y\log n_X) \) and only the sender works in \( n_X \).

metadata.title: Efficient malicious two-party PSI

sections.content:
The application that practical two-party PSI keeps returning to is private
contact discovery: a phone checks which of its contacts use a messaging
service without revealing its address book (PSI-PAPER-2017-CLR,
PSI-PAPER-2019-KRSSW). The sets are unbalanced, so communication should
depend on the phone's set rather than on the user base, as it does without
privacy (PSI-PAPER-2017-CLR); and either side may cheat. Security against
malicious parties is the property that the fastest and the most
communication-efficient protocols each weaken (PSI-PAPER-2018-CHLR,
PSI-PAPER-2019-KRSSW). The goal is all three at once.
sections.heading: Why this goal

sections.content:
Rows group protocols by technique and by the security they prove. A malicious
row may let a corrupt party use a constant factor more items than it
declared, as every fast malicious protocol does; tighter bounds on that slack
follow only from unproven conjectures that overfitting a polynomial or a
key-value encoding to a random oracle is hard (PSI-PAPER-2021-RS,
PSI-PAPER-2021-RT, PSI-PAPER-2021-GPRTY). The last column asks whether a
protocol fits the deployment Signal's developers described, as reported by
Kales et al. (PSI-PAPER-2019-KRSSW, §7): a server database of \( 10^{9} \) users,
address books of up to 10,000 contacts, lookups in under 2 s, and one server
core handling 1,600 contacts per second. Balanced protocols fail it because
their communication grows with the user base; the unbalanced ones are too
slow at a quarter of that scale and do not resist a malicious server. Times
come from different machines and are compared only with the budget, not with
each other.

metadata.title: Multiparty threshold PSI at optimal communication without FHE

sections.content:
Computing an intersection needs communication linear in the set size, but
when parties only want the intersection if it is large, communication can
depend on the threshold \( t \) instead (PSI-PAPER-2019-GS). For any number of
parties the cost is now pinned down: at least \( \Omega(\ell t) \) bits over
point-to-point channels, and that much suffices with threshold fully
homomorphic encryption (PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR). The area asks for the same cost
from the weaker assumptions behind ordinary PSI (PSI-PAPER-2023-GS).
sections.heading: Why this goal

sections.content:
Each row gives up one requirement: more than two parties, an assumption weaker
than FHE, the exact functionality, or communication counted over
point-to-point channels. The row for threshold additively homomorphic
encryption is marked partial on the first column because it solves a stricter
functionality, which bounds the elements outside the intersection over all
sets together rather than per party. The last row counts a broadcast message
once; over point-to-point channels each broadcast is sent to every party, and
the source does not state the resulting cost.

named_open_by.statement: Notes that a malicious sender can evaluate an arbitrary function on the receiver's encrypted set and so steer the receiver's output, for example to the receiver's whole set, and says that efficiently preventing such behavior by the sender appears extremely challenging.

Calls full simulation-based security against a malicious sender extremely challenging in its setting; names the requirement of communication sublinear in the sender's set as the main barrier, because it rules out extracting that set with zero-knowledge proofs of linear size, and enforcing correct computation by the sender as the second; it therefore proves only privacy against a malicious sender.

metadata.resolution_condition: A two-party protocol in which the receiver, holding \( Y \) with \( |Y| = N_y \), learns \( X^* \cap Y \) and the sender, holding \( X \) with \( |X| = N_x \), learns nothing, that is fully simulation-secure (stand-alone, static corruption, in the plain or the random oracle model) against a malicious receiver whose effective set has at most \( N_y \) items and against a malicious sender, for whom the simulator extracts an effective set \( X^* \) of polynomial size; and whose total communication is at most \( p(\lambda, N_y) \cdot g(N_x) \) for some polynomial \( p \) and some function \( g \) with \( g(N) = o(N) \). metadata.summary: Can a receiver with a small set learn its intersection with a much larger sender set, with full simulation-based security against either party acting maliciously, while communication stays sublinear in the sender's set? Solved for a malicious receiver; open for a malicious sender.
metadata.title: Unbalanced PSI against a malicious sender with sublinear communication

sections.content:
In unbalanced PSI a receiver with a small set \( Y \), such as a phone's
contact list, learns which of its items lie in a sender's much larger set
\( X \), as in private contact discovery. Protocols built on fully homomorphic
encryption let the receiver send its encrypted set and the sender evaluate the
intersection on it, so that communication grows with \( |Y| \) and only
logarithmically with \( |X| \) (PSI-PAPER-2017-CLR). The sender then holds an
encrypted copy of the receiver's set and may compute on it whatever it likes,
which makes security against a malicious sender the hard direction.
sections.heading: Background

sections.content:
Is there a two-party protocol in which the receiver learns \( X \cap Y \) and
the sender learns nothing, that is fully simulation-secure against a malicious
receiver and against a malicious sender, possibly in the random oracle model,
and whose total communication is sublinear in \( |X| \) for every fixed
receiver set size and security parameter?
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
Against a malicious receiver the question is settled: if both sets first pass
through a Diffie-Hellman oblivious PRF keyed by the sender, a simulator reads
the receiver's set off its random-oracle queries, and communication stays
\( O(|Y|\log|X|) \) (PSI-PAPER-2018-CHLR; [security against a malicious
receiver with privacy against the sender](PSI-OP-002)). Against a malicious
sender the same protocol gives only privacy: the receiver's messages reveal
nothing, but the sender still decides what the receiver outputs, for instance
by returning encryptions of zero so that the receiver accepts its whole set
(PSI-PAPER-2018-CHLR, §7.2). Full simulation needs an effective input
extracted from the sender, and the usual tool, zero-knowledge proofs as in
earlier malicious PSI, costs communication linear in \( |X| \); the sender
must also be held to the prescribed homomorphic computation. Making the sender
return, for each match, an encryption of a hash of the item's PRF value
confines it to [removing matches as a function of the receiver's other
items](PSI-OP-004), but only under a heuristic assumption that leveled
homomorphic encryption cannot evaluate the hash.
sections.heading: Why it is open

sections.content:
- Privacy against a malicious sender, which guarantees neither input
  independence nor a correct output for the receiver.
- Leaky functionalities, in which the receiver's output may depend on its items
  outside the intersection.
- Protocols whose communication is linear in the sender's set, such as
  balanced malicious-secure PSI, or protocols that transfer an encoding of the
  whole sender set in a setup phase (PSI-PAPER-2019-KRSSW).
sections.heading: What would not resolve it

sections.content:
Parties: a sender with \( X \), \( |X| = N_x \), and a receiver with \( Y \),
\( |Y| = N_y \); \( N_x \), \( N_y \) and the item length are public. Ideal
functionality: the receiver obtains \( X^* \cap Y \), where \( X^* \) is the
sender's input, and the sender obtains nothing. Security: stand-alone
simulation against a static malicious adversary corrupting either party; the
simulator for a corrupt receiver submits a set of at most \( N_y \) items, and
the simulator for a corrupt sender submits a set of polynomial size. Model:
plain or random oracle model; any computational assumption. Efficiency: total
communication at most \( p(\lambda, N_y)\cdot g(N_x) \) for a polynomial
\( p \) and some \( g(N) = o(N) \).
sections.heading: Formal target

sections.content:
Hashing gives a malicious sender further ways to make the receiver's output
depend on items outside the intersection: it can perform its simple hashing
incorrectly, and when it reuses its preprocessing across receivers and
chooses the hash functions it can provoke cuckoo-hashing failures that depend
on the receiver's set, which leaks one bit (PSI-PAPER-2018-CHLR, §7.2 and
§7.3).
sections.heading: Known obstacles

sections.content:
PSI-PAPER-2017-CLR introduced the homomorphic approach with communication
\( O(|Y|\log|X|) \) against semi-honest parties and noted that a malicious
sender can steer the output. PSI-PAPER-2018-CHLR added oblivious PRF
preprocessing, which gives one-sided simulation against a malicious receiver
and privacy against a malicious sender, and a variant that limits a malicious
sender to a leakage function under the H-limited assumption.
PSI-PAPER-2021-CONG reduced computation and communication while keeping the
same guarantees.

metadata.title: Unbalanced PSI against a malicious receiver with sublinear communication

sections.content:
Give an unbalanced PSI protocol with communication sublinear in the sender's
set that is simulation-secure against a malicious receiver and keeps the
receiver's set private from a malicious sender, in the sense of Hazay and
Lindell: the sender's view reveals nothing about the receiver's input, while
input independence and output correctness are not required.
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
PSI-PAPER-2018-CHLR first maps both sets through the Diffie-Hellman oblivious
PRF \( F_\alpha(x) = H'(H(x)^\alpha) \), whose key the sender holds, and then
runs the homomorphic intersection of PSI-PAPER-2017-CLR on the outputs. In the
random oracle model and in a group where One-More-Gap-Diffie-Hellman is hard,
a simulator extracts a malicious receiver's set, of the honest size, from its
oracle queries (Theorem 1). Semantic security of the homomorphic encryption
and the same group assumption give privacy against a malicious sender
(Theorem 2). Communication is \( O(|Y|\log|X|) \) (§4.2). Because the sender's
non-matching items look random to the receiver, noise flooding is no longer
needed, and the sender can reuse its processed set across receivers.
PSI-PAPER-2021-CONG keeps these guarantees with lower cost.
sections.heading: Resolution

metadata.title: Semi-honest unbalanced PSI with sublinear communication

sections.content:
Give a two-party PSI protocol, secure against semi-honest parties, in which
the receiver learns \( X \cap Y \) and total communication is sublinear in the
sender's set size \( |X| \).
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
PSI-PAPER-2017-CLR has the receiver cuckoo-hash its items, pack the table into
batched ciphertexts of a leveled fully homomorphic scheme, and send them with
some encrypted powers; the sender, holding its items in simple-hashed bins,
evaluates for each bin a polynomial that vanishes on the bin's items and
returns the results, and the receiver reads its matches off the zero slots
(Figure 4). Windowing and partitioning of the bins keep the multiplicative
depth low. Communication is \( O(|Y|\log|X|) \) (abstract), and the protocol
is secure against semi-honest parties in the standard model, assuming an
IND-CPA scheme with circuit privacy, which noise flooding provides in the
leveled setting (Theorem 2).

metadata.title: Unbalanced PSI against a malicious sender with bounded leakage

sections.content:
Give an unbalanced PSI protocol with communication sublinear in the sender's
set that is fully secure against a malicious receiver and simulation-secure
against a malicious sender for a weaker functionality: the sender submits a
set \( X^* \) and a leakage function \( L \), and the receiver obtains
\( X^* \cap Y \cap L(Y) \). A malicious sender can thus withhold matches
depending on the receiver's other items, but cannot add items it does not
hold.
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
PSI-PAPER-2018-CHLR runs its labeled protocol, whose communication is
sublinear in the sender's set (§1.3, p. 3), with the label of each sender item
set to a hash \( H(\mathrm{OPRF}_k(x)) \); the receiver accepts \( y \) only
if the decrypted label at its position equals \( H(\mathrm{OPRF}_k(y)) \), and
the sender proves in zero knowledge that it used one PRF key (Figure 8).
Definition 1 calls a leveled scheme H-limited if no efficient party can turn an
encryption of \( z \) into an encryption of \( H(z) \). In the random oracle
model, with a One-More-Gap-Diffie-Hellman group and a semantically secure
H-limited leveled scheme, the protocol realizes the leaky functionality with
non-black-box simulation, a malicious receiver held to its declared set size,
and a malicious sender's set of polynomial size (Theorem 3). The theorem
covers a sender that does not reuse its preprocessing; with reuse and
sender-chosen hash functions, selective cuckoo-hashing failures leak one bit
(§7.3, p. 18).

metadata.title: Multiparty threshold PSI with optimal communication without FHE

sections.content:
In threshold PSI the parties learn the intersection of their sets only if it is
large, here if it contains at least \( n - t \) of each party's \( n \)
elements, so for small \( t \) communication can fall far below the set size,
which plain PSI cannot achieve in general (PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR, §1). For two
parties PSI-PAPER-2019-GS proved an \( \Omega(t) \) lower bound and an almost
matching protocol from fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR
extended both to \( \ell \) parties: every protocol communicates
\( \Omega(\ell t) \) over point-to-point channels, and threshold FHE achieves
\( O(\ell t\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)) \). Whether that cost is reachable from
weaker assumptions is the remaining question.
sections.heading: Background

sections.content:
Let \( \ell \ge 2 \) parties each hold a set of \( n \) elements, and let
\( t < n \). Without fully homomorphic or threshold fully homomorphic
encryption, is there a protocol, secure against a semi-honest adversary
corrupting up to \( \ell - 1 \) parties, that gives every party the
intersection if it has at least \( n - t \) elements and nothing otherwise,
over point-to-point channels, with total communication
\( \ell t\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)\cdot\mathrm{polylog}(t) \) bits?
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
With threshold FHE the bound is met: PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR tests the
intersection size homomorphically and then computes the intersection with
threshold additively homomorphic encryption ([the threshold-FHE
case](PSI-OP-006)). Because that second phase needs no FHE, [a cardinality
test of the same cost without FHE](PSI-OP-010) would suffice, but
PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR builds a test from threshold additively homomorphic
encryption only for its other functionality, which releases the intersection
when all elements outside it together number at most \( t \), a stricter
condition. For [two parties](PSI-OP-007) the question is settled.
PSI-PAPER-2023-GS reaches \( O(\lambda^2\ell t\,\mathrm{polylog}\,t) \) bits
from oblivious transfer or additively homomorphic encryption by splitting the
sets into buckets and running a quadratic cardinality test on small
thresholds, but in a model where each broadcast message counts once
([the broadcast case](PSI-OP-009)). It does not state the cost over
point-to-point channels, where the \( \Omega(\ell t) \) bound holds and each
broadcast becomes \( \ell - 1 \) private messages, and it does not call its
protocol optimal. With a broadcast channel the known lower bound is only
\( \Omega(t\log\ell + \ell) \) (PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR, Appendix C).
sections.heading: Why it is open

sections.content:
- Protocols that use plain or threshold fully homomorphic encryption.
- Protocols for the functionality that bounds all elements outside the
  intersection together, rather than each party's.
- Bounds that count a broadcast message once, unless they are also shown over
  point-to-point channels.
- Communication of order \( \ell t^2 \), or with factors in \( \ell \) or
  \( t \) beyond \( \mathrm{polylog}(t) \).
sections.heading: What would not resolve it

sections.content:
Parties \( P_1,\dots,P_\ell \), \( \ell \ge 2 \), hold sets
\( X_1,\dots,X_\ell \) of exactly \( n \) elements from a universe of
\( \mathrm{poly}(\lambda) \)-bit strings; \( t < n \) is public. Ideal
functionality: if \( |\bigcap_i X_i| \ge n - t \), every party receives
\( \bigcap_i X_i \); otherwise every party receives \( \bot \). Security:
simulation against a static semi-honest adversary corrupting any \( \ell - 1 \)
parties. Network: pairwise private channels, each message counted at its
length; a star topology is allowed. Efficiency: total communication
\( O(\ell t\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)\cdot\mathrm{polylog}(t)) \) bits for
every \( n \); rounds unrestricted. Assumptions: any that do not include
fully homomorphic or threshold fully homomorphic encryption.
sections.heading: Formal target

sections.content:
PSI-PAPER-2019-GS initiated sublinear threshold PSI for two parties, with an
\( \Omega(t) \) bound, an almost matching FHE protocol, an
\( \tilde O(t^2) \) protocol from additively homomorphic encryption, and a
multiparty extension. PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR defined two multiparty
functionalities, proved \( \Omega(\ell t) \) for both, met it with threshold
FHE, gave \( \tilde O(\ell t) \) without FHE for the stricter functionality,
and thereby settled the two-party case. PSI-PAPER-2023-GS compiled quadratic
cardinality tests into quasilinear ones, counting broadcast messages once.

sections.content:
Give an \( \ell \)-party threshold PSI protocol, secure against a semi-honest
adversary corrupting up to \( \ell - 1 \) parties, that releases the
intersection exactly when it has at least \( n - t \) elements, with
communication \( \ell t\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) \) up to polylogarithmic
factors over point-to-point channels, assuming threshold fully homomorphic
encryption.
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR works in a star network. In the first phase each party
sends a central party \( O(t) \) threshold-FHE encryptions of evaluations of
its set polynomial; the central party homomorphically interpolates a rational
function and tests it at a random point, and the parties jointly decrypt one
bit (Theorem 5.1, with \( O(\ell t\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)) \)
communication, p. 19). If the test passes, a second phase from threshold
additively homomorphic encryption gives every party \( 3t + 4 \) evaluations
of a randomized combination of all set polynomials, from which it interpolates
the elements of its own set outside the intersection (Theorem B.1). The whole
protocol communicates \( O(\ell t\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)) \) bits in a
constant number of rounds (Corollary B.2, whose statement names the other
functionality although it instantiates this protocol), matching the
\( \Omega(\ell t) \) bound for point-to-point networks (Theorem 4.1,
Corollary 4.2).

sections.content:
Give a two-party protocol, secure against semi-honest parties and without
fully homomorphic encryption, that reveals the intersection of two sets of
\( n \) elements exactly when it has at least \( n - t \) elements, with
communication \( \tilde O(t) \), that is \( t\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda) \)
up to polylogarithmic factors.
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
PSI-PAPER-2019-GS reduces two-party threshold PSI to a private intersection
cardinality test followed by an intersection step that already costs
\( \tilde O(t) \) (Theorem 4 and the following paragraph). Its own test, a
singularity test of a Hankel matrix built from the parties' polynomial
encodings, cost \( \tilde O(t^2) \). PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR observes that the
Hankel structure reduces the test to the half-GCD problem, solvable in
quasi-linear time, so that the parties can obtain additive shares of the
matrix and test it with Yao's garbled circuits or additively homomorphic
encryption at quasi-linear cost (§3.3); its second phase needs only additively
homomorphic encryption for two parties (§7.1). The paper states that this
gives two-party threshold PSI with communication \( \tilde O(t) \) from
additively homomorphic encryption and settles the question of
PSI-PAPER-2019-GS (abstract; §1.2), with \( \mathrm{poly}(\lambda) \) factors omitted.
PSI-PAPER-2023-GS credits the bound \( O(\lambda t\,\mathrm{polylog}\,t) \)
without FHE to this combination (footnote 5, p. 4).
sections.heading: Resolution

sections.content:
Is there a two-party protocol, secure against semi-honest parties and without
fully homomorphic encryption, that outputs whether two sets of \( n \)
elements share at least \( n - t \) of them, with communication
\( t\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)\cdot\mathrm{polylog}(t) \) bits?
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
In the test of PSI-PAPER-2019-GS the sets are encoded so that the size of
their symmetric difference is the number of monomials of a polynomial, whose
sparsity is decided by the singularity of a Hankel matrix; testing it with a
protocol for arbitrary matrices costs \( \tilde O(t^2) \).
PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR observes that a Hankel matrix has only linearly many
distinct entries and that its singularity reduces to the half-GCD problem,
solvable in quasi-linear time, so the parties can obtain additive shares of the
matrix and test it with additively homomorphic encryption or Yao's garbled
circuits at quasi-linear communication (§3.3). Theorem 6.5 and Corollary 6.6
give the protocol for any number of parties from threshold additively
homomorphic encryption; for more than two parties it decides whether all
elements outside the intersection together number at most \( t \).
sections.heading: Resolution

sections.content:
Give an \( \ell \)-party threshold PSI protocol, without fully homomorphic
encryption and secure against a semi-honest adversary corrupting up to
\( \ell - 1 \) parties, with communication
\( \ell t\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)\cdot\mathrm{polylog}(t) \) bits, in a
network of private channels together with a broadcast channel on which
sending a message costs its length once, whatever the number of recipients.
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
PSI-PAPER-2023-GS assumes pairwise private channels and a unit-cost broadcast
channel, against a static passive adversary corrupting all but one party
(§2.1). Each party hashes its set into \( t \) buckets, independently
\( \epsilon \) times for a statistical parameter \( \epsilon = O(\lambda) \);
in every bucket the parties obtain secret shares of the bucket's exact
intersection size when it is within a logarithmic threshold of full, and of a
default value otherwise, and a final secure computation checks whether one of
the \( \epsilon \) sums of these shares shows a large enough intersection
(Theorem 7). The bucket test is built from a quadratic cardinality test of
earlier work run at logarithmic thresholds (Theorem 8), which the paper states
can be rewritten over generic secure computation at
\( O(\lambda\ell\,\mathrm{poly}(t)) \). The result is an \( \ell \)-party
cardinality test and, with the multiparty intersection step that
PSI-PAPER-2019-GS sketches without a theorem (§8.2 there), passively secure
threshold PSI with
\( O(\epsilon^2\ell t\,\mathrm{polylog}\,t) \) bits from oblivious transfer or
additively homomorphic encryption (Corollaries 5 and 6).
sections.heading: Resolution

sections.content:
Is there an \( \ell \)-party protocol, secure against a semi-honest adversary
corrupting up to \( \ell - 1 \) parties and without fully homomorphic
encryption, that tells every party whether the intersection of their sets of
\( n \) elements has at least \( n - t \) elements, with total communication
\( \ell t\cdot\mathrm{poly}(\lambda)\cdot\mathrm{polylog}(t) \) bits over
point-to-point channels?
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR builds this test only from threshold FHE (Theorem 5.1); its
test from threshold additively homomorphic encryption decides the stricter
union-based condition instead (Corollary 6.6). PSI-PAPER-2023-GS gives an
\( \ell \)-party test with secret-shared output and
\( O(\epsilon^2\ell t\,\mathrm{polylog}\,t) \) bits from oblivious transfer or
additively homomorphic encryption (Corollary 5), but in a model where a
broadcast message counts once (§2.1), and it does not state the cost over
point-to-point channels.

recognized_by.statement: Reports Signal's developers' requirements for deploying PSI-based contact discovery (\( 10^{9} \) users, address books of up to 10,000 contacts, lookups under 2 s, 1,600 contacts per second on one core) and states that its protocols, secure against malicious clients only, do not yet meet them.
Presents private contact discovery from a phone as the motivating application of unbalanced PSI, where earlier protocols send data proportional to both entire sets.
Calls full simulation-based security against a malicious sender extremely challenging when communication must stay sublinear in the sender's set.

metadata.resolution_condition: An implementation of a two-party PSI protocol with a proof of simulation-based security against a malicious client and against a malicious server (a corrupt party's effective set may exceed its declared size by a constant factor; random oracles allowed), together with a measurement in which a client on a smartphone checks 10,000 contacts against a server set of \( 10^{9} \) items in under 2 s end to end, and the server's computation per contact, including any per-client precomputation and amortized over clients, is at most 1/1,600 core-second. One-time processing of the server's set, one-time downloads, and the network are reported but not bounded.
metadata.summary: Can PSI secure against a malicious client and a malicious server check 10,000 contacts against \( 10^{9} \) users in under 2 s, with one server core handling 1,600 contacts per second, as Signal's developers require? Protocols secure against both parties run only on balanced sets; those measured at this scale trust the server.
metadata.title: Malicious PSI deployable for contact discovery

sections.content:
Messaging services find which of a user's contacts are registered by
comparing the phone's address book with the user base. Signal's developers
considered PSI for this and, as Kales et al. report, stated what a deployable
protocol must handle: a server database of \( 10^{9} \) users, address books of up to
10,000 contacts, lookups in under 2 s, and one server core handling 1,600
contacts per second (PSI-PAPER-2019-KRSSW, §7). Private contact discovery from
a phone is also the application that motivates unbalanced PSI
(PSI-PAPER-2017-CLR). A server that runs the protocol can cheat as well as a
client, so the goal asks for security against both.
sections.heading: Background

sections.content:
Build and measure a two-party PSI protocol, simulation-secure against a
malicious client and against a malicious server (a corrupt party may use a
constant factor more items than it declared; random oracles allowed), in
which a phone checks 10,000 contacts against \( 10^9 \) registered users in
under 2 s, while the server spends at most 1/1,600 core-second per contact.
sections.heading: Problem

sections.content:
Protocols secure against both parties are balanced: their communication is at
least 128 bits per item of either set (PSI-PAPER-2022-RR), so a lookup against
\( 10^9 \) users would move at least 16 GB, and the largest measured run has
\( 2^{24} \) items per party. The protocols built for contact discovery give
up security against the server. Precomputed OPRF PSI on a phone checks 1,024
contacts against \( 2^{28} \) users in 2.92 s over WiFi and 6.53 s over LTE
after a one-time 1,072 MiB download, is secure only against a malicious
client, and its authors state that Signal's requirements are not met
(PSI-PAPER-2019-KRSSW). FHE-based unbalanced PSI keeps communication small but
only keeps the server from learning the client's items, not from changing the
client's output (PSI-PAPER-2018-CHLR), and for 2,048 contacts against
\( 2^{28} \) users its sender needs 4.75 s on 24 threads
(PSI-PAPER-2021-CONG). Full simulation against a malicious sender with
communication sublinear in its set is itself open
([PSI-OP-001](PSI-OP-001)).
sections.heading: Why it is open

sections.content:
- Protocols secure only against a malicious client, or that trust the server
  in any other way, however fast.
- Measurements at a smaller user base or address book, or extrapolations.
- Latency amortized over several lookups, or server throughput that leaves
  out per-client precomputation.
- Designs that add servers assumed not to collude, which change the setting.
sections.heading: What would not resolve it

sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title, authors, venue, and pages were checked against the ACM PDF (first page, p. 78). The PDF carries the ACM copyright line "E-COMMERCE 99, Denver, Colorado" and printed pages 78-86. No other version was compared.
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-1999-HFH-DH-PREFERENCE-MATCHING: a protocol, related by the authors to Diffie-Hellman key exchange and to encrypted key exchange, in which two parties exponentiate hashes of their list items with secret exponents and count the matches (Appendix A, p. 85). The protocol is the construction PSI-CONSTRUCTION-1999-HFH. Not recorded, outside the topic: community discovery by posting key pairs for yes/no answers (§3, p. 80; Appendix A, p. 85), deniable and convertible signatures (§4, pp. 81-82; Appendix A, p. 86), and 1-out-of-n and t-out-of-n proofs of knowledge for anonymous group membership (§5, pp. 82-83; Appendix A, p. 86).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: The paper does not use the terms "set intersection" or "PSI". It calls the task private preference matching: the basic function takes two lists of yes/no answers and a threshold and outputs whether the number of matching answers reaches the threshold (§3, p. 81). The protocol it gives in Appendix A instead lets each party count the matches, and the paper says that this leaks the number of matches rather than the one-bit threshold decision, as a trade-off for efficiency (§3, p. 81). Revealing which items are shared appears only as a variation in which the last two lists are not permuted (Appendix A, p. 85). Later papers describe this protocol as the classic Diffie-Hellman PSI protocol (for example PSI-PAPER-2021-RT, §1, p. 1); that description is theirs. The paper states no adversary model and no security argument for the matching protocol. Its assumptions appear only as context: a prime \( p \) with a large prime factor \( q \) of \( p - 1 \) in which discrete logarithms are believed hard (Appendix A, p. 85), and a hash function whose output "cannot be easily influenced or predicted" (§2, p. 79). It adds that a zero-knowledge proof could be incorporated so that active cheating other than strategic choice of inputs is detected, without giving one (Appendix A, p. 85).

sections.content: Efficient Private Matching and Set Intersection
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title, authors, venue, and pages were checked against the chapter's first page (p. 1: "C. Cachin and J. Camenisch (Eds.): EUROCRYPT 2004, LNCS 3027, pp. 1-19, 2004"). LITERATURE_COVERAGE.md records the 2016 Journal of Cryptology version with Hazay as a second version of this identity; it was not read, and no claim here depends on it. The paper calls set intersection "private matching" (PM), with the client learning \( X \cap Y \) (§3.1, p. 3).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: The paper lists its contributions on p. 2. PSI-CONTRIB-2004-FNP-OPE-PSI: set intersection from oblivious evaluation of an encrypted polynomial whose roots are the client's items, semi-honest, standard model (§4.1, p. 5; Protocol PM-Semi-Honest, p. 6; Lemmas 1-3, p. 8). PSI-CONTRIB-2004-FNP-BALANCED-ALLOCATION-HASHING: balanced-allocation hashing into low-degree bin polynomials, which reduces the server's exponentiations to \( O(k_C + k_S \ln \ln k_C) \) (§4.2, pp. 6-8). PSI-CONTRIB-2004-FNP-MALICIOUS-OPE: protocols against a malicious client (cut-and-choose, standard model) and a malicious server (random oracle model) (§5, pp. 9-13). PSI-CONTRIB-2004-FNP-CARDINALITY-THRESHOLD: variants that output the intersection size or a threshold decision (§4.4-4.5, p. 9). PSI-CONTRIB-2004-FNP-APPROX-LOWER-BOUND: an \( \Omega(N) \) communication lower bound for multiplicatively approximating the intersection size (§6, pp. 13-14). PSI-CONTRIB-2004-FNP-MULTIPARTY-OPE: a sketched multi-party protocol for semi-honest parties (§7, pp. 15-17). PSI-CONTRIB-2004-FNP-OT-REDUCTION: private matching implies oblivious transfer, so it has no black-box reduction from one-way functions (§3.1, pp. 3-4). Not carded separately: the sampling-based private approximation protocol Intersect-Approx, whose expected number of sampling invocations matches the lower bound for distinguishing intersection sizes (§6, pp. 14-15); it is described in PSI-CONTRIB-2004-FNP-APPROX-LOWER-BOUND. Not carded, outside the topic: fuzzy matching and fuzzy search, including a 2-out-of-3 fuzzy matching protocol (§8, p. 17). Fuzzy PSI is excluded by SCOPE.md.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: Only the client learns the output (§3.1, p. 3). Security definitions are informal in this version (§3.2, p. 4), and the security lemmas carry proof sketches. The protocol against both malicious parties is described only in outline (§5.3, p. 13). The authors note that the number of rounds of Intersect-Approx depends on its output, which the security definitions do not capture (§6, "Caveat", p. 15). The paper leaves open more efficient fuzzy matching and malicious-secure fuzzy matching (§8, p. 17).

sections.content: The paper lists its contributions in §3 (p. 2). PSI-CONTRIB-2010-DT-BLIND-RSA: PSI from RSA blind signatures with server precomputation, in which the client performs no online exponentiations (§5.6, Figure 4, p. 9; Appendix B.3, p. 16). PSI-CONTRIB-2010-DT-LINEAR-APSI: authorized PSI with linear computation and communication, obtained from the quadratic APSI protocol derived from RSA-PPIT, and its PSI version in a prime-order group (§5.3-5.5, Figures 1-3, pp. 7-9; Appendices B.1-B.2, pp. 14-16). Not carded separately: adding data transfer (PSI-DT, APSI-DT) to all four protocols by deriving symmetric keys from the matching values, following the earlier PPIT work (§5.7, p. 10). Not carded separately: the asymptotic and experimental comparison with prior PSI and APSI protocols (§6, Tables 2-3, pp. 10-11); its figures are recorded in the construction rows.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: All PSI protocols assume an honest-but-curious client and server; in APSI the server is honest-but-curious, the certification authority is not malicious, and the client may lack authorizations for some items (§5.1, p. 6). Malicious security is left to future work (§5.1, p. 6; §7, p. 12), as are formal proofs of unlinkability (Appendix B.1-B.3, pp. 14-16), a security proof for shorter exponents in the APSI protocol (§6, p. 11), and removing an extra oracle query from the One-More-Gap-DH reduction (Appendix B.2, p. 16). The APSI protocol has no comparison row: authorization by a certification authority has no facet in the topic vocabulary, and the APSI rows of Table 2 are not comparable with PSI rows.

sections.content: Private Set Intersection: Are Garbled Circuits Better than Custom Protocols?
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the 15-page PDF dated 2011-11-28. The PDF itself does not name the venue. NDSS 2012 is the venue given in the reference lists of PSI-PAPER-2018-PSWW (reference [HEK12]) and PSI-PAPER-2019-PSTY (reference [HEK12]) and on the NDSS 2012 programme page. The authors' framework and protocol implementations are announced at www.MightBeEvil.com (p. 14).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2012-HEK-SORT-COMPARE-SHUFFLE: the sort-compare-shuffle circuit, with a bitonic merger of the locally sorted sets, DupSelect-3 filtering, and shuffling by a Waksman network, so that the circuit has \( \Theta(n \log n) \) non-free gates (§5, pp. 5-10; Table 1, p. 2). PSI-CONTRIB-2012-HEK-GC-VERSUS-CUSTOM: the measured comparison of the garbled-circuit protocols with the one-more-DL-based protocol of De Cristofaro and Tsudik on the same hardware (§7, pp. 11-14; Figure 11 and Table 2, p. 13). PSI-CONTRIB-2012-HEK-SIZE-AUDITING: an extension of the circuits that withholds the intersection when its size exceeds a threshold (§6, pp. 10-11). Not listed as separate contributions: the bit-vector protocol (Bitwise-AND, §3, pp. 4-5), the pairwise-comparison protocol with early reveal (§4, p. 5), and the shuffling by sorting or by homomorphic encryption (§§5.3.1-5.3.2, pp. 8-9). They are comparison rows PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2012-HEK-BWA, PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2012-HEK-PWC, and PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2012-HEK-SCS-HE.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: All protocols are semi-honest and two-party; stronger threat models are left to future work (§1.1, p. 2). The paper states that the protocols can be proven secure from decisional Diffie-Hellman, used for the oblivious transfer, in the random oracle model, without giving proofs (§2, p. 4). The bit-vector protocol does not bound the set sizes, so a dishonest party could input the whole universe; the paper says it should not be used standalone (§3, pp. 4-5). The introduction says the SCS-WN protocol on 160-bit elements is faster than the De Cristofaro-Tsudik protocol except at the ultra-short security level (§1.1, p. 2), while §7.3 calls it competitive at all security levels (p. 13); the plotted times (Figure 11, p. 13) show it about five times slower at the ultra-short level and faster at every other level.

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2016-KKRT-BATCHED-OPRF: the batched, related-key OPRF (BaRK-OPRF) from OT extension with a pseudorandom code. PSI-CONTRIB-2016-KKRT-ITEM-LENGTH-INDEPENDENT-PSI: PSI in the hashing paradigm of Pinkas, Schneider, Segev, and Zohner with BaRK-OPRF in place of their OPRF, so that the OT cost per bin no longer grows with item length, and with the hash index appended to each bin input (§5, pp. 10-13; Figure 3, p. 13; Table 1, p. 14). The protocol itself is PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2016-KKRT.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: The paper is strictly in the semi-honest model (§1.1, p. 3). Theorem 6 (p. 9) covers BaRK-OPRF; the security of the PSI protocol is argued in prose (§5.2, p. 11). Footnote 3 (p. 12) notes that the earlier protocol did not account for collisions among the cuckoo hash functions, which the hash-index optimization of §5.2 (Figure 3, p. 13) handles.

sections.content: Fast Private Set Intersection from Homomorphic Encryption
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the ePrint PDF dated 2017-09-06 (PDF metadata; the PDF itself carries no date). Venue and pages are taken from the reference list of PSI-PAPER-2018-CHLR (reference [12]) and were not checked against the ACM Digital Library. The paper calls the protocol of Pinkas, Schneider, and Zohner "[PSZ16]" and cites it as IACR ePrint 2016/930, which is PSI-PAPER-2018-PSZ. The implementation uses SEAL v2.1 (§6.1, p. 13).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2017-CLR-FHE-SUBLINEAR-COMMUNICATION: semi-honest PSI from leveled fully homomorphic encryption with communication linear in the smaller set and logarithmic in the larger set, made practical by batching, cuckoo and permutation-based hashing, windowing, partitioning, and modulus switching. The complete protocol of Figure 4 (p. 12) is PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2017-CLR. Not recorded separately: the basic protocol of Figure 1 (p. 5), which the paper calls a strawman with \( O(N_x N_y) \) homomorphic operations (§3, p. 6); the variant for a receiver holding the larger set, in which the parties switch roles and the result is returned masked (§5.2, p. 13); and the comparison with the protocols of Pinkas et al. and Kolesnikov et al. (§§6.2-6.3, pp. 14-17).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: Security is proved only against semi-honest parties (Theorem 2, p. 11), with output to the receiver only (Figure 3, p. 11). The paper discusses but does not address malicious behavior: a malicious sender can influence the receiver's output, and a malicious receiver could add noise to its ciphertexts so that noise flooding no longer hides the sender's set (§5.2, pp. 12-13). Experiments use 32-bit items; longer items require larger FHE parameters, which the authors leave to future work (§6.1, p. 14). Cuckoo-hashing failure probabilities were determined empirically, without a stash (§4.2, pp. 7-8). Reusing the sender's pre-processing across executions is safe only against adversaries that do not force hashing failures (§6.1, p. 14).

sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the ePrint PDF dated 2017-08-24, whose first footnote calls it the full version of an ACM CCS 2017 paper (p. 1). The page range is taken from reference [3] of PSI-PAPER-2024-VCE and was not checked against the ACM Digital Library. The implementation is at github.com/osu-crypto/MultipartyPSI (§7, p. 17).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2017-KMPRT-OPPRF: the oblivious programmable PRF, its three single-query constructions (polynomial, garbled Bloom filter, table), and the hashing-based extension to many points and queries (§§3-4, pp. 4-10). PSI-CONTRIB-2017-KMPRT-SYMMETRIC-KEY-MPSI: multiparty PSI against any number of colluding semi-honest parties from conditional zero-sharing and conditional reconstruction over OPPRFs (§5, pp. 10-13; Theorem 1, p. 12). PSI-CONTRIB-2017-KMPRT-AUGMENTED-ZERO-SHARING: the augmented semi-honest variant with zero-sharing from pairwise PRF seeds (§6.1, pp. 14-15; Theorem 2, p. 14). Not yet recorded: the optimized three-party protocol with three sequential OPPRF executions instead of four (§6.3, pp. 16-17; Figure 10, p. 16), described in PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2017-KMPRT-3PARTY; the stash-free cuckoo-hashing variant with three primary and two supplementary hash functions (§4, p. 9; Appendix B, pp. 24-25), which §7.2 (p. 19) reports as 168 ms against 211 ms for two-party PSI-PAPER-2016-KKRT at \( 2^{12} \) items; and the hint-size optimizations of §6.2 (pp. 15-16).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: All protocols are semi-honest or augmented semi-honest (§2.1, p. 4); no malicious security is claimed. Theorem 1 is stated for the protocol of Figure 8 with an ideal OPPRF functionality (p. 12). The OPPRF constructions are built on the KKRT OPRF, which has related keys and leaks slightly more than the PRF output; the paper works with cleaner definitions and states that the PSI protocol remains secure in the standard sense when built from the relaxed building blocks (§3.1, p. 5). Table 1 (p. 3) compares asymptotic costs with Kissner-Song, Cheon-Jarecki-Seo, and Hazay-Venkitasubramaniam, none of which is recorded yet.

sections.content: Malicious-Secure Private Set Intersection via Dual Execution
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the ePrint PDF, which describes itself as the full version of the CCS 2017 paper (p. 1). Alice is the sender and Bob the receiver who learns the intersection (§2.1, p. 3). The implementations are in github.com/osu-crypto/libPSI (§7, p. 18).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2017-RR-CCS-MALICIOUS-DUAL-EXECUTION: malicious security for the OT-based PSI paradigm of Pinkas, Schneider, and Zohner by running oblivious encodings in both directions and comparing common encodings, with simple hashing, phasing, and aggregation of encodings across bins (§5.1-5.2, pp. 7-8; §6.1-6.3, pp. 10-15; Figure 4, p. 12; Theorem 2, p. 13). PSI-CONTRIB-2017-RR-CCS-ENCODE-COMMIT: the encode-commit variant, in which Alice commits to her items and sends masked decommitments (§5.3, pp. 8-10; §6.4-6.5, pp. 15-17; Theorem 3, p. 16; Figure 9, p. 27). Not carded separately: the oblivious encoding functionality F_encode and its two instantiations (§4, Figure 2, pp. 5-7); its programmable-random-oracle instantiation is the 1-out-of-N OT extension of Orrù, Orsini, and Scholl. Not carded separately: the experimental comparison with De Cristofaro, Kim, and Tsudik, with Rindal and Rosulek (EUROCRYPT 2017), and with the semi-honest protocol of Kolesnikov et al. (§7, Figures 6-8, pp. 18-22); its figures are recorded in the construction rows.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: Both protocols give output only to Bob; §6.7 (pp. 17-18) explains why the natural symmetric extension to two-party output fails against a malicious Bob. The ideal functionality allows a corrupt party up to \( n' > n \) items, with \( n' < 4n \) for \( n = 2^{20} \) in the dual-execution protocol (Figure 1, p. 4; §6.3, p. 15); the encode-commit protocol restricts Alice to exactly \( n \) items (§6.5, p. 17). Footnote 1 (p. 7) states that it is not known how to make OT of random secrets cheaper without the programmable random oracle model.

sections.content: Labeled PSI from Fully Homomorphic Encryption with Malicious Security
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the ePrint PDF dated 2018-08-27 (PDF metadata). Venue, pages, and DOI are taken from reference [14] of PSI-PAPER-2021-CONG and were not checked against the ACM Digital Library. The paper builds on PSI-PAPER-2017-CLR, which it cites as [12] and reviews in §2 (pp. 6-7). The implementation is built on SEAL v2.3.0-4 with BFV (§1.2, p. 2; §8, p. 18).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2018-CHLR-OPRF-MALICIOUS-RECEIVER: OPRF pre-processing before the FHE intersection, giving security against a malicious receiver and removing noise flooding (§4, pp. 8-11; Theorems 1-2, pp. 15-16). PSI-CONTRIB-2018-CHLR-LONG-ITEMS: arbitrary-length items through SIMD slots over extension fields and a lazy encoding algorithm (§3, pp. 7-8; Table 1, p. 9). PSI-CONTRIB-2018-CHLR-LABELED-PSI: labeled PSI with communication sublinear in the sender's set from label-interpolation polynomials (§5, pp. 11-12; Figures 1-2, pp. 13-14). PSI-CONTRIB-2018-CHLR-LEAKY-MALICIOUS-SENDER: security against a malicious sender up to a sender-chosen leakage function, from hash-valued labels and an H-limited leveled FHE assumption (§7.3, pp. 17-18; Appendix A, pp. 25-26). Not recorded separately: PSI with computation, which returns additive secret shares of the per-bin results and labels for a further secure computation with communication \( O(|Y| \log |X| + |f|) \), described without a security theorem (§6, pp. 13-15); the symmetric-key BFV variant that nearly halves fresh ciphertexts (§8.1, p. 18). The complete protocols are PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2018-CHLR (unlabeled), PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2018-CHLR-LABELED, and PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2018-CHLR-MAL-LEAKAGE.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: Theorem 1 (p. 15) gives one-sided simulation security against a malicious receiver and Theorem 2 (p. 16) privacy, not simulation, against a malicious sender, both for the unlabeled PSI functionality of Figure 3 (p. 15); no theorem is stated for the labeled functionality. Theorem 3 (p. 25) relies on a leveled FHE scheme being H-limited (Definition 1, p. 17), which the authors argue heuristically and support by experiments, without a reduction (§7.3, p. 17). When the sender reuses its pre-processing across receivers and picks the hash functions, a selective cuckoo-hashing failure leaks one bit of the receiver's set (§7.3, p. 18). The authors call full simulation-based security against a malicious sender extremely challenging when communication must stay sublinear in the sender's set (§7.2, p. 16). The OT-based OPRF alternative of §4.4 (pp. 10-11) is discussed but not part of the full protocol.

sections.content: Efficient Circuit-based PSI via Cuckoo Hashing
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The ePrint PDF asks to be cited as the EUROCRYPT 2018 paper (footnote on p. 1). Its first page gives no proceedings pages; those are taken from the reference list of PSI-PAPER-2019-GS. The hashing simulation code and the PSI implementation in the ABY framework are announced in §6.1 (p. 19) and §6.3 (p. 24).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2018-PSWW-ALMOST-LINEAR-CIRCUIT: mirror cuckoo hashing and the resulting circuit-based PSI with \( \omega(n) \) comparisons and negligible failure probability, including the stash bound for non-constant stash size (§4, pp. 10-13; Appendix C, p. 34). PSI-CONTRIB-2018-PSWW-2D-CUCKOO-HASHING: two-dimensional cuckoo hashing, its \( O(1/n) \) failure analysis, and the concretely efficient PSI protocol with two-item bins and a combined stash (§5, pp. 13-18; §6, pp. 19-26; Appendix A, pp. 29-33). Not listed as separate contributions: the generalization of 2D cuckoo hashing to more parties with \( 2^{m} \) tables (§5.3, p. 18), the use of lookup-table evaluation to cut communication by up to 4.1 times (§6.2, p. 23), and the extension of PSI-CAT to privacy-preserving ridesharing (§6.3, p. 26).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: Security is semi-honest only; the authors see no way to extend their hashing to malicious adversaries (§5.4, p. 18). The parameters of the concrete protocol rest on about 5.5 million core hours of simulations rather than on an analysis of two-item bins (§3.3, p. 10; §6.1, p. 20; Appendix A, p. 29). No security proof is given; security follows from the generic two-party computation protocol (§5.2, p. 16).

sections.content: Scalable Private Set Intersection Based on OT Extension
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The paper asks to be cited as the ACM TOPS 2018 journal version and describes itself as a combined and extended version of the USENIX Security 2014 and 2015 papers (PSI-PAPER-2014-PSZ and PSI-PAPER-2015-PSSZ), with the additions listed in §1.4 and marked "ADDED" or "EXTENDED" in section headings (first footnote, p. 1; §1.4, pp. 6-7). Locators cite the ePrint PDF dated 2019-07-28.
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: §1.2 (pp. 3-5) discusses PSI protocols under the headings "A naive solution" (insecure hashing), "Third Party-Based PSI", "Public-Key-Based PSI", "Circuit-Based PSI", and "OT-Based PSI". §6.2.3 (pp. 29-30) runs the best protocol of each class on unequal set sizes. Three of the five PSI subfields of this atlas take their scope from the public-key-based, circuit-based, and OT-based classes.
sections.heading: Source role

sections.content: The paper lists its contributions in §1.3 (pp. 5-6) and its additions to the conference versions in §1.4 (pp. 6-7). PSI-CONTRIB-2018-PSZ-BIT-LENGTH-INDEPENDENT-OT-PSI: the OT-based PSI protocol with per-bin OPRFs from 1-out-of-N random OT over a fixed 512-bit BCH code, whose communication no longer depends on item bit length (§2.2.3, p. 11; §5, Protocol 3, pp. 21-23). The construction is PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2018-PSZ-OT. PSI-CONTRIB-2018-PSZ-HASHING-PARAMETERS: concrete parameters for simple and cuckoo hashing in PSI (§3, pp. 12-18). Not carded here because they first appeared in the conference papers, which are separate identities without full text in this release: permutation-based hashing for PSI (§3.3, pp. 17-18; from PSI-PAPER-2015-PSSZ, whose title names it); circuit-based PSI with the sort-compare-shuffle circuit on GMW and the pairwise-comparison circuit with hashing (§4.1-4.2, pp. 18-20). Not carded: the description and benchmark of the circuit-based OPRF protocol of Pinkas, Schneider, Smart, and Williams (§4.3, pp. 20-21, marked ADDED), which the paper finds close to server-aided PSI in run-time for unequal set sizes (§6.2.3, p. 30; Table 12, p. 30); and the same-platform comparison of naive hashing, server-aided, public-key, circuit-based, and OT-based protocols (§6, Tables 8-13, pp. 24-31).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: All protocols compared are semi-honest (§2.1, p. 8). The paper observes that existing two-party PSI protocols all seem to have communication linear in both set sizes (§6.2.3, p. 30) and that dependence on the larger set seems inevitable if brute-force searches are to be prevented (§1.1, p. 3). The text of §6.2.3 gives client sets of \( 2^{8} \) and \( 2^{16} \) items while Tables 11-13 use \( 2^{8} \) and \( 2^{12} \) (p. 29; pp. 30-31).

sections.content: The Communication Complexity of Threshold Private Set Intersection
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The ePrint page describes the PDF as a minor revision of the CRYPTO 2019 paper. The version read includes §8, multiparty threshold PSI, which §1.3 (p. 4) says was added after the CRYPTO extended abstract; footnote 7 (p. 18) thanks Badrinarayanan, Miao, and Rindal for pointing out that numerator and denominator polynomials may share roots in the multiparty cardinality test.
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2019-GS-LOWER-BOUND: an \( \Omega(t) \) communication lower bound for any two-party threshold PSI protocol (§3, pp. 7-8). PSI-CONTRIB-2019-GS-FHE-UPPER-BOUND: an \( O(t \log p) \) protocol from fully homomorphic encryption and set reconciliation (§3, p. 8). PSI-CONTRIB-2019-GS-AHE-THRESHOLD-PSI: the main protocol with communication \( \tilde O(t^{2}) \) from additively homomorphic encryption and OLE, through private intersection cardinality testing and noisy polynomial addition (§§4-7, pp. 9-17). Not listed as separate contributions: the garbled-circuit sketch with communication at least \( \tilde O(t^{3}) \) (§3, p. 9); the treatment of unequal set sizes by padding (§6.4, p. 15); and the multiparty cardinality test from threshold FHE with communication \( \tilde O(t) \) and the multiparty threshold PSI from generic MPC (§8, pp. 17-19), which are sketches without theorems.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: Security is against static passive adversaries in the UC framework (§2.2, p. 6). The authors present the results as feasibility results of theoretical interest and do not claim practicality (§1.1, p. 2). \( \tilde O \) hides polylogarithmic factors (§2, p. 4); set elements lie in a field \( \mathbb{F}_p \) with \( p \) a \( \Theta(\kappa) \)-bit prime (§2, p. 4).

sections.content: Mobile Private Contact Discovery at Scale
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the ePrint full version (PDF metadata dated 2019-05-24). The title page lists the authors as Kales, Rechberger, Schneider, Senker, Weinert; the paper's own reference to the USENIX Security 2019 version lists Kales, Rechberger, Senker, Schneider, Weinert. Both orders give the same initials. Venue details were not checked against the USENIX proceedings. The implementation is at contact-discovery.github.io (§5, footnote 6, p. 11).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: The paper optimizes two precomputed unbalanced PSI protocols of Kiss, Liu, Schneider, Asokan, and Pinkas (PoPETs 2017): GC-PSI, an OPRF evaluated by garbled circuits, and NR-PSI, an oblivious evaluation of the Naor-Reingold PRF (§1.1, p. 2; §3.5, p. 6). PSI-CONTRIB-2019-KRSSW-COT-PRECOMPUTATION: correlated-OT precomputation that halves online OT communication (§4.3, p. 8; §4.4, p. 10). PSI-CONTRIB-2019-KRSSW-CUCKOO-FILTER-COMPRESSION: a compressed cuckoo-filter encoding of the server set, smaller updates, and realistic false-positive parameters (§4.1, pp. 6-7). PSI-CONTRIB-2019-KRSSW-LOWMC-OPRF: LowMC parameters for the garbled-circuit OPRF with 8.2 times fewer AND gates than AES-128 (§4.2, pp. 7-8). PSI-CONTRIB-2019-KRSSW-MOBILE-IMPLEMENTATION: native ARMv8 implementations with security against malicious clients and their measurement (§4.5, pp. 10-11; §§5-6, pp. 11-14). Not recorded separately: the survey of contact discovery in twelve mobile messengers (§1.2, p. 3; Table 1, p. 3); the proposed combinations with multi-server PIR and with FHE-based PSI, a dedicated filter server, and database partitioning, none of them implemented (§4.6, p. 11; Appendix A, pp. 18-19); the Signal prototype (Appendix C, p. 19). The complete protocols are PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2019-KRSSW-GC (Figure 1, p. 9) and PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2019-KRSSW-NR (Figure 2, p. 10).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: The server is assumed semi-honest; a malicious server could learn about client items whenever the client reveals the intersection to it, as messaging apps do (§4.5, p. 11). Enumeration attacks by repeated queries remain possible and are left to rate limiting (§4.5, p. 11). The setup phase sends the client a filter linear in the server set, about 1 GiB for \( 2^{28} \) items, which the authors name as the bottleneck for very large sets (§4.6, p. 11). Cuckoo filters give a nonzero false-positive probability, about \( 2^{-29} \) per item in the experiments (§4.1, p. 6; Table 4, p. 13). The authors report Signal's stated requirements for deploying PSI-based contact discovery, a server database of \( 10^{9} \) users, address books of up to 10,000 contacts, lookups under 2 s, and 1,600 contacts per second on one core, and state that these are not yet met (§7, p. 14; the figures were rechecked on 2026-10-12 in the §7 of the USENIX Security 2019 version).
sections.heading: Claim boundary

sections.content: Efficient Circuit-based PSI with Linear Communication
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the PDF dated 2019-02-28. Venue and pages are taken from the reference list of PSI-PAPER-2020-ION and the ePrint page, which says the paper was published by the IACR in EUROCRYPT 2019. The implementation is at github.com/encryptogroup/OPPRF-PSI (footnote 8, p. 26).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2019-PSTY-BATCHED-OPPRF: the one-time programmable PRF with correlated targets and its batched version, whose single polynomial hint over all bins has size linear in the total number of programmed points (§3, pp. 10-16). PSI-CONTRIB-2019-PSTY-LINEAR-COMMUNICATION: circuit-based PSI with \( O(n) \) communication, through one comparison per bin and either a role-reversed phase for the stash or stash-less cuckoo hashing with three hash functions (§§4-5, pp. 16-21). PSI-CONTRIB-2019-PSTY-PAYLOAD: injection of the sender's payloads into the circuit through a second batched OPPRF (§6, pp. 21-22). Not listed as separate contributions: the mega-bin split that lowers the cost of polynomial interpolation (§4.3, p. 18; §7.2, pp. 23-24) and the PSI-CAT comparison with earlier public-key threshold protocols (§7.4, pp. 27-28).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: Security is semi-honest (§2.2, p. 8). The protocol's security is stated to follow from the OPPRF and generic two-party computation (§4.1, p. 17); the OPPRF is proved in the F_OPRF-hybrid model (Theorem 8, p. 15). Only the stash-less protocol was implemented; the run times of the basic and dual-execution protocols are estimates (§7.4, p. 26; Table 5, p. 27).

sections.content: On Deploying Secure Computing: Private Intersection-Sum-with-Cardinality
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors follow the PDF dated 2020-09-05; the ePrint page lists the same nine authors with Mariana Raykova placed after Sarvar Patel. The venue is taken from the ePrint page. PSI-PAPER-2018-PSWW and PSI-PAPER-2019-PSTY cite an earlier version of the deployed protocol as the 2017 ePrint report "Private intersection-sum protocol with applications to attributing aggregate ad conversions" (reference [IKN+17] in both).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2020-ION-DDH-INTERSECTION-SUM: the deployed private intersection-sum-with-cardinality protocol from Diffie-Hellman double masking and additively homomorphic encryption (§3, pp. 5-7; Figure 2, p. 6). PSI-CONTRIB-2020-ION-ROT-INTERSECTION-SUM: the protocol from batched random OT with a shuffle and re-masking of the OPRF outputs (§4.3.1, pp. 9-10; Figure 3, p. 10). Not listed as separate contributions: the "Tag, Shuffle, Aggregate" recipe for turning a PSI protocol into an intersection-sum-with-cardinality protocol (§4.2, pp. 8-9); the encrypted-Bloom-filter protocol (§4.3.2, pp. 10-11; Figure 4), which is the comparison row PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2020-ION-BF; the monetary cost model for batch computation (§2.5, p. 4; Table 1, p. 5); and the reverse variants in which the identifier-only party receives the sum (§3.4, p. 7; Appendix G).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: All protocols are semi-honest (§1, p. 2; §2.3, p. 4) and reveal the intersection size besides the sum, which the authors note may be undesirable leakage in other settings (§4.2, p. 9). The comparison with garbled-circuit protocols mixes measurement settings, as the authors state (§5.3, p. 12).

sections.content: PSI from PaXoS: Fast, Malicious Private Set Intersection
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the ePrint PDF dated 2020-02-16. Venue, volume, and pages are taken from the reference list of PSI-PAPER-2021-GPRTY and were not checked against the publisher. The authors point to their source code under github.com/cryptobiu; the repository name is split across a page break in the PDF (§1.1, pp. 2-3).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-PAXOS: the probe-and-XOR of strings, an input-independent binary key-value encoding with XOR-homomorphic decoding (Definition 3, p. 6; §3, pp. 5-9). PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-GARBLED-CUCKOO: the garbled cuckoo table, a PaXoS of constant rate with linear-time encoding (§5, pp. 16-21), and its DFS-based variant (Appendix B, pp. 29-31). PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-MALICIOUS-PAXOS-PSI: two-party PSI from any PaXoS and the OOS OT extension, malicious or semi-honest by the choice of code (Figure 3, p. 11; Theorem 4, p. 10). PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-RECEIVER-SET-SIZE-BOUND: the incompressibility bound on a malicious receiver's effective set (Claim 7, p. 15; Appendix A, pp. 27-29). Not separately recorded: the bound on the number of cycles in a cuckoo graph (Lemma 12, Appendix C, pp. 31-32), which is part of the garbled cuckoo table's analysis, and the qualitative comparison of PSI paradigms (Appendix D, pp. 32-36). The complete protocols are PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2020-PRTY-SH and PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2020-PRTY-MAL.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: The adversary corrupts one of two parties statically (§2, p. 5), and only the receiver learns the intersection (Figure 1, p. 6). The ideal functionality lets a corrupt party use a set larger than advertised (§2, p. 5). Theorem 4 (p. 10) is proved in the random oracle model with OOS as an ideal functionality; Appendix D (p. 33) states standard-model security for the semi-honest case without a separate proof. The introduction's claim that the semi-honest instantiation improves on KKRT's communication by 25% (§1.1, p. 2) does not match Table 1 (p. 21) or §7.3 (p. 23), which put PaXoS-PSI above KKRT; this was not resolved. The protocol targets sets of roughly equal size (Appendix D, p. 36).
