sections.content: Multi-Party Threshold Private Set Intersection with Sublinear Communication
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the PDF dated 2021-02-25; the venue is taken from the ePrint page. The paper treats the multiparty extension in the full version of PSI-PAPER-2019-GS as concurrent work and reports that it initially overlooked an unexpected degree reduction, fixed after notification (§1.3, p. 5; footnote 6, p. 11).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2021-BMRR-FUNCTIONALITIES: two multiparty threshold PSI functionalities, equal for two parties and different for more (§1.1, p. 2; §2.3, p. 6; Figures 1-4). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-BMRR-LOWER-BOUND: \( \Omega(nT) \) communication for both functionalities in point-to-point networks, and \( \Omega(T \log n + n) \) for the first in the broadcast model (§4, pp. 15-17; Appendix C, pp. 40-42). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-BMRR-TFHE-UPPER-BOUND: matching \( O(nT) \) protocols for both functionalities from threshold FHE (§5, pp. 17-23; §7, pp. 28-30; Appendix B, pp. 39-41). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-BMRR-TAHE-THRESHOLD-PSI: an \( \tilde O(nT) \) protocol for the second functionality from threshold additively homomorphic encryption, whose two-party case gives \( \tilde O(T) \) from additively homomorphic encryption (§6, pp. 24-28; §7, pp. 28-30; §1.2, p. 4). Not listed as separate contributions: the use of repeated threshold PSI with \( T = 1, 2, 4, \dots \) to obtain multiparty PSI with communication independent of the set sizes, and the observation that the protocols are compact MPC in the plain model (§1.2, p. 4).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: All protocols are semi-honest with up to \( n - 1 \) corruptions and run in a star network (§1.1, p. 3; §2.3, p. 6). Upper bounds omit a \( \mathrm{poly}(\lambda) \) factor and \( \tilde O \) hides polylogarithmic factors (footnote 1, p. 3). Whether the first functionality admits a protocol from assumptions weaker than threshold FHE is marked unknown (Table 1, p. 3). On the claim to settle the open problem of PSI-PAPER-2019-GS: the abstract says that, as a direct implication, the paper designs a two-party protocol with communication \( \tilde O(T) \) from assumptions weaker than FHE (p. 1); §1.2 says the case \( n = 2 \) gives \( \tilde O(T) \) from additively homomorphic encryption, referring to §§6-7 (p. 4); §3.3 attributes the gain to testing Hankel-matrix singularity through the half-GCD connection of Brent, Gustavson, and Yun, quasi-linear instead of the quadratic protocol of Kiltz et al. (p. 13). In the two-party case the singularity test is instantiated with Yao's garbled circuits at communication \( \tilde O(k \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\lambda)) \) for a \( (k + 1) \times (k + 1) \) Hankel matrix (§6.1, p. 26), and the intersection step uses additively homomorphic encryption alone with communication \( O(T \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\lambda)) \) (§7.1, p. 29). The later paper of Ghosh and Simkin, PSI-PAPER-2023-GS (ePrint 2023/919, PDF dated 2023-06-12), accepts the two-party result: it states that communication \( O(\lambda t\,\mathrm{polylog}\,t) \) without fully homomorphic encryption follows from the construction of PSI-PAPER-2019-GS combined with an observation of Badrinarayanan et al., and that its own two-party protocol does not improve on this (paper outline and footnote 5, p. 4). For more than two parties it notes that this paper's quasilinear protocol without FHE additionally requires fewer than \( t \) distinct elements outside the intersection among all sets (§1, pp. 1-2), and it counts this paper among the works that leave asymptotically optimal multiparty threshold PSI from assumptions other than FHE open (§1, p. 2).
sections.heading: Claim boundary

sections.content: Labeled PSI from Homomorphic Encryption with Reduced Computation and Communication
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the ePrint PDF dated 2021-11-14 (PDF metadata). The PDF names no venue; ACM CCS 2021 was not checked against the proceedings. The paper refines PSI-PAPER-2017-CLR and PSI-PAPER-2018-CHLR, cited as [15] and [14] (§1.1, p. 3; §1.2, p. 3). The SEAL-based implementation is the open-source APSI library (§5, footnote 7, p. 15); the HElib implementation is a proof of concept without OPRF or networking (§5, p. 15).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2021-CONG-PATERSON-STOCKMEYER: evaluation of each bin's intersection polynomial with \( O(\sqrt{B}) \) ciphertext-ciphertext multiplications (§3.1, pp. 7-9; Appendix A). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-CONG-POSTAGE-STAMP-BASES: extremal postage-stamp bases in place of windowing for the receiver's encrypted powers (§3.1, pp. 10-11). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-CONG-FROBENIUS-POWERS: depth-free Frobenius powers giving communication nearly constant in the larger set (§3.1, pp. 11-12; §5.4, pp. 18-20). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-CONG-PRIME-FIELD-SLOTS: arbitrary-length items and labels over prime-field SIMD slots, with OPRF hashing made mandatory (§3.1, p. 7; §4.2, pp. 13-14). Not recorded separately: a hash-to-curve map for the FourQ curve used by the OMGDH-based OPRF, measured at about 12,000 cycles (§3.1, p. 12); the partitioning of very large sender sets into several protocol runs (§5.2, p. 18); and the security sketch for the labeled case (§4.2, p. 14). The complete protocols are PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-CONG (unlabeled, SEAL), PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-CONG-LABELED (labeled, SEAL), and PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-CONG-FROBENIUS (HElib proof of concept).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: The paper states that its security guarantees and proof are those of the earlier labeled-PSI paper: security against a malicious receiver and privacy against a malicious sender in the random oracle model (§3, p. 6); the labeled case is argued as a straightforward extension (§4.2, p. 14). The low-communication variant has impractically high computation on current CPUs (abstract, p. 1; §6, p. 20). Experiments use a false-positive probability of at most \( 2^{-40} \) per execution (§5.1, p. 16). Comparisons with the earlier protocol use a 24-core machine that the authors assume comparable to the earlier 32-core one (§5, p. 14).
sections.heading: Claim boundary

sections.content: Oblivious Key-Value Stores and Amplification for Private Set Intersection
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title, authors, and date were checked against the ePrint PDF dated 2021-11-30. Venue, volume, and pages are taken from the reference list of PSI-PAPER-2022-RR and were not checked against the publisher.
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2021-GPRTY-OKVS: the definition of oblivious key-value stores, with linear, binary, and overfitting notions (§2, pp. 5-7), and the catalog of existing instances (§3, pp. 7-9). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-GPRTY-3H-GCT: the three-hash garbled cuckoo table (§4.1, pp. 9-11). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-GPRTY-AMPLIFICATION: replication and star architectures for amplifying OKVS correctness, with a concrete instantiation (§5, pp. 13-18). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-GPRTY-LINEAR-OKVS-VOLE: PSI from any linear OKVS and vector OLE (§7.1, pp. 20-22). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-GPRTY-MALICIOUS-MULTIPARTY: malicious security for the zero-sharing multiparty PSI of Kolesnikov et al. (§7.2, pp. 21-22; Appendix B, pp. 29-39). Not separately recorded: the OKVS from simple hashing into bins with dense matrices and its sharper failure analysis (§4.2, pp. 11-12); the observation that OKVS can replace polynomials in sparse OT extension, OPPRF, and covert computation (§6.1, §6.2, §6.4, pp. 18-20); the benchmarks of OKVS constructions (Appendix A.2, pp. 28-29). The complete protocols are PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-GPRTY-MAL-3HGCT, PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-GPRTY-MAL-STAR, PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-GPRTY-VOLE, and PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-GPRTY-MULTIPARTY. The semi-honest PaXoS-PSI rows with the new encodings in Table 1 (p. 24) are not recorded as separate rows.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: The two-party protocols are PaXoS-PSI of PSI-PAPER-2020-PRTY with a different binary OKVS (§6.3, p. 19) or with vector OLE (§7.1, pp. 20-22); the paper does not re-prove the former. The parameter \( 1.3n \) of the three-hash table is a heuristic choice (§8.1, p. 23), and the failure probability of the star instantiation rests on an empirical measurement (§5.4, pp. 17-18). A later analysis in PSI-PAPER-2022-RR (§5.1, p. 24) argues that this measurement overstates the security level by a few bits; that claim was not checked here. The vector-OLE protocol and the multiparty protocol are not implemented.

sections.content: Simple, Fast Malicious Multiparty Private Set Intersection
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the ePrint PDF dated 2021-09-17, whose acknowledgments thank the CCS 2021 reviewers (p. 12). The page range is taken from reference [32] of PSI-PAPER-2024-VCE and was not checked against the ACM Digital Library. The implementation is at github.com/asu-crypto/mPSI (§5, p. 11).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2021-NTY-MALICIOUS-NO-COLLUSION: malicious multiparty PSI when at most one party is corrupted, from PRF keys, OKVS encodings, and a two-party PSI between two designated parties instantiated as server-aided PSI (§3, pp. 5-9; Protocols 3.1 and 3.3; Theorems 3.2 and 3.4). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-NTY-MALICIOUS-THRESHOLD-CALIBRATED: malicious multiparty PSI against \( t < n \) colluding parties with clients, a pivot, and \( t \) servers, whose cost decreases with \( t \) (§4, pp. 9-11; Protocol 4.4; Theorem 4.5). Not yet recorded separately: the ZeroXOR functionality and protocol (Functionality 4.1, Protocol 4.2, Theorem 4.3, pp. 9-10), which the second contribution uses; the observation that replacing the OKVS by an OPPRF in Protocol 3.1 gives a three-party protocol against two colluding parties (§3.1.3, p. 6).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: Both main protocols are proved against a malicious adversary in the random oracle model with ideal subfunctionalities (Theorems 3.2, 3.4, 4.5; pp. 7-11), and the ideal functionality gives the output to \( P_n \) only (Functionality 2.1, p. 4). The implementation uses the table-based OPPRF code of PSI-PAPER-2017-KMPRT, which footnote 2 calls semi-honest secure and about three times slower than the malicious PaXoS-based OPPRF (p. 11). Runtimes of the protocol of Ben Efraim et al. are copied from that paper rather than rerun (§5.1, p. 11). Table 1 lists five rounds for Protocol 3.3 while §3.2.2 (p. 8) counts four.

sections.content: VOLE-PSI: Fast OPRF and Circuit-PSI from Vector-OLE
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and date were checked against the ePrint PDF dated 2024-08-08. The title page spells the second author "Phillipp Schoppman"; the spelling "Schoppmann" follows the paper's own reference [SGRR19] and the citations in PSI-PAPER-2021-GPRTY and PSI-PAPER-2022-RR. Venue, volume, and pages are taken from the reference list of PSI-PAPER-2022-RR and were not checked against the publisher. The revision adds the Strong OKVS Extraction Conjecture and its discussion (§2, pp. 11-13).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2021-RS-VOLE-OPRF: a batched OPRF from vector OLE and a PaXoS encoding, malicious-secure (§3, pp. 13-18; Figure 4, p. 36). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-RS-SHORT-OPRF-OUTPUTS: a tighter analysis of the malicious OPRF-to-PSI transformation that allows κ-bit outputs (§4, pp. 18-20). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-RS-CIRCUIT-PSI: circuit-PSI from an OPPRF built on the VOLE OPRF and XoPaXoS (§2, pp. 10-11; §§5-6, pp. 21-24). Not separately recorded: the variant with a polynomial-interpolation encoding of rate 1, analyzed only in theory (§7.1, pp. 24-25; Table 1, p. 25), and the Strong OKVS Extraction Conjecture (Conjecture 2.1, p. 12), which the authors leave open. The complete protocols are PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-RS-SH, PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-RS-MAL, and PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-RS-CIRCUIT.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: The OPRF and PSI are proved in the random oracle and F_vole-hybrid model; the implementation instantiates VOLE from LPN with regular noise (§3.1, p. 14; §7.2, p. 26). Circuit-PSI is semi-honest, and its proof is deferred to Pinkas, Schneider, Tkachenko, and Yanai (§6, p. 23). Table 1 (p. 25) prints the malicious communication formula with a \( (\lambda + \log(n_x n_y)) n_y \) term while its numeric column uses \( 128 n_y \); the numeric column and the measurements of Table 3 (p. 29) are recorded.

sections.content: Compact and Malicious Private Set Intersection for Small Sets
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title, authors, and the CCS DOI were checked against the author version (p. 1). The protocol has a sender and a receiver; only the receiver learns \( X \cap Y \) (Figure 2, p. 6). The implementation is at github.com/osu-crypto/MiniPSI (§5.1, p. 16).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2021-RT-KA-TO-MALICIOUS-PSI: a transformation from two-round key agreement with pseudorandom second messages and non-malleability to malicious PSI, by encoding the receiver's key-agreement responses in a polynomial, in the ideal permutation and random oracle model (§4, Figure 4, pp. 10-16). PSI-CONTRIB-2021-RT-SEMI-HONEST-DH-COMMUNICATION: two semi-honest variants, instantiated with Diffie-Hellman, that lower the communication of Diffie-Hellman PSI (Appendix A, Figures 5-6, pp. 23-28; Table 1, p. 4). Not carded separately: the unconditional bound on how many items a corrupt receiver can effectively input (§4.1, pp. 15-16; Appendix C, pp. 28-29); it is recorded in the qualifiers of the malicious contribution. Not carded separately: the optimizations of Appendix B (sender without elligator encoding; OKVS instead of polynomials), whose security the paper leaves to the reader (p. 28).
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: The paper compares protocols on small sets and records that OT-based protocols overtake it between 500 and 1,000 items on a 10 Gbps network (§1, p. 2). It conjectures, without proof, that overfitting polynomials are hard to find even when they exist, which would tighten the enforcement of a corrupt receiver's set size (§4.1, p. 16). It describes De Cristofaro-Tsudik 2010 and its improvement as RSA-accumulator protocols (§1.1, p. 3); PSI-PAPER-2010-DT's own protocols use blind RSA signatures and RSA-PPIT, not accumulators.

sections.content: Blazing Fast PSI from Improved OKVS and Subfield VOLE
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the ePrint PDF dated 2022-11-02, whose header gives only the year 2022. The venue follows LITERATURE_COVERAGE.md and was not checked against the ACM Digital Library. The implementation is at github.com/Visa-Research/volepsi (§5, p. 23).
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2022-RR-TRIANGULATION-OKVS: the OKVS by sparse triangulation with a small gap, its clustering, and its failure-probability analysis and parameter selection (§§2-3, pp. 5-21; Figure 1, p. 7; Appendix A, pp. 30-31). PSI-CONTRIB-2022-RR-SUBFIELD-VOLE: semi-honest VOLE-based PSI with subfield VOLE and communication \( O(n\lambda + n \log n) \) (§4, pp. 21-23; Figure 9, p. 23; Theorem 3, pp. 33-35). Not separately recorded: the application of the new OKVS, in its doubly oblivious form, to the circuit-PSI of PSI-PAPER-2021-RS (§4, p. 23; Table 2, p. 25), which appears as a construction row, and the argument that the greedy triangulation is not a matroid algorithm for \( w > 2 \) (Appendix B, pp. 32-33). The complete protocols are PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2022-RR-FAST, PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2022-RR-SD, PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2022-RR-MAL, and PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2022-RR-CIRCUIT.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: The malicious and circuit-PSI protocols are those of PSI-PAPER-2021-RS with the new OKVS; the paper proves only the semi-honest subfield-VOLE protocol (Theorem 3, p. 33). Concrete failure probabilities rest on empirical fits (§3.1-3.2, pp. 13-19). The paper's improvement factors differ by passage: the abstract reports \( 187n \) bits and a 6× circuit-PSI speedup, §1 a 6.8× and 2.3× reduction, §1.1 \( 180n \) bits and 1.5× and 23× improvements; Table 2 (p. 25) is recorded. All measurements were taken on one laptop over a local network of about 1 Gbps (§5, p. 23).

sections.content: Threshold Private Set Intersection with Better Communication Complexity
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title, authors, and affiliations (Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur; Ethereum Foundation) were checked against the PDF dated 2023-06-12. The venue is taken from the ePrint page, which describes the PDF as a minor revision of the PKC 2023 paper.
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2023-GS-PICT-COMPILER: a transformation from any private intersection cardinality test with secret-shared output and communication \( O(\lambda \ell\,\mathrm{poly}(t)) \) to one with communication \( O(\lambda^{2} \ell t\,\mathrm{polylog}\,t) \), by random partitioning into \( t \) buckets (abstract, p. 1; §1.2, p. 2; §§3-4, pp. 6-16). PSI-CONTRIB-2023-GS-MULTIPARTY-QUASILINEAR: passively secure \( \ell \)-party threshold PSI, releasing the intersection when it has at least \( n - t \) elements, with communication \( O(\epsilon^{2} \ell t\,\mathrm{polylog}\,t) \) bits from oblivious transfer or additively homomorphic encryption (Corollaries 5-6, p. 16). Not listed as separate contributions: the two-party instantiation (Corollaries 2-3, p. 10), which the authors say does not improve the two-party state of the art asymptotically (p. 4), and the use of threshold PSI with thresholds \( 2, 2^{2}, 2^{4}, \dots \) to compute plain PSI with communication sublinear in the set sizes for large intersections (§1.1, p. 2). The two-party instantiation is the comparison row PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2023-GS-TWO-PARTY.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: Security is against a static passive adversary corrupting all but one party, with pairwise authenticated private channels and a broadcast channel of unit cost (§2.1, p. 4). The partitioning uses random functions, which the authors say may be replaced by pseudorandom functions with a key known to all parties (footnote 4, p. 3). The authors consider the protocols too inefficient for most real-world parameters (§1.2, p. 3). On the earlier claim of PSI-PAPER-2021-BMRR: the paper states that two-party threshold PSI with communication \( O(\lambda t\,\mathrm{polylog}\,t) \) can be obtained without fully homomorphic encryption from the construction of PSI-PAPER-2019-GS combined with an observation of Badrinarayanan et al., and that its own two-party protocol does not improve on this (p. 4 and footnote 5). Its abstract sentence that current protocols rely on FHE or depend at least quadratically on \( t \) concerns the \( \ell \)-party setting (abstract, p. 1); for \( \ell > 2 \) it notes that Badrinarayanan et al. additionally require fewer than \( t \) distinct elements outside the intersection among all sets (§1, pp. 1-2).

sections.content: SoK: Collusion-resistant Multi-party Private Set Intersections in the Semi-honest Model
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Title and authors were checked against the ePrint PDF dated 2023-11-16. The PDF ends with a meta-review (Appendix C, p. 19) but does not name the venue.
sections.heading: Version and bibliographic notes

sections.content: The paper covers multiparty PSI in which only the leader \( P_1 \) learns the intersection, at most \( t \) parties collude, and no external party helps; it excludes server-aided protocols and treats only the semi-honest model, noting whether malicious versions exist (§1, pp. 1-2; Definition 1, p. 2). It defines size-hiding and size-revealing privacy and exact protocols with error at most \( 2^{-40} \) (Definitions 2-4, p. 3), and notes that augmented semi-honest security neither implies nor follows from semi-honest security, while malicious security implies it (§2.3, pp. 3-4). Network topologies are star, mesh, wheel, and tree (§3.1, p. 4). It sorts all protocols into three constructions (§4, pp. 5-9): private homomorphic set representations (bitsets, hash sets, sorted multisets, polynomial roots), leaky homomorphic set representations (Bloom filters and garbled Bloom filters), and aggregatable membership queries (payloads in polynomial roots, oblivious programmable PRFs, oblivious key-value stores). Table 2 (p. 10) lists the protocols without known attacks in these classes, with communication, computation, rounds, topology, collusion resistance, and whether a malicious version exists; PSI-PAPER-2017-KMPRT and PSI-PAPER-2021-NTY appear under aggregatable membership queries. Section 6 (p. 12) collects recurring flaws: revealing a Bloom filter of the intersection, randomness contributed by only one party, and difficulties of moving to the malicious model.
sections.heading: What it classifies

sections.content: PSI-CONTRIB-2024-VCE-ANALYTICAL-COST-COMPARISON: worst-case counts of elliptic-curve multiplications, OTs, and OLEs for semi-honest collusion-resistant protocols, and the conclusion that no single protocol is the state of the art (§7, pp. 12-13; Table 3, p. 13; Appendices A-B, pp. 16-18). Not yet recorded: the argument that the multiparty protocol of Bay and Kayan is insecure because the leader can enumerate the universe to invert hashed PRF values (§5.2.1, p. 11); the paper states it as an argument, without proof. Section 6.2 (p. 12) also describes an error in the protocol of Wei et al. without attributing the finding to another source.
sections.heading: Contributions

sections.content: The complexities in Table 2 are derived by the authors (Appendix A, pp. 16-17), partly copied from the original papers, and in some cases after modifying a protocol so that only the leader receives the output. Table 3 counts sub-protocol calls, not running time, and the authors caution that experiments in the surveyed papers ran on different hardware (§5.1.1, p. 10). The open questions the paper names (abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2; §§7-9, pp. 12-14) are not restated here.

historical_context.narrative: Huberman, Franklin, and Hogg wanted members of online communities to find others who share their preferences without handing their answers to a trusted intermediary, since such a party is hard to agree on and becomes a single point of failure. Generic methods for comparing private data were already known, but the authors chose a direct scheme modelled on Diffie-Hellman key exchange. Each side hashes its entries and applies a secret exponent; after a second exchange, values that coincide mark the entries both sides hold. Counting coincidences gives the size of the overlap, and skipping a shuffle reveals the overlap itself. The authors presented it as simple and efficient, accepting that it reveals a count rather than only whether a threshold is met, and gave no formal security analysis.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The paper motivates the protocol by the difficulty of agreeing on a trusted third party in an open community and by the single point of failure such a party creates (§1, p. 79); it notes that techniques for two or more parties to compute preference-matching functions exist under various fault and leakage assumptions, citing Fagin-Naor-Winkler and Naor-Pinkas (§3, p. 81).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors present it as one technique for private preference matching that is easier to describe and quite efficient, at the price of leaking the number of matches instead of a threshold bit (§3, p. 81), and as part of mechanisms that avoid trusted third parties (abstract, p. 78).
historical_context.technical_delta: Each party hashes its items, exponentiates them with its own secret exponent modulo \( p \), and re-exponentiates the other party's values, so equal items yield equal values \( H(x)^{ab} \); the parties then count matches (Appendix A, steps 1-5, p. 85). Permuting the exchanged lists hides positions; dropping the final permutations reveals the shared items instead of only their number (Appendix A, p. 85).

limitations: no adversary model, security definition, or proof is given for the protocol (Appendix A, p. 85)
the terms 'set intersection' and 'PSI' do not appear; the task is called private preference matching (§3, p. 81)
protection against active cheating is only mentioned as a possible zero-knowledge addition, not specified (Appendix A, p. 85)
no costs are stated beyond the four messages of the protocol (Appendix A, p. 85)
qualifiers: both parties receive output: each counts the matches (Appendix A, step 5, p. 85)

the computation is modulo a large prime \( p \); the appendix sets up a prime \( r \) dividing \( p - 1 \) and an element g of order \( r \), but does not say into which group H maps (Appendix A, p. 85)
the hash function is required to have output that cannot be easily influenced or predicted ahead of time (§2, p. 79)
the basic preference-matching function in §3 takes a threshold, but the appendix protocol reveals the count of matches instead of the threshold bit (§3, p. 81)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 78); §1 (p. 79); §2 (p. 79); §3 'Private Preference Matching' (p. 81); Appendix A 'Discrete Log Problem' and 'Private Preference Matching' (p. 85). ACM EC 1999 proceedings PDF, printed pages.

metadata.statement: Two parties holding lists \( x_1, \ldots, x_{n_X} \) and \( y_1, \ldots, y_{n_Y} \) each raise hashes of their own items modulo a prime \( p \) to a secret random exponent, exchange the permuted results, raise the other party's values to their own exponent, and return them permuted, so that both parties learn how many items the lists share; if the last two lists are not permuted, both learn which items are shared. The paper relates the protocol to Diffie-Hellman key exchange and states no adversary model or security proof for it.
metadata.title: Two-party count of shared list items by commutative exponentiation of hashed items modulo a prime, without a trusted third party

sections.content: Diffie-Hellman preference matching
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Alice holds \( x_1, \ldots, x_{n_X} \) and Bob holds \( y_1, \ldots, y_{n_Y} \). Alice sends \( H(x_1)^a, \ldots, H(x_{n_X})^a \bmod p \) in random order; Bob sends \( H(y_1)^b, \ldots, H(y_{n_Y})^b \bmod p \) in random order; Alice returns the values \( H(y_j)^{ab} \) and Bob returns the values \( H(x_i)^{ab} \), each list permuted; each party then counts the matches (Appendix A, steps 1-5, p. 85). The paper lists variations: without the permutations in steps 3 and 4 both parties learn which elements they have in common; without the permutations in steps 1 and 2 they learn the positions of matches; with a fresh exponent per element they learn only matches in equal positions (Appendix A, p. 85). The authors relate the protocol to the Diffie-Hellman key exchange and to Bellovin and Merritt's encrypted key exchange (Appendix A, p. 85).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: PKE-RESULT-1976-DH-INTERACTIVE-PUBLIC-CHANNEL-KEY-AGREEMENT: Diffie-Hellman key agreement, which the paper names as the protocol's relative (Appendix A, p. 85, reference [10]). Bellovin-Merritt encrypted key exchange (reference [7]) has no record in any topic.

historical_context.narrative: Exact computation of an intersection's size inherits the linear communication cost of set disjointness, a classical communication complexity result, while approximations with additive error are cheap. That raised the hope that a multiplicative approximation could be private and sublinear at once. Freedman, Nissim, and Pinkas ruled this out by a short reduction: padding disjointness instances so that disjoint and intersecting inputs land on intersection sizes a factor \( (1 + \varepsilon) \) squared apart, which any good approximation separates. The resulting linear lower bound holds whether or not privacy is required. They pair it with a sampling protocol whose expected number of rounds adapts to the true size and is optimal for telling such sizes apart, while noting that the round count itself reveals information about the result.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The randomized communication complexity of disjointness is \( \Theta(u) \), \( u \) the length of the input strings, so computing \( |a \cap b| \) exactly needs \( \Theta(u) \) communication; with additive error \( \varepsilon u \), very efficient protocols exist, namely \( O(\log u) \) bits in the private randomness model (§2, pp. 2-3).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The bound shows that approximation does not circumvent the linear communication of computing the intersection size (§2, p. 3); the paper's sampling protocol Intersect-Approx then matches the bound for distinguishing intersection sizes \( k \) and \( k(1 + \varepsilon) \) in an expected \( O(u/k) \) sampling invocations, \( k \) the smaller intersection size and \( u \) the domain size (§6, p. 15).
historical_context.technical_delta: Padding the disjointness inputs a and b with \( \eta \) leading ones and \( (2 + \varepsilon^2)\eta \) copies of themselves maps disjoint inputs to intersection size \( \eta \) and intersecting inputs to size at least \( \eta(1 + \varepsilon)^2 \), so an \( (\varepsilon, \delta) \)-approximation decides disjointness (§6, pp. 13-14).

limitations: approximation with additive error \( \varepsilon u \) is not covered; it admits \( O(\log u) \)-bit protocols, \( u \) the domain size (§2, p. 3)
the matching protocol Intersect-Approx is for semi-honest parties, and its number of rounds depends on the output, which the security definitions do not capture (§6, p. 15)
qualifiers: inputs are \( u \)-bit strings X, Y, \( u \) the domain size, with \( \alpha = |X \cap Y| \) (§6, p. 13)

multiplicative error with constant \( \varepsilon \); the bound \( \Omega(u/\eta) \) becomes \( \Theta(u) \), \( u \) the domain size, when \( \eta \), the intersection size the reduction starts from, is a constant (§6, p. 14)
the bound is a communication complexity bound and holds regardless of privacy (§2, p. 3)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 1); contributions (p. 2); §2 'Disjointness and set intersection' (pp. 2-3); §6 'A lower bound' (pp. 13-14); Protocol Private-Sample-B (p. 14); Intersect-Approx and 'Caveat' (p. 15). EUROCRYPT 2004, LNCS 3027, printed pages.

metadata.statement: For sets given as characteristic strings of \( u \) bits, \( u \) the domain size, any protocol that outputs an \( (\varepsilon, \delta) \)-approximation of \( |X \cap Y| \), that is a value within a factor \( 1 \pm \varepsilon \) with probability at least \( 1 - \delta \), can distinguish intersection size at most \( \eta \) from at least \( \eta(1 + \varepsilon)^2 \) and hence decide disjointness on inputs of length about \( u/\eta \); for constant \( \varepsilon \) and constant \( \eta \) its randomized communication complexity is therefore \( \Theta(u) \), with or without privacy. Intersection size thus has no private approximation with sublinear worst-case communication, \( o(u) \), under multiplicative error.
metadata.title: Linear communication lower bound for approximating intersection size within a multiplicative factor, by reduction from disjointness

sections.content: Communication lower bound for approximate intersection size
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Given disjointness inputs a, b of length m, the client sets \( X = 1^{\eta} | a^{(2 + \varepsilon^2)\eta} \) and the server sets \( Y = 1^{\eta} | b^{(2 + \varepsilon^2)\eta} \), so \( |X \cap Y| = \eta \) if a and b are disjoint and at least \( \eta(1 + \varepsilon)^2 \) otherwise; an \( (\varepsilon, \delta) \)-approximation separates the two cases, so its randomized communication is \( \Omega(m) = \Omega(u/\eta) \) (§6, pp. 13-14). The accompanying protocol Intersect-Approx repeats the private sampler Private-Sample-B with the AND predicate until \( T \) positive samples occur and outputs \( T/s \), \( s \) the number of samples drawn; it is a private approximation for semi-honest parties whose communication is dominated by 1-out-of-\( u \) oblivious transfers (Protocol Private-Sample-B, p. 14; §6, p. 15).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: PIR-RESULT-1999-CMS-POLYLOGARITHMIC-SINGLE-SERVER-COMMUNICATION: the paper instantiates the 1-out-of-\( u \) oblivious transfer of Private-Sample-B with a computational PIR scheme of Cachin, Micali, and Stadler, through the Naor-Pinkas combination, for \( \kappa \cdot \mathrm{polylog}(u) \) communication (§6, p. 14).

historical_context.narrative: The basic polynomial protocol makes the server evaluate a polynomial whose degree equals the client's set size at every one of its own items, so its work grows with the product of the two set sizes. Freedman, Nissim, and Pinkas cut this by letting the client spread her items over many bins and send a short polynomial for each. They used balanced allocations, placing each item in the emptier of two random bins, which keeps the fullest bin at about \( \ln\ln n_Y \) items. The server then evaluates just two short polynomials per item. With short exponents and Horner's rule on top, the construction reaches the linear communication and near-linear computation advertised in the abstract, and the authors note that full-length exponentiations, one per server item, dominate in practice.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Evaluating the client's encrypted degree-\( n_Y \) polynomial naively costs \( O(n_Y) \) exponentiations per server item, \( O(n_Y n_X) \) in total, for Protocol PM-Semi-Honest (§4.2, p. 6).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: These steps give the \( O(n) \) communication and \( O(n \ln\ln n) \) computation stated in the abstract (p. 1); in practice the server's cost is dominated by \( n_X \) full-length exponentiations (§4.2, p. 8).
historical_context.technical_delta: Items are hashed to short representations so that Horner's rule uses short exponents (§4.2, pp. 6-7); the client then splits her set into \( B \) bins by balanced allocations, \( B \) the number of bins, where each item goes to the less loaded of two random bins, and sends \( B \) encrypted polynomials of degree \( M \); the server evaluates two of them per item (§4.2, p. 7). By Azar et al., the maximum load is \( (1 + o(1)) \ln\ln B / \ln 2 + \Theta(n_Y / B) \) (§4.2, p. 7).

limitations: the maximum-load bound holds with probability \( 1 - o(1) \); for concrete constants the paper cites Broder and Mitzenmacher (\( M = 5 \) fails with probability about \( 10^{-58} \)) and says simple experimentation can give finer bounds (§4.2, p. 8)
the protocol does not specify what happens if a bin overflows (§4.2, p. 8)
qualifiers: semi-honest parties; the hashing-based protocol's security is argued informally (§4.3, p. 9)
items are first mapped to about \( 2 \log(\max(n_X, n_Y)) \) bits by pairwise-independent hashing, with a small collision probability (§4.2, p. 6)
the server returns, for every item, the encryptions for both candidate bins (§4.2, p. 7)
the mapping to bins may be chosen pseudorandomly, jointly or by either party (footnote 9, p. 7)
with \( B = n_Y \) bins and \( n \le 2^{24} \), communication is at most four times that of the protocol without hashing (§4.2, p. 8)

EUROCRYPT 2004, LNCS 3027, printed pages.

metadata.statement: In polynomial-evaluation PSI, the client maps her items into \( B \) bins with the two-choice balanced-allocation hash of Azar et al., pads each bin with zero roots to a common degree \( M \), and sends one encrypted polynomial per bin; the server evaluates, for each of its items, only the two polynomials of the bins the item could occupy. With \( B = n_Y / \ln\ln n_Y \), \( M = O(\ln\ln n_Y) \), so communication and client work remain \( O(n_Y) \) coefficients while the server's work falls from \( O(n_Y n_X) \) to \( O(n_Y + n_X \ln\ln n_Y) \) exponentiations; Horner's rule and hashing items to short representations reduce the constant further.

sections.content: Balanced-allocation hashing for polynomial-evaluation PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The client chooses a random hash h with range \( B \); each item goes to the less occupied of its two candidate bins, and every bin polynomial is padded with the root 0 to degree \( M \) (0 is assumed not to be a valid input). The client sends the \( B \) encrypted polynomials and the mapping; for each item y, the server evaluates the polynomials of both candidate bins and returns \( \mathrm{Enc}(r \cdot P(y) + y) \) for each (§4.2, p. 7). Communication and the client's work equal the number of coefficients \( B \cdot M \), which is \( O(n_Y) \) for \( B = n_Y / \ln\ln n_Y \) (§4.2, p. 8).

historical_context.narrative: Some uses of set intersection need less than the shared items: only how many there are, or whether their number passes a threshold. Freedman, Nissim, and Pinkas observed that their polynomial protocol adapts with almost no change. If the server attaches a fixed string instead of its item, the client can count matches but cannot tell which items matched. If the server attaches random values, the client ends up holding values that agree with the server's exactly on the matches, and a small secure circuit over those values can then compute a threshold test or another function of the matches. The authors point out that this circuit depends only on the server's set size and a statistical parameter, not on the size of the domain from which items are drawn.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The paper defines private cardinality matching and private threshold matching, and more generally simple functions of the intersection, as variants of private matching (§3.1, p. 3); its basic protocol reveals the intersection itself to the client (Protocol PM-Semi-Honest, p. 6).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The circuit's cost depends on \( n_X \) and a statistical parameter, not on the domain size, and the same approach computes any function of the intersection, such as whether its size lies in a range (§4.5, p. 9).
historical_context.technical_delta: Only the server's payload changes: \( 0^{s} \) for the size (§4.4, p. 9); random values \( r_y \) followed by a circuit with \( n_X \cdot \lambda \) gates, \( \lambda \) a statistical parameter, for the bitwise equality tests and a threshold function for the threshold decision (§4.5, p. 9).

limitations: no separate security argument is given for the threshold variant beyond its composition with a secure circuit evaluation (§4.5, p. 9)
no costs are stated beyond the polynomial protocol plus \( n_X \cdot \lambda \) equality gates, \( \lambda \) a statistical parameter, and the threshold circuit (§4.5, p. 9)
qualifiers: semi-honest parties; for the cardinality variant the paper says the proof follows trivially from that of PM-Semi-Honest (§4.4, p. 9)
the threshold variant adds a generic secure circuit evaluation protocol after the polynomial step, whose engine is not specified (§4.5, p. 9)
the client is the only party with output (§3.1, p. 3)

source_locator.primary_source: Contributions (p. 2); §3.1 'PM Variants' (p. 3); §4.4 'Variant: Private Matching for Set Cardinality' (p. 9); §4.5 'Variants: Private Matching for Cardinality Threshold and Other Functions' (p. 9). EUROCRYPT 2004, LNCS 3027, printed pages.

metadata.statement: In polynomial-evaluation PSI, if the server encodes a fixed string \( 0^{s} \) of \( s \) zero bits instead of its item as the payload, the client learns only how many of its decryptions equal that string, that is \( |X \cap Y| \), with security following from the semi-honest protocol. If the server instead encodes fresh random values \( r_y \) and the parties then run a secure circuit evaluation that compares the client's \( n_X \) decryptions with the server's \( r_y \) values and applies a threshold, the client learns only whether \( |X \cap Y| > t \); the same circuit step can compute other functions of the matches.
metadata.title: Intersection size or a threshold decision on it, instead of the intersection, from polynomial-evaluation PSI, semi-honest

sections.content: Cardinality and threshold variants of polynomial-evaluation PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Cardinality (\( \mathrm{PM}_C \)): the server computes \( \mathrm{Enc}(r \cdot P(y) + 0^{s}) \), and the client outputs the number of decryptions equal to \( 0^{s} \), a string of \( s \) zero bits (§4.4, p. 9). Threshold (\( \mathrm{PM}_t \)): the server computes \( \mathrm{Enc}(r \cdot P(y) + r_y) \) with random \( r_y \); the client's ordered decryptions and the server's ordered \( r_y \) values enter a circuit that tests equality bit by bit (\( n_X \cdot \lambda \) gates) and then applies the threshold function (§4.5, p. 9).

sections.content: None. The secure circuit evaluation protocol is not named.

historical_context.narrative: The polynomial protocol is fragile against deviation. A cheating client can hide extra roots, especially when its items are spread over many bins, and a cheating server can blend two of its items into one reply so that the client's verdict depends on both. Freedman, Nissim, and Pinkas treated the two sides separately. The client commits to several copies of its bin polynomials built from pseudorandom item identities, and the server has half of them opened before answering with the rest, so that cheating is caught except with probability exponentially small in the number of copies. The server, in turn, must derive all of its randomness from a seed it encrypts, letting the client replay each answer. Only the first fix avoids random oracles, and the combination is outlined only.
historical_context.prior_boundary: In the semi-honest protocol a client could send a polynomial with more than \( n_Y \) roots, which with hashing means more nonzero roots across bins than allowed (§5.1, pp. 10-11), and a server could use two different inputs for the evaluation and the payload, for example encrypting \( r \cdot (P(y) + P(y')) + y' \) so that y' is reported only if both y and y' are client items (§5.2, p. 11).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The paper presents these as protocols for malicious environments with the same \( O(n) \) communication and \( O(n \ln\ln n) \) computation as the semi-honest case up to the factor L, the client-side protocol in the standard model and the server-side one in the random oracle model (abstract, p. 1; footnote 4, p. 2; §5, p. 10).
historical_context.technical_delta: Cut-and-choose over L copies with pseudorandom item identities bounds the client's effective set (Protocol PM-Malicious-Client, p. 10; proof sketch, p. 11). Deriving the server's evaluation randomness and a hash tag from an encrypted seed lets the client verify each reply against her own items (Protocol PM-Malicious-Server, p. 12; Lemma 4, p. 12).

limitations: the protocol against both malicious parties is only outlined; its detailed description is deferred to the full version (§5.3, p. 13)
the malicious-server protocol is given without hashing; the paper says the balanced-allocation version may be modified similarly (§5.2, p. 11)
security arguments are proof sketches (pp. 11-13)
qualifiers: malicious client: standard model, overhead L times the semi-honest protocol, error exponentially small in L (§5.1, p. 11)
malicious server: random oracle model, random oracles H1 and H2 (Protocol PM-Malicious-Server, p. 12)
without hashing, a client polynomial with more than \( n_Y \) roots is excluded by fixing the constant coefficient to 1 (§5.1, p. 11)
the client protocol uses a pseudorandom function F and a collision-resistant hash G (Protocol PM-Malicious-Client, step 1(b), p. 10; footnote 10, p. 11)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 1); contributions and footnote 4 (p. 2); §3.2 'Malicious adversaries' (p. 4); §5 introduction (pp. 9-10); Protocol PM-Malicious-Client (p. 10); §5.1 and proof sketch (pp. 10-11); §5.2 (p. 11); Protocol PM-Malicious-Server and Lemma 4 (p. 12); proof sketch (pp. 12-13); §5.3 (p. 13). EUROCRYPT 2004, LNCS 3027, printed pages.

metadata.statement: Against a malicious client, the client builds L copies of her bin polynomials over pseudorandom identities \( F_s(G(x)) \) of her items, the server opens \( L/2 \) copies to check that each has \( n_Y \) nonzero roots and evaluates the rest with XOR shares of each item as payloads, giving error exponentially small in L at L times the semi-honest cost, in the standard model. Against a malicious server, the server derives all randomness for item y from \( r = H1(s) \) for a random s, returns \( (\mathrm{Enc}(r' \cdot P(y) + s), H2(r'', y)) \), and the client recomputes each reply to check consistency, in the random oracle model. A protocol secure against both is only outlined.
metadata.title: Polynomial-evaluation PSI secure against a malicious client by cut-and-choose (standard model) and against a malicious server by derandomized replies (random oracle model)

sections.content: Malicious-secure polynomial-evaluation PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: PM-Malicious-Client: the client sends L copies, the server asks to open \( L/2 \) of them, the client opens their encrypted coefficients without revealing their PRF keys and reveals the keys of the other \( L/2 \) copies, and the server, after checking \( n_Y \) roots per opened copy, evaluates the unopened copies with \( L/2 \) random shares whose XOR is its item as payloads (Protocol PM-Malicious-Client, p. 10). PM-Malicious-Server: the server computes \( r = H1(s) \) for a random s and returns \( (\mathrm{Enc}(r' \cdot P(y) + s), H2(r'', y)) \); the client decrypts s, recomputes r, and accepts x if the pair is consistent with x (Protocol PM-Malicious-Server, p. 12). The simulator extracts the server's input from its random-oracle queries (Lemma 4 and proof sketch, pp. 12-13).

historical_context.narrative: Extending the polynomial protocol to many parties looks easy: let one party, the leader, evaluate every other party's encrypted polynomial on its own items, splitting each item into shares that only a matching client can unlock. Freedman, Nissim, and Pinkas show that this naive version leaks, since the leader created the shares and can see which clients return the right ones even for items that are not shared by everyone. Their fix has every client contribute additional random shares that cancel out, so the values clients publish look random unless an item lies in every set. The resulting protocol for honest-but-curious parties needs only three rounds of postings, which the authors contrast with many-round protocols whose communication grows quadratically in the number of parties, as \( O(\ell^2) \).
historical_context.prior_boundary: The paper's two-party protocol gives the intersection to one client (Protocol PM-Semi-Honest, p. 6). A strawman extension in which the leader shares each item among the clients fails, because the leader can tell which clients hold an item outside the intersection from which of them publish correct shares (§7, pp. 15-16).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors note that the communication involves two rounds of client submissions and one of the leader, which they prefer to protocols with many rounds and \( \ell^2 \) communication, \( \ell \) the number of parties, and that hashing to bins can lower the leader's computation (§7, p. 17).
historical_context.technical_delta: Each client adds, for each leader item, random shares that XOR to zero, encrypted to the other clients, so that published values look random to the leader unless the item is in the intersection (§7, steps 1-4, p. 16).

limitations: no proof and no formal collusion threshold are given; the text says that for items outside the intersection the published XOR looks random to any coalition (§7, p. 16)
no costs are stated beyond the round count; the leader's computation can be reduced by the hashing of §4.2 (§7, p. 17)
qualifiers: semi-honest parties only; the protocol is sketched (§7, p. 15)
each list is assumed to contain \( n \) items without loss of generality (§7, p. 15)
data is posted to a public bulletin board, or to the leader acting as one (§7, step 1, p. 16)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 1); contributions (p. 2); §7 'The Multi-party Case', 'A strawman protocol', and 'Achieving security with respect to semi-honest parties', steps 1-4 (pp. 15-17). EUROCRYPT 2004, LNCS 3027, printed pages.

metadata.statement: For \( \ell \) parties with \( n \) items each, \( \ell - 1 \) clients publish polynomials encoding their items under their own additively homomorphic keys, together with encrypted random shares that XOR to zero for each of the leader's \( n \) items; the leader evaluates every client polynomial on each of its items with one XOR share of the item as payload; each client decrypts what is encrypted under its key and publishes the XOR of the leader's share with the other clients' zero shares, and an item is in the intersection if all published values for its row XOR to it. The protocol is sketched for semi-honest parties and uses two rounds of client submissions and one round of leader submissions.
metadata.title: Multi-party set intersection from encrypted client polynomials and XOR-shared payloads with re-randomizing zero shares, semi-honest (protocol sketch)

sections.content: Multi-party polynomial-evaluation PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Client \( P_i \) (\( 1 \le i \le \ell - 1 \)) posts encrypted coefficients of a degree-\( n \) polynomial \( Q_i \) with its items as roots, and an \( n \times (\ell - 1) \) matrix of random numbers whose rows XOR to zero, column \( j \) encrypted under \( P_j \)'s key. The leader \( P_\ell \) splits each of its items y into \( \ell - 1 \) XOR shares \( s_{y,j} \) and posts, for each y, the tuple of encryptions of \( r_{y,j} \cdot Q_j(y) + s_{y,j} \), in permuted order. Each client decrypts its column from the leader and from the other clients, XORs each row, and posts the \( n \) results; every party checks whether a row's published values XOR to one of its items (§7, steps 1-4, p. 16).

historical_context.narrative: Before this work, two parties could compute a set intersection privately with generic circuits or with many pairwise equality tests, both with communication \( O(n^2 \log u) \), \( u \) the domain size, while cheaper constructions using a linear number of exponentiations had been argued only with random oracles and only for honest-but-curious parties. Freedman, Nissim, and Pinkas turned the client's set into the roots of a polynomial and sent its coefficients under additively homomorphic encryption, so that the server could evaluate it blindly on each of its own items and hide everything except matches behind a random multiplier. Security against semi-honest parties then rests on semantic security alone, in the standard model, and communication is linear in the set sizes, \( O(n_X + n_Y) \), which the authors present as an improvement over earlier solutions.
historical_context.prior_boundary: A generic circuit for private matching of length-\( n \) lists needs \( O(n^2 \log u) \) communication and \( O(n \log u) \) oblivious transfers, \( u \) the domain size, and comparing all pairs with private equality tests costs \( O(n^2 \log u) \) communication; constructions with only \( O(n) \) exponentiations had been analyzed only in the random oracle model against semi-honest parties (§2, p. 2).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors state that their protocols are more efficient than previous solutions, with \( O(n) \) communication (p. 2), and that the semi-honest protocol is secure in the standard model, unlike the earlier \( O(n) \)-exponentiation constructions (abstract, p. 1; §2, p. 2).
historical_context.technical_delta: The client's set becomes the root set of a polynomial sent under additively homomorphic encryption; the server evaluates it on each of its items, masks the result with a random multiplier, and adds the item, so shared items decrypt to themselves (§4.1, p. 5; Protocol PM-Semi-Honest, p. 6). Client privacy follows from semantic security and server privacy from simulating with the polynomial's roots (Lemmas 2-3, p. 8).

limitations: security is argued by lemma statements with proof sketches (§4.3, p. 8)
a malicious server can break correctness, for example by encrypting \( r \cdot (P(y) + P(y')) + y' \) (§5.2, p. 11); malicious security is a separate contribution
the \( O(n_Y n_X) \) server cost of this basic protocol is reduced only by the hashing of §4.2 (p. 6)
qualifiers: only the client learns the intersection (§3.1, p. 3)
the plaintext space is a field that represents the input domain but is exponentially larger (Protocol PM-Semi-Honest, step 1(a), p. 6)
the server may attach a payload \( v_y \) by computing \( \mathrm{Enc}(r \cdot P(y) + (y|v_y)) \); the client obtains \( v_y \) iff y is shared (Protocol PM-Semi-Honest, step 2(b), p. 6)
deciding whether a ciphertext encrypts a client item suffices, so exponential ElGamal can replace Paillier (footnote 8, p. 5)
re-randomization of the result ciphertexts is neglected in the description (footnote 6, p. 5)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 1); contributions (p. 2); §2 (p. 2); §3.1 (p. 3); §3.3 (pp. 4-5); §4.1 (p. 5); Protocol PM-Semi-Honest (p. 6); §4.3, Lemmas 1-3 (p. 8). EUROCRYPT 2004, LNCS 3027, printed pages.

metadata.statement: The client encodes her \( n_Y \) items as the roots of a polynomial P and sends its coefficients encrypted under a semantically secure additively homomorphic scheme; for each of his \( n_X \) items y the server homomorphically computes \( \mathrm{Enc}(r \cdot P(y) + y) \) with a fresh random r and returns the permuted ciphertexts, so the client decrypts exactly the shared items and random values otherwise. The protocol computes the intersection for the client with security against semi-honest parties in the standard model, assuming semantic security; without the hashing optimization the server performs \( O(n_Y n_X) \) exponentiations.
metadata.title: Set intersection for the client from oblivious evaluation of an encrypted polynomial whose roots are the client's items, semi-honest, standard model

sections.content: Polynomial-evaluation PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The client interpolates \( P(y) = (x_1 - y) \cdots (x_{n_Y} - y) \), encrypts its \( n_Y + 1 \) coefficients, and sends them; the server computes \( \mathrm{Enc}(P(y)) \) by homomorphic operations for each of its items, then \( \mathrm{Enc}(r \cdot P(y) + y) \), and sends the permuted results; the client outputs every x in its set that appears among the decryptions (Protocol PM-Semi-Honest, p. 6). The authors note that the construction generalizes oblivious transfer protocols in which the client sends a predicate that is zero exactly at its index (footnote 7, p. 5).

historical_context.narrative: A natural question about any new secure-computation task is how weak an assumption could possibly suffice. Freedman, Nissim, and Pinkas answered it for set intersection with a two-line encoding. If the sender's set holds each of its two bits tagged with its position, and the chooser's set holds both possible bits tagged with its choice, then the one common element tells the chooser exactly the bit it selected and nothing more. Any private matching protocol thus yields oblivious transfer, and the known black-box separation between one-way functions and oblivious transfer carries over. Set intersection therefore cannot be built from one-way functions alone in a black-box way, which the authors state as an impossibility result and do not develop further.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Impagliazzo and Rudich bounded what can be proved from one-way permutations in a black-box way (reference [13], cited in §3.1, p. 3); the paper uses this result through oblivious transfer.
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It follows that no black-box reduction of private matching from one-way functions exists (§3.1, p. 3); the authors use the reduction only for this impossibility statement (§3.1, p. 4).
historical_context.technical_delta: A two-element set encoding of the sender's bits and the chooser's choice bit turns any private matching protocol into a 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious transfer protocol (§3.1, p. 3); the semi-honest PM protocol also supports oblivious transfer of strings, and 1-out-of-N bit transfer can be built directly (§3.1, p. 4).

limitations: no non-black-box impossibility is claimed (§3.1, p. 3)
the reduction is given in prose without a formal proof (§3.1, pp. 3-4)
qualifiers: the reduction is stated for semi-honest 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious transfer (§3.1, p. 3)
the impossibility concerns black-box reductions only (§3.1, p. 3)

source_locator.primary_source: §3.1 'Private Matching and Oblivious Transfer' (pp. 3-4). EUROCRYPT 2004, LNCS 3027, printed pages.

metadata.statement: Semi-honest 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious transfer reduces to private matching: the sender inputs the set \( \{0|b_0, 1|b_1\} \), the chooser inputs \( \{\sigma|0, \sigma|1\} \), and the chooser's output of the matching protocol is \( \sigma|b_\sigma \). By the result of Impagliazzo and Rudich, private matching therefore has no black-box reduction from one-way functions.
metadata.title: Private matching implies oblivious transfer, so set intersection has no black-box construction from one-way functions

sections.content: Private matching implies oblivious transfer
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: From a private matching protocol in which the chooser learns \( X \cap Y \), the sender's set \( \{0|b_0, 1|b_1\} \) and the chooser's set \( \{\sigma|0, \sigma|1\} \) intersect in exactly \( \sigma|b_\sigma \), giving the chooser \( b_\sigma \) and the sender nothing (§3.1, p. 3). The authors combine this with Impagliazzo and Rudich to conclude that private matching cannot be reduced to one-way functions in a black-box manner (§3.1, p. 3).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-COMP-CORR-BASEOT: oblivious transfer, the primitive that private matching is shown to imply (§3.1, p. 3).

nodes.subtitle: Efficient Private Matching and Set Intersection
nodes.summary: Semi-honest 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious transfer reduces to private matching: the sender inputs the set \( \{0|b_0, 1|b_1\} \), the chooser inputs \( \{\sigma|0, \sigma|1\} \), and the chooser's output of the matching protocol is \( \sigma|b_\sigma \). By the result of Impagliazzo and Rudich, private matching therefore has no black-box reduction from one-way functions.
nodes.title: Private matching implies oblivious transfer, so set intersection has no black-box construction from one-way functions

historical_context.narrative: Linear-cost PSI protocols existed by 2009, but they made the client perform one modular exponentiation per item, which is heavy for a phone, and the best known oblivious-PRF protocol carried extra setup. De Cristofaro and Tsudik borrowed an idea from adaptive oblivious keyword search: the server signs the hashes of its items with an RSA key ahead of time and publishes hashes of those signatures, and the client obtains signatures on its own items by blind signing, so that matching items produce equal tags. Online, the client multiplies and divides but never exponentiates, and the server performs one exponentiation per client item. The authors recommend the protocol when the client is weak and the server can precompute, and they note that reusing tags lets a client track changes to the server's set.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Polynomial-evaluation PSI cost \( O(n_X n_Y) \) or \( O(n_X \log\log n_Y) \) server exponentiations; the OPRF-based protocol of Jarecki and Liu needed a common reference string with a safe RSA modulus and a polynomial input domain; the UPF-based protocol of Jarecki and Liu used \( O(n_X + n_Y) \) short server exponentiations and \( O(n_Y) \) client exponentiations (§4.1, pp. 3-4; Table 2, p. 11). The paper's own prime-order protocol also needs \( O(n_Y) \) client exponentiations (§5.5, p. 8).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The client performs no online exponentiations, which suits resource-poor clients (§5.6, p. 9); in the paper's measurements the client's online time for 5,000 items per party is 1,422 ms against 5,344 ms for the prime-order protocol, while the server's is 4,662 ms against 2,072 ms (Table 3, p. 11).
historical_context.technical_delta: Adapting Ogata and Kurosawa's adaptive oblivious keyword search, the server reveals as keys the hashes of RSA signatures on its items, and the client obtains signatures on its own items by blinding (§5.6, Figure 4, p. 9); server privacy is reduced to one-more-RSA in the random oracle model (Appendix B.3, p. 16).

limitations: no server unlinkability: tags \( H'(H(s_j)^d) \) repeat across runs, so a client observes changes in the server's set; the paper sketches patches such as fresh RSA keys or per-run hash functions (§5.6, pp. 9-10)
without precomputation it is slower than the prime-order protocol, which uses shorter server exponents (§5.6, p. 10)
client privacy and unlinkability proofs are deferred; server privacy is a proof sketch (Appendix B.3, p. 16)
no security against malicious parties is claimed (§5.1, p. 6; §7, p. 12)
qualifiers: honest-but-curious client and server (§5.1, p. 6)
the server sets up its RSA parameters a priori and precomputes \( n_X \) signatures and tags; the client precomputes its blinded values (Figure 4, steps 1-2, p. 9)
only the client learns the intersection; mutual PSI is obtained by two one-way runs if neither party aborts (§2, p. 2)
data transfer can be added by deriving symmetric keys from the matching values (§5.7, p. 10)

metadata.statement: The server signs the full-domain hash of each of its \( n_X \) items with its RSA key offline and sends the tags \( H'(H(s_j)^d) \); the client blinds each hashed item as \( H(c_i) \cdot R_i^e \), the server returns \( (H(c_i) \cdot R_i^e)^d \), and the client divides by \( R_i \) to obtain \( H(c_i)^d \) and compares tags. Against honest-but-curious parties, in the random oracle model under the one-more-RSA assumption, the protocol is server-private, client-private, and client-unlinkable; online the server performs \( O(n_Y) \) exponentiations and the client \( O(n_Y) \) modular multiplications, after \( n_X \) RSA signatures of server precomputation, with \( O(n_Y + n_X) \) communication.

sections.content: Blind-RSA PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Offline, the server computes \( K_{s:j} = H(s_j)^d \bmod N \) and \( t_j = H'(K_{s:j}) \) for each of its items, and the client computes \( y_i = H(c_i) \cdot (R_{c:i})^e \bmod N \). Online, the client sends the \( y_i \), the server returns \( y_i^d \) together with the tags \( t_j \), and the client computes \( K_{c:i} = y_i^d / R_{c:i} = H(c_i)^d \) and outputs the items whose tag \( H'(K_{c:i}) \) appears among the \( t_j \) (Figure 4, p. 9). The simulator for an honest-but-curious client answers random-oracle queries and reduces any client that learns more than \( n_Y \) outputs to the one-more-RSA problem (Appendix B.3, p. 16).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: SIG-CONSTRUCTION-1978-RSA: RSA signatures, computed obliviously by blinding (Figure 4, p. 9; Appendix B.3, p. 16, which cites Chaum's blind signatures). Ogata-Kurosawa adaptive oblivious keyword search, the stated source of the idea (§5.6, p. 9), has no record in any topic.

historical_context.narrative: Authorized set intersection asks that a client may only match items that a trusted authority has signed, which suits queries such as checking vetted suspects against a bank's records. The available construction, extended from a policy-based information transfer protocol, compared every client authorization with every server item, so its cost grew with the product of the set sizes; identity-based alternatives were linear but lost forward security. De Cristofaro and Tsudik restructured the RSA protocol so that the client folds all its signatures into one aggregate value, letting the server derive a single key per item of its own. Costs become linear, and moving the same pattern into a prime-order group gives a plain set-intersection protocol with short exponents, which the authors prove secure only for honest-but-curious parties.
historical_context.prior_boundary: APSI obtained by extending RSA-PPIT to clients with several authorizations has quadratic computation and communication (§4.2, p. 5; §5.3, Figure 1, p. 7); IBE-based PPIT is linear but not forward secure, and PEKS-based APSI needs a quadratic number of tests and bilinear maps (§4.2, p. 5).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors report that the linear APSI protocol needs 12,037 ms of server time against 99,118 ms for the RSA-PPIT protocol for 5,000 items per party, with the gap growing for larger sets (Table 3 and §6.1, p. 11), and that it relies on RSA rather than bilinear maps (§4.2, p. 5).
historical_context.technical_delta: The client aggregates its authorizations into \( \mathrm{PCH}^* \) and sends \( X = (\mathrm{PCH}^*)^2 \cdot g^{R_c} \) plus, for each item, a value built from \( \mathrm{PCH}^*/\sigma_i \), so the server computes one key per own item from \( X \) instead of one per pair (§5.4, Figure 2, pp. 7-8). Dropping the RSA setting for a subgroup of prime order \( r \) of \( \mathbb{Z}_p^* \) gives the PSI version, with \( |r| \)-bit exponents and precomputable \( (h_{sj})^{-R_s} \) (§5.5, Figure 3, p. 8).

limitations: no security against malicious parties is claimed; the authors' work-in-progress malicious proofs seem to depend on the product-of-hashes structure (§5.5, p. 9)
unlinkability is argued informally, with formal proofs deferred (Appendix B.1-B.2, pp. 14-15)
shorter exponents for the APSI protocol are suggested without a security proof (§6, p. 11)
authorization by a certification authority has no facet value in this topic; it is stated here in prose
qualifiers: APSI involves an offline certification authority that is assumed not to behave maliciously; the server is honest-but-curious and the client may lack authorizations for some items (§5.1, p. 6)
in the PSI version both client and server are honest-but-curious (§5.1, p. 6)
the server privacy reduction for the PSI version gives the reduction one additional DH-oracle query; removing it is stated as ongoing work (Appendix B.2, p. 16)
simplified versions for honest-but-curious parties that drop the product of hashes are given in Appendix C (Figures 5-6, p. 17)
only the client learns the intersection (§2, p. 2)

metadata.statement: In authorized PSI, where each client item must carry an RSA signature issued by an offline certification authority, the client sends one aggregate value X built from the product of its signatures and one blinded value per item; the server returns one exponentiated value per client value and one tag per own item, and the client recomputes the tags of its authorized items. Computation and communication are \( O(n_Y + n_X) \), against \( O(n_X n_Y) \) for the APSI protocol derived from RSA-PPIT, with an honest-but-curious server and a client that may lack authorizations, proved server-private in the random oracle model under the RSA assumption. The same structure in a prime-order subgroup of \( \mathbb{Z}_p^* \) gives a PSI protocol with \( O(n_Y + n_X) \) costs and short exponents, whose server privacy is argued under the One-More-Gap-DH assumption in the random oracle model.
metadata.title: Authorized PSI with computation and communication linear in both set sizes, \( O(n_X + n_Y) \), and its prime-order-group PSI version, semi-honest, random oracle model

sections.content: Linear-cost authorized PSI and its PSI version
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: APSI (Figure 2, p. 8): the client computes \( \mathrm{PCH}^* = \prod \sigma_i \), sends \( X = (\mathrm{PCH}^*)^2 \cdot g^{R_c} \) and \( y_i = (\mathrm{PCH}^*/\sigma_i)^2 \cdot g^{R_{c:i}} \); the server picks \( R_s \), sends \( Z = g^{eR_s} \), \( y_i' = y_i^{eR_s} \), and tags \( t_j = H'((X^e / h_{sj}^2)^{R_s}) \); the client computes \( K_{c:i} = y_i' \cdot Z^{R_c} \cdot Z^{-R_{c:i}} \) and matches \( H'(K_{c:i}) \) against the tags. Server privacy reduces to RSA in the random oracle model (Appendix B.1, pp. 14-15). PSI (Figure 3, p. 8): the same flow in a subgroup of prime order \( r \) of \( \mathbb{Z}_p^* \) with \( \mathrm{PCH} = \prod H(c_i) \), \( X = \mathrm{PCH} \cdot g^{R_c} \), and \( t_j = H'((X/h_{sj})^{R_s}) \); server privacy reduces to One-More-Gap-DH in the random oracle model (Appendix B.2, pp. 15-16).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: SIG-CONSTRUCTION-1978-RSA: the certification authority's authorizations are RSA signatures on hashed items (Figure 2, p. 8). The RSA-PPIT protocol of De Cristofaro, Jarecki, Kim, and Tsudik (PETS 2009), the stated starting point (§5.3, p. 7), has no record in any topic.

historical_context.narrative: Through the late 2000s, designers of set-intersection protocols built them from public-key primitives and justified this by the presumed slowness of generic secure computation, without measuring the alternative. Huang, Evans, and Katz tested the presumption directly. They rebuilt the fastest custom semi-honest protocol as a real client-server program in the same Java framework as their own garbled circuits and timed both on one pair of desktop machines at five security levels. The garbled circuit used vastly more bandwidth, hundreds of megabytes against one or two, but almost no exponentiations, so its running time grew slowly with the security level while the public-key protocol grew steeply. The measurements turned an untested assumption about generic computation into a comparison with stated settings.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Custom PSI protocols from homomorphic encryption and other public-key techniques were designed on the stated belief that generic garbled-circuit solutions would be impractical, a claim the authors say had never been substantiated (abstract and §1, p. 1). The fastest semi-honest PSI protocol reported was that of De Cristofaro and Tsudik (§1.3, p. 3).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: For 32-bit elements SCS-WN was always comparable to or faster than the custom protocol, and for 160-bit elements more than ten times faster at the highest security level, at the cost of two to three orders of magnitude more bandwidth (§7.3, pp. 12-13). The conclusion states that generic protocols can be competitive with the best custom PSI protocols (§8, p. 14).
historical_context.technical_delta: The authors reimplemented the De Cristofaro-Tsudik protocols in Java as client-server protocols with the same tools as their garbled-circuit framework (§7.3 and footnote 3, p. 12) and measured both at five NIST security levels, scaling OT parameters, OT-extension security, wire-label length, and hash function together (Table 3, p. 12; Figure 11, p. 13). They also counted the expensive operations of each protocol for \( n = 1024 \) and \( \sigma = 160 \) (Table 2, p. 13).

limitations: for 160-bit elements at the ultra-short level SCS-WN took 51.5 s against 10.9 s for the custom protocol (Figure 11, p. 13); the introduction says it is faster except at that level (§1.1, p. 2)
the comparison covers semi-honest security only (§1.1, p. 2)
timings depend on the implementations of the cryptographic operations, which is why Table 2 also counts operations (§7.3, pp. 13-14)
qualifiers: two Dell desktops with Intel Core 2 Duo E8400 at 3 GHz, 100 Mbps LAN, one core per party (§7, p. 11; §7.2, p. 12)

times include OT and garbled-circuit execution but exclude one-time setup, about 1.2 s for circuit construction and under 1 s for OT-extension initialization, which would add about two seconds to the first run per pair (§7, p. 11; §7.3, p. 12)
the custom protocol is the one-more-DL-based variant, which the authors found faster in total running time than the one-more-RSA-based one (footnote 4, p. 12)
both sides are the authors' Java implementations; De Cristofaro and Tsudik's own C code was single-process and not used for timing (footnote 3, p. 12)
times in this statement are read from the bar labels of Figure 11 for \( n = 1024 \) (p. 13)

metadata.statement: With both protocols implemented on the same two desktops (Intel Core 2 Duo E8400, 100 Mbps LAN), the garbled-circuit SCS-WN protocol computed the intersection of two sets of 1024 elements in 10.5 to 22.7 seconds for 32-bit elements and 51.5 to 122.7 seconds for 160-bit elements across NIST security levels from 80 to 256 bits, while the one-more-DL-based protocol of De Cristofaro and Tsudik took 10.9 to 1972.0 seconds; SCS-WN used 147 to 470 MB of bandwidth against 0.4 to 2.0 MB, and needs far fewer public-key operations but about 2000 times as many operations in total.

sections.content: Garbled circuits against custom PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Besides the comparison with the custom protocol, the paper measures its own protocols against each other. The bit-vector protocol is the fastest for element spaces up to about \( \sigma = 20 \), for example for \( n > 40 \) at \( \sigma = 12 \) and \( n > 500 \) at \( \sigma = 16 \) (§7.1 and Figure 8, p. 11). For \( \sigma = 32 \) and 128 to 8192 elements, SCS-WN is more than seven times faster than SCS-HE and 10 to 70 times faster than pairwise comparison, and the oblivious transfers take about 5% of the cost (§7.2, p. 12; Figure 10, p. 13). SCS-WN intersected two sets of \( 2^{20} \) 32-bit elements in about six hours (§7.2, p. 12).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-COMP-EVAL-YAO: all measured generic protocols use Yao's garbled-circuit protocol, cited as reference [39] (§1.2, p. 2). MPC-CONTRIB-2003-IKNP-OTEXT: the implementation uses OT extension, whose statistical parameter \( \lambda \) is varied with the security level (§2, p. 4; Table 2, p. 13).

historical_context.narrative: A protocol that returns the intersection reveals a great deal, and when the universe of possible elements is small a dishonest participant can simply submit everything and read off the other set. Custom PSI protocols offered no easy way to restrict what is released, since any change to the output means redesigning the protocol. Huang, Evans, and Katz used the fact that their protocols are ordinary garbled circuits: a few extra gates can count the matches and suppress the result when there are too many. For the sort-based circuits the counter rides on signals the circuit already computes and adds no measurable time, while for the very cheap bit-vector circuit it multiplies the cost several times over. The example illustrates the argument that generic protocols compose with further computation.
historical_context.prior_boundary: A PSI output leaks much about the inputs, and for small universes a dishonest party can input every value and learn the other set (§6, p. 10; §3, pp. 4-5). The authors judge that such self-auditing appears difficult to add to custom-designed PSI protocols (§6, p. 10).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It is the paper's demonstration that generic PSI protocols can be combined with further computation at little cost, the modularity argument for generic protocols in the introduction and conclusion (§1, pp. 1-2; §6, p. 10; §8, p. 14).
historical_context.technical_delta: Auditing logic is appended to the garbled circuit: for the sort-compare-shuffle family, a Counter circuit that lazily widens its state sums the MUX selection signals of the duplicate-selection circuits, and a comparison circuit tests the threshold; for the bit-vector protocol, a Counter sums the outputs of the AND gates (§6, pp. 10-11).

limitations: the paper calls the implementations prototypes and an initial study (§6, p. 10)
no security argument specific to the audited circuits is given (§2, p. 4)
the released condition is an upper bound on the intersection size (§6, p. 10), so it should not be read as threshold PSI in the sense of releasing the intersection only when it is large
qualifiers: the policy studied is an upper bound on the intersection size; above it no output is revealed except that the bound was exceeded (§6, p. 10)
semi-honest parties, as for all protocols of the paper (§1.1, p. 2)
when the threshold is known for an application the Counter can be made smaller (§6, p. 11)
metadata.statement: Because the PSI protocols are pure garbled circuits, the circuit can obliviously count the intersection size \( \hat{n} \) and compare it with a threshold, revealing nothing but that fact when \( \hat{n} \) exceeds it; in the sort-compare-shuffle protocols a Counter circuit of \( n \log n - n \) non-free gates sums the duplicate-selection signals with no measurable overhead in the authors' experiments, while in the bit-vector protocol the count uses \( \sigma \cdot 2^{\sigma} \) non-free gates instead of \( 2^{\sigma} \) and raised the running time for \( \sigma = 16 \) from 2.48 s to 12.22 s.
metadata.title: Size-based auditing inside garbled-circuit PSI: the intersection is withheld when its size exceeds a threshold

sections.content: Size-based auditing
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The auditing circuit computes \( \hat{n} \) obliviously, which is the main cost, and compares it with a threshold, which is negligible (§6, p. 10). In the sort-compare-shuffle protocols the Counter takes as inputs the selection signals of the MUX circuits inside DupSelect-2 and DupSelect-3 (§6, p. 11; Figure 5, p. 8). The authors measured no performance overhead for those protocols and a roughly fivefold slowdown for the bit-vector protocol at \( 12 \le \sigma \le 16 \), because its garbled-circuit part is only 35 to 45% of its running time (§6, p. 11).
