historical_context.narrative: Before 2012 nearly every semi-honest PSI protocol was a custom design from public-key techniques, and generic secure computation was dismissed, in part because comparing all pairs of elements seemed to force a quadratic circuit. Huang, Evans, and Katz observed that each party may sort its own set before the computation starts. The garbled circuit then only has to merge two sorted lists, which a bitonic merger does with \( n \log 2n \) small sorters, keep any element equal to a neighbour, and finally permute the surviving values, because their sorted positions would reveal information about elements outside the intersection. A Waksman network programmed by the circuit generator performs that permutation cheaply. The resulting quasi-linear circuit ran on million-element sets on ordinary desktops and became the generic baseline for computing PSI with secure computation.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The custom semi-honest PSI protocols of the time used public-key techniques, and the most efficient was the De Cristofaro-Tsudik protocol, secure under one-more-DL or one-more-RSA in the random oracle model (§1.3, p. 3; §2, p. 3). Generic protocols were held impractical, partly from the belief that a circuit for the intersection of two \( n \)-sets needs \( \Theta(n^{2}) \) size (§1, p. 1); the generic weighted-PSI circuit of Jónsson et al. had \( \Theta(n \log^{2} n) \) gates and required an honest majority (§1.3, p. 3).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The SCS-WN variant computed the intersection of two sets of \( 2^{20} \) 32-bit elements in about six hours with 1.7 billion non-free gates (§7.2, p. 12), was faster than every other variant of the paper for 128 to 8192 elements (Figure 10, p. 13), and is the protocol the paper compares with the De Cristofaro-Tsudik protocol (§7.3, p. 12).
historical_context.technical_delta: Each party sorts its set locally, so the circuit only merges two sorted lists with a bitonic merger built from 2-Sorters of \( 2\sigma \) non-free gates (§5.1, pp. 6-7; Figures 2-4), filters matches with DupSelect-3 using that three consecutive sorted elements contain at most one match (§5.2, p. 7; Figure 5), and shuffles with a Waksman network whose swapper gates the generator programs, each garbled as a single ciphertext with garbled-row reduction (§5.3.3, pp. 9-10; Algorithm 2). The total is \( 2\sigma n \log(2n) + ((3n - 1)\sigma - n) + \sigma(n \log n - n + 1)/3 \) gates (Table 1, p. 2).

limitations: no security against malicious parties is claimed; stronger threat models are left to future work (§1.1, p. 2)

the \( \Theta(n \log n) \) count is in non-free gates with free XOR; the Waksman stage is counted as \( \sigma(n \log n - n + 1)/3 \) gate equivalents because each programmed swapper gate costs one ciphertext (Table 1, p. 2; §5.3.3, p. 9)
the gate counts and timings concern the plain intersection, not a function of it (§2, p. 3)
qualifiers: semi-honest parties; security follows from Yao's protocol in the semi-honest model, with oblivious transfer from decisional Diffie-Hellman in the random oracle model; no proof is given (§1.2, p. 2; §2, p. 4)
both sets have the same known size \( n \), contain no duplicates, and use \( \sigma \)-bit elements; padding handles other cases (§2, p. 3)
\( 0^{\sigma} \) must not be a valid element, since DupSelect outputs it for non-matches (§5.2, p. 7)
the circuit generator chooses the random permutation and configures the Waksman network locally (§5.3.3, pp. 9-10)
either or both parties may receive the intersection (§2, p. 3)

metadata.statement: Against semi-honest parties holding \( n \) elements of \( \sigma \) bits each, the intersection can be computed by evaluating with Yao's garbled-circuit protocol a circuit that merges the two locally sorted sets with a bitonic merger of \( 2\sigma n \log(2n) \) non-free gates, keeps each element that equals a neighbour with DupSelect-3 circuits of \( (3n - 1)\sigma - n \) non-free gates in total, and destroys positional information with a Waksman switching network whose control bits the circuit generator sets from a random permutation; the circuit has \( \Theta(n \log n) \) non-free gates, whereas pairwise comparison needs \( \Theta(n^{2}) \).
metadata.title: Sort-compare-shuffle garbled circuit for two-party PSI with \( \Theta(n \log n) \) non-free gates, semi-honest

sections.content: Sort-compare-shuffle circuit
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The circuit has three stages (Figure 1, p. 6). Sorting: the two locally sorted lists form a bitonic sequence, and a bitonic merger of \( n \log(2n) \) 2-Sorters sorts their union; each 2-Sorter is a comparison plus a conditional swap with \( 2\sigma \) non-free gates (§5.1, pp. 6-7). Filtering: DupSelect-3 outputs the middle of three consecutive elements if it equals a neighbour and \( 0^{\sigma} \) otherwise, which leaves \( n \) outputs instead of \( 2n - 1 \) (§5.2, p. 7). Shuffling: the \( n \) outputs are permuted before they are revealed, because their positions leak information (§5.3, p. 8). Of the three shuffles studied, the Waksman network (SCS-WN) costs about 15% of the sorting stage (§5.3.3, p. 10), sorting the outputs again (SCS-SORT) is less efficient (§5.3.1, p. 8), and a homomorphic-encryption shuffle (SCS-HE) is linear in \( n \), \( O(n) \), but slower in practice (§5.3.2, p. 9).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-COMP-EVAL-YAO and MPC-COMP-ENC-GARBLED: the circuit is evaluated with Yao's garbled-circuit protocol, which the paper cites as its reference [39] (§1.2, p. 2; §2, pp. 3-4). MPC-CONTRIB-2008-FREEXOR: XOR gates are free and not counted (§1.2, p. 3; §2, p. 4). MPC-CONTRIB-2009-PRACTICAL2PC: garbled-row reduction to three ciphertexts per gate, and to one for the programmed swapper gates (§2, p. 4; §5.3.3, p. 9). MPC-CONTRIB-2003-IKNP-OTEXT: input-wire labels are transferred with OT extension on top of Naor-Pinkas OT (§2, p. 4).

historical_context.narrative: Oblivious transfer extension had made large batches of 1-out-of-2 transfers cheap, and Kolesnikov and Kumaresan had read its matrix as a repetition code that a better code could replace, reaching transfers with up to about 256 choices. Oblivious PRFs, by contrast, were still built from algebraic PRFs, and the OPRF hidden inside the PSI protocol of Pinkas, Schneider, Segev, and Zohner, which this paper calls the fastest at the time, spent one random OT on every byte of an item. Kolesnikov, Kumaresan, Rosulek, and Trieu observed that the code is never decoded and needs only large pairwise distance with overwhelming probability, so a pseudorandom code suffices. Each row of the extension matrix then gives an OPRF evaluation on an arbitrary string, with keys related across the batch, and item length drops out of the cost.
historical_context.prior_boundary: IKNP OT extension produced many 1-out-of-2 OTs from \( \kappa \) base OTs and symmetric-key work, and the Kolesnikov-Kumaresan coding view of IKNP gave 1-out-of-many OT, with up to about 256 choices per matrix row (§1, p. 2; §1.1, p. 3). Earlier OPRF protocols evaluated algebraic PRFs with exponentiations (§1.1, p. 3), and the OPRF implicit in the PSI protocol of Pinkas, Schneider, Segev, and Zohner used one 1-out-of-256 random OT per byte of the effective item length (§5.1, pp. 10-11; §5.3, p. 12).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The OT cost of one OPRF instance became 424-448 bits for the parameters considered, independent of item length (§5.3, p. 12; Table 2, p. 15). The authors use this to replace the OPRF inside the PSI protocol that their abstract calls the fastest at the time, which is the source of their PSI speedup for long items (abstract, p. 1; §5.1, p. 11).
historical_context.technical_delta: The error-correcting code of the Kolesnikov-Kumaresan framework is replaced by a pseudorandom code of minimum distance \( \kappa \) that is never decoded (§2, p. 5; Definition 2, p. 7), so one row of a width-k OT-extension matrix yields one OPRF instance on arbitrary strings. The m instances share the code and the sender's secret, so their keys are related and the receiver learns a relaxed output (Definition 4 and Lemma 5, p. 8); the protocol realizes this functionality against semi-honest adversaries (Theorem 6, p. 9; Figure 2, p. 10) at about the cost of \( 3.5m \) 1-out-of-2 OTs (abstract, p. 1).

limitations: no security against malicious parties is claimed (§1.1, p. 3)
the related-key batch is not a standard OPRF; §5.2 (p. 11) argues that it suffices for the PSI protocol of Figure 3
the matrix width k is 424-448 bits for the parameters of Table 2 (p. 15), against \( \kappa = 128 \) for IKNP, so communication grows with \( km \) rather than \( \kappa m \) (footnote 1, p. 6)
qualifiers: semi-honest sender and receiver (Theorem 6, p. 9)
related keys: every instance shares the pseudorandom code C and the sender's secret s (§3.3, pp. 7-8)
the receiver learns a relaxed output, the row of the extension matrix, rather than only the PRF value (§3.3, p. 8)
one receiver input per instance (§1, p. 2)
proved with an ideal functionality for the k base OTs (Figure 2, p. 10)
assumes a \( \kappa \)-Hamming correlation-robust hash H and a pseudorandom code C; the implementation derives C from AES used as a PRF (Lemma 3, p. 7; §6.3, p. 16)

metadata.statement: Against semi-honest adversaries, the BaRK-OPRF protocol produces a batch of m oblivious PRF instances with related keys, each of which the receiver evaluates on one input from \( \{0,1\}^* \), using k base OTs and symmetric-key operations; it replaces the error-correcting code of Kolesnikov-Kumaresan OT extension with a pseudorandom code of minimum distance \( \kappa \), and m instances cost roughly as much as \( 3.5m \) 1-out-of-2 OTs.
metadata.title: Batched related-key OPRF from OT extension, with per-instance cost independent of input length

sections.content: BaRK-OPRF
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The sender picks a pseudorandom code C and a random k-bit string s. For each of m instances the receiver secret-shares the codeword \( C(r_j) \) of its input \( r_j \) across two matrices, and the parties run k base OTs with their roles reversed, so that the sender obtains the row \( q_j = t_j \oplus (C(r_j) \wedge s) \) (Figure 2, p. 10). The sender can then evaluate \( H(j, q_j \oplus (C(r) \wedge s)) \) on any string r, while the receiver learns only the value for its own \( r_j \). Recovering another value requires guessing at least \( \kappa \) bits of s, because two codewords differ in at least \( \kappa \) positions with overwhelming probability (§2, pp. 4-5).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-2003-IKNP-OTEXT: IKNP OT extension. BaRK-OPRF starts from the IKNP paradigm (§2, p. 4), and the implementation uses IKNP to extend 128 Naor-Pinkas base OTs to the k base OTs it needs (footnote 1, p. 6; §6.3, p. 16). The Kolesnikov-Kumaresan 1-out-of-N OT extension, the direct predecessor, has no record in any topic yet.

historical_context.narrative: The fastest semi-honest PSI protocol of 2015, from Pinkas, Schneider, Segev, and Zohner, hashed items into bins and ran an oblivious PRF in each bin, but that PRF consumed one oblivious transfer per byte of an item, so long identifiers made the protocol slower. Kolesnikov, Kumaresan, Rosulek, and Trieu kept the hashing structure and swapped in their batched OPRF, whose cost per bin is one fixed-width row of the extension matrix. They also fixed a subtle leak: when two cuckoo hash functions sent an item to the same bin, duplicated values revealed it, so they tag each bin input with its hash index. The result runs in the same time for 32-, 64-, and 128-bit items and was three to four times faster than its predecessor on long items.
historical_context.prior_boundary: In the PSSZ protocol, which the paper calls the fastest PSI protocol at the time, each bin's OPRF uses one 1-out-of-256 random OT per byte of the effective item length \( \sigma^* = \sigma - \log n \), an OT cost of \( 32\sigma^* \) bits (abstract, p. 1; §5.1, pp. 10-11; §5.3, p. 12). Its protocol and implementation do not account for collisions among the cuckoo hash functions, which leak through duplicate PRF values (§5.2, p. 12, footnote 3).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: Communication is lower than PSSZ whenever \( \sigma^* > 14 \), which covers every reported PSSZ configuration except \( n \ge 2^{20} \) with 32-bit items (§5.3, p. 13); PSI of \( 2^{20} \) items takes 3.8 s regardless of item length, and \( 2^{24} \) 128-bit items take about one minute against 214 s for PSSZ (abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2; Table 3, p. 15).
historical_context.technical_delta: Each bin consumes one BaRK-OPRF instance, one row of a k-bit-wide OT-extension matrix with \( k = 424\text{--}448 \), so the OT cost no longer depends on the item length (§5.3, p. 12; Table 1, p. 14). Appending the hash index z to each bin input makes Alice's PRF calls distinct and lets Bob search a single set \( H_z \) or \( S_j \) of \( n \) values (§5.2, pp. 11-12; Figure 3, p. 13).

limitations: for short items PSSZ can be faster: its OT cost is lower when the effective item length \( \sigma^* = \sigma - \log n \) is below 14, as for 32-bit items with \( n \ge 2^{20} \) (§5.3, p. 13; Table 1, p. 14; §6.2, pp. 16-17)
no security against malicious parties is claimed (§1.1, p. 3)
communication grows with the code width k of 424-448 bits per bin rather than with \( \kappa = 128 \) (Table 1, p. 14; Table 5, p. 15)
qualifiers: semi-honest Alice and Bob; PSI security is argued in prose from the RK-PRF security of BaRK-OPRF, Definition 4 (§5.2, p. 11)
both parties learn the intersection: Bob sends it to Alice (Figure 3, step 6, p. 13)
described for equal set sizes \( |X| = |Y| = n \) (§5.2, p. 11; Figure 3, p. 13)
stash sizes are taken from PSSZ for a hashing failure probability of \( 2^{-40} \) (§6.1, p. 14)
PRF outputs of \( \lambda + \log_2(n^2) \) bits bound spurious collisions by \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (§5.2, p. 12)
the hash-index optimization reduces running time by about 10% in the implementation (§5.2, p. 11)

metadata.statement: Replacing the OPRF implicit in the PSSZ protocol, which spends one 1-out-of-256 random OT per byte of the effective item length, with BaRK-OPRF gives a semi-honest PSI protocol whose OT-extension cost is 424-448 bits per bin for \( n = 2^{8} \) to \( 2^{24} \), independent of item length. Bob cuckoo-hashes his items into \( 1.2n \) bins with three hash functions and a stash and appends the hash index to each bin input, so that Alice evaluates the PRF only on distinct key-input pairs and Bob searches one set of \( n \) values per item. Communication is \( k(1.2n + s) + (3 + s)nv \) bits excluding base OTs, and the authors report PSI 3.1-3.6 times faster than PSSZ for 128-bit items and sufficiently large sets.
metadata.title: Semi-honest two-party PSI with OT-extension cost per bin independent of item length, from BaRK-OPRF in the cuckoo-hashing paradigm of Pinkas, Schneider, Segev, and Zohner

sections.content: BaRK-OPRF PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Bob places his items in \( 1.2n \) bins by three-way cuckoo hashing with a stash of size \( s \) and uses \( y \| z(y) \) as the OPRF input of the bin holding y (or y itself in the stash); the parties run \( 1.2n + s \) BaRK-OPRF instances with Bob as receiver; Alice sends permutations of \( H_i = \{F(k_{h_i(x)}, x \| i)\} \) for \( i = 1, 2, 3 \) and \( S_j = \{F(k_{1.2n+j}, x)\} \) for each stash position; Bob outputs his items whose PRF value lies in the one set that corresponds to its hash index or stash position (Figure 3, p. 13). The paper notes that hashing long items to \( \lambda + \log n \) bits before PSI cannot remove its advantage, since effective item lengths stay above 14 bits for \( \lambda \ge 40 \) (§5.3, p. 13).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-2003-IKNP-OTEXT: the implementation obtains the k base OTs of BaRK-OPRF by extending 128 Naor-Pinkas OTs with IKNP (§6.3, p. 16).

historical_context.narrative: In 2017 the fastest PSI protocols, built from oblivious transfer and hashing, made both parties send encodings of their entire sets, so a phone checking a few thousand contacts against a service with millions of users paid for the size of the service's set. Encrypting the small set under fully homomorphic encryption and letting the server compute on it was an obvious idea, but the depth of the intersection circuit made it impractical. Chen, Laine, and Rindal made it practical by combining SIMD batching with cuckoo and permutation-based hashing, sending extra encrypted powers to flatten the circuit, splitting the server's bins, and shrinking replies by modulus switching. Communication fell to the small set times a logarithm of the large one, and nearly all computation moved to the server, at the price of semi-honest security and 32-bit items.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The most efficient PSI protocols at the time, the OT-based protocols of Pinkas et al. and Kolesnikov et al., have communication linear in both set sizes, \( O(n_X + n_Y) \) (§1.1, p. 1; §1.3, p. 2), and the paper states that all prior PSI protocols send data proportional to both entire sets, whereas the insecure solution sends only the smaller set (§1.4, p. 3). A naive FHE solution would send only twice the ciphertext expansion times the smaller set, but its computation grows with the size and depth of the intersection circuit (§1.2, pp. 1-2); the concurrent online/offline protocol of Kiss et al. still needs communication or storage linear in the larger set, \( O(n_X) \) (§1.3, p. 2).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: For 5535 receiver items against \( 2^{24} \) sender items of 32 bits, the paper reports 11.0 to 20.1 MB of total communication depending on parameters, against 480.4 MB for the protocol of Pinkas et al. and 962.1 MB computed from the formula of Kolesnikov et al. (Table 5, p. 16), and 1.7 s of receiver computation in one setting (§6.2, p. 16). The authors present private contact discovery from a phone as the motivating application (§2.2, p. 4) and describe the work as a first step in applying FHE to PSI (§7, p. 17).
historical_context.technical_delta: The receiver encrypts its permutation-based cuckoo hash table with SIMD batching, and the sender evaluates per bin the polynomial \( r\prod(y - x) \) from its simple-hashed bins, using encrypted powers of y supplied by the receiver (windowing) and splitting its bins into \( \alpha \) partitions, then switches the reply ciphertexts to a smaller modulus (§4, pp. 6-10; Figure 4, p. 12). Communication becomes \( O(n_Y \log n_X) \), only the sender performs work linear in \( n_X \) (p. 4), and the protocol is proved secure against semi-honest parties assuming an IND-CPA FHE scheme with circuit privacy (Theorem 2, p. 11).

limitations: no security against malicious parties is claimed: a malicious sender can steer the receiver's output, for example to the receiver's full set, and a malicious receiver could add noise to its ciphertexts so that noise flooding no longer hides the sender's set (§5.2, pp. 12-13)
the implementation restricts items to 32 bits; arbitrary lengths are possible in principle but need much larger FHE parameters (§4.2, p. 9; §6.1, p. 14)

communication is lower than that of the protocol of Pinkas et al. only when the sender's set exceeds about \( 2^{16} \) items, and in a single-threaded LAN run with \( n_X = 2^{20} \) and \( n_Y \le 5535 \) that protocol is faster (3.1 s against 8.6 s) (§6.2, p. 15; Table 5, p. 16)
simulation-based security requires fresh hash functions in each execution; reusing the sender's pre-processing is safe only against adversaries that do not force hashing failures (§6.1, p. 14)
qualifiers: semi-honest sender and receiver (§2.2, p. 3; Theorem 2, p. 11)
one-sided output: the receiver learns \( X \cap Y \) and the sender learns nothing (Figure 3, p. 11)
the set sizes \( n_X \) and \( n_Y \) and the item length \( \sigma \) are public (§2.2, p. 3)

security assumes an IND-CPA FHE scheme with circuit privacy; with leveled parameters the sender obtains statistical function privacy by adding encryptions of zero with large noise (noise flooding) (Theorem 2, p. 11; §5.2, p. 11)
the proof of Theorem 2 uses no random oracle; the hash functions are sampled at random and treated as public parameters (p. 11)

correctness holds when hashing succeeds, which happens with probability \( 1 - 2^{-\lambda} \); cuckoo hashing uses three hash functions and no stash, and its failure probability was estimated empirically (§4.2, pp. 7-8; p. 11)
the communication bound assumes the sender holds the larger set; a role-switched variant handles the opposite case with the same asymptotic communication (§2.2, p. 4; §5.2, p. 13)

metadata.statement: Against semi-honest adversaries, a two-party PSI protocol in which the receiver, holding \( n_Y \) items, encrypts its cuckoo hash table under a leveled fully homomorphic encryption scheme with SIMD batching, and the sender, holding \( n_X \) items in simple-hashed bins, homomorphically evaluates for each bin the product of differences \( r\prod(y - x) \) and returns it, has communication \( O(n_Y \log n_X) \), requires work linear in \( n_X \) only from the sender, and gives the intersection to the receiver only; windowing (the receiver also sends encrypted powers of its items) and partitioning of the sender's bins reduce the homomorphic circuit depth to \( \lceil \log_2(\lfloor \log_2(B/\alpha)/w \rfloor + 1) \rceil + 1 \), \( B \) the bin size, \( w \) the window size, and \( \alpha \) the number of partitions.
metadata.title: Communication \( O(n_Y \log n_X) \), linear in the smaller set and logarithmic in the larger set, for semi-honest two-party PSI, from leveled FHE with batching and hashing

sections.content: FHE-based PSI with communication logarithmic in the larger set
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The receiver cuckoo-hashes its items into \( m \) bins with three hash functions and no stash, and the sender inserts each of its items into all three candidate bins of a simple hash table with bin size \( B \) (Figure 2, p. 8). Permutation-based hashing stores only part of each item, and items longer than \( 2\log_2(n_X + n_Y) + \lambda - 1 \) bits are first hashed to that length (§4.2, pp. 7-9). The receiver batches its table into \( m/s \) plaintexts of the FV scheme, \( s \) the number of slots per plaintext, encrypts the powers \( y^{i \cdot 2^{wj}} \) of each slot value, \( w \) the window size, and sends them (Figure 4, step 5, p. 12). The sender, holding precomputed coefficients of the polynomial with roots in each partition of each bin, computes encryptions of all needed powers and a plaintext-ciphertext dot product per partition, optionally switches the results to a smaller modulus, and returns \( \alpha \cdot m/s \) ciphertexts (Figure 4, steps 4 and 6, p. 12). A slot decrypts to zero exactly when the receiver's item lies in the sender's bin (§3, pp. 5-6). Windowing raises the receiver-to-sender communication by a factor \( (2^{w} - 1)(\lfloor \log_2(B)/w \rfloor + 1) \) to lower the depth, and partitioning multiplies the reply by \( \alpha \) (§4.3, pp. 9-10). Modulus switching reduces reply ciphertexts to about 15-20% of their size (§4.4, p. 10). The paper gives the concrete communication as about \( 1.5C\sigma n_Y \log_2 n_X \) bits, with \( C \) a small ciphertext-expansion constant (§6.3, p. 17).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: HE-PAPER-2012-FV and HE-RESULT-2012-FV-RLWE-EXACT-ARITHMETIC-SCHEME-WITH-RELINEARIZATION: the implementation uses SEAL v2.1, which implements the Fan-Vercauteren scheme, and §2.3 names FV as a scheme of the required plaintext and ciphertext form (§2.3, p. 4; §6.1, p. 13). HE-RESULT-2012-SV-SIMD-CIPHERTEXT-SLOT-PACKING-AND-PARALLEL-RECRYPTION: the batching step cites Smart-Vercauteren SIMD operations among its sources (§4.1, p. 6). HE-RESULT-2012-BGV-MODULUS-SWITCHING-NOISE-MANAGEMENT: replies are shrunk by modulus switching, citing Brakerski-Gentry-Vaikuntanathan (§4.4, p. 10). HE-PAPER-2016-DS: the paper notes that circuit privacy can be obtained with the sanitization techniques of Ducas and Stehlé, and uses the weaker statistical function privacy by noise flooding instead (§5.2, p. 11).

historical_context.narrative: In the semi-honest protocol, the step that hands out shares of zero is the expensive one: every pair of parties runs a programmable OPRF so that a share reaches a party only if both hold the item. Kolesnikov, Matania, Pinkas, Rosulek, and Trieu observed that if parties may fix their inputs before the run, as the augmented semi-honest model allows, the shares need not be conditional at all. Pairs exchange short PRF seeds once, and each party derives its share of zero for any item locally, so only the reconstruction with the leader still uses programmable OPRFs. The price is that a corrupt party can compute the share for an item it does not hold, which standard semi-honest security forbids; the gain was a run on million-item sets roughly three times faster.
historical_context.prior_boundary: In the semi-honest protocol of the same paper, conditional zero-sharing runs a multi-query OPPRF between every pair of parties and is the most expensive part of the protocol (§5.3, p. 13; §6.1, p. 14), giving per-client communication \( O(n t_c \lambda) \) bits (Table 1, p. 3).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The abstract reports 22 seconds for 5 parties with \( 2^{20} \) items each, against 72 seconds for the semi-honest protocol (abstract, p. 1); Table 3 (p. 18) gives 21.93 seconds and 467.66 MB of client communication with the table-based OPPRF on a LAN. The authors argue that in PSI the only useful choice for a coalition is a common input set, so the extra power is relatively harmless (§2.1, p. 4; Appendix A, pp. 23-24).
historical_context.technical_delta: The zero-sharing protocol of Figure 9 (p. 14) derives unlimited shares of zero from seeds exchanged in a one-time initialization, and the PSI protocol replaces steps 1-3 of Figure 8 by it, keeping step 4 onward (§6.1, p. 14). Theorem 2 states security in the augmented semi-honest model, defined in §2.1 (p. 4) and Appendix A (pp. 23-24), with a proof sketch (pp. 14-15); the authors explain that a corrupt party can compute the share it would have held for an item it lacks, which rules out standard semi-honest security (§6.1, p. 15).

limitations: not secure in the standard semi-honest model; §2.3 of PSI-PAPER-2024-VCE (p. 3) notes that augmented semi-honest security does not imply semi-honest security
unlike the semi-honest protocol, its cost does not decrease with a smaller tolerated coalition, as PSI-PAPER-2021-NTY observes (§1.1.1, p. 1)
qualifiers: augmented semi-honest model: the adversary may change the corrupted parties' inputs once, then runs the protocol honestly (§2.1, p. 4; Definition 3, p. 24)
Theorem 2 is given with a proof sketch that assumes the underlying OPRF protocol is secure (pp. 14-15)
the security argument for the zero-sharing considers a coalition of \( t_c < \ell - 1 \) corrupt parties (§6.1, p. 14); Table 1 (p. 3) lists corruption threshold \( \ell - 1 \) for both variants
the reported 22 seconds uses the table-based OPPRF, which models a hash function as a random oracle (Figure 6, p. 8; §7.1, pp. 17-18)

metadata.statement: In the multiparty PSI protocol with conditional zero-sharing, the pairwise OPPRF phase is replaced by unconditional zero-sharing: each pair of parties exchanges a PRF seed once, and each party derives its share of zero for any index as the XOR of PRF values under its \( \ell - 1 \) seeds. The parties then run only the conditional-reconstruction phase, in which each party programs an OPPRF to the leader. The modified protocol is secure in the augmented semi-honest model, where corrupt parties may change their inputs before running the protocol honestly, and not in the standard semi-honest model; per-client communication becomes \( O(n \lambda) \) bits against \( O(n t_c \lambda) \) for the semi-honest protocol.
metadata.title: Augmented semi-honest multiparty PSI with per-client communication \( O(n \lambda) \), by replacing the pairwise OPPRF zero-sharing phase with zero-sharing from pairwise PRF seeds

sections.content: Augmented semi-honest multiparty PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Each party \( P_i \) picks a random seed \( r_{i,j} \) for every \( j > i \) and sends it to \( P_j \); on index ind, \( P_i \) computes \( S_i(\mathrm{ind}) \) as the XOR of \( F(r_{j,i}, \mathrm{ind}) \) over \( j < i \) and \( F(r_{i,j}, \mathrm{ind}) \) over \( j > i \), so every term appears twice across all parties and the shares XOR to zero (Figure 9, p. 14). Used as the mapping \( S_i \) of Figure 8, these shares feed directly into the reconstruction phase with the leader (§6.1, p. 14). Correctness is unchanged: a party without x does not program its OPPRF at x, so the leader receives a random value (§6.1, p. 14). In the proof sketch, a simulator for a coalition that contains the leader submits the leader's set as every corrupt party's input, which is the extra power the augmented model grants (p. 14).

historical_context.narrative: An oblivious PRF lets a receiver learn PRF values on inputs of its choice while the sender keeps the key, and the batched construction of Kolesnikov, Kumaresan, Rosulek, and Trieu had made such instances cost a few hundred bits each. This paper asked for more: the sender should be able to fix the outputs on chosen inputs, and the receiver should not learn whether its query hit one of them. The authors obtained this with a public hint that corrects the OPRF output on the programmed points, stored as an interpolated polynomial, a garbled Bloom filter, or a small table indexed through a random oracle, and they scaled it to many points and queries by hashing items into bins. A party could now pass a secret value to another party only when both hold the same item.
historical_context.prior_boundary: An oblivious PRF gives the sender a key and the receiver PRF values on its chosen inputs (§3.1, p. 4), and the batched OPRF of Kolesnikov, Kumaresan, Rosulek, and Trieu produces many instances from OT extension at roughly 500 bits of communication and a few symmetric-key operations each (§3.1, pp. 4-5). The paper presents programmability, the sender fixing outputs on chosen points without the receiver learning whether its query was programmed, as a new notion (§1.3, p. 3; §3.1, p. 5).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The abstract calls the OPPRF the technical core of the multiparty PSI protocol and suggests it may be of independent interest (abstract, p. 1). In the evaluation the table-based OPPRF gives the fastest PSI and the polynomial hint with separate bins the lowest communication for practical sizes (Table 3, p. 18; §7.1, pp. 17-18).
historical_context.technical_delta: The programmable PRF adds a public hint to the syntax, with \( (n, Q) \)-security defined by an indistinguishability experiment (§3.1, pp. 5-6), and the OPPRF functionality hands the hint to the receiver (Figure 3, p. 5). The hint masks programmed values with OPRF outputs and is stored as a polynomial (Figure 4, p. 7), a garbled Bloom filter (Figure 5, p. 8), or a random-oracle-indexed table for \( Q = 1 \) (Figure 6, p. 8). Bins built with stash-free cuckoo hashing for the receiver and simple hashing for the sender scale it to large \( n \) and \( Q \) (§4, pp. 9-10; Figure 7, p. 11; Table 2, p. 10).

limitations: no security against malicious senders or receivers is claimed (§2.1, p. 4)
no theorem covers the OPPRF constructions or the hashing extension; their security is argued in prose (§§3.2-3.4, pp. 6-9; §4, p. 10)
the polynomial hint combined over all bins grows quadratically in the number of points, \( O(n^2) \), and did not finish within an hour at \( 2^{16} \) items (Table 3, p. 18)
qualifiers: semi-honest sender and receiver; the OPPRF protocols are given in the OPRF-hybrid model, and simulation of the polynomial protocol is called trivial (§3.2, p. 6)
the table-based construction supports one query (\( Q = 1 \)) and models H as a random oracle (Figure 6, p. 8; §3.4, pp. 8-9)
built on the KKRT OPRF, whose instances have related keys and leak slightly more than the PRF value; the paper uses cleaner definitions and says the relaxations can be incorporated (§3.1, p. 5)
the hashing extension programs the same point in several bins and relies on the receiver never querying two bins on the same item (§4, Caveats, p. 10)
hashing parameters, including the stash-free scheme, were determined empirically with failure probability below \( 2^{-30} \) or \( 2^{-40} \) (§4, p. 9; Table 2, p. 10; Appendix B, pp. 24-25)

metadata.statement: A programmable PRF takes a set of \( n \) points at key generation and outputs a key and a public hint; it is \( (n, Q) \)-secure if the hint and \( Q \) outputs do not reveal which points were programmed when the programmed values are random. The OPPRF functionality gives the sender the key and hint and gives the receiver the hint and the PRF values on its \( Q \) queries. From an OPRF, three semi-honest OPPRFs are built: an interpolated polynomial hint of \( n \) values with \( O(n^2) \) interpolation, a garbled Bloom filter hint of about \( 60n \) entries with \( O(n) \) insertion, and, for a single query, a table of at most \( 2n \) entries indexed through a random oracle. Receiver-side cuckoo hashing and sender-side simple hashing extend single-query OPPRFs to many points and queries with one single-query instance per bin.
metadata.title: Oblivious programmable PRF: sender-programmed OPRF outputs that the receiver cannot tell apart from unprogrammed ones, from an OPRF plus a hint, semi-honest

sections.content: Oblivious programmable PRF
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: For a programmable PRF built from a PRF F, the sender masks each programmed value \( y_i \) with \( F(k, x_i) \) and publishes the masked points in a structure that the receiver can evaluate anywhere: the coefficients of an interpolated polynomial \( P \), so that the output on a query z is \( F(k, z) \oplus P(z) \) (§3.2, p. 6); a garbled Bloom filter (§3.3, pp. 6-7); or, for one query, a table T of size the next power of two above \( n \) together with a nonce v chosen so that the positions \( H(F(k, x_i) \| v) \) are distinct (§3.4, pp. 7-9). When the \( y_i \) are random the hint is uniform, so it hides which points were programmed (§§3.2-3.4). To handle many queries the receiver cuckoo-hashes its items into bins with three primary and two supplementary hash functions and no stash, the sender maps every item under all five functions, and the parties run one single-query OPPRF per bin (§4, pp. 9-10; Figure 7, p. 11). The polynomial and garbled Bloom filter constructions use no random oracle in their description; the table construction models H as a random oracle (Figure 6, p. 8).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-COMP-CORR-OTEXT: the OPPRF constructions are instantiated with the KKRT OPRF, which the paper describes as based on OT extension with a constant number of base-OT public-key operations (§3.1, p. 4).

historical_context.narrative: Multiparty PSI had been built from oblivious polynomial evaluation under homomorphic encryption or from bilinear groups, so every item cost public-key operations, and no protocol had been implemented. Kolesnikov, Matania, Pinkas, Rosulek, and Trieu replaced that machinery with oblivious programmable PRFs running on OT extension. Every party splits zero into shares for each of its items and lets another party receive its share only if that party holds the same item; a designated leader then collects, again through programmable PRFs, one combined value per party and keeps the items whose values cancel. Security holds against any number of colluding semi-honest parties, and a smaller tolerated coalition means fewer pairwise instances. Their implementation intersected million-item sets among five parties in about a minute.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Multiparty PSI protocols were built from oblivious polynomial evaluation with additively homomorphic encryption or from bilinear groups. Kissner and Song have computation and communication quadratic in the set size and the number of parties; Cheon, Jarecki, and Seo reach quasi-linear complexity but assume at most \( n/2 \) corrupted parties; Hazay and Venkitasubramaniam need a linear number of exponentiations in the input sets and give no implementation (§1.2, p. 2; Table 1, p. 3).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: Public-key operations no longer depend on the set size (§1.2, p. 2; Table 1, p. 3), and the authors call their implementation the first of a multiparty PSI protocol (abstract, p. 1). It computes PSI of \( 2^{20} \) items among 5 parties in 72 seconds and among 15 parties in about 5 minutes on a LAN, with cost linear in the number of parties (abstract, p. 1; §7.2, p. 20; Figure 11, p. 19).
historical_context.technical_delta: Conditional zero-sharing uses an OPPRF between every pair of parties so that a party receives another's share of zero for an item only if it holds the item (§5.1, p. 11); conditional reconstruction uses one OPPRF from each party to the leader, which outputs items whose values XOR to zero (§5.2, p. 12; Figure 8, p. 12). Theorem 1 gives security against any number of colluding semi-honest parties (p. 12), outputs of \( \lambda + \log_2 n \) bits bound false positives by \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (§5.3, p. 12), and a bound \( t_c \) on corruptions limits sharing to \( t_c + 1 \) parties (§5.3, p. 13).

limitations: no security against malicious parties is claimed (§1, p. 1; §2.1, p. 4)
communication \( O(n t_c \lambda) \) per client grows with the tolerated coalition and reaches gigabytes for \( n = 2^{20} \) (§7.2, p. 20; Table 5, p. 19)
measurements are for one machine with simulated LAN and WAN links and 128-bit items (§7, p. 17)
qualifiers: semi-honest parties, any number of whom may be corrupt and collude (Theorem 1, p. 12)
proved with an ideal OPPRF functionality (Figure 8, p. 12); the evaluated instantiation uses the table-based OPPRF, which models a hash function as a random oracle (Figure 6, p. 8; §7.2, p. 18)
exponentiation counts are for an offline preprocessing phase (Table 1, p. 3)

the generalization to at most \( t_c \) corrupt parties has each party \( P_i \) deal shares only to \( P_{i+1}, \ldots, P_{i+t_c+1} \) (§5.3, p. 13); in the evaluation each party runs OPPRFs with \( \min\{t_c + 1, \ell - 1\} \) others, so \( t_c = \ell - 1 \) and \( t_c = \ell - 2 \) cost the same (§7.2, p. 20)
the leader P1 announces the intersection (Figure 8, step 5, p. 12); the ideal functionality gives it to all parties (Figure 1, p. 5)

metadata.statement: For \( \ell \) parties with \( n \) items each, every party deals XOR-shares of zero for each of its items and, through a pairwise multi-query OPPRF, lets each other party obtain its share only for items both hold (conditional zero-sharing); each party then programs an OPPRF to the leader P1 with the XOR of the shares it holds per item, and P1 announces the items of its set whose values XOR to zero (conditional reconstruction). With an ideal OPPRF functionality the protocol is secure in the semi-honest model against any number of corrupt, colluding parties, and to tolerate at most \( t_c \) corruptions each party deals shares only to the next \( t_c + 1 \) parties. Exponentiations are confined to an offline phase, \( O(\ell \kappa) \) for the leader and \( O(t_c \kappa) \) per client, and communication is \( O(\ell n \lambda) \) bits for the leader and \( O(n t_c \lambda) \) bits per client.
metadata.title: Multiparty PSI secure against any number of colluding semi-honest parties with public-key operations independent of set size, via conditional zero-sharing and reconstruction over OPPRFs

sections.content: Multiparty PSI from conditional zero-sharing
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Each party \( P_i \) chooses, for each of its items x, random strings \( s^{i,1}, \ldots, s^{i,\ell} \) that XOR to zero and runs a multi-query OPPRF with every other party \( P_j \) as sender programmed on \( (x, s^{i,j}) \); \( P_j \) queries its own set (Figure 8, steps 1-2, p. 12). Each party XORs its own share with the outputs it received into a value \( S_i(x) \), and in the second phase every \( P_i \) with \( i > 1 \) programs an OPPRF to P1 on \( (x, S_i(x)) \); P1 announces its items x with \( S_1(x) \) equal to the XOR of the received outputs (steps 3-5, p. 12). If some party lacks x, at least one term is pseudorandom and x is excluded except with probability \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (§5.3, p. 12). The proof of Theorem 1 argues that a party without x leaves the honest parties' values for x independent of the coalition's view, and that programming an OPPRF on a random value is indistinguishable from not programming it (pp. 12-13). All OPPRF instances of a phase run in parallel, so the protocol has a constant number of rounds (§5.3, p. 13).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-COMP-CORR-OTEXT: every OPPRF instance runs on the KKRT OPRF, which the paper describes as based on OT extension (§3.1, p. 4).

historical_context.narrative: Dual execution forces the sender to bind herself to her items by obtaining encodings of them, which works but costs encoding work and lets a cheating sender spread up to a few times \( n \) candidate items over the bins. Rindal and Rosulek noted that those encodings act as commitments and asked what happens if an ordinary commitment takes their place. The sender commits to each item and attaches openings hidden under the receiver's encodings, together with short tags so the receiver knows which opening to try. Security needs only an extractable, hiding commitment, which a hash function provides in the random oracle model. The variant computes less and sends more, so it was the faster of the two on a fast local network and the slower one over a wide-area link.
historical_context.prior_boundary: In the dual-execution protocol of the same paper, Alice's encodings under Bob's instances act as commitments to her items, which bounds her effective set only by \( m\mu \) items (§5.3, pp. 8-9; §6.3, p. 15), and Alice must act as encoding receiver for every bin position (Figure 4, p. 12).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The commitment-based approach needs less computation and more communication, making it faster in LAN (§5.3, p. 10): 12.6 s against 18 s for dual execution at \( n = 2^{20} \) on one thread, but 255 s against 106 s in WAN (Figure 6, p. 19), with 1,322 MB against 1,092 MB of communication (Figure 8, p. 20); it also restricts Alice to exactly \( n \) items (§6.5, p. 17).
historical_context.technical_delta: Alice commits with a standard non-interactive commitment and sends decommitments masked under Bob's encodings (§5.3, p. 9); PRF-derived tags let Bob find the right decommitment to try without \( O(n^2) \) trial openings (§6.4, pp. 15-16; Figure 9, p. 27). Security needs straight-line extraction and standalone hiding, not equivocation (Appendix A, Definition 4, p. 26; Theorem 3, p. 16).

limitations: communication is higher than dual execution because \( O(n \log n) \) tag-decommitment pairs are sent (§7.1, p. 21)

the paper states the exact bound only for Alice; Bob still acts as encoding receiver for all \( m\mu \) bin positions and the simulator extracts his set from those inputs, as in the dual-execution protocol where this gives up to \( m\mu \) items (Figure 9, step 3, p. 27; §6.5, p. 16; §6.3, p. 15)
Theorem 3 is supported by simulator descriptions without hybrids (§6.5, pp. 16-17)
qualifiers: UC security in the \( F_{\mathrm{encode}} \)-hybrid model with a commitment satisfying Definition 4 (Theorem 3, p. 16); only Bob receives output (Figure 1, p. 4)
Alice's set is restricted to exactly \( n \) items, unlike the dual-execution protocol (§6.5, p. 17)
the standard model needs a UC-secure non-interactive commitment, which the authors did not implement because of its communication (Appendix A, p. 26; §7, p. 18)
uses the same simple hashing and phasing as the dual-execution protocol (§6.4, p. 16; Figure 9, step 2, p. 27)

metadata.statement: Instead of acting as encoding receiver, Alice sends for each item a commitment \( \mathrm{Comm}(x; r_x) \) and, for each position of the item's bin, a tag and the decommitment \( r_x \) masked under two PRF values derived from her encoding under Bob's instance; Bob builds a hash table from the tags of his own encodings and outputs his item when the unmasked value opens the commitment. With an extractable and hiding commitment, such as \( H(x \| r) \) in the non-programmable random oracle model, the protocol UC-realizes PSI with output to Bob against malicious adversaries in the \( F_{\mathrm{encode}} \)-hybrid model at cost \( O(Cn \log n) \), \( C \) the cost of one oblivious encoding, and restricts Alice to exactly \( n \) items.
metadata.title: Encode-commit malicious PSI with commitments to the sender's items and decommitments masked under oblivious encodings, trading communication for computation and fixing the sender's set size, UC

sections.content: Encode-commit malicious PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Bob acts as encoding receiver for every bin position and stores \( \llbracket y' \rrbracket^{\mathrm{tag}}_{b,i} = \mathrm{PRF}(\llbracket y' \rrbracket^{A}_{b,i}, \mathrm{tag}) \) together with \( \llbracket y' \rrbracket^{\mathrm{enc}}_{b,i} \), for bin b and position \( i \), in a hash table. For each item x, in random order, Alice sends \( \mathrm{Comm}(x; r_x) \) and, for \( j = 1, \ldots, \mu \), the pair \( \llbracket x' \rrbracket^{\mathrm{tag}}_{b,j} \| (\llbracket x' \rrbracket^{\mathrm{enc}}_{b,j} \oplus r_x) \); Bob looks up each tag and adds y to the output if the recovered value opens the commitment to y (Figure 9, p. 27). The simulator extracts Alice's items from her commitments in extraction mode and Bob's from his \( F_{\mathrm{encode}} \) inputs (§6.5, pp. 16-17).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: None. The commitment scheme \( H(x \| r) \) and the Orrù-Orsini-Scholl OT extension have no record in any topic.

historical_context.narrative: By 2017 the fastest semi-honest PSI protocols all followed one pattern: hash items into bins, let one party learn an oblivious encoding of its item in each bin, and compare encodings. Making this pattern resist a cheating sender had failed, partly because the sender's encoding cannot be inverted to extract its input and partly because cuckoo hashing makes item placement depend on the whole set. Rindal and Rosulek adapted dual execution: each party encodes its own items under the other's keys, and only a combination of both encodings is compared, so neither side can count an item it never encoded. Simple hashing and a proof that phasing remains secure complete the protocol. It needs only symmetric-key operations, can avoid random oracles, and ran far faster than the previous malicious protocols in their experiments.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The OT-based paradigm of Pinkas, Schneider, and Zohner, fastest against semi-honest adversaries, had a variant secure only against a malicious Alice (§1.1, p. 2); three features block malicious security: the encoding map is not invertible for extraction, cuckoo-hashing placement depends on Bob's whole set, and Alice may use different sets in different instances (§3.2, p. 5). The fastest malicious protocol, Rindal-Rosulek's Bloom-filter protocol, appears to depend inherently on the random oracle model (§1.1, p. 2; §1.2, p. 3).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The paper presents this as the first fully malicious variant of the fastest semi-honest paradigm (§1.2, p. 3); the dual-execution random-oracle protocol takes 18 s in LAN and 106 s in WAN for \( n = 2^{20} \) on one thread, against 148 s and 1,080 s for the Bloom-filter protocol (Figure 6, p. 19), and a standard-model instantiation is faster than that protocol in LAN (§7.1, p. 20).
historical_context.technical_delta: Inspired by Mohassel-Franklin dual execution, each party is encoding receiver once, and the XOR of the two one-sided encodings forms a common encoding that a party can compute only for values it encoded (§5.1, pp. 7-8; Theorem 1, p. 8). Simple hashing replaces cuckoo hashing, phasing is shown secure against malicious adversaries, and aggregating Alice's encodings across bins removes dummy encodings (§6.1-6.2, pp. 10-12; Figure 4, p. 12; Theorem 2, p. 13).

limitations: two-party output is not supported: a malicious Bob could make Alice learn \( X \cap Y' \) for any \( Y' \subseteq Y \) (§6.7, pp. 17-18)
the protocol does not strictly enforce the size of a corrupt party's set (Figure 1, p. 4; §6.3, p. 15)

the protocols carry a \( \log n \) factor more communication and computation than the semi-honest protocol of Kolesnikov et al., which the paper reports as a 3.3-4 times running-time gap in LAN for its fastest variant and 25 times in WAN (§7.1, p. 22)
qualifiers: UC security in the \( F_{\mathrm{encode}} \)-hybrid model (Theorem 2, p. 13); only Bob receives output (Figure 1, p. 4)
a corrupt party may input up to \( n' = m\mu \) items, \( n' < 4n \) for \( \lambda = 40 \), \( n = 2^{20} \), \( \mu = 68 \) (§6.3, p. 15)
the programmable-random-oracle instantiation of \( F_{\mathrm{encode}} \) is the 1-out-of-N OT extension of Orrù, Orsini, and Scholl, at about three semi-honest 1-out-of-2 OTs per encoding (§4, p. 6)
the standard-model instantiation uses \( \sigma \) chosen-message OTs and a PRF per encoding, so its cost grows with the item length, as \( O(\sigma) \) per encoding (§4, pp. 6-7)
bins are padded to \( \mu \) positions and each bin position uses its own \( F_{\mathrm{encode}} \) session (§6.6, p. 17)

metadata.statement: Both parties act as receiver of an oblivious encoding for every position of every bin, so each obtains one-sided encodings of its own items; for each of her items Alice sends the \( \mu \) common encodings that combine her encoding under Bob's instance with her encodings under Alice's instances for the positions of the item's bin, and Bob outputs his items whose own common encodings appear. With simple hashing into \( m = O(n / \log n) \) bins of \( \mu = O(\log n) \) positions, phasing to shorten items, and Alice's encodings aggregated across bins, the protocol UC-realizes PSI with output to Bob against malicious adversaries in the \( F_{\mathrm{encode}} \)-hybrid model at cost \( O(Cn \log n) \), where \( C \approx \kappa \) is the cost of one oblivious encoding. \( F_{\mathrm{encode}} \) is realized in the programmable random oracle model by 1-out-of-N OT extension, or in the standard model by \( \sigma \) oblivious transfers per encoding; a corrupt party's set may hold up to \( m\mu \) items, fewer than \( 4n \) for \( n = 2^{20} \).
metadata.title: Malicious security for OT-based PSI in the Pinkas-Schneider-Zohner paradigm by dual execution of oblivious encodings, with simple hashing and phasing, UC in the oblivious-encoding hybrid model

sections.content: Dual-execution malicious PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: For each bin b and position \( i \), Alice encodes her item x' under the instance \( (B, b, i) \), and Bob encodes his item y' under \( (A, b, i) \). For each of her items, Alice sends \( \llbracket x' \rrbracket^{A}_{b,j} \oplus \llbracket x' \rrbracket^{B}_{b,i} \) for \( j = 1, \ldots, \mu \), in random order across all bins; Bob outputs y if \( \llbracket y' \rrbracket^{A}_{b,i} \oplus \llbracket y' \rrbracket^{B}_{b,j} \) lies in this set for some j (Figure 4, p. 12). Encodings have \( \lambda + 2\log(n\mu) \) bits so that spurious matches occur with probability at most \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (§6.2, p. 12). The simulator extracts each party's candidate set from its \( F_{\mathrm{encode}} \) inputs and, for a corrupt Alice, keeps the candidates whose common encodings appear in her message (Theorem 2 proof, pp. 13-15).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: Dual execution of Mohassel and Franklin (PKC 2006), the Orrù-Orsini-Scholl 1-out-of-N OT extension, and the Keller-Orsini-Scholl actively secure OT extension used in the standard-model instantiation (§4, pp. 6-7; §7, p. 18) have no record in any topic. MPC-CONTRIB-2003-IKNP-OTEXT: IKNP is cited among the OT-extension protocols on which the paradigm relies (§1.1, p. 2); the paper's instantiations use the later protocols named above.

historical_context.narrative: Returning data attached to matching items, such as a public key for each contact found on a messaging service, was easy in OPRF-based PSI: encrypt each label under its item's PRF value and ship them all. But shipping them all costs communication linear in the server's set, \( O(n_X) \), and the keyword-search protocol of Freedman, Ishai, Pinkas, and Reingold, which used an interpolating polynomial, was linear as well. Chen, Huang, Laine, and Rindal let the server evaluate, next to the homomorphic intersection polynomial, a second polynomial that interpolates the labels of each bin. A match decrypts to its label, a miss to a random value, and the cost stays logarithmic in the server's set, \( O(\sigma \log n_X + \sigma_{\mathrm{L}}) \) per client item for \( \sigma_{\mathrm{L}} \)-bit labels. The result is a batched symmetric PIR by keywords.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Existing PSI protocols could return labels by encrypting each label under its item's OPRF value, but their communication is linear in the sender's set (§1.3, p. 3). The single-server PIR by keywords of Freedman, Ishai, Pinkas, and Reingold uses the same interpolation polynomial under additively homomorphic encryption with communication \( n_X \sigma_{\mathrm{L}} \) for \( \sigma_{\mathrm{L}} \)-bit labels, and the Diffie-Hellman labeled PSI of Jarecki and Liu is also linear in the larger set (§1.5, p. 5).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The paper notes that labeled PSI with a single receiver item is single-server symmetric PIR by keywords, so the protocol is a batched keyword PIR (§1.1, p. 2; §1.5, p. 5). Replacing the multi-query keyword retrieval of the Pung messaging system, for \( 2^{20} \) messages of 288 bytes and 256 retrievals, it reports 4.6 s server online time and 17.6 MB against 20.5 s and 120 MB for multi-query SealPIR (§8.4, p. 21; Figure 6, p. 22).
historical_context.technical_delta: For each bin the sender interpolates H with \( H(x_i) = v_i \) and evaluates \( G = H + rF \), where F is the randomized intersection polynomial, so \( G(y) \) is the label on a match and uniformly random otherwise; longer labels are split into chunks (§5.1, pp. 11-12). With OPRF pre-processing the sender interpolates labels padded with the second half of each item's OPRF output, which needs no randomization and no help from the FHE scheme to hide non-matching labels (§5.2, p. 12; Figures 1-2, pp. 13-14).

limitations: the security theorems (Theorems 1-2, pp. 15-16) are stated for the unlabeled PSI functionality of Figure 3 (p. 15); no theorem covers the labeled functionality, which PSI-PAPER-2021-CONG later notes and sketches (§4.2, p. 14 of that paper)
Figure 6 (p. 22) does not state thread counts for this comparison
qualifiers: items and labels are first assumed to lie in one finite field; longer labels are split into item-size chunks and the sender repeats the evaluation per chunk (§5.1, p. 11)
complexity figures are for the CLR17-compatible variant of §5.1, with items hashed to \( \sigma = \lambda + \log n_X + \log n_Y \) bits (§5.1, p. 12)

offline, the sender interpolates polynomials of degree about \( n_X/(m\alpha) \) per bin, \( O(n_X^2/(m\alpha)) \cdot \sigma_{\mathrm{L}}/\sigma \) operations in total, \( m \) the number of bins and \( \alpha \) the number of partitions (§5.1, p. 12)
in the OPRF-optimized variant the one-time pad can be extended to longer labels with a PRG (§5.2, footnote 7, p. 12)
metadata.statement: In labeled PSI the sender holds a label \( v_i \) of \( \sigma_{\mathrm{L}} \) bits for each item \( x_i \) and the receiver learns the labels of the items in the intersection; if, besides the intersection polynomial, the sender homomorphically evaluates on each receiver bin a polynomial that interpolates the labels of the sender's bin (as \( G = H + rF \), or, after OPRF pre-processing, interpolating labels one-time-padded with a second part of each item's OPRF output), the receiver obtains the label exactly for matching items, with communication \( O(n_Y \log n_X \, \sigma + n_Y \sigma_{\mathrm{L}}) \) and sender online computation \( O(n_X \sigma_{\mathrm{L}}) \), a factor \( \sigma_{\mathrm{L}}/\sigma \) above unlabeled PSI.
metadata.title: Labeled PSI with communication sublinear in the sender's set, \( O(n_Y \log n_X \, \sigma + n_Y \sigma_{\mathrm{L}}) \) for \( \sigma_{\mathrm{L}} \)-bit labels, from homomorphically evaluated label-interpolation polynomials

sections.content: Labeled PSI from FHE
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Without OPRF pre-processing the sender evaluates, for a receiver item y in a bin, both \( F(y) = r^* \prod(x - y) \) over the bin and \( G(y) = H(y) + rF(y) \) with H the interpolation of the bin's labels; the receiver decrypts \( (F(y), G(y)) \), which is \( (0, v_i) \) when \( y = x_i \) and uniformly random in \( F^* \times F \) otherwise (§5.1, p. 11). With OPRF pre-processing the sender computes \( (x'_i, x''_i) = \mathrm{OPRF}_k(x_i) \), uses \( x'_i \) as the item and \( v'_i = v_i + x''_i \) as the label, and interpolates G with \( G(x'_i) = v'_i \) (§5.2, p. 12). The full protocol batches the label polynomials like the intersection polynomials and returns their evaluations on the receiver's encrypted powers (Figure 1, step 5(b)ii, p. 13; Figure 2, steps 8-9, p. 14).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: PIR-PAPER-2018-SEALPIR: the labeled-PSI experiment replaces the multi-query PIR by keywords of the Pung system, built on the multi-query SealPIR of Angel, Chen, Laine, and Setty, and compares with it (§8, p. 18; §8.4, p. 21; Figure 6, p. 22). PIR by keywords (Chor, Gilboa, and Naor, 1997), to which the paper relates labeled PSI, has no record in any topic (§1.1, p. 2; §1.5, p. 5).

historical_context.narrative: Homomorphic PSI with a small client set gave a malicious server a lot of room: it held the client's encrypted items and could simply return encryptions of zero, making the client believe that its whole set was in the intersection. Full simulation against such a server looked out of reach, because extracting the server's set seemed to need communication linear in it, \( \Omega(n_X) \). Chen, Huang, Laine, and Rindal instead asked the server to prove each match by returning, as a label, a hash of the item's oblivious PRF value. Under the assumption that leveled homomorphic encryption cannot evaluate a deep hash on encrypted data, the server must actually know an item to produce its label, so it can only remove matches as a function of the client's other items, not invent them.
historical_context.prior_boundary: In the protocol of Chen, Laine, and Rindal, and in the semi-honest version of this paper, a sender can return encryptions of zero and make the receiver output its full set (§1.3, p. 3; §7.2, p. 16). With OPRF pre-processing the paper proves only privacy against a malicious sender, without input independence or output correctness (Theorem 2, p. 16), and it names two obstacles to full simulation: communication sublinear in the sender's set, \( o(n_X) \), rules out extracting that set by zero-knowledge proofs, and the sender holds the encrypted receiver set and may evaluate any circuit on it (§7.2, p. 16).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: A malicious sender can no longer add receiver items it does not hold; it can only drop matches depending on the receiver's other items, which the authors call significantly less leakage than in the earlier protocol (§7.3, pp. 17-18). Labeled PSI is what makes this possible, and the variant saves work by not evaluating the intersection polynomial (§5.2, p. 12).
historical_context.technical_delta: The label of each processed item \( x' \) is set to \( H(x') \), the receiver accepts y only if the decrypted label at its bin equals \( H(y') \), the symmetric polynomial is neither evaluated nor sent, and the sender proves that one OPRF key was used (Figure 8, p. 25). Definition 1 (p. 17) states the F-limited property, and Theorem 3 (p. 25) proves that the protocol realizes the leaky functionality of Figure 7 (p. 25): the simulator extracts the OPRF key from the proof, takes the sender's set from its random-oracle queries, and reads the leakage function off the sender's code (pp. 25-26).

limitations: this is not full simulation-based security against a malicious sender: the receiver's output may depend on items in \( Y \setminus X \) through the sender-chosen leakage function (§7.3, p. 17)

if the sender reuses its pre-processing with many receivers and picks the hash functions, cuckoo-hashing failures can leak one bit of the receiver's set; sampling hash functions from a public reference string is suggested as a countermeasure (§7.3, p. 18)
no measurement of this variant is reported
qualifiers: the H-limited property is an assumption about the leveled FHE scheme and its fixed parameters, supported by a heuristic argument and experiments in which noise overflows after a few extra multiplications, not by a reduction (§7.3, p. 17)
the depth of H can be increased by iterating the hash after the FHE parameters are fixed (§7.3, p. 17)
the sender is not committed to its set and may use any subset of it in each execution (§7.3, p. 17)

the theorem first assumes the sender does not reuse pre-processing across receivers; the zero-knowledge proof of one OPRF key may be replaced by aborting on degenerate OPRF answers, with extra cases in the leakage function (§7.3, p. 17; remarks, p. 26)
simulation against a malicious sender is non-black-box (Theorem 3, p. 25)

source_locator.primary_source: §1.3 (pp. 3-4); §5.2 (p. 12); §7.2 (p. 16); §7.3 and Definition 1 (pp. 17-18); Appendix A, Figures 7-8, and Theorem 3 (pp. 25-26). IACR ePrint 2018/787, PDF dated 2018-08-27.

metadata.statement: If the receiver accepts an item y only when the sender returns, as its label, an encryption of \( H(\mathrm{OPRF}_k(y)) \) for a hash function H modeled as a random oracle, the intersection polynomial is no longer returned, and the sender proves in zero knowledge that all OPRF answers use one key, then, assuming One-More-Gap-Diffie-Hellman and a semantically secure leveled FHE scheme that is H-limited (no efficient sender can compute an encryption of \( H(z) \) from encryptions of the fixed powers of z), the protocol securely computes, with non-black-box simulation in the random oracle model, a leaky PSI functionality that gives the receiver \( X \cap Y \cap \mathrm{leakage}(Y) \) for a leakage function chosen by a malicious sender whose set may have polynomial size.
metadata.title: Malicious-sender FHE-based unbalanced PSI with bounded leakage \( X \cap Y \cap \mathrm{leakage}(Y) \), from hash-valued labels and an H-limited leveled FHE assumption

sections.content: Leaky security against a malicious sender
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Figure 8 (p. 25) runs steps 1-7 of the labeled protocol with labels \( H(x') \) and a zero-knowledge proof of one OPRF key, evaluates and returns only the label polynomials, and lets the receiver output y when the decrypted label at \( y' \)'s cuckoo position equals \( H(y') \). The ideal functionality of Figure 7 (p. 25) takes the sender's set and a leakage function and outputs \( X \cap Y \cap \mathrm{leakage}(Y) \). In the proof, a sender that produced a correct label for an item outside its extracted set would contradict the H-limited property, because outputs of the OPRF and the random oracle on such items are uniform (pp. 25-26).

historical_context.narrative: Homomorphic PSI with a small client set had been demonstrated only on 32-bit strings, because the plaintext modulus had to be as large as an item, and a modulus of 80 bits, the length needed for hashed items of any length, inflated every parameter and cost. Chen, Huang, Laine, and Rindal used the more general form of SIMD packing in which each slot is an extension field with \( p^d \) elements, so a long item occupies one slot while the modulus stays small. They encode with only the Chinese remainder map, skipping the slot isomorphisms that the protocol never needs, and show that wider slots trade a slightly larger query for less server computation. Arbitrary-length items became practical at roughly the cost of the earlier 32-bit runs.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Chen, Laine, and Rindal set the plaintext modulus to about \( 2^{\sigma} \) for \( \sigma \)-bit items, so their communication grows linearly and computation quadratically with \( \sigma \), as \( O(\sigma) \) and \( O(\sigma^2) \), and a larger plaintext prime \( p \) and ciphertext modulus \( q \) force a larger ring dimension that can leave slots unused (§3, p. 7). Their examples compare 22-bit items extended to 32 bits by permutation-based hashing (§8.3, p. 21), while hashing arbitrary items to \( \lambda + \log n_X + \log n_Y \) bits needs \( p \) of about 80 bits, which the authors say hurts that protocol severely (§3, p. 8).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: With this encoding the protocol compares 80-bit items inside FHE; for \( 2^{24} \) sender items and 5535 receiver items the paper reports 16 MB and 22 s online against 20 MB and 40 s for the 32-bit protocol (§8.3, p. 21; Figure 5, p. 22). The lazy encoder ran 2.2 to 21.8 times faster than FFT-based encoding for d between 8 and 64 (Table 1, p. 9). The earlier paper had left efficient support for long items to future work (PSI-PAPER-2017-CLR, §6.1, p. 14).
historical_context.technical_delta: For a prime \( p \), \( m \) the ring dimension, and \( d \) the degree of the irreducible factors of \( x^m + 1 \) modulo \( p \), the plaintext ring splits into \( m/d \) copies of \( \mathbb{F}_{p^d} \), so one slot holds a \( d \cdot \log p \)-bit item (§3, p. 8). The encoder applies only the CRT map \( \phi \) and omits the field isomorphisms \( \psi \), which are needed only to permute slots (§3.2, p. 8). The cost analysis gives query size growing with \( \log d \) and online computation \( \Theta(1/d) \), with only logarithmic dependence on \( m \) (§3.1, pp. 7-8).

limitations: the trade-off analysis of §3.1 is heuristic, with constants hidden (§3.1, p. 8)
the reported comparison with the 32-bit protocol also reflects the removal of noise flooding by OPRF pre-processing, so the speedup is not attributable to the encoding alone (§8.3, p. 21)
qualifiers: items are first hashed to \( \lambda + \log n_X + \log n_Y \) bits, about 80 bits for \( \lambda = 40 \) (§3, p. 8; Figure 1, step 1, p. 13)
requires \( p \) prime and \( d \) the smallest positive integer with \( p^d \equiv 1 \bmod 2m \) (§3, p. 8)
the cost model treats \( n_Y \), \( n_X \), \( m \), and the depth \( L \) as constants (§3.1, p. 8)
metadata.statement: Encoding each hashed item into one SIMD slot holding an element of an extension field \( \mathbb{F}_{p^d} \), with \( m/d \) slots per BFV plaintext of ring dimension \( m \) and an encoder that skips the slot-permutation isomorphism, lets FHE-based unbalanced PSI compare items of about 80 bits inside the homomorphic computation, enough for arbitrary-length inputs at 40-bit statistical security, without the plaintext modulus \( p \approx 2^{\sigma} \) that the 32-bit protocol of Chen, Laine, and Rindal would need; larger d increases the query size and reduces the sender's online computation in proportion to \( 1/d \).
metadata.title: Arbitrary-length items in FHE-based unbalanced PSI without a plaintext modulus of the item length, via SIMD slots over extension fields

sections.content: Long items through extension-field SIMD slots
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The BFV plaintext ring \( \mathbb{Z}_p[x]/(x^m + 1) \) is mapped by CRT to the product of the fields \( \mathbb{Z}_p[x]/(F_j(x)) \) and then to \( m/d \) copies of \( \mathbb{F}_{p^d} \) (§3, p. 8). Only the first map is used: items are placed directly in the factor rings, which saves the time and storage of the field isomorphisms (§3.2, p. 8). The full protocol chooses \( p \) and \( d \) with \( d \log_2 p \ge \sigma \) (Figure 1, step 3, p. 13).

sections.content: HE-RESULT-2012-SV-SIMD-CIPHERTEXT-SLOT-PACKING-AND-PARALLEL-RECRYPTION: the general SIMD encoding with slots of flexible width is that of Smart and Vercauteren, cited as [50] (§3, p. 8; §3.2, p. 8). HE-PAPER-2012-FV: BFV as implemented in SEAL (§1.2, p. 2).

historical_context.narrative: The first FHE-based unbalanced PSI protocol protected the server's set only against an honest client, and it did so by flooding reply ciphertexts with noise, padding every bin, and randomizing the evaluated polynomial. Those countermeasures cost depth and parameter size, and a client that tampered with the noise in its own ciphertexts could defeat them. Chen, Huang, Laine, and Rindal moved the protection into a preprocessing step: both sets pass through an oblivious PRF keyed by the server, so the server's non-matching items look random to the client whatever it decrypts. The homomorphic part can then run with smaller parameters, and a simulator reads the client's inputs off its random-oracle queries, which yields security against a malicious client and privacy against a malicious server.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The FHE-based protocol of Chen, Laine, and Rindal was proved secure only against semi-honest parties and protected the sender's set by noise flooding, padding of every bin, and a random multiplier on the evaluated polynomial (§2, pp. 6-7; §4.1, p. 9; §4.2, p. 10). Flooding needs a heuristic noise bound and spare noise room, which rules out small FHE parameters, and a receiver that inserts extra noise into its ciphertexts can defeat it (§4.1, p. 9). The OPRF-based unbalanced protocols of Resende and Aranha and of Kiss et al. send the sender's processed set, so their communication is linear in it, \( O(n_X) \) (§1.4, p. 4; §4.2, p. 9).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors state that dropping noise flooding lets them choose smaller FHE parameters (§1.3, p. 3). For \( 2^{24} \) sender items and 5535 receiver items they report 16 MB and 22 s online, single-threaded, against 20 MB and 40 s for the earlier protocol, while also comparing 80-bit instead of 22-bit items (§8.3, p. 21; Figure 5, p. 22). The sender's Diffie-Hellman pre-processing is non-interactive and reusable across receivers, which suits contact discovery with a large, slowly changing server set (§4.3, p. 10; Figure 4, p. 20).
historical_context.technical_delta: Both sets are first hashed with an OPRF keyed by the sender, either the Diffie-Hellman OPRF of Jarecki and Liu, reusable across receivers, or an OT-based OPRF applied after cuckoo hashing that cannot be reused and keeps the padding (§4.2-4.4, pp. 9-11). The FHE intersection then runs on OPRF outputs without flooding, padding, or multiplier (§4.2, pp. 9-10). A simulator that observes the receiver's random-oracle queries extracts its set, giving one-sided simulation security against a malicious receiver (Theorem 1, p. 15), and the receiver's messages are hidden by OMGDH and FHE semantic security, giving privacy against a malicious sender (Theorem 2, p. 16).

limitations: full simulation-based security against a malicious sender is not achieved; a malicious sender can still make the receiver output its full set (§7.2, p. 16)
with the OT-based OPRF the sender cannot reuse OPRF values across receivers and must still pad its bins (§4.2, p. 10; §4.4, p. 11)
when the sender reuses its pre-processing and chooses the hash functions, a selective cuckoo-hashing failure leaks one bit of the receiver's set (§7.3, p. 18)
qualifiers: one-sided simulation in the sense of Hazay and Lindell against a malicious receiver, with the malicious receiver's set size equal to the honest one (Theorem 1, p. 15)
against a malicious sender only privacy holds: the receiver's messages reveal nothing about its set, but input independence and output correctness are not guaranteed (§7.2, p. 16; Theorem 2, p. 16)
random oracle model: H is a random oracle into the group, \( H' \) an outer hash, and the group must be One-More-Gap-Diffie-Hellman hard (§4.3, p. 10; Theorem 1, p. 15)
the OPRF output is hashed to \( \sigma = \log_2(n_X n_Y) + \lambda \) bits with a random-oracle hash sampled by coin flipping (Figure 1, step 1, p. 13)
simulation extracts the receiver's input only before it learns OPRF values, not when it sends its first message, which the authors state suffices (§4.3, p. 10)

sections.content: OPRF pre-processing for FHE-based unbalanced PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The sender samples a key k and replaces its set by \( X' = \{H(F_k(x))\} \); the receiver obtains \( F_k(y) \) for its items interactively, by sending \( H(y)^\beta \) and unblinding \( (H(y)^{\beta\alpha})^{1/\beta} \) (§4.3, p. 10; Figure 1, step 1, p. 13; Figure 2, step 7a, p. 14). Because \( X' \setminus Y' \) is pseudorandom to the receiver, the number of items in each bin can be public, the evaluated polynomial need not be randomized, and the sender does not flood noise (§4.2, pp. 9-10). In the proof of Theorem 1 the simulator collects the receiver's random-oracle queries to H, extracts its input set when the receiver queries \( H' \), obtains \( X \cap Y^* \) from the ideal functionality, pads it with random values to size \( n_X \), and plays the honest sender (pp. 15-16).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: HE-PAPER-2012-FV: the FHE scheme is BFV as implemented in SEAL v2.3.0-4 (§1.2, p. 2; §8, p. 18). The Diffie-Hellman OPRF of Jarecki and Liu (SCN 2010), which the protocol uses, has no record in any topic.

historical_context.narrative: Hashing makes circuit-based PSI cheaper only if a common item lands where both parties look for it. Earlier constructions guaranteed this by letting one party copy each item into every candidate bin, which forced the bins, and the circuit, to grow. Pinkas, Schneider, Weinert, and Wieder arranged two tables of two subtables each so that one party fills whole sides while the other fills one subtable per side; the two choices always cross in exactly one place. They proved that placing items fails with probability inversely proportional to \( n \) when each table is somewhat more than four times the input size, and set concrete parameters for bins holding two items by running about \( 2^{40} \) simulated insertions. The resulting circuits were several times smaller than both earlier circuit-based approaches.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Hashing-based circuit PSI let one party use cuckoo hashing and the other simple hashing, because two cuckoo-hashing parties may place a common item in different bins; simple hashing forces bins of \( O(\log n / \log\log n) \) items and \( O(n \log n / \log\log n) \) comparisons (§2, p. 7). A related layout with items in two of three tables, by Amossen and Pagh, had no tight stash analysis, and its follow-up needed stashes that grew with \( n \) (§2, pp. 6-7).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: With two-item bins, no stash for Alice, a combined stash for Bob, and permutation-based hashing, the circuit has \( 4 \cdot 2.4n(\sigma - \log_2(2.4n) + 1) + sn(\sigma - 1) \) AND gates, \( s \) the size of Bob's combined stash, 1.8 to 3.8 times fewer than the best earlier circuit for \( n = 2^{12} \) to \( 2^{20} \) and fixed or arbitrary bitlength (§6.2, pp. 22-23; Table 3), and PSI-CAT ran 1.4 to 2.8 times faster than Circuit-Phasing (§6.3, p. 24; Table 4).
historical_context.technical_delta: Alice's items occupy both subtables of one side and Bob's items one subtable on each side, so a common item shares exactly one subtable (§5, pp. 13-14; Figures 2-3). Alice inserts with Algorithm 2 or, with two items per bin, Algorithm 3 (pp. 15-16). An inference-graph argument bounds the probability that an item is bad by \( ((1 + \varepsilon)/\varepsilon)^3 \cdot 2/m^2 \) per item (Theorem 1, p. 32), and also yields the tight space bound for standard cuckoo hashing and a bound of \( k^2 n \) per table for k copies (Appendix A.4, p. 33).

limitations: the \( 2^{-40} \) bound for \( n \ge 2^{13} \) is extrapolated from experiments up to \( n = 2^{12} \) and the observed \( n^{-3} \) dependence, for which Appendix B gives only a heuristic explanation (§6.1, p. 20; Appendix B, pp. 33-34)
the authors see no way to make the construction secure against malicious parties, since item placement depends on the whole input set (§5.4, p. 18)
the PSI-CAT protocol remained 19 to 36 times slower than the specialized BaRK-OPRF PSI protocol, which computes only the intersection (§6.3, p. 25)
qualifiers: Theorem 1 covers single-item bins with tables larger than \( 4(1 + \varepsilon)n \) each (Appendix A.3, p. 32)
the two-item-bin variant has no analysis; its failure probability and stash size rest on simulations (§3.3, p. 10; Appendix A, p. 29)
the hash functions must be chosen independently of the inputs and cannot be replaced after a failure without leaking information (§3, pp. 7-8; §5.2, p. 16)
semi-honest parties (§2, p. 6)
