metadata.statement: In two-dimensional cuckoo hashing one party places each item in both subtables of one of two tables, using an iterative insertion that moves evicted items to the other table, and the other party places each item in one subtable of each table by standard cuckoo hashing, so that an item held by both meets in exactly one subtable; with one item per bin and tables of more than \( 4(1 + \varepsilon)n \) bins the probability that some item cannot be placed is \( O(1/n) \) (Theorem 1); the variant with two-item bins and tables of \( 2.4n \) bins was measured to fail with probability at most \( 2^{-37} \) for \( n = 2^{12} \) at 99.9% confidence, with failure scaling as \( n^{-3} \), which the authors take as at most \( 2^{-40} \) for \( n \ge 2^{13} \).
metadata.title: Two-dimensional cuckoo hashing for circuit-based PSI: one shared bin per common item with \( O(1/n) \) failure above \( 4(1 + \varepsilon)n \) bins per table

sections.content: Two-dimensional cuckoo hashing
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Two tables \( T_L \) and \( T_R \) of \( 4(1 + \varepsilon)n \) entries each are used, each with two hash functions (§5.1, pp. 14-15). Bob maps an item to one location in each table by standard cuckoo hashing; Alice maps it to both locations in one table, evicting occupants and their second copies to the other table (Algorithm 2, p. 15). With bins of two items the tables have \( 2.4n \) bins of capacity two, the same memory (Algorithm 3, p. 16). For PSI, Bob keeps one combined stash instead of one per table, which roughly halves the stash comparisons (§5.2 and Table 1, p. 17), and permutation-based hashing shortens the stored items (§5.2, pp. 16-17).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-COMP-EVAL-GMW: the measured protocol evaluates the circuit with GMW, which the authors chose because GMW ran faster than Yao in earlier experiments (§6.3, p. 24; §2, p. 6). MPC-PAPER-2015-ABY and MPC-CONTRIB-2015-ABY-MIXED: the implementation is part of the ABY framework (§1.2, p. 3; §6.3, p. 24). MPC-PAPER-1987-GMW: GMW protocol, cited as [GMW87], for the measured protocol (§2, p. 6; Table 4, p. 25).

historical_context.narrative: Circuit-based PSI pays for every comparison inside a secure computation, so the number of comparisons sets its cost. Sorting networks gave \( n \log n \) comparisons, and the hashing approach of Circuit-Phasing, which pairs cuckoo hashing on one side with simple hashing on the other, gave slightly fewer, because simple hashing leaves logarithmically full bins. Pinkas, Schneider, Weinert, and Wieder let both parties use cuckoo hashing and resolved the problem that two parties may place a common item in different places by using a second set of tables whose hash functions mirror the first. Every common item then meets in exactly one bin, bins hold one item, and only a slowly growing stash must be compared with everything. Proving that such a stash keeps failure negligible completed an almost linear construction.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The best circuit constructions for PSI computed \( O(n \log n) \) comparisons (sort-compare-shuffle of Huang, Evans, and Katz) or \( O(n \log n / \log\log n) \) comparisons (Circuit-Phasing of Pinkas, Schneider, Segev, and Zohner), the latter because one party maps items by cuckoo hashing and the other by simple hashing into bins of \( O(\log n / \log\log n) \) items (abstract, p. 1; §1.4, p. 5; §2, p. 7). The known stash bound \( O(n^{-(s+1)}) \) for cuckoo hashing, \( s \) the stash size, was stated only for constant \( s \) (§3.3, p. 9).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: Against the best known circuit constructions named in the abstract, the number of comparisons becomes arbitrarily close to linear, so that symmetric functions such as cardinality, threshold tests, or sums over the intersection need circuits of total size \( \omega(n) \) instead of \( O(n \log n) \) (abstract, p. 1; §1.3, p. 4; §6.2, p. 22).
historical_context.technical_delta: Two sets of tables are used, the right set reusing the left hash functions with the lower row in mirror order; Bob cuckoo-hashes each item into one subtable of each of the four tables, and Alice cuckoo-hashes into the two left rows and moves every item that lands in different columns to the right tables without new insertions (§4.1, pp. 10-12; Figure 1 and Algorithm 1). Appendix C shows that the Kirsch-Mitzenmacher-Wieder bound also holds for non-constant stash size, so a stash of size \( \omega(1) \), for example \( \log\log n \), gives negligible failure (Appendix C, p. 34; §4.1, p. 13).

limitations: the analysis is asymptotic and not intended to be tight (§4, p. 10)
concretely the mirror construction is worse than the 2D construction and was not implemented or timed (§6.2, p. 22; §6.3, p. 24)
no security against malicious adversaries (§5.4, p. 18)
qualifiers: semi-honest parties (§2, p. 6)
both sets have \( n \) items of bitlength \( \sigma \); the parties agree on a symmetric function \( f \) and a circuit for it (§2, p. 5)
the hash functions are chosen at random and independently of the inputs (§3, pp. 7-8)
any symmetric function of the intersection; non-symmetric functions or the intersection itself need an \( O(n \log n) \) shuffle (§1.3, p. 4)
the stash bound for a non-constant stash size \( s \) is derived from Theorem 5.5 of Wieder's survey (Appendix C, p. 34)
metadata.statement: For two parties with \( n \) items of \( \sigma \) bits each, mirror cuckoo hashing places every item of each party into four standard cuckoo tables of total size \( 8(1 + \varepsilon)n \) so that an item held by both meets in exactly one subtable, with stashes of size \( \omega(1) \); a circuit that compares items bin by bin and compares every stashed item with all items of the other party then computes any symmetric function of the intersection with \( \omega(n) \) comparisons, that is \( o(f(n)) \) for every \( f(n) \in \omega(n) \), and circuit size \( \omega(\sigma n) \), against \( O(\sigma n \log n) \) for sort-compare-shuffle and \( O(\sigma n \log n / \log\log n) \) for Circuit-Phasing, with failure probability negligible in \( n \).
metadata.title: Circuit-based PSI with \( \omega(n) \) comparisons and negligible failure probability from mirror cuckoo hashing, semi-honest two-party

sections.content: Mirror cuckoo hashing for circuit-based PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The circuit (§4.2, p. 13) compares, for each bin, the item Alice mapped there with the item Bob mapped there, and compares every stashed item of either party with all items of the other. Mirror hashing guarantees that a common item is input to exactly one comparison, and the comparisons number \( \omega(n) \) (§4.2, p. 13). The tables have total size \( 8(1 + \varepsilon)n \); Bob keeps four stashes and Alice two (§4.1, p. 12). Concretely the circuit has \( 4 \cdot 2.4n(\sigma - \log_2(2.4n) + 1) + 3s'n(\sigma - 1) \) AND gates with a combined stash \( s' \le 2s \) (§6.2, p. 22).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-COMP-EVAL-YAO and MPC-COMP-EVAL-GMW: the circuit may be evaluated with Yao's protocol or GMW, both named as the two main approaches (§2, p. 6).

historical_context.narrative: In the authors' earlier OT-based protocol, each bin's oblivious PRF used transfers proportional to the item length, so longer identifiers cost more. Kolesnikov and coauthors had just removed that dependence with a pseudorandom code. Pinkas, Schneider, and Zohner reached the same goal differently in their journal version: they kept a genuine error-correcting code and fixed one BCH code with 512-bit codewords, large enough that, after shortening items with permutation-based hashing, sets of up to about 100 billion items need no larger code. Communication ends up slightly above the pseudorandom-code version but, the authors note, the structured code allows a published extension to malicious receivers. On a single platform comparing many paradigms, it ran fastest, with communication close to that of the public-key protocols.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The authors' conference protocols scaled linearly in the bit length \( \sigma \) of the inputs, as \( O(\sigma) \) (§1.4, 'Optimizations', p. 7). Kolesnikov et al. had replaced the error-correcting code of the implicit OPRF by a pseudorandom code of 424-448 bits, making its cost independent of \( \sigma \) (§1.2, p. 4; Table 1, p. 5).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors report communication 1.10-1.15 times that of Kolesnikov et al. and note that their code choice permits the malicious-receiver extension of Orrù, Orsini, and Scholl, which the pseudorandom code does not (§1.2, pp. 4-5); in their benchmarks it is the fastest protocol, with about the communication of public-key protocols (§6.2.2, p. 28), and it intersects two billion-element sets in 34.2 hours (§6.2.4, p. 31).
historical_context.technical_delta: The OPRF keeps an error-correcting code but fixes one linear BCH code that encodes up to \( 2^{77} \) words into 512-bit codewords with distance 129 (§2.2.3, p. 11); with permutation-based hashing this covers sets of up to \( 2^{37} \) elements for \( \lambda = 40 \) regardless of \( \sigma \) (§2.2.3, p. 11; §5, pp. 21-23; Protocol 3, p. 22). Smaller custom codes of 255-271 bits would suffice when \( \sigma - \log_2(n) \) is 8 to 13 (Table 1, p. 5).

limitations: communication is 1.10-1.15 times that of Kolesnikov et al. for the fixed 512-bit code (§1.2, p. 5)
smaller custom-tailored codes would lower communication for small \( \sigma - \log_2(n) \), but generating them is described as a non-trivial problem (§1.2, p. 5)
no security against malicious parties is claimed (§2.1, p. 8)
for small sets it is slower than the Bloom-filter protocols because of the base OTs (§6.2.2, pp. 28-29)
qualifiers: semi-honest P1 and P2; the proof assumes an ideal 1-out-of-N random OT functionality (§5, 'Security', p. 23)
efficient random OT extension relies on a function modeled as a random oracle (§2.1, p. 8; §2.2.2, p. 10)
only P2 learns the intersection (Protocol 3, 'Output', p. 22)
the 1-out-of-N OT extension needs 512 base OTs, four times as many as 1-out-of-2 OT extension, which dominates for small sets (§2.2.3, p. 11; §6.2.2, pp. 28-29)
the OT-based protocol first appeared in the USENIX 2014 and 2015 versions; independence of \( \sigma \) is an addition of this version (§1.4, p. 7; §5, p. 21)

metadata.statement: P1 hashes its items into \( b \) bins by simple hashing with \( k \) hash functions and P2 by cuckoo hashing with a stash of size \( s \), \( b \) the number of bins and \( k \) the number of hash functions, with permutation-based hashing shortening stored items to \( \mu = \sigma - \log b + \log k \) bits; for each bin and stash position the parties run one 1-out-of-\( 2^{\mu} \) random OT of the Kolesnikov-Kumaresan OT extension with a fixed linear \( [2^{77}, 512, 129] \) BCH code, which serves as an OPRF; P1 evaluates the OPRF on its own items and sends the permuted outputs, and P2 outputs its items whose outputs appear. Against semi-honest adversaries, P2 sends \( 512(s + b) \) bits and P1 sends about \( k \cdot n_X \cdot v \) bits with \( v = \lambda + \log_2(kn_X) + \log_2(n_Y) \), independent of \( \sigma \) for sets of up to \( 2^{37} \) items at \( \lambda = 40 \), and P1 performs \( (k + s)n_X \) correlation-robust function evaluations.

sections.content: Bit-length-independent OT-based PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: For each bin i, P1 obtains a random OPRF key \( t_i \), which corresponds to the values \( q_i \) and s of the 1-out-of-N OT extension, and P2 obtains \( F_{t_i}(T2[i]) \); P1 computes \( M1[i][j] = H(q_i \oplus (s \wedge c_{v_j})) \) for each of its items \( v_j \) in bin i, collects all values, permutes them, and sends them; stash positions are handled by evaluating the OPRF on P1's whole set (Protocol 3, p. 22; §5, p. 22). Mask length \( v = \lambda + \log_2(kn_X) + \log_2(n_Y) \) gives correctness with probability \( 1 - 2^{-\lambda} \) (§5, 'Correctness', p. 23).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-2003-IKNP-OTEXT: the 1-out-of-2 OT extension of Ishai et al., on which the 1-out-of-N OT extension builds (Protocol 1, p. 10; §2.2.3, p. 10). The Kolesnikov-Kumaresan 1-out-of-N OT extension, which this protocol instantiates (§2.2.3, Protocol 2, pp. 10-11), has no record in any topic.

historical_context.narrative: Hashing items into bins is what makes OT-based and circuit-based PSI run in linear time, but its parameters decide both correctness and cost: bins that overflow leak information or lose items, while oversized bins waste comparisons. Earlier work had given only asymptotic bounds for these schemes, with constants too vague to pick a concrete setting. Pinkas, Schneider, and Zohner computed the bounds numerically and ran about a billion cuckoo-hashing trials per configuration, extrapolating to a failure probability of two to the minus forty. Their tables list bin sizes, stash sizes, and bin counts, show that three hash functions work best when the parties' sets are equally large, and give low-stash choices for a small client set against a large server set, which other protocols adopted as well.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Freedman, Nissim, and Pinkas, and the later journal version with Hazay, suggested hashing to bins for PSI but analyzed its parameters only asymptotically and left setting them to future work (§1.3, p. 5; §3, p. 12); cuckoo hashing with a stash fails with probability \( O(n^{1-c(s+1)}) \), \( s \) the stash size and \( c \) the constant in the exponent, with unclear constants, and the utilization gains for more than two hash functions were known only asymptotically (§3.2.2, p. 15).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The parameters let PSI protocols meet a stated hashing failure probability with concrete costs, show that three hash functions minimize comparisons for equal set sizes (§3.2.2, p. 16), and give low-stash settings for unequal set sizes (§3.2.2, p. 17; Table 11, p. 30); the authors note that the protocols of Kolesnikov et al. and of Orrù et al. benefit from this analysis (§1.2, p. 5).
historical_context.technical_delta: The paper computes the bin-size bound with 1,024-bit floating-point precision and measures cuckoo-hashing failures over \( 2^{30} \) repetitions, extrapolating by linear or logarithmic regression or a 4/3 margin, and tabulates trade-offs among stash size, number of hash functions, and number of bins (§3.1.2-3.2.2, pp. 13-18; Tables 3-7, Figures 1-2).

limitations: the \( 2^{-40} \) values are extrapolated from \( 2^{-30} \) experiments, because \( 2^{40} \) trials were too costly (§3, p. 13; §3.2.2, pp. 15-17)
the cuckoo-hashing parameters are empirical estimates, not proved bounds (§3.2.2, p. 15)
the unequal-set parameters were computed for client sets of \( 2^{8} \) and \( 2^{12} \) items, while the text of §6.2.3 mentions \( 2^{8} \) and \( 2^{16} \) (Table 4, p. 14; §6.2.3, p. 29)
qualifiers: the hashing failure parameter \( \eta \) is kept separate from the statistical security parameter \( \lambda \) (§3, p. 13)
cuckoo hashing is used by P2 and simple hashing with the same k functions by P1, who pads bins with dummy items (§3.2.1, p. 14)
part of the analysis appeared in the conference versions, which bounded the failure for one parameter set; the trade-offs and unequal-set parameters are additions of this version (§1.4, p. 7)

historical_context.narrative: Threshold PSI from fully homomorphic encryption reached communication close to the lower bound but was computationally out of reach, while generic garbled circuits paid a cubic price for solving the interpolation system. Ghosh and Simkin separated the problem in two. First the parties test, privately, whether their sets are close: writing each set as a sum of monomials makes the difference polynomial sparse exactly when the sets nearly agree, and sparsity reduces to whether a Hankel matrix is singular, which can be checked under additively homomorphic encryption. Only if the test passes do they compute randomized evaluations from which each party recovers its own exclusive elements and nothing about the other's. The second step is already cheap, so the cardinality test became the remaining bottleneck.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Threshold PSI protocols of Freedman-Nissim-Pinkas, Hallgren-Orlandi-Sabelfeld, Ghosh-Nilges, Pinkas et al., and Zhao-Chow first computed PSI or its cardinality and so communicated at least linearly in the smaller set (§1, p. 2). Sublinear communication was available only from FHE, or from generic garbled circuits at \( \tilde O(t^3) \) because interpolation needs Gaussian elimination (§3, pp. 8-9).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors present it as the first threshold PSI protocols whose communication depends mainly on \( t \) and only logarithmically on \( n \), from assumptions weaker than FHE and with less computation than the FHE protocol (abstract, p. 1; §3, p. 7). Since the intersection step already costs \( \tilde O(t) \), an \( \tilde O(t) \) cardinality test would give \( \tilde O(t) \) threshold PSI (§6.3, p. 14; §9, p. 19).
historical_context.technical_delta: Threshold PSI is split into a cardinality test and an intersection step (§1.2, pp. 2-4). The test uses a monomial set encoding, so sparsity of \( p_A - p_B \) measures the symmetric difference, and checks singularity of an encrypted Hankel matrix (Theorem 1, p. 9; Figure 5 and Theorem 3, p. 11). The intersection step uses generic computation only to produce noisy evaluations, which the parties interpolate in the clear; Lemma 1 of Kissner and Song makes the noise uniformly random (Figure 7, p. 13; Theorem 4, p. 14; Theorem 5, p. 16).

limitations: the authors do not claim practical efficiency (§1.1, p. 2; §9, p. 20)
the \( \tilde O(t^2) \) cost comes from the private cardinality test; the intersection step alone is \( \tilde O(t) \) (§6.3, p. 14)
qualifiers: static passive adversaries in the UC framework (§2.2, p. 6)

Theorem 4 is in the \( (F_{\mathrm{PICT}}, F_{\mathrm{NPA}}) \)-hybrid model and Theorem 5 in the \( F_{\mathrm{OLE}} \)-hybrid model (pp. 14, 16); the \( \tilde O(t^2) \) bound holds in the plain model after instantiation (Lemmas 3-4, pp. 12, 14)
the cardinality test needs a field \( \mathbb{F}_r \) whose size \( r > (4t^2 + 2t)(p - 1)2^{\lambda} \) is a prime power, and errs with probability at most \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (Theorem 1, p. 9)
the parties' sets have equal size \( n \); unequal sizes are handled by padding, at most doubling the threshold (§2, p. 4; §6.4, p. 15)
both parties learn the intersection or \( \perp \) (Figure 6, p. 12)

metadata.statement: Against passive adversaries, two-party threshold PSI is realized with communication \( \tilde O(t^2) \) in the plain model from IND-CPA additively homomorphic encryption and OLE: a private intersection cardinality test encodes each set as the polynomial with one monomial \( x^a \) per element, so the difference of the two encodings has at most \( 2t \) monomials exactly when the symmetric difference is at most \( 2t \), and tests this with the Hankel-matrix sparsity test of Grigorescu, Jung, and Rubinfeld under encryption and the singularity test of Kiltz, Mohassel, Weinreb, and Franklin (\( \tilde O(t^2) \)); if the test passes, an OLE-based noisy polynomial addition gives both parties \( 3t + 1 \) evaluations of \( p_A R_1 + p_B R_2 \) for random degree-\( t \) polynomials \( R_1, R_2 \), from which each interpolates its exclusive elements and hence the intersection (\( \tilde O(t) \)).

sections.content: Threshold PSI from additively homomorphic encryption
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: \( \Pi_{\mathrm{TPSI}} \) (Figure 7, p. 13): the parties call \( F_{\mathrm{PICT}} \) and output \( \perp \) if it returns different; otherwise they call \( F_{\mathrm{NPA}} \) for \( 3t + 1 \) evaluation points \( \alpha_i \) and receive \( V(\alpha_i) = p_A(\alpha_i)R_1(\alpha_i) + p_B(\alpha_i)R_2(\alpha_i) \). Alice divides by \( p_A(\alpha_i) \), interpolates a rational function whose denominator is \( p_{A \setminus B} \), and removes its roots from \( S_A \); Bob does the same. \( \Pi_{\mathrm{PICT}} \) (Figure 5, p. 11) sends Alice's encrypted Hankel matrix, Bob subtracts his own homomorphically, and \( F_{\mathrm{INV}} \) decides singularity. \( \Pi_{\mathrm{NPA}} \) (Figure 10, p. 17) uses \( 2(3t + 1) \) OLE calls, adapting a protocol of Ghosh and Nilges (§7.2, p. 15).

historical_context.narrative: Set reconciliation, a technique from distributed systems, lets two parties learn the union of their sets by exchanging a number of polynomial evaluations proportional to how much the sets differ, but it reveals both sets' differences. Ghosh and Simkin placed it under fully homomorphic encryption: one party sends encrypted evaluations of the polynomial whose roots are its elements, and the other interpolates the ratio of the two set polynomials on ciphertexts, verifies the result at a random point, and returns only the part describing the first party's exclusive elements. Communication becomes linear in the threshold and logarithmic in the field size, \( O(t \log p) \) bits, close to the lower bound, although interpolating homomorphically is expensive enough that the authors treat the protocol as a feasibility result.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Before this work all threshold PSI protocols had communication \( \Omega(n) \) in the set size (abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2). The set reconciliation protocol of Minsky, Trachtenberg, and Zippel computes a set union with communication proportional to the symmetric difference but is not private (§1.2, p. 3).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It is an upper bound within polylogarithmic factors of the \( \Omega(t) \) lower bound, establishing that threshold PSI communication can depend on the threshold rather than the set size; the authors consider it of mainly theoretical interest because of the homomorphic interpolation cost (§3, pp. 7-8; Figure 2, p. 7).
historical_context.technical_delta: The set reconciliation protocol is run under fully homomorphic encryption, so the rational-function interpolation and the consistency check at z happen on ciphertexts and only the numerator encoding Alice's exclusive elements is returned (§3, p. 8).

limitations: not claimed practical: homomorphic rational-function interpolation is computationally heavy (§3, p. 8)
relies on fully homomorphic encryption; whether \( \tilde O(t) \) is possible from weaker assumptions is left open (§9, p. 19)
qualifiers: a high-level sketch; the details are left to the reader (§3, p. 8)
assumes FHE ciphertexts larger than plaintexts by at most a constant factor and elements from \( \mathbb{F}_p \) (§3, p. 8)
security follows from the security of FHE; known instantiations rest on lattice assumptions such as LWE or ring-LWE (§3, p. 8)

metadata.statement: Against passive adversaries, two parties can run threshold PSI with communication \( O(t \log p) \) bits for set elements in \( \mathbb{F}_p \), that is \( \tilde O(t) \) independent of the set size \( n \): Alice sends FHE encryptions of her set polynomial at \( 2t + 1 \) points plus a random point z, Bob homomorphically interpolates the rational function \( p_A/p_B \) from the first \( 2t \) points, checks the candidate at z, and returns \( t \) ciphertexts holding the numerator \( p_{A \setminus B} \) or \( \perp \), from which Alice computes the intersection.

sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Alice encodes \( S_A \) as \( p_A(x) = \prod(x - a_i) \) and sends \( \mathrm{Enc}(p_A(\alpha_1)), \ldots, \mathrm{Enc}(p_A(\alpha_{2t})) \), \( \mathrm{Enc}(p_A(z)) \), and z. Bob interpolates \( p_A/p_B \), whose numerator and denominator have gcd 1, on ciphertexts, and returns \( p_{A \setminus B} \) if the candidate agrees with \( p_A(z)/p_B(z) \) and \( \perp \) otherwise. Total communication is \( 2t + 1 \) ciphertexts from Alice and \( t \) from Bob (§3, p. 8).

historical_context.narrative: The communication of ordinary set intersection had long been known to grow at least linearly with the sets, as \( \Omega(n) \), through the hardness of deciding set disjointness. Threshold PSI asks for less: the intersection is released only when the two sets differ in at most \( t \) elements. Ghosh and Simkin asked what that relaxation is worth and showed that it cannot be worth everything. A threshold protocol that communicated \( o(t) \) bits would, after both parties pad small sets with the same public dummy elements, compute an ordinary intersection too cheaply. The bound depends only on \( t \), leaving room for protocols whose cost is independent of the set size, and it frames the upper bounds of the same paper.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Freedman, Nissim, and Pinkas observed that the \( \Theta(n) \) communication complexity of set disjointness yields an \( \Omega(n) \) lower bound for any PSI protocol on sets of size \( n \), which extends to intersection cardinality (§1, p. 1; §3, p. 8). All earlier threshold PSI protocols started from PSI and communicated at least linearly in the smaller set (§1, p. 2).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: With the FHE-based protocol it gives the first characterization of the communication complexity of threshold PSI, showing that communication depending on \( t \) rather than \( n \) is not ruled out (§1.1, p. 2; §3, p. 7; Figure 2, p. 7).
historical_context.technical_delta: The bound is restated in terms of the threshold: padding both inputs with a common set of dummy elements turns any threshold PSI protocol into a PSI protocol for the unpadded sets, so threshold PSI inherits an \( \Omega(t) \) bound, measured by the symmetric set difference rather than the set size (§3, pp. 7-8).

limitations: the bound concerns protocols that output the intersection when the threshold condition holds, not cardinality testing alone (§3, p. 8)
it is stated for two parties (§3, p. 7)
qualifiers: unconditional: the bound holds for any protocol, without computational assumptions (§3, p. 7)
\( t \) is an upper bound on the size of the symmetric set difference (§3, p. 7)
the argument is a sketch that relies on the \( \Omega(n) \) bound for set intersection derived from set disjointness (§3, p. 8)

metadata.statement: Any two-party protocol that outputs the intersection of two sets whenever their symmetric difference is at most \( t \) must communicate \( \Omega(t) \) bits, unconditionally: a protocol with \( o(t) \) communication, run on two size-\( t \) sets each padded with the same \( n' - t \) public dummy elements, would compute the intersection of size-\( t \) sets with \( o(t) \) communication, contradicting the \( \Omega(n) \) set-intersection bound that follows from the communication complexity of set disjointness.
metadata.title: \( \Omega(t) \) communication lower bound for two-party threshold PSI, \( t \) the bound on the symmetric set difference

sections.content: \( \Omega(t) \) lower bound for threshold PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Suppose protocol \( \Pi \) computes the intersection of sets of size \( n' \) that share at least \( n' - t \) elements with \( o(t) \) communication. For sets \( S_A \) and \( S_B \) of size \( t \), both parties run \( \Pi \) on \( S_A \cup S_D \) and \( S_B \cup S_D \) for a fixed public set \( S_D \) of \( n' - t \) dummies; the threshold condition always holds, and removing \( S_D \) from the output yields \( S_A \cap S_B \) with \( o(t) \) communication, contradicting the \( \Omega(t) \) bound for PSI on size-\( t \) sets (§3, p. 8).

historical_context.narrative: Precomputed unbalanced PSI pushes all heavy work into phases that run before the client's contacts are known, leaving an online phase in which the client fetches the keys that let it evaluate a precomputed oblivious PRF on each item. Those fetches were ordinary oblivious transfers. Free-XOR garbling invites correlated transfers, which cost half as much, but precomputed correlated transfers seemed to require regarbling whenever the client's random choice bit differed from its real input. Kales and coauthors fixed the label pair from the correlated transfer, added a fresh random mask per label, and let a one-bit correction decide which masked value the server returns. The same idea applies to the Naor-Reingold OPRF, and in both protocols the online transfers shrink by half.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Kiss et al. split unbalanced PSI into base, setup, online, and update phases and precomputed OTs and garbled circuits in the base phase with ordinary OTs (§3.5, p. 6; §4.3, p. 8). Correlated OTs suit Free-XOR labels \( l_1 = l_0 \oplus \Delta \), but with OT precomputation the sender must swap the precomputed messages whenever the client's random choice differs from its input, which would force re-garbling at least the first layer of each precomputed circuit (§4.3, p. 8).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: OT messages are the only online communication of GC-PSI, so its online phase sends half as much; the authors state the technique is of independent interest for Yao's protocol with precomputation (§1.1, p. 2; §4.3, p. 8). The measured online phase for 1024 client items sends 2,048 KiB from server to client in GC-PSI and 4,147 KiB in NR-PSI (Table 5, p. 13).
historical_context.technical_delta: For GC-PSI the input labels are derived from correlated OTs through per-label masks \( \delta \), so the swap moves into the masks: the client sends \( b = c \oplus y \), the garbler replies \( B = r_b \oplus l_0 \), and the client sets its label to \( r_c \oplus B \) (§4.3, p. 8; Figure 1, p. 9). For NR-PSI the correlation between r and \( r \cdot a_j \) in the OPRF of Hazay and Lindell lets correlated OTs replace ordinary ones, combined with OT precomputation (§4.4, p. 10; Figure 2, p. 10).

limitations: the factor 2 concerns the online OT messages; base-phase garbled circuits and the setup-phase filter are unchanged (§4.3, p. 8; Tables 3-4, p. 13)
qualifiers: applies to the precomputation setting, in which the number of precomputed OTs and circuits bounds the client items checked before the base phase must be rerun (Figure 1 caption, p. 9)
security is argued from the arguments for standard OT precomputation and the uniformity of the fresh masks \( \delta \); no proof is given (§4.3, p. 8)
the GC-PSI variant relies on Free-XOR labels with a global offset \( \Delta \) known only to the garbler (§4.3, p. 8)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 1); §1.1 (p. 2); §3.1 (pp. 4-5); §3.5 (p. 6); §4.3 (p. 8); Figure 1 (p. 9); §4.4 (pp. 9-10); Figure 2 (p. 10); Table 5 (p. 13). IACR ePrint 2019/517, full version, PDF dated 2019-05-24.

metadata.statement: In unbalanced PSI whose client-side OPRF evaluations rely on OTs precomputed in an input-independent base phase, the online OT messages can come from correlated OTs: in garbled-circuit OPRF evaluation the garbler builds each input-wire label pair as \( l_0 = r_0 \oplus \delta \) and \( l_1 = l_0 \oplus \Delta \) from a correlated OT \( (r_0, r_1 = r_0 \oplus \Delta) \) and a fresh mask \( \delta \), and answers the client's correction bit \( b = c \oplus y \) with the single value \( r_b \oplus l_0 \); in Naor-Reingold OPRF evaluation, where the client chooses between r and \( r \cdot a_j \), a correlated OT combined with OT precomputation sends one message of the symmetric security parameter instead of two. In both cases online OT communication halves, and garbled circuits stay precomputable before the client's input is known.
metadata.title: Correlated-OT precomputation that halves the online OT communication of precomputed garbled-circuit and Naor-Reingold OPRF evaluation in unbalanced PSI

sections.content: Correlated-OT precomputation
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: In the base phase the parties run random correlated OTs by OT extension: the garbler, with input \( \Delta \), learns \( r_0 \) and \( r_1 = r_0 \oplus \Delta \), and the evaluator, with a random choice c, learns \( r_c \) (§4.3, p. 8). Each precomputed circuit's input labels are \( l_0 = r_0 \oplus \delta \) and \( l_1 = l_0 \oplus \Delta \) with \( \delta \) fresh per label. Online, the evaluator sends \( b = c \oplus y \) and receives \( B = r_b \oplus l_0 \), and \( r_c \oplus B \) is the label for its input bit y in all four cases of \( (c, b) \) (§4.3, p. 8; Figure 1, p. 9). For NR-PSI the client's correction bit decides which precomputed random message the server treats as r and which masks the correlated message \( r \cdot a_j \) (§4.4, p. 10).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-2003-IKNP-OTEXT: the base phase runs correlated and random OTs by OT extension, which the paper introduces with IKNP (§3.1, p. 4); the implementation uses the correlated-OT extension of Keller, Orsini, and Scholl (§5.1, p. 12). MPC-CONTRIB-2008-FREEXOR: the GC-PSI variant depends on Free-XOR labels with a global offset (§4.3, p. 8). Beaver's OT precomputation (CRYPTO 1995), on which the technique builds, has no record in any topic (§3.1, p. 5; §4.3, p. 8).

historical_context.narrative: In precomputed unbalanced PSI the server encrypts its entire user base under a PRF once and ships it to every client as a compact filter, so the size of that filter and of its daily updates decides whether the approach works on a phone plan. Resende and Aranha had used cuckoo filters with short tags, accepting a false-positive rate near one in eight thousand, and sent every update as a full elliptic-curve point. Kales and coauthors observed that empty entries need not be sent, that the position of a tag within its bucket carries no information, and that a tag plus one bucket index is enough to insert or delete. With longer tags the false-positive rate drops to about one in half a billion, while the filter shrinks and updates become four times smaller.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Resende and Aranha represented the server's encrypted set by a cuckoo filter with 16-bit tags, bucket size 3, and a false-positive probability of about \( 2^{-13} \), which the authors call impractical, and sent each updated element as a 256-bit compressed point on GLS-254 (§2, p. 4; §4.1, pp. 6-7). Kiss et al. used Bloom filters (§2, p. 4). Dictionary compression with LZMA, suggested for Bloom-filter updates, takes over 8 min to compress a filter for \( 2^{28} \) items (§4.1, p. 6).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The setup transfer for \( 2^{28} \) server items is 1,072 MiB (Table 4, p. 13), and a filter at 10% occupancy, as in a fast-growing service, compresses 8.3 times (§4.1, p. 6). The encoding runs on the fly, while LZMA would be infeasible on a phone for regular updates (§4.1, pp. 6-7). The authors still name the filter size as the bottleneck for very large server sets (§4.6, p. 11).
historical_context.technical_delta: The filter is sent as a bit map of occupied entries plus the list of tags, or with a per-bucket tag count, since tag positions within a bucket do not matter (§4.1, p. 6). An update carries a tag and one bucket index, from which the client computes the other candidate bucket for relocations or deletion (§4.1, p. 7). Tags of 32 bits with bucket size 3 set the false-positive probability per item near \( 2^{-29} \) (§4.1, p. 6; Table 4, p. 13).

limitations: the filter remains linear in the server set, \( O(n_X) \), about 1 GiB for \( 2^{28} \) items and about 8 GiB for \( 2^{31} \), and must be stored by the client (§4.6, p. 11)

the paper does not discuss what updates reveal; PSI-PAPER-2018-CHLR notes that in filter-based protocols of this kind the receiver learns how many items were inserted and removed and that deletions cannot be enforced (§8.3, p. 21 of that paper)
qualifiers: the 30% figure is for load ≈66%, tag size 32 bits, and bucket size 3; sparser filters compress more (§4.1, p. 6)
the 59-bit update assumes \( 2^{28} \) items, 27-bit bucket indices, and 32-bit tags (§4.1, p. 7)
false-positive probabilities are per item; the authors note that one false positive per ten clients querying \( 2^{10} \) items follows from \( 2^{-13} \) (§4.1, p. 6)
metadata.statement: In unbalanced PSI where the server sends its set once as a cuckoo filter of PRF values, transmitting an occupancy bit per entry plus the nonempty tags, or the number of tags per bucket in \( \log_2(b + 1) \) bits, \( b \) the bucket size, reduces the filter by about 30% at load ≈66% (from 6 MiB to 4.19 MiB for \( 2^{20} \) items with 32-bit tags and bucket size 3), and sending only a tag and one candidate bucket index per inserted or deleted item makes an update 59 bits for \( 2^{28} \) items instead of a 256-bit group element; 32-bit or 42-bit tags give false-positive probabilities of about \( 2^{-29} \) or \( 2^{-39} \) instead of about \( 2^{-13} \).

sections.content: Compressed cuckoo filters
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: A cuckoo filter stores a v-bit tag of each item in one of two buckets of b entries; lookups compare tags in both candidate buckets, so equal tags cause false positives at a rate set mainly by v (§3.4, pp. 5-6). The compressed encoding sends an occupancy bit map and the stored tags, or a \( \log_2(b + 1) \)-bit tag count per bucket followed by the tags (§4.1, p. 6). Updates send \( (t_i, p_i) \) for each changed item; the client inserts or deletes the tag at \( p_i \) or at \( p_i \oplus H(t_i) \) (§4.1, p. 7; Figure 1, update phase, p. 9).

historical_context.narrative: In the garbled-circuit flavor of precomputed unbalanced PSI, the server sends one garbled PRF circuit per client contact before the contacts are known, so the PRF's AND-gate count sets the cost of the base phase. Every implementation had used AES-128, with about five thousand AND gates, and LowMC had been named only as a possibility. Kales and coauthors chose LowMC parameters for this setting: a single S-box per round and many rounds, which costs nothing extra in Yao's constant-round protocol, and a data-complexity bound tied to how many queries the service will ever answer. The circuit shrinks to about six hundred AND gates, the key schedule is garbled once because the key never changes, and precomputation traffic falls roughly sevenfold.
historical_context.prior_boundary: All earlier GC-PSI implementations evaluated AES-128, whose circuit with the Boyar-Peralta S-box has 5,120 AND gates without key schedule (§4.2, p. 7). Kiss et al. had mentioned LowMC as a possible replacement without fixing parameters (§1.1, p. 2; §4.2, p. 7). With Free-XOR and half-gates only AND gates cost communication, two \( \kappa \)-bit labels each (§4.2, p. 7; §5.2, p. 12).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: In the base phase, which sends the garbled circuits, LowMC reduces communication 7.4 times relative to AES while the online phase stays comparable; the one-time server setup becomes slower than hardware-accelerated AES (§6.1, pp. 12-13; Tables 3-4, p. 13). The \( 2^{64} \) data complexity allows \( 2^{20} \) contact discoveries of \( 2^{10} \) items for each of \( 2^{28} \) clients (§4.2, p. 7).
historical_context.technical_delta: The authors compare five LowMC instances under the round formula updated after recent cryptanalysis and recommend instance (3), with one S-box per round and 624 AND gates, accepting 208 rounds because Yao's protocol has constant round complexity (§4.2, pp. 7-8; Table 2, p. 8). Data complexity \( 2^{64} \) is matched to the number of queries the service allows, and bundling all client circuits lets the fixed key schedule be garbled once, saving about 2 KiB per further item (§4.2, p. 7).

limitations: the one-time server setup takes 1,869.13 s with LowMC against 23.94 s with AES for \( 2^{28} \) items, because AES has hardware support (Table 4, p. 13; §6.1, p. 13)
the number of client queries must be bounded to stay within the data complexity (§4.2, p. 7)
qualifiers: security of the OPRF rests on LowMC instance (3) being a secure PRF up to data complexity \( 2^{64} \), with rounds from the LowMC designers' updated formula (§4.2, pp. 7-8)
the 8.2x figure counts AND gates; the measured base-phase communication ratio is 7.4x (abstract, p. 1; §6.1, p. 12)
for small data complexity the authors recommend instance (4), with \( 2^{32} \) and 576 AND gates, which needs re-keying once the bound is reached (§4.2, pp. 7-8)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 1); §1.1 (p. 2); §4.2 (pp. 7-8); Table 2 (p. 8); §6.1 (pp. 12-13); Tables 3-4 (p. 13). IACR ePrint 2019/517, full version, PDF dated 2019-05-24.

metadata.statement: Instantiating the PRF evaluated by garbled circuits in GC-PSI with the LowMC instance of block and key size 128, one S-box per round, data complexity \( 2^{64} \), and 208 rounds gives 624 AND gates per client item, against 5,120 for AES-128 without key schedule (8.2x fewer); since the server's key is fixed, the key schedule is garbled once for all client circuits, and the data-complexity bound is enforced by limiting client queries. In the authors' measurement the base-phase communication for \( 2^{10} \) client items falls from 162.52 MiB to 22.01 MiB.

sections.content: LowMC as the garbled OPRF
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Table 2 (p. 8) lists LowMC instances with block and key size 128: (1) 42 S-boxes and 13 rounds, 1,638 AND gates; (2) 31 S-boxes and 13 rounds, 1,209; (3) one S-box and 208 rounds, 624; (4) one S-box, data complexity \( 2^{32} \), 192 rounds, 576; (5) one S-box, data complexity \( 2^{128} \), 287 rounds, 861; and AES-128 with 5,120. Instance (3) is used in all experiments (§6.1, p. 12). Other MPC- and FHE-oriented ciphers are set aside: three of them are stream ciphers designed for FHE ciphertext expansion, and MiMC works over large prime fields, which does not fit Boolean garbled circuits (§4.2, p. 8).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-1982-YAO-2PC and MPC-CONTRIB-2015-HALFGATES: the OPRF is evaluated by Yao's garbled circuits with Free-XOR and half-gates, so AND gates determine the communication (§3.2, p. 5; §5.2, p. 12). SYM-RESULT-2001-AES-AES-128-BIT-BLOCK-CIPHER-STANDARD: AES-128 is the replaced PRF and the baseline of Table 2 (§4.2, p. 7). MPC-PAPER-2009-PRACTICAL2PC: OPRF evaluation by garbled circuits follows Pinkas, Schneider, Smart, and Williams (§4.3, p. 8). LowMC (Albrecht et al., EUROCRYPT 2015) has no record in any topic.

historical_context.narrative: Private contact discovery had a protocol design that suited phones, with an input-independent precomputation, a one-time transfer of the server's encrypted user base, and a cheap online phase, but its only phone implementation ran in Java with semi-honest security and needed close to a minute to check a single contact. Kales and coauthors rewrote both variants natively for ARMv8, garbling with the hardware AES instructions of recent phones and running the algebraic variant on an elliptic curve. Malicious clients came almost for free, because a client only sends oblivious-transfer messages, so swapping in actively secure transfers suffices. A thousand contacts against a quarter of a billion users then took about three seconds on WiFi, and the protocols ran inside a modified Signal client.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Kiss et al. gave the only unbalanced PSI implementation on real phones, in Java and with semi-honest security; their fastest protocol that can easily be made secure against malicious clients needed more than 52 s on WiFi to check one contact against \( 2^{20} \) entries, and one garbled AES-128 circuit took over a second (§1, p. 2; §5, p. 11). The FHE-based protocols of Chen et al. had been evaluated only on servers in a 10 Gbit/s network (§6.2, p. 13).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: For 1024 contacts the combined base and online time improves by more than 300 times (GC-PSI) and 30 times (NR-PSI) over the implementations of Kiss et al. run in the same environment, with 7.5 and 10.9 times less communication (Table 6, p. 14). A prototype was integrated into the Signal Android client (§1.1, p. 3; Appendix C, p. 19), although the authors state that Signal's stated requirements for a billion users are not yet met (§7, p. 14).
historical_context.technical_delta: Garbling uses fixed-key AES through the ARM Cryptography Extensions, which speed AES up 35 times, and NEON registers for 128-bit labels; NR-PSI runs over P-256, which shrinks online values 8 times relative to a finite field; libOTe is ported to ARMv8 (§5.1-5.3, pp. 11-12). Because the client sends only OT messages and correction bits, maliciously secure base OTs and OT extension suffice for malicious clients (§4.5, pp. 10-11; §5.1, pp. 11-12).

limitations: the server setup takes 52,332.38 s for ECC-NR-PSI and 1,869.13 s for LowMC-GC-PSI on \( 2^{28} \) items, single-threaded (Table 4, p. 13)
enumeration attacks by repeated queries are not prevented; the authors recommend rate limiting (§4.5, p. 11)
a malicious server can learn about non-matching client items whenever the client reveals its intersection to the server, so a semi-honest server is assumed (§4.5, p. 11)
qualifiers: malicious clients and a semi-honest server; security is argued in prose, with no simulation proof (§4.5, pp. 10-11)
the reported 2.92 s and 6.53 s are base plus online time (Table 6, p. 14), which the abstract calls the online phase (p. 1)
server on an Intel Core i7-4600U, client a Google Pixel XL 2, one thread each; WiFi with about 230 Mbit/s and 70 ms RTT, LTE with 42 Mbit/s down, 4 Mbit/s up, and 80 ms RTT; 128-bit items (§6, p. 12)
the numbers for Kiss et al. come from running their implementations in the authors' environment (Table 6, p. 14)
metadata.statement: C/C++ implementations of precomputed LowMC-GC-PSI and ECC-NR-PSI for Android, using ARMv8 Cryptography Extensions for fixed-key AES garbling, the P-256 curve for the Naor-Reingold PRF, and an ARMv8 port of libOTe with Chou-Orlandi base OTs and Keller-Orsini-Scholl OT extension, are secure against malicious clients when the server is semi-honest, as argued in prose; checking 1024 client contacts against \( 2^{28} \) server items takes 2.92 s on WiFi and 6.53 s on LTE of base plus online time with 6.07 MiB of communication for ECC-NR-PSI, after a one-time 1,072 MiB filter transfer, and a garbled AES-128 circuit is evaluated more than 1,000 times faster than in the earlier Java implementation of Kiss et al.

sections.content: Smartphone implementation of precomputed unbalanced PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Both protocols follow the four phases of precomputed unbalanced PSI: an input-independent base phase, a setup phase in which the server sends a compressed cuckoo filter of PRF values of its whole set, an online phase of OPRF evaluations on the client's items followed by local filter lookups, and an update phase (§3.5, p. 6). The implementation measures each phase separately (Tables 3-5, p. 13) and compares with the Android implementations of Kiss et al. (Table 6, p. 14) and, on x86 hardware, with the FHE-based and Diffie-Hellman protocols using numbers taken from Chen et al. (Appendix D, Table 8, p. 20).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-2003-IKNP-OTEXT: OT extension, which the paper introduces with IKNP (§3.1, p. 4); the implementation uses the actively secure extension of Keller, Orsini, and Scholl, which has no record in any topic (§5.1, p. 12). MPC-CONTRIB-2008-FREEXOR and MPC-CONTRIB-2015-HALFGATES: the garbling scheme of the GC-PSI implementation (§5.2, p. 12).

historical_context.narrative: An oblivious programmable PRF lets one party fix the outputs on chosen inputs while the other evaluates it without learning which inputs were chosen. In its original form each programmed input needed its own random target and its own polynomial coefficient, so programming every item that simple hashing places in a bin cost as much as the largest bin allowed. Pinkas, Schneider, Tkachenko, and Yanai observed that a single query suffices in circuit-based PSI, and that the targets may then be correlated, even identical, without loss of security. They also merged the polynomials of all bins into one, so the hint grows with the total number of items rather than with the number of bins times the maximum load. Programming every bin then costs linear communication overall.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The OPPRF was introduced by Kolesnikov, Matania, Pinkas, Rosulek, and Trieu with a polynomial-based construction and a security definition that allows many queries but requires an independent target per programmed point (§1, p. 2; §3.2, p. 12). One standalone OPPRF per bin costs communication linear in the number of programmed values, which for bins of maximal size \( O(\log n / \log \log n) \) gives \( O(n \log n / \log \log n) \) overall (§1.1, p. 3; §3.3, p. 13).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The total hint size becomes \( K \cdot n \) coefficients for cuckoo hashing with K hash functions (footnote 6, p. 13), at most 3% of the protocol's communication (§7.3, p. 24), which removes the logarithmic factor that bounded earlier circuit-based PSI (§1.1, pp. 3-4).
historical_context.technical_delta: The definition is changed to one query but correlated targets, including all targets equal (Definition 1, p. 11; §3.2, p. 12), which lets every item of a bin be programmed to the same value. The hints of all bins are merged into one polynomial over all programmed points, keyed per bin (Definition 2 and Construction 4, pp. 13-14), and security is reduced to a batch PRF (Theorem 5, pp. 14-15).

limitations: the definition is weaker than the earlier one in allowing a single query (§3.2, p. 12)
interpolating a polynomial of degree \( O(n) \) costs \( O(n^2) \) or \( O(n \log^2 n) \) operations, which the protocol reduces by splitting bins into mega-bins (§4.3, p. 18)
qualifiers: one query per programmed function; querying twice could break security when targets are correlated (§3.2, p. 11)
the sets \( X_1, \ldots, X_\beta \) must be disjoint; the protocol appends the bin index to each item (Definition 2, p. 14; Protocol 9, p. 17)
security reduces to a pseudorandom function (Theorems 3 and 5, pp. 12-15) and is proved in the \( F_{\mathrm{OPRF}} \)-hybrid model (Theorem 8, p. 15)
semi-honest parties (§2.2, p. 8)

IACR ePrint 2019/241, PDF dated 2019-02-28.

metadata.statement: A one-time programmable PRF publishes as hint the polynomial interpolated through the points \( (x, F'_k(x) \oplus v) \) for each programmed input x with target \( v \), so that a single evaluation returns \( v \) on programmed inputs and a pseudorandom value elsewhere even when the targets are correlated (Construction 2, Theorem 3); interpolating one polynomial through the points of \( \beta \) such functions with independent keys gives a hint of \( \kappa M \) bits for \( M \) programmed points in total (Construction 4, Theorem 5), and combined with \( \beta \) one-time OPRF instances it securely realizes a batched oblivious programmable PRF in the \( F_{\mathrm{OPRF}} \)-hybrid model (Protocol 7, Theorem 8), so the hints for bins of \( O(\log n / \log \log n) \) items cost \( O(\kappa n) \) in total instead of \( O(\kappa n \log n / \log \log n) \).
metadata.title: Batched OPPRF with a single polynomial hint of \( \kappa M \) bits over all bins, \( M \) the number of programmed points, from a one-time programmable PRF with correlated targets

sections.content: Batched OPPRF
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: In Protocol 7 (p. 16) the parties run \( \beta \) one-time OPRF instances in which the sender receives the keys \( k_j \) and the receiver learns \( F'(k_j, x_j) \); the sender then sends the batched hint polynomial \( P \), and the receiver outputs \( F'(k_j, x_j) \oplus P(x_j) \). The receiver learns \( t_j \) when \( x_j \) is a programmed point of bin j and a pseudorandom value otherwise (Functionality 6, p. 16).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: None: the OPPRF and the one-time OPRF are PSI-specific mechanisms.

historical_context.narrative: Circuit-based PSI had come within a slowly growing factor of linear cost, but two obstacles kept it there: the party that copies each item into all its candidate bins needs bins with room for a logarithmic number of items, and the cuckoo-hashing party has a stash whose items must be compared with everything. Pinkas, Schneider, Tkachenko, and Yanai removed the first obstacle by moving the work out of the circuit: an oblivious programmable PRF maps all of a bin's items to one secret value, so the circuit checks a single equality per bin. They removed the second either by running the protocol again with roles swapped on the stashed items or by using three hash functions and no stash. Communication became linear in the set size, \( O(n\kappa) \), and the measured cost fell several times.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Circuit-Phasing needed \( O(n \log n / \log \log n) \) comparisons because the simple-hashing party fills bins of up to \( O(\log n / \log \log n) \) items, and the private set membership protocol of Ciampi and Orlandi kept that overall communication (§1.1, p. 3). Two-dimensional cuckoo hashing reached \( \omega(n) \) comparisons, with \( s \cdot n \) of them spent on a stash of size \( \omega(1) \) (§1, p. 2; §5, p. 19), and the linear protocol of Falk, Noble, and Ostrovsky achieved \( O(n) \) only when the output is the intersection itself (§5, p. 19).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors call it the first circuit-based PSI with linear communication, matching the obvious lower bound on the number of comparisons (abstract, p. 1; §1.1, p. 4). The stash-less protocol ran 2.8 to 4.2 times faster in the LAN and 3.9 to 5.8 times faster in the WAN setting than the 2D cuckoo-hashing protocol (Table 5, p. 27).
historical_context.technical_delta: Circuit-Phasing's hashing is kept but the per-bin sub-circuit of S comparisons is replaced by a batched OPPRF whose output the circuit compares with one target per bin (§1.1, p. 3; Protocol 9, p. 17). The stash is handled by dual execution, comparing \( X_T \times Y \), \( X_S \times Y_T \), and \( X_S \times Y_S \) in three groups of circuit sections (§5.1, pp. 19-20; Protocol 10), or avoided with \( K = 3 \) hash functions, whose cost the OPPRF makes independent of the bin load (§5.2, pp. 20-21).

limitations: the \( O(n) \) bound concerns symmetric functions; non-symmetric functions or the intersection itself need an \( O(n \log n) \) shuffle (§1.3, p. 5)
the stash-less variant has no analytic failure bound (§5, p. 19)
only the stash-less protocol was implemented; times for the other variants are estimates (§7.4, p. 26)
the stash-less protocol was 41 times slower than BaRK-OPRF PSI for \( n = 2^{20} \) in the WAN setting (§7.4, p. 27)
qualifiers: semi-honest parties (§2.2, p. 8)
both sets have \( n \) items of bitlength \( \sigma \); outputs \( f(X \cap Y) \) to both parties for a symmetric function \( f \) (§1, p. 1; §2.1, p. 8; §1.3, p. 5)
Protocol 10 assumes a stash of size \( O(\log n) \) (§5.1, p. 19)
the stash-less parameters \( K = 3 \) and \( \beta = 1.27n \) rely on the empirical failure analysis of Pinkas, Schneider, and Zohner (§5.2, p. 20; §7.1, p. 22)

OPPRF outputs are truncated to \( \gamma = 40 + \log_2 \beta \) bits, \( \beta \) the number of bins, so a false positive occurs with probability at most \( \beta \cdot 2^{-\gamma} \) (§4.2, p. 18; §7.1, p. 22)
security follows from that of the OPPRF and the two-party computation functionality (§4.1, p. 17; §5.1, p. 20)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 1); §1 (pp. 1-2); §1.1 (pp. 3-4); §1.5 (pp. 7-8); §4.1-4.2 with Protocol 9 (pp. 16-18); §5 with Protocol 10 (pp. 19-21); §7.1 and Table 1 (p. 22); §7.3 and Table 3 (pp. 24-25); §7.4 and Table 5 (pp. 26-28). IACR ePrint 2019/241, PDF dated 2019-02-28.

metadata.statement: Against semi-honest parties with \( n \) items each, letting the sender program a batched OPPRF so that all of its items in a cuckoo bin map to one random target lets the circuit test a single equality per bin; handling the receiver's stash by a second OPPRF phase with the roles reversed, restricted to the stashed items, plus \( s^2 \) comparisons between the two stashes (Protocol 10) yields \( O(n) \) comparisons and \( O(n\kappa) \) communication with failure probability negligible in the statistical security parameter, and the stash-less variant with \( K = 3 \) hash functions and \( 1.27n \) bins, whose failure is below \( 2^{-40} \) by earlier experiments, needs 2,540 MB for \( n = 2^{20} \) and 2.6 to 12.8 times less communication than two-dimensional cuckoo hashing for \( n = 2^{12} \) to \( 2^{20} \).
metadata.title: Circuit-based PSI with \( O(n) \) communication through one OPPRF comparison per bin, semi-honest two-party

sections.content: Circuit-based PSI with linear communication
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: In Protocol 9 (p. 17) the receiver P1 cuckoo-hashes its items into \( \beta = 2(1 + \varepsilon)n \) bins and P2 places each item in both candidate bins; the batched OPPRF gives P1 the value \( y^*_j \), equal to P2's target \( t_j \) when P1's item in bin j is among P2's items there; the circuit compares the first \( \gamma \) bits of \( y^*_j \) and \( t_j \) per bin and every stashed item with all of P2's items. Protocol 10 (p. 20) removes the stash comparisons with a role-reversed second phase. The stash-less version uses \( K = 3 \) hash functions, so the circuit compares \( 1.27n \) values; the OPRF and the hint polynomials are about 4% of its communication (Table 3, p. 25).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-COMP-EVAL-GMW: the circuit is evaluated with GMW (Table 5 caption, p. 27; §2.3, pp. 8-9). MPC-PAPER-2015-ABY and MPC-CONTRIB-2015-ABY-MIXED: the secure circuit evaluation uses the ABY framework (§7.4, p. 27). MPC-PAPER-1987-GMW: GMW protocol, cited as [GMW87] (§2.3, p. 9; §7.3, p. 25).

nodes.summary: Against semi-honest parties with \( n \) items each, letting the sender program a batched OPPRF so that all of its items in a cuckoo bin map to one random target lets the circuit test a single equality per bin; handling the receiver's stash by a second OPPRF phase with the roles reversed, restricted to the stashed items, plus \( s^2 \) comparisons between the two stashes (Protocol 10) yields \( O(n) \) comparisons and \( O(n\kappa) \) communication with failure probability negligible in the statistical security parameter, and the stash-less variant with \( K = 3 \) hash functions and \( 1.27n \) bins, whose failure is below \( 2^{-40} \) by earlier experiments, needs 2,540 MB for \( n = 2^{20} \) and 2.6 to 12.8 times less communication than two-dimensional cuckoo hashing for \( n = 2^{12} \) to \( 2^{20} \).
nodes.title: Circuit-based PSI with \( O(n) \) communication through one OPPRF comparison per bin, semi-honest two-party

historical_context.narrative: Many uses of circuit-based PSI need more than the matching identifiers: an advertiser and a merchant want the total spent by common customers, so each item carries a value that must reach the circuit only when it matches. In the OPPRF approach a bin collapses all of the sender's items to one secret value, which leaves no room for their individual payloads. Pinkas, Schneider, Tkachenko, and Yanai added a second programmable PRF in which each item's target is the bin's mask combined with that item's payload. The receiver's output for a matching item therefore carries the right payload under a mask that only the sender knows and inputs to the circuit, while the circuit still performs one comparison per bin.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Circuit-Phasing and the private set membership approach of Ciampi and Orlandi did not consider payloads (§1.1, p. 4). Two-dimensional cuckoo hashing handles payloads naturally because each comparison involves one item from each party, but the basic OPPRF protocol maps all of a bin's items to one output and cannot encode their different payloads in one value (§6, p. 21).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It supports functions of data associated with intersecting items, such as aggregate revenue over common users, which the authors list among their contributions as unsupported by the Phasing circuit (§1.5, p. 7; §1.2, pp. 4-5).
historical_context.technical_delta: A second batched OPPRF uses non-equal targets, \( \widetilde{t}_j \) XORed with each item's payload, so the receiver's output for a matching item hides exactly that item's payload under \( \widetilde{t}_j \), which the sender inputs to the circuit (§6, p. 21).

limitations: the section describes the payload variant for the cuckoo table and does not discuss stashed items separately (§6, pp. 21-22)
no measurement of the payload variant is reported (§7, pp. 22-28)
qualifiers: all payloads have the same length \( \delta \) (§6, p. 21)
semi-honest parties (§2.2, p. 8)
the circuit has \( O(n(\sigma + \rho)) \) input wires for items of \( \sigma \) bits, \( \rho \) the payload length in bits (§2.1, p. 8)
metadata.statement: In OPPRF-based circuit-PSI, where the sender maps several items with different payloads to one bin, a second batched OPPRF in which the sender programs each item y of bin j to the target \( \widetilde{t}_j \oplus V(y) \) lets the receiver feed its output \( \widetilde{y}_j \) into the circuit, which forwards the receiver's item and payload and the sender's payload \( \widetilde{y}_j \oplus \widetilde{t}_j \) to the function sub-circuit exactly when the per-bin equality test succeeds; the number of comparisons and the asymptotic complexity stay those of the protocol without payloads.

sections.content: Payloads in OPPRF-based circuit-PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: For bin j the receiver inputs its item, its own payload U(item), and the two OPPRF outputs \( y^*_j \) and \( \tilde y_j \); the sender inputs \( t_j \) and \( \tilde t_j \). If \( y^*_j = t_j \) the circuit forwards the item, U(item), and \( \tilde y_j \oplus \tilde t_j \), which equals the sender's payload V(item) (§6, p. 21). The efficiency is that of the basic protocol (§6, p. 22).

historical_context.narrative: Measuring ad conversions requires two companies to learn how many users both saw an ad and bought, and how much those users spent, without exchanging customer lists. Commutative Diffie-Hellman masking had long answered the first half: hashed identifiers raised to both parties' secret exponents can be compared, and shuffling hides which ones matched. Ion and colleagues at Google attached an additively homomorphic encryption of each purchase value to the masked identifier, so the party that finds the matches can add the corresponding ciphertexts without learning any individual value, and only the holder of the key learns the total. The protocol is simple, uses widely deployed primitives, and keeps communication small, which the authors identify as the dominant monetary cost in batch computation between companies.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The Diffie-Hellman set-intersection protocol of Meadows computes the intersection, and Huberman, Franklin, and Hogg added a shuffle so that only its size is learned (§3.1, p. 5; §4.2, p. 8). Neither aggregates values attached to the intersecting items (§3.1, p. 5).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The protocol had been used in practice for several years to attribute aggregate ad conversions (abstract and §1, p. 1); with Paillier encryption a run on 100,000 items per party cost 0.084 US cents in the authors' cost model, and it was 20 to 30 times cheaper in that model than the cheapest garbled-circuit protocol compared (§1, p. 3; Table 2, p. 8; §5.3, p. 12; §6, p. 13).
historical_context.technical_delta: The party holding values sends additively homomorphic encryptions of them alongside its doubly masked identifiers, and the other party sums the ciphertexts whose identifiers match in the shuffled intersection (§3.1, p. 5; Figure 2, p. 6). Security against each party is proved by simulation from the intersection size, and for P2 also the sum (Theorems 1-2, p. 6; Appendix D).

limitations: the intersection size is revealed in addition to the sum (§4.2, p. 9)
no security against malicious parties is claimed (§2.3, p. 4)
the threshold variant only lets P1 abort before the sum is computed if the intersection is too small (§3.4, p. 7)
qualifiers: semi-honest parties (§2.3, p. 4; Theorems 1-2, p. 6)
the hash function H into a DDH group is modeled as a random oracle; a fresh oracle per execution is simulated by prepending a common random seed (§3.1, p. 5; §3.2, pp. 6-7)
P1 learns the intersection size and P2 learns the size and the sum; a reverse variant gives the sum to P1 (Figure 1, p. 3; §3.4, p. 7)
associated values and their sum are assumed small enough not to wrap around the plaintext space (§3.2, p. 7; Appendix A.4, footnote 5)
both parties use the same identifier space; finding one is outside the scope (§2.1, p. 3)

metadata.statement: In the private intersection-sum-with-cardinality functionality, P1 holds identifiers, P2 holds identifier-value pairs, both learn the intersection size, and P2 also learns the sum of values over the intersection; a three-round protocol realizes it against semi-honest parties under DDH with the hash modeled as a random oracle and a CPA-secure additively homomorphic encryption scheme: both parties raise hashed identifiers to secret exponents, the sets are exchanged in shuffled order, P2's identifiers travel with encryptions of their values, and P1 homomorphically adds the ciphertexts of matching items and returns a rerandomized ciphertext for P2 to decrypt; for \( n \) items per party it sends \( 3n \) group elements and \( n + 1 \) ciphertexts.

sections.content: Deployed DDH-based intersection-sum
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Round 1: P1 sends \( H(v_i)^{k_1} \) in shuffled order. Round 2: P2 returns \( H(v_i)^{k_1 k_2} \) shuffled, and sends pairs \( (H(w_j)^{k_2}, \mathrm{AEnc}(t_j)) \) shuffled. Round 3: P1 raises the first components to \( k_1 \), finds the matches, sums their ciphertexts, rerandomizes, and sends the result to P2 (Figure 2, p. 6). The deployment uses the NIST curve prime256v1 with SHA-256 hashing and Paillier with the Damgård-Jurik optimization, packing 65 values per ciphertext (§3.2, pp. 6-7). Variants allow a threshold abort, segmented inputs, and several values per item (§3.4, p. 7).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: PKE-RESULT-1976-DH-INTERACTIVE-PUBLIC-CHANNEL-KEY-AGREEMENT: the DDH assumption is stated with reference to Diffie and Hellman (Appendix A.2, p. 15). HE-RESULT-1999-PAILLIER-PRACTICAL-ADDITIVELY-HOMOMORPHIC-PUBLIC-KEY-ENCRYPTION and he_paillier99: the deployment encrypts the values with Paillier and the Damgård-Jurik optimization (§1, p. 2; §3.2, p. 7; Appendix B.1).

nodes.title: Private intersection-sum with cardinality from Diffie-Hellman double masking and additively homomorphic tags, semi-honest, random oracle model

historical_context.narrative: The fastest set-intersection protocols of the late 2010s replace each party's items by outputs of a batched oblivious PRF computed with random oblivious transfer, after cuckoo hashing places the items into bins. Such protocols expose which items match, so they could not directly compute a sum over a hidden intersection. Ion and colleagues inserted a shuffle: the PRF outputs of the receiving party are encrypted under its own key, masked and permuted by the other party, and so become fresh pseudorandom values in an order the receiver does not know. Encrypted purchase values ride along as tags, and the matching values are summed homomorphically. The result computes the same aggregate as the deployed protocol from symmetric-key oblivious transfer plus homomorphic encryption.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The most efficient PSI protocols evaluated a batched OPRF from random OT per cuckoo bin, building on the hashing of Pinkas, Schneider, Segev, and Zohner and the batched OPRF of Kolesnikov, Kumaresan, Rosulek, and Trieu, but they reveal which items intersect (§1, p. 2; §4.1, pp. 7-8). Circuit-based approaches hid the intersection with a garbled-circuit sub-protocol per bucket (§4.3.1, p. 9).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors believe it is the first construction of private intersection-sum with cardinality from random OT (§4.3.1, p. 9). In their cost model it was cheaper than every garbled-circuit protocol compared but about 15 times more expensive than the deployed Diffie-Hellman protocol (§5.2-5.3, p. 12; Table 7, p. 13).
historical_context.technical_delta: A shuffle step is inserted after the batched OPRF: P1's encrypted OPRF outputs are additively re-masked and permuted by P2, so P1 learns the new OPRF values of its inputs only in shuffled order, and homomorphically encrypted values travel as tags with P2's items (§4.3.1, p. 9; Figure 3, p. 10). Security against each party is proved by simulation from the intersection size and sum (Theorems 3-4, pp. 9-10; Appendix E).

limitations: the intersection size is revealed (§4.2, p. 9)

communication \( 3.6n + 1 \) homomorphic ciphertexts plus random OTs and \( 96n \) bytes for \( n \) items per party, about 15 times that of the deployed protocol in the measurements (Table 4, p. 12; §5.2, p. 12)
qualifiers: semi-honest parties (Theorems 3-4, pp. 9-10)
correctness assumes cuckoo hashing fails and random-OT outputs collide only with negligible probability (§4.3.1, p. 9)
the batched random OT of Kolesnikov et al. yields a relaxed PRF with related keys, which the authors say does not affect their protocol or proofs (Appendix A.6, p. 16)
P1 learns the intersection size and P2 the size and the sum (Figure 1, p. 3; Figure 3, p. 10)

metadata.statement: Against semi-honest parties, private intersection-sum with cardinality can be computed from batched random OT: P1 cuckoo-hashes its identifiers and obtains one OPRF value per bin and stash slot, encrypts these values under its own additively homomorphic key, and P2 adds a fresh random mask to each ciphertext and returns them shuffled, which turns them into evaluations of new, still pseudorandom functions in unknown order; P2 sends, for each of its items, the masked evaluations at all candidate positions together with an encryption of its value under P2's key, and P1 adds the value ciphertexts of items that hit a decrypted evaluation and returns the rerandomized sum for P2 to decrypt.
metadata.title: Private intersection-sum with cardinality from batched random OT with shuffled, re-masked OPRF outputs, semi-honest

sections.content: Random-OT-based intersection-sum
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: P1 cuckoo-hashes into \( b \) bins and a stash of size \( s \); for each of the \( b + s \) positions a random OT gives P2 a key \( k_i \) and P1 the value \( f_{k_i}(v_i) \). P1 sends \( \mathrm{AEnc}(pk_1, f_{k_i}(v_i)) \); P2 adds random \( r_i \), rerandomizes, and returns the ciphertexts shuffled. For each \( (w_j, t_j) \), P2 sends the set \( \{f_{k_i}(w_j) + r_i\} \) over the hash positions and stash slots, padded and in permuted order, with \( \mathrm{AEnc}(pk_2, t_j) \). P1 decrypts the shuffled values, sums the tags of matching items, and sends the rerandomized sum (Figure 3, p. 10). The measured instance uses three hash functions, no stash, at most \( 1.5n \) bins, and the batched random OT of Kolesnikov et al. with 128 base OTs and a 448-bit pseudorandom code (§5.1, p. 11).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-2003-IKNP-OTEXT: the paper describes random OT as a modification of OT extension (§4.1, p. 8) and instantiates it with the batched random OT of Kolesnikov et al. on 128 base public-key OTs (§5.1, p. 11); IKNP itself is not cited by name.

historical_context.narrative: Cuckoo hashing had made semi-honest PSI fast, but a party's choice of bin leaks information about its other items, and garbled Bloom filters, the encodings that suited malicious protocols, cost a factor of \( \lambda \) in size. The garbled cuckoo table removes the choice. Each item becomes an edge between two table positions, and the encoder sets the positions so that their XOR, together with a short random tail, equals the item's value. Positions on acyclic parts of the graph are fixed by a simple traversal, and the few constraints on cycles are solved jointly using the tail. Because a random cuckoo graph has only logarithmically many cycles, the table keeps constant rate with linear-time encoding and probes of \( O(\lambda) \) positions.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Garbled Bloom filters have rate \( \Theta(1/\lambda) \) with \( O(n\lambda) \) encoding and \( \lambda \)-position decoding; a random Boolean matrix has rate \( n/(n + \lambda) \) but \( O(n^3) \) encoding; the Bloomier-filter variant of Charles and Chellapilla encodes in linear time only by re-sampling hash functions until the graph is acyclic, which makes them depend on the input (§3.5, pp. 8-9; Figure 2, p. 9; §5, p. 16).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors present it as matching the encoding and decoding costs of garbled Bloom filters at constant rate, about \( 1/(2 + \varepsilon) \), with hash functions chosen independently of the keys (§5, p. 16; §5.3, pp. 20-21); with \( 2.4n \) main positions it is the encoding of the variant that the authors report as their faster implementation (§7.1, p. 22; §7.3, p. 23).
historical_context.technical_delta: Each key is an edge \( \{h_1(x), h_2(x)\} \), and the table is \( D = L \| R \) with \( |R| = d + \lambda \) (§5.1-5.2, pp. 17-19; Figure 6, p. 19). Theorem 8 (p. 20) bounds the failure probability using Lemma 12 (p. 31), which shows that a cuckoo graph has at most \( \log n \) cycles except with negligible probability. A DFS-based variant handles each back edge with one constraint on R (Appendix B, Figure 7, p. 30; Theorem 11, p. 29).

limitations: the rate is about \( 1/(2 + \varepsilon) \), well below 1 (§5, p. 16; Figure 2, p. 9)
the paper gives asymptotic failure bounds and no concrete failure probability for the \( 2.4n \) setting used in its implementation (Theorem 8, p. 20; §7.1, p. 22)
qualifiers: the failure bound rests on bounding the cyclomatic number of a random \( (n, m) \)-cuckoo graph by \( d = (1 + \varepsilon) \log n \), where \( \varepsilon \) is a positive constant (Theorem 8, p. 20; Lemma 12, p. 31)
Lemma 12 is stated for a cuckoo graph with \( (2 + \varepsilon)n \) nodes; the implementation uses \( 2.4n \) main positions for the 2-core variant and \( 2n \) for the DFS variant (§7.1, p. 22)
items are placed in a global order determined by the graph, unlike the online insertion of garbled Bloom filters (§5.3, p. 20)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 1); Figure 2 (p. 9); §5.1-5.3 (pp. 17-21); Figure 6 (p. 19); Theorem 8 (p. 20); Appendix B, Theorem 11 and Figure 7 (pp. 29-31); Appendix C, Lemma 12 (pp. 31-32); §7.1 (p. 22). IACR ePrint 2020/193, PDF dated 2020-02-16.

metadata.statement: Two hash functions map each key to an edge of a cuckoo graph on the m main positions L, and a random vector r(x) selects positions among \( d + \lambda \) extra positions R. The encoder solves the constraints of the edges in the graph's 2-core by Gaussian elimination over the 2-core positions and R, then fixes every other position by traversing the remaining forest away from the 2-core. With \( d = (1 + \varepsilon) \log n \), where \( \varepsilon \) is a positive constant, this is a PaXoS whose failure probability is the probability that the cyclomatic number of a random cuckoo graph exceeds \( \log n + O(1) \), plus \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (Theorem 8). Encoding costs \( O((d + \lambda)^3 + n\lambda) \), and decoding one key XORs about \( (\lambda + d + 2)/2 \) positions on average.
metadata.title: Garbled cuckoo table: a PaXoS of size \( (2 + \varepsilon)n + d + \lambda \) with \( O(n\lambda) \) encoding and \( O(\lambda) \)-position decoding, hash functions independent of the keys

sections.content: Garbled cuckoo table
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The table has \( m \) main positions and \( d + \lambda \) extra positions. A key x has two main positions \( h_1(x), h_2(x) \) and a random extra vector r(x); its value is the XOR of the two main positions and of the extra positions selected by r(x) (Figure 6, p. 19). Encoding builds the cuckoo graph whose edges are the keys, solves the linear constraints of the edges in its 2-core with Gaussian elimination using the extra positions, picks a root value for every tree component, and then sets each remaining position while traversing edges directed away from the 2-core or the root (Figure 6, steps 1-5, p. 19). The rows of a cycle are linearly dependent in the main part, which is why the random extra part is needed; with at most d cycles the kernel has dimension at most d, and \( d + \lambda \) random columns make the system solvable except with probability \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (Theorem 8 and proof, p. 20). The DFS variant instead adds, for each back edge, one constraint on the extra positions equal to the XOR of the values on that cycle (Appendix B, pp. 29-31). This is the encoding used in PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-MALICIOUS-PAXOS-PSI's implementation.
