historical_context.narrative: Malicious PSI lagged far behind semi-honest PSI. The leading semi-honest protocols relied on cuckoo hashing, which leaks through the choice of bin, and the leading malicious protocol, Rindal and Rosulek's dual execution, paid \( O(n \log n) \) communication for hashing into small bins. Pinkas, Rosulek, Trieu, and Yanai noticed that the outputs of the malicious OOS OT extension are XOR-homomorphic, the property that PaXoS decoding respects. If the receiver feeds an encoding of its hashed items into OOS, both parties can compute the same masked value for a common item, and the sender sends one hash per item. Random-oracle hashing on both sides lets a simulator extract inputs, and changing only the code turns the semi-honest protocol into a malicious one.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Semi-honest OT-based PSI used cuckoo hashing, but in the malicious setting a party's choice of cuckoo location leaks information about its other items, and how to use cuckoo hashing there was unknown (§1, p. 2). The malicious protocol that the authors name the most concretely efficient, Rindal and Rosulek's dual execution, hashes items into \( O(n/\log n) \) bins and has \( O(n \log n) \) communication (§1, p. 2; §1.1, p. 3; Appendix D, pp. 34-35).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors call it the first concretely efficient PSI with linear communication and malicious security in the OT-hybrid model with a non-programmable random oracle, and the first to use cuckoo hashing for malicious PSI (abstract, p. 1; §1.1, pp. 2-3). For \( 2^{20} \) items the malicious 2-core variant sends 202.04 MB against 1,322 MB for the encode-commit variant of Rindal and Rosulek (Table 2, p. 24).
historical_context.technical_delta: The protocol combines the XOR-homomorphism of OOS outputs, which OOS itself uses for a consistency check, with PaXoS decoding (§4.1, pp. 9-10; Figure 3, p. 11). H1 lets the simulator extract a malicious receiver's set from D, and including x in H2 lets it extract a malicious sender's set (§4.2, p. 10); Theorem 4 (p. 10) is proved in Lemmas 5-6 (pp. 12-14). The code and hash lengths select the semi-honest or malicious instantiation (§4.4, pp. 14-16; Figures 4-5, pp. 15-16).

limitations: the introduction states a 25% communication improvement over KKRT for the semi-honest instantiation (§1.1, p. 2), but Table 1 gives about \( 1268n \) bits against \( 1018n \) for KKRT at \( n = 2^{20} \) (p. 21) and §7.3 reports the best variant within 10% above KKRT (p. 23)
in the semi-honest setting the 2-core variant is 18% slower than KKRT on a LAN and about 80% slower over the two WANs for \( 2^{20} \) items (§7.3, p. 23)
the protocol is designed for sets of roughly equal size (Appendix D, p. 36)
qualifiers: static corruption of one of the two parties (§2, p. 5; Theorem 4, p. 10)
OOS is used as an ideal functionality, and H1, H2 are non-programmable random oracles (abstract, p. 1; §4.2, p. 10)

the ideal functionality lets a corrupt party contribute a set of size \( n' > n \); for a malicious receiver the paper bounds \( n' \) between \( 2m \) and \( 5m \), \( m \) the number of PaXoS strings, in its parameter tables (§2, p. 5; Claim 7, p. 15; Figure 5, p. 16)
only the receiver learns the intersection (Figure 1, p. 6)
linear communication means \( O(n\kappa) \); the authors note that concrete hash lengths may involve an \( O(\log n) \) term, as in any intersection protocol (§6, p. 22)

IACR ePrint 2020/193, PDF dated 2020-02-16.

metadata.statement: The receiver encodes the pairs \( (y, H_1(y)) \) for its set into a PaXoS D and uses the strings of D as its choice inputs to the OOS 1-out-of-N OT extension. Because the code C is linear and PaXoS decoding is XOR-homomorphic, the receiver's value \( \mathrm{Decode}(R, x) \) equals \( \mathrm{Decode}(Q, x) \oplus C(H_1(x)) \wedge s \), which the sender can compute, whenever x is in the receiver's set; the sender sends \( H_2(x, \mathrm{Decode}(Q, x) \oplus C(H_1(x)) \wedge s) \) for each of its items. The protocol is a secure two-party PSI against a malicious sender or receiver in the random oracle model with OOS as an ideal functionality, where a corrupt party may use a set of size \( n' > n \) (Theorem 4). The semi-honest instantiation is the same protocol with a shorter code and hash outputs.
metadata.title: Malicious-secure two-party PSI with communication linear in the set size, \( O(\kappa n) \), from any PaXoS and OOS OT extension, random oracle model

sections.content: PaXoS-PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The OOS functionality gives the sender a secret s and strings \( q_i \), and the receiver \( r_i = q_i \oplus C(d_i) \wedge s \) for its choice strings \( d_i \), where C is a linear code of minimum distance at least \( \kappa \) (§2, pp. 4-5). If the receiver's choice strings form a PaXoS D (PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-PAXOS) encoding \( y \mapsto H_1(y) \), then decoding R at x equals decoding Q at x XOR \( C(\mathrm{Decode}(D, x)) \wedge s \), so the two parties obtain the same string for every x in the receiver's set (§4.1, pp. 9-10). For any other x, the difference \( C(\mathrm{Decode}(D, x) \oplus H_1(x)) \) is a nonzero codeword, and the hashed value looks random by the code-correlation robustness of a random oracle (Lemma 1, p. 4; Lemma 5, Hybrid 4, p. 13). The sender sends one hash per item, randomly permuted, and the receiver outputs the items whose own hash appears (Figure 3, p. 11). Semi-honest security needs only H1, H2 outputs of \( \lambda + 2 \log n \) bits; the malicious instantiation lengthens H1 to bound the receiver's effective set (PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-RECEIVER-SET-SIZE-BOUND) and sets H2 to \( 2\kappa \) bits to bound the sender's (§4.4, pp. 14-16). The implementation uses the garbled cuckoo table of PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-GARBLED-CUCKOO; the complete configurations are PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2020-PRTY-SH and PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2020-PRTY-MAL.
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-CONTRIB-2003-IKNP-OTEXT: the protocols compared in the paper reduce PSI to many OTs implemented with OT extension (§1, p. 2); the OOS extension that PaXoS-PSI runs is a 1-out-of-N extension in the IKNP paradigm (§2, p. 4; §4.1, p. 9). OOS itself and the Kolesnikov-Kumaresan paper behind Lemma 1 (p. 4) have no record in any topic yet.

nodes.subtitle: PSI from PaXoS: Fast, Malicious Private Set Intersection
nodes.summary: The receiver encodes the pairs \( (y, H_1(y)) \) for its set into a PaXoS D and uses the strings of D as its choice inputs to the OOS 1-out-of-N OT extension. Because the code C is linear and PaXoS decoding is XOR-homomorphic, the receiver's value \( \mathrm{Decode}(R, x) \) equals \( \mathrm{Decode}(Q, x) \oplus C(H_1(x)) \wedge s \), which the sender can compute, whenever x is in the receiver's set; the sender sends \( H_2(x, \mathrm{Decode}(Q, x) \oplus C(H_1(x)) \wedge s) \) for each of its items. The protocol is a secure two-party PSI against a malicious sender or receiver in the random oracle model with OOS as an ideal functionality, where a corrupt party may use a set of size \( n' > n \) (Theorem 4). The semi-honest instantiation is the same protocol with a shorter code and hash outputs.
nodes.title: Malicious-secure two-party PSI with communication linear in the set size, \( O(\kappa n) \), from any PaXoS and OOS OT extension, random oracle model

historical_context.narrative: Garbled Bloom filters already let a party hide a set of keys inside a table whose values are recovered by XOR, but the table grew with the statistical parameter, and a random linear system, the compact alternative, was too slow to solve for large sets. Pinkas, Rosulek, Trieu, and Yanai isolated what such encodings must provide: a public probing rule, fixed before the inputs are known, whose rows for any \( n \) keys are linearly independent with overwhelming probability, and a decoder that commutes with XOR, linear maps, and bitwise AND. Treating garbled Bloom filters and random matrices as instances of one object let them write a PSI protocol once for any encoding and made rate and encoding time explicit targets for new constructions.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Garbled Bloom filters, introduced by Dong, Chen, and Wen, encode \( n \) items into \( \Theta(\lambda n) \) positions with \( O(n\lambda) \) encoding and decode by XOR of at most \( \lambda \) positions; a random Boolean matrix reaches \( m = n + \lambda \) but needs \( O(n^3) \) Gaussian elimination and decodes by XOR of about \( n/2 \) positions; a Bloomier-filter variant reaches linear time only by choosing hash functions that depend on the input set (§3.5, pp. 8-9; Figure 2, p. 9).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The abstraction separates the PSI protocol from the data structure: the protocol of Figure 3 is written for any PaXoS (§4, pp. 9-11). The authors require the map to be independent of the inputs, since an input-dependent choice would leak them, which excludes the Bloomier-filter variant (§3.1, p. 6; §3.5, p. 9).
historical_context.technical_delta: Definition 3 (p. 6) abstracts these structures as a probe-and-XOR of strings, with Encode solving a linear system and Decode computing the inner product of v(x) with the data structure (§3.2, pp. 6-7); §3.3 (p. 7) states the homomorphic properties that the PSI protocol uses, and §3.4 (pp. 7-8) names rate, encoding cost, and decoding cost as the efficiency measures.

limitations: Definition 3 requires only linear independence of the probe vectors; it defines no hiding property for the encoded data structure (Definition 3, p. 6)
rate and encoding cost are efficiency measures, not part of the definition; a random matrix satisfies the definition with poor encoding cost (§3.1, p. 6; §3.5, p. 8)
qualifiers: failure probability \( 2^{-\lambda} \) over the choice of the random function H (Definition 3, p. 6)
the probing rule must not depend on the inputs; the Bloomier-filter variant of Charles and Chellapilla is not a PaXoS for this reason (§3.1, p. 6; §3.5, pp. 8-9)
values are bit strings and decoding uses only 0/1 coefficients (§3.2, pp. 6-7)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 1); §1.1 (p. 2); Definition 3 (p. 6); §3.2-3.4 (pp. 6-8); §3.5 and Figure 2 (pp. 8-9). IACR ePrint 2020/193, PDF dated 2020-02-16.

metadata.statement: An \( (n, m, 2^{-\lambda}) \)-PaXoS is a randomized map v from strings to m-bit vectors such that, for any \( n \) distinct inputs, the vectors are linearly independent except with probability \( 2^{-\lambda} \) over the random function. It encodes \( n \) key-value pairs as m strings D by solving \( M \cdot D = (y_1, \ldots, y_n) \), and decodes a key x as the XOR of the positions of D selected by v(x). Decoding commutes with XOR of two encodings, with linear maps, and with bitwise AND by a fixed string, and the map is fixed independently of the inputs.
metadata.title: Probe-and-XOR of strings (PaXoS): an input-independent binary key-value encoding with XOR-homomorphic decoding

sections.content: Probe-and-XOR of strings
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: A PaXoS is given by a probe function v that maps each string to an m-bit vector (Definition 3, p. 6). To encode pairs \( (x_i, y_i) \), the encoder forms the matrix whose rows are \( v(x_i) \) and solves for \( D = (d_1, \ldots, d_m) \) with \( M \cdot D = (y_1, \ldots, y_n) \); to decode x, one XORs the positions \( d_j \) with \( v(x)_j = 1 \) (§3.2, pp. 6-7). Decoding can be applied to any string, not only to encoded keys. Because decoding is linear over \( \mathrm{GF}(2) \), it commutes with XOR of two encodings, with any linear map applied position by position, and with bitwise AND by a fixed string (§3.3, p. 7); these are the properties that the PSI protocol of PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-MALICIOUS-PAXOS-PSI combines with the outputs of OT extension. The paper measures a PaXoS by its rate \( n/m \), its encoding cost, and its decoding cost (§3.4, pp. 7-8), and lists random matrices and garbled Bloom filters as instances (§3.5, p. 8). The construction of the same paper that achieves constant rate with linear-time encoding is PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-GARBLED-CUCKOO.

historical_context.narrative: In malicious PSI a simulator must read off the set that a corrupt receiver effectively used, and an encoding sized for \( n \) items might be crafted to agree with a random oracle on more of them. Pinkas, Rosulek, Trieu, and Yanai bounded this slack without any computational assumption. A PaXoS of m strings that matched the oracle on many queried points could be used to describe the oracle in fewer bits than it contains, which is possible only with small probability. For practical parameters the extracted set exceeds a small multiple of m with probability below \( 2^{-40} \), at the price of longer oracle outputs and longer codewords in the malicious instantiation.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Malicious PSI functionalities, as in Rindal and Rosulek's protocols, already let a corrupt party use more items than it advertises (§2, p. 5). In PaXoS-PSI the simulator extracts a malicious receiver's set as the queried y with \( \mathrm{Decode}(D, y) = H_1(y) \), and the protocol by itself does not limit how many such y a crafted D satisfies (§4.4, p. 15).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The bound fixes the slack between the advertised and extracted set sizes in the malicious instantiation and is why its hash outputs and codewords are longer than in the semi-honest one (§4.4, pp. 14-16; Figures 4-5, pp. 15-16); it applies only once \( n' \) exceeds m, since a structure of m strings can always encode m values (§4.4, p. 16).
historical_context.technical_delta: Claim 7 (p. 15), proved as Lemma 10 (pp. 27-29), shows that a D agreeing with H1 on many queried points would compress H1, which Proposition 9 (p. 27) rules out; Figure 5 (p. 16) turns the bound into parameters with probability below \( 2^{-40} \) of extracting more than \( n' \) items, for \( n' \) from \( 2m \) to \( 5m \) and \( 2^{128} \) queries.

limitations: the bound allows the extracted set to exceed the advertised size by a constant factor; it does not enforce \( n' = n \) (§4.3, p. 10; §4.4, p. 16)
the sender side is handled separately by choosing H2 outputs of \( 2\kappa \) bits so that collisions are negligible (§4.4, p. 15)
qualifiers: random oracle model; the probability is over H1 and holds against unbounded adversaries making \( Q \) queries (Claim 7, p. 15; Lemma 10, pp. 27-29)
the parameters of Figure 5 assume \( 2^{128} \) queries; the authors note that \( 2^{80} \) queries would allow \( \ell_1 \) of 70 to 90 bits (p. 16, footnote 4)

source_locator.primary_source: §2 (p. 5); §4.3 (p. 10); §4.4, Claim 7 (p. 15); Figure 5 (p. 16); Appendix A, Proposition 9 and Lemma 10 (pp. 27-29). IACR ePrint 2020/193, PDF dated 2020-02-16.

metadata.statement: If an adversary makes \( Q \) queries to a random oracle H1 with \( \ell_1 \)-bit outputs and then outputs a PaXoS D of m strings, the probability that \( \mathrm{Decode}(D, y) = H_1(y) \) holds for at least \( n' \) of the queried values y is at most the binomial coefficient \( \binom{Q}{n'} \) divided by \( 2^{(n' - m)\ell_1} \). The bound is information-theoretic and bounds the set that the simulator extracts from a malicious receiver in PaXoS-PSI; it constrains \( n' \) only when \( n' \) exceeds m.
metadata.title: Bound on the number of random-oracle values a malicious receiver can encode in a PaXoS of m strings, by an incompressibility argument

sections.content: Bound on a malicious receiver's effective set
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The proof builds a compression scheme for the random oracle H1 from any adversary that produces a PaXoS consistent with H1 on \( n' \) queried points (Lemma 10, pp. 27-29). The compressed description lists D (\( m \cdot \ell_1 \) bits), the indices of the \( n' \) consistent queries, and the oracle answers for all other points; the decompressor recovers each consistent answer by decoding D. Proposition 9 (p. 27) bounds the success probability of any such scheme by the ratio of description sizes, which yields the stated bound. The simulator of PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-MALICIOUS-PAXOS-PSI extracts exactly this set from a malicious receiver (Lemma 5, p. 12), so the bound determines how many items a corrupt receiver can test. Figure 5 (p. 16) lists, for PaXoS sizes \( m \) from \( 2^{12} \) to \( 2^{24} \), output lengths \( \ell_1 \) from 129 to 233 bits and the corresponding codes for extracted sets of size \( 2m \) to \( 5m \).

historical_context.narrative: Threshold PSI had been defined for two parties, where saying that each set is close to the intersection and saying that the two sets are close to each other amount to the same thing. With more parties the two readings separate: if each of \( \ell \) parties holds \( t \) elements that no one else has, every set lies within \( t \) of the intersection, yet the union exceeds it by \( \ell t \) elements. Badrinarayanan, Miao, Raghuraman, and Rindal therefore defined two multiparty functionalities, one requiring every party's set to lie within \( t \) of the intersection and one requiring the union to lie within \( t \) of it, with matching tests that only reveal whether the condition holds. Applications choose between them, and the known techniques reach them from different assumptions.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Ghosh and Simkin defined two-party threshold PSI, releasing the intersection when the symmetric set difference is small, and studied its communication (§1, p. 2). Earlier threshold PSI protocols computed the cardinality first and compared it with the threshold (§1, p. 2).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The distinction organizes the paper's results: both functionalities need \( \Omega(\ell t) \) communication and admit \( O(\ell t) \) from threshold FHE, but only the union-based one has a protocol from threshold additively homomorphic encryption (Table 1, p. 3).
historical_context.technical_delta: The two-party condition is generalized in two inequivalent ways, by each party's distance to the intersection and by the union's distance to it, with ideal functionalities for threshold PSI and for cardinality testing in the UC framework (§1.1, p. 2; §2.3-2.4, pp. 6-7; Figures 1-4).

limitations: the functionalities are defined for sets of equal size (§2.3, p. 6)
qualifiers: all sets have the same size \( n \) and elements lie in a field \( \mathbb{F}_p \) with \( p \) a \( \Theta(\kappa) \)-bit prime (§2.3, p. 6)
with equal set sizes, under \( F_{\text{TPSI-int}} \) either all parties learn the output or none does (§2.3, p. 6)
which functionality and threshold to use depends on the application (§1.1, pp. 2-3)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 1); §1.1 (pp. 2-3); §2.3 with Figures 1-2 (p. 6); §2.4 with Figures 3-4 (pp. 6-7); Table 1 (p. 3). IACR ePrint 2020/600, PDF dated 2021-02-25.

metadata.statement: For \( \ell \) parties each holding \( n \) elements with intersection I, \( F_{\text{TPSI-int}} \) releases I to every party if and only if \( |S_i \setminus I| \le t \) for all i, equivalently \( |I| \ge n - t \), and \( F_{\text{TPSI-diff}} \) releases I if and only if \( |(S_1 \cup \cdots \cup S_\ell) \setminus I| \le t \); for two parties the conditions coincide up to the factor 2 in \( |(S_1 \cup S_2) \setminus I| = 2|S_i \setminus I| \), while for \( \ell > 2 \) only \( 2|S_i \setminus I| \le |(\cup S_i) \setminus I| \le \ell|S_i \setminus I| \) holds, so the two can lead to very different outcomes; matching cardinality-testing functionalities \( F_{\text{CTest-int}} \) and \( F_{\text{CTest-diff}} \) output only similar or different.
metadata.title: Two multiparty threshold PSI functionalities: release when every party's set is close to the intersection, or when the union is close to it

historical_context.narrative: Once two-party threshold PSI was known to need communication linear in the threshold, the multiparty question was whether more parties must pay proportionally more. Badrinarayanan, Miao, Raghuraman, and Rindal answered with a simple simulation argument: if any one party could take part while exchanging \( o(t) \) bits, a two-party protocol could be built in which one side plays that party and the other plays everyone else, and that protocol would beat the two-party bound. Every party therefore carries \( \Omega(t) \) communication, and with only point-to-point channels the total is \( \Omega(\ell t) \). A separate reduction from multiparty set disjointness gives a weaker bound when broadcast is available, a setting the authors leave for further study.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Ghosh and Simkin proved an \( \Omega(t) \) lower bound for two-party threshold PSI (§1, p. 2; §3.5, p. 15). No multiparty bound was known; the paper asks whether sublinear lower and upper bounds extend to more parties (§1, p. 2).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: Together with the paper's \( O(\ell t) \) protocols from threshold FHE, the bound settles the point-to-point communication complexity of both functionalities up to the omitted \( \mathrm{poly}(\kappa) \) factor (Table 1, p. 3).
historical_context.technical_delta: A protocol in which some party \( P_{i^*} \) communicates \( o(T) \) is turned into a two-party threshold PSI protocol by letting one party emulate \( P_{i^*} \) and the other emulate all remaining parties with the same input, contradicting the two-party bound (Theorem 4.1, pp. 15-16; Theorem 4.3, pp. 16-17). The broadcast bound reduces multiparty set disjointness, whose complexity Braverman and Oshman showed to be \( \Omega(N \log n + n) \), to \( F_{\text{TPSI-int}} \) with \( T = N - 1 \) (Theorem C.1, pp. 40-42).

limitations: the point-to-point bound does not necessarily apply with broadcast channels (Appendix C, p. 40)
a broadcast lower bound for \( F_{\text{TPSI-diff}} \) is left open (Appendix C, p. 42)
qualifiers: semi-honest adversary corrupting up to \( \ell - 1 \) parties (Theorems 4.1 and 4.3, pp. 15-16)
a party's communication counts both incoming and outgoing messages (footnote 7, p. 15)
the \( \Omega(\ell t) \) total holds for point-to-point networks, which include the star network (§1.1, p. 4; §4, p. 15)
the broadcast bound is proved only for \( F_{\text{TPSI-int}} \) (Theorem C.1, p. 40)

metadata.statement: In any multiparty threshold PSI protocol for \( F_{\text{TPSI-int}} \) or \( F_{\text{TPSI-diff}} \) secure against a semi-honest adversary corrupting up to \( \ell - 1 \) of \( \ell \) parties, every party sends and receives \( \Omega(t) \) bits, so in a network of point-to-point channels the total communication is \( \Omega(\ell t) \) (Theorems 4.1 and 4.3, Corollaries 4.2 and 4.4); in the broadcast model any protocol for \( F_{\text{TPSI-int}} \) needs \( \Omega(t \log \ell + \ell) \) (Theorem C.1).

sections.content: \( \Omega(\ell t) \) lower bound for multiparty threshold PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: For \( F_{\text{TPSI-int}} \), the emulating parties learn the output iff \( |X_1 \setminus I| \le t \), which for equal set sizes is the two-party condition \( |(X_1 \setminus X_2) \cup (X_2 \setminus X_1)| \le 2t \); for \( F_{\text{TPSI-diff}} \) the reduction yields the two-party condition with threshold \( t \) (§4.1-4.2, pp. 15-17). Corruption of either emulating party is simulated by corrupting \( P_{i^*} \) alone or all other parties (Theorem 4.1, p. 15).

historical_context.narrative: The two-party threshold PSI protocol from additively homomorphic encryption had communication quadratic in the threshold, \( \tilde O(t^2) \), because its cardinality test checked singularity of a general encrypted matrix. Badrinarayanan, Miao, Raghuraman, and Rindal observed that the matrix in question is a Hankel matrix, determined by a linear number of entries, and that a classical result of Brent, Gustavson, and Yun ties its singularity to a half-GCD computation that runs in quasi-linear time. Shared among the parties and tested with a garbled circuit or homomorphic evaluation, the test costs quasi-linear communication. Combined with an encoding whose monomials count the elements outside the intersection across all parties, this gave a multiparty protocol without fully homomorphic encryption and, for two parties, quasi-linear communication in the threshold, \( \tilde O(t) \).
historical_context.prior_boundary: Ghosh and Simkin's two-party threshold PSI from additively homomorphic encryption cost \( \tilde O(t^2) \), dominated by the Kiltz-Mohassel-Weinreb-Franklin singularity test for arbitrary matrices, and they left \( \tilde O(t) \) from assumptions weaker than FHE open (§1, p. 2; §1.2, p. 4; §3.3, p. 13).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The paper states that the case \( \ell = 2 \) solves the Ghosh-Simkin open problem (abstract, p. 1; §1.2, p. 4; §3.3, p. 13). Its multiparty protocol is computationally more efficient than the threshold-FHE protocol and almost matches the \( \Omega(\ell t) \) bound (abstract, p. 1; §1.1, p. 3).
historical_context.technical_delta: The \( (t + 1) \times (t + 1) \) Hankel matrix has only \( 2t + 1 \) distinct entries, and by Brent, Gustavson, and Yun their singularity reduces to a half-GCD computation of \( O(t \log^2 t) \) cost (Imported Theorems 6.1-6.3, p. 25). The parties share the Hankel matrix additively and run \( F_{\mathrm{SingTest}} \), instantiated either by homomorphic evaluation following Franklin-Haber and Cramer-Damgård-Nielsen, with \( O(t \log^2 t) \) rounds, or by jointly generating a Yao garbled circuit for the test, with \( O(1) \) rounds (§6.1, pp. 25-26; Figure 8 and Theorem 6.5, p. 27).

limitations: only \( F_{\text{TPSI-diff}} \) is covered; for \( F_{\text{TPSI-int}} \) a protocol from threshold additively homomorphic encryption is marked unknown (Table 1, p. 3; §1.1, p. 4)
no security against malicious parties is claimed (§1.1, p. 3)
no implementation or measurement is reported (§§6-7, pp. 24-30)
qualifiers: semi-honest adversary corrupting up to \( \ell - 1 \) parties (Theorem 7.1, p. 28)

Theorem 6.5 is proved in the \( F_{\mathrm{SingTest}} \)-hybrid model and needs a prime \( r > t(t + 1)(p - 1)2^{\lambda} \); the sparsity test errs with probability at most \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (Imported Theorem 6.4 and Theorem 6.5, p. 27)
the constant-round singularity test assumes a PRG computable in \( \mathrm{NC}^1 \) (§6.1, p. 26)
threshold additive homomorphic encryption can be obtained from ElGamal under DDH or Paillier under decisional composite residuosity (§2.6, p. 10)
\( \tilde O \) hides polylogarithmic factors and the bounds omit \( \mathrm{poly}(\kappa) \) (footnote 1, p. 3)

in the two-party case \( F_{\mathrm{SingTest}} \) uses Yao's garbled circuits with communication \( \tilde O(t \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\kappa)) \) for the \( (t + 1) \times (t + 1) \) Hankel matrix (§6.1, p. 26), and the second phase uses additively homomorphic encryption with Alice holding the secret key, at \( O(t \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\kappa)) \) (§7.1, p. 29)

sections.content: \( \tilde O(\ell t) \) threshold PSI from threshold additively homomorphic encryption
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: \( \Pi_{\text{CTest-diff}} \) (Figure 8, p. 27): the central party picks u; party 1 encodes its set as \( \sum (\ell - 1)x^a \) and every other party as \( -\sum x^a \); each party evaluates its polynomial at \( u^0, \ldots, u^{2t} \), and these values define additive shares of the Hankel matrix H; \( F_{\mathrm{SingTest}} \) reports whether H is singular, which happens exactly when the encoding has at most \( t \) monomials, except with probability \( 2^{-\lambda} \). If the test passes, the second phase of Figure 9 (p. 30) computes the intersection. The communication is \( \tilde O(\ell \cdot t \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\kappa)) \) with \( O(1) \) rounds (Corollaries 6.6 and 7.2, p. 28).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-COMP-EVAL-YAO and MPC-COMP-ENC-GARBLED: the constant-round singularity test generates and evaluates a Yao garbled circuit, and the two-party test uses Yao's garbled circuits, cited as [Yao86] (§6.1, p. 26; §3.3, p. 13). HE-RESULT-1999-PAILLIER-PRACTICAL-ADDITIVELY-HOMOMORPHIC-PUBLIC-KEY-ENCRYPTION: Paillier is named as a basis for threshold additive homomorphic encryption (§2.6, p. 10).

historical_context.narrative: Two-party threshold PSI from fully homomorphic encryption had shown that communication can depend on the threshold alone, but extending it to many parties raised a subtle problem: adding the set polynomials of several parties may cancel roots by accident, so a test based on the degree of a rational function can wrongly report that the sets are close. Badrinarayanan, Miao, Raghuraman, and Rindal multiplied each party's polynomial by a random linear factor, which makes such cancellations negligible, and ran the test under threshold fully homomorphic encryption with one central party. A second phase, built only on threshold additively homomorphic encryption and economical in randomizing polynomials, then lets every party recover its own excess elements, so total communication meets the lower bound.
historical_context.prior_boundary: For two parties, Ghosh and Simkin obtained communication \( O(t) \) from FHE by homomorphically interpolating the ratio of the two set polynomials and checking it at a random point (§1, p. 2; §3.1, p. 11). Summing several parties' polynomials in the numerator can cancel roots, so the natural multiparty extension may accept sets that differ too much (§3.1, pp. 11-12).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The protocols match the \( \Omega(\ell t) \) lower bound for both functionalities up to the omitted \( \mathrm{poly}(\kappa) \) factor, and their communication does not depend on the set size (Table 1, p. 3; §1.2, p. 4).
historical_context.technical_delta: Each party multiplies its set polynomial by a random linear factor \( (x - r_i) \), which makes accidental cancellation negligible (Lemma 2.4, p. 10; §3.1, p. 12); for \( F_{\text{CTest-diff}} \) the central party instead interpolates \( p_i/p_1 \) for every i and counts the union of differences under encryption (§3.2, p. 12; §5.2, pp. 21-23). The second phase lets each party contribute two randomizing polynomials, reducing \( O(\ell^2 t) \) to \( O(\ell t) \) communication (§3.4, p. 14; Figure 9, p. 30).

limitations: no security against malicious parties is claimed (§1.1, p. 3)
relies on threshold FHE for the cardinality test; for \( F_{\text{TPSI-int}} \) no protocol from weaker assumptions is given (Table 1, p. 3)
qualifiers: semi-honest adversary corrupting up to \( \ell - 1 \) parties (Theorems 7.1 and B.1, pp. 28, 40)
\( \ell \)-out-of-\( \ell \) threshold FHE with distributed setup, available from circular-secure LWE (Imported Theorem 2.2, p. 9; footnote 4)
star network with a designated central party; not all parties need be online at once (§1.1, p. 4; §2.3, p. 6)
the bounds omit a \( \mathrm{poly}(\kappa) \) factor (footnote 1, p. 3)
equal set sizes \( n \) and a field of order \( \Omega(2^{\kappa}) \) (§2.3, p. 6; Figure 5, p. 18)

metadata.statement: Assuming \( \ell \)-out-of-\( \ell \) threshold FHE with distributed setup, both \( F_{\text{TPSI-int}} \) and \( F_{\text{TPSI-diff}} \) are securely realized against a semi-honest adversary corrupting up to \( \ell - 1 \) parties in a star network with communication \( O(\ell \cdot t \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\kappa)) \) and \( O(1) \) rounds: each party sends encrypted evaluations of its set polynomial, randomized by a factor \( (x - r_i) \), to a central party that homomorphically interpolates and tests a rational function, the parties jointly decrypt one bit, and if the test passes a second phase from threshold additively homomorphic encryption gives every party \( 3t + 4 \) evaluations of a randomized combination of all set polynomials, from which it interpolates \( S_i \setminus I \).
metadata.title: Multiparty threshold PSI with \( O(\ell t) \) communication and \( O(1) \) rounds from threshold FHE, matching the \( \Omega(\ell t) \) bound, semi-honest

sections.content: \( O(\ell t) \) multiparty threshold PSI from threshold FHE
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: \( \Pi_{\text{TFHE-CTest-int}} \) (Figure 5, p. 18): each party sends encryptions of \( p'_i(j) = p_i(j)(x - r_i) \) evaluated at \( j = 1, \ldots, 2t + 3 \) and at a random z; the central party interpolates \( (p'_2 + \cdots + p'_\ell)/p'_1 \) homomorphically, compares it with the value at z, and the parties decrypt the resulting bit (§5.1, p. 17). \( \Pi_{\text{TFHE-CTest-diff}} \) (Figure 6) interpolates \( p_i/p_1 \) for each i (§5.2, pp. 21-23). The second phase, \( \Pi_{\text{TPSI-diff}} \) (Figure 9, p. 30) and \( \Pi_{\text{TPSI-int}} \) (Figure 10, p. 41), evaluates \( V(x) = \sum p'_i(x) U_i(x) \) at \( 3t + 4 \) points under threshold additively homomorphic encryption.
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: TSIG-PAPER-2018-BGGJKRS: the threshold FHE with distributed setup follows the definition of Boneh et al. and is instantiated by their scheme (§2.5, p. 7; Imported Theorem 2.2, p. 9). HE-RESULT-1999-PAILLIER-PRACTICAL-ADDITIVELY-HOMOMORPHIC-PUBLIC-KEY-ENCRYPTION: Paillier, like ElGamal, can be converted into the threshold additively homomorphic encryption used in the second phase (§2.6, p. 10).

historical_context.narrative: In homomorphic PSI with a small client set, the client's upload is dominated by the extra encrypted powers it sends so that the server can stay within a shallow circuit, and their number grows with the logarithm of the server's bin size. Cong and coauthors observed that the Frobenius automorphism, available in BGV and BFV, raises an encrypted value to a power of the plaintext modulus without consuming depth. With a small modulus, the server can then build every power it needs from a constant number of ciphertexts, and the upload becomes nearly independent of the server's set size. Their prototype in HElib kept online communication under one megabyte for server sets of up to tens of millions of items, but the server computation took minutes, so the variant demonstrates a communication bound rather than a deployable protocol.
historical_context.prior_boundary: With windowing, the earlier protocols need \( O(\log B) \) encrypted powers, \( B \) the bin size, for the sender to compute all powers up to \( B \) at depth \( O(\log \log B) \), which gives communication \( \tilde O(2^C C^2) \) for \( C = \log \log n_X \) (§1.2, p. 3; §3.1, p. 11).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: For 210 receiver items, online communication stays at 0.76 MB for sender sets of \( 2^{22} \) to \( 2^{26} \) items, which the authors compare with 18.32 MB for 128 receiver items in the earlier protocol at \( 2^{24} \) (abstract, p. 1; Table 6, p. 20). Evaluation keys of 6 to 9 MB are sent once (Table 5, p. 19). Sender online time is 38.7 s at \( 2^{20} \) and 354 s at \( 2^{24} \) on 24 threads (Table 8, p. 27), and the authors call the variant not practical today (§6, p. 20).
historical_context.technical_delta: A Frobenius operation costs about one key switch, adds only additive noise, and is counted as depth-free (§2.3, p. 5). Lemma 2 (p. 12, proved in Appendix C) gives the number \( e_D \) of consecutive powers reachable at depth D, so \( O(1) \) encrypted powers suffice (§3.1, pp. 11-12). The HElib implementation over BGV, whose cyclotomic order can be chosen freely, demonstrates the effect without partitioning or windowing and without implementing the OPRF or networking (§5, p. 15; §5.4, pp. 18-19).

limitations: the HElib implementation does not implement the OPRF or networking; communication is computed from ciphertext sizes plus 32 bytes of OPRF per receiver item (§5, p. 15)
sender online computation is impractically high on current CPUs (abstract, p. 1; Table 8, p. 27; §6, p. 20)
the comparison with the earlier protocol uses public-key-mode sizes supplied by its authors and different receiver set sizes (§5.4, p. 19; Table 6, p. 20)
qualifiers: requires a small plaintext modulus \( p \); the number of SIMD slots is the ring dimension divided by \( d \), \( d \) the order of \( p \) modulo the cyclotomic order \( m \), so smaller \( p \) gives fewer slots (§3.1, p. 12)

the receiver sends \( \lfloor \log_p B \rfloor \) Frobenius evaluation keys, \( B \) the bin size, or one key at the cost of more Frobenius operations; keys are independent of the receiver's set and can be cached (§3.1, p. 12; §5.4, p. 19)
SEAL's fixed ring orders leave no suitable small primes, so the technique was implemented only in HElib (§5, p. 15)
the HElib runs use 80-bit hashed items, \( \alpha = 1 \), no windowing or postage-stamp bases, and parameters with at least 128-bit security except one set at 106 bits (§5.4, p. 19; Table 6, p. 20)

metadata.statement: Since the Frobenius automorphism maps an encryption of y to an encryption of \( y^{p^i} \) without consuming a multiplicative level, the sender can compute all powers \( y, y^2, \ldots, y^{e_D} \) within depth D from the single ciphertext of y (Lemma 2), so evaluating the intersection circuit at depth \( O(\log \log n_X) \) needs only \( O(1) \) query ciphertexts, and the communication complexity becomes \( \tilde O(C^2) \) with \( C = \log \log n_X \) instead of \( \tilde O(2^C C^2) \); the receiver must also send Frobenius evaluation keys, which the sender can cache, and a small plaintext modulus reduces the number of SIMD slots.
metadata.title: Online communication nearly constant in the larger set for FHE-based unbalanced PSI, from depth-free Frobenius powers

sections.content: Depth-free Frobenius powers
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: With plaintext modulus \( p \), the Frobenius operation maps an encryption of y to an encryption of \( y^{p^i} \) by a permutation of the Double-CRT representation and a key switch (§2.3, p. 5). For \( p = 2 \), from y alone the sender obtains \( y^2 \), \( y^4 \), \( y^8 \) at depth zero, the odd powers up to 15 at depth at most two, and the remaining low and high powers of Paterson-Stockmeyer evaluation by further Frobenius maps, so a degree-255 polynomial is evaluated at depth three from one ciphertext (Example 2, p. 11). Lemma 2 (p. 12) generalizes the count to any \( p \) and depth \( D \).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: HE-PAPER-2012-GHS-AES: the Frobenius operation and the Double-CRT representation are used as described by Gentry, Halevi, and Smart, cited as [27] (§2.3, p. 5). HE-PAPER-2012-BGV: the low-communication variant is implemented over BGV in HElib (§2.3, p. 4; §5, p. 14).

nodes.title: Online communication nearly constant in the larger set for FHE-based unbalanced PSI, from depth-free Frobenius powers

historical_context.narrative: Homomorphic PSI with a small client set evaluates, for every bin of the server's hash table, a polynomial whose roots are the bin's items, and the earlier protocols did so by computing every power of the client's encrypted value, one ciphertext multiplication per power. With bins of a few thousand items these multiplications dominated the server's online work. Cong and coauthors applied the classic Paterson-Stockmeyer method: compute about the square root of the degree in low powers and as many high powers, combine the low powers with plaintext coefficients, which is cheap, and multiply only by the high powers. The number of expensive multiplications drops from linear to square root in the bin size, from about \( B \) to \( O(\sqrt{B}) \) for \( B \) the bin size, costing at most one extra level of depth, and it combines with partitioning.
historical_context.prior_boundary: In the protocols of Chen et al., the sender computes all powers of the receiver's encrypted item up to \( \lceil B/\alpha \rceil \) for \( \alpha \) partitions of a bin of size \( B \), using \( \lceil B/\alpha \rceil - 1 \) non-scalar multiplications, so computation is \( O(n_X) \) homomorphic multiplications with depth \( O(\log \log n_X) \) (§1.1, p. 3; §3.1, p. 7). When \( B \) is in the thousands and \( \alpha \) about ten, these multiplications can dominate the online time (§3.1, p. 7).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors call the result a quadratic improvement in homomorphic multiplications over the earlier labeled-PSI protocol (§1.2, p. 3). With all their optimizations, for \( 2^{28} \) sender items and 2048 receiver items they report 4.75 s sender online time on 24 threads against 28.5 s on 32 threads, and 15.09 MB against 22.28 MB of online communication (Table 2, p. 17).
historical_context.technical_delta: The intersection polynomial is rewritten as a sum over i of \( y^{iL} \) times an inner sum of low powers with plaintext coefficients, so only the multiplications by high powers are non-scalar (eq. (2), p. 8). The count is \( L + 2H - 4 \) (eq. (3), p. 8), or \( L_\alpha + (\alpha + 1)H_\alpha - (\alpha + 3) \) with partitioning (eq. (4), p. 8), with the optimum derived in Appendix A; Lemma 1 (p. 9) bounds the receiver powers needed for a target depth.

limitations: the reported speedups combine this method with the other optimizations of the paper and different FHE parameters, so they are not attributable to it alone (§5.1, p. 15; Table 2, p. 17)
the comparison runs use 24 threads against the earlier protocol's 32, on machines the authors assume comparable (§5, p. 14; Table 1, p. 16)
qualifiers: costs are counted in non-scalar multiplications, which dominate both running time and noise growth (§2.3, p. 5)
the slightly faster original Paterson-Stockmeyer variant is not used, because the coefficient ring \( R_p \), \( p \) the plaintext modulus, is not Euclidean (§3.1, p. 8)

with partitioning the naive method can need fewer multiplications for larger \( \alpha \); Example 1 (p. 8) shows the crossover at \( \alpha = 6 \) for \( B = 81 \), and Appendix A gives the general condition

metadata.statement: In FHE-based unbalanced PSI, the sender can evaluate each bin's intersection polynomial of degree \( B = LH - 1 \) on the receiver's encrypted item by computing the low powers \( y^2, \ldots, y^{L-1} \) and the high powers \( y^L, \ldots, y^{(H-1)L} \) and summing high powers times scalar combinations of low powers, which costs \( L + 2H - 4 \) ciphertext-ciphertext (non-scalar) multiplications, minimal \( O(\sqrt{B}) \) for \( L \approx \sqrt{2(B + 1)} \), instead of the \( \lceil B/\alpha \rceil - 1 \) needed to compute all powers for \( \alpha \) partitions; with partitioning the count is \( L_\alpha + (\alpha + 1)H_\alpha - (\alpha + 3) \), the depth grows by at most one, and the protocol needs \( O(\sqrt{n_X}) \) homomorphic multiplications.
metadata.title: \( O(\sqrt{B}) \) ciphertext-ciphertext multiplications per sender bin, \( B \) the bin size, in FHE-based unbalanced PSI, by Paterson-Stockmeyer evaluation of the intersection polynomial

sections.content: Paterson-Stockmeyer evaluation of the intersection polynomial
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Choose \( L \) and \( H \) with \( B = LH - 1 \). The sender computes \( y^2, \ldots, y^{L-1} \) and \( y^L, y^{2L}, \ldots, y^{(H-1)L} \), and evaluates P(y) as the sum over \( i < H \) of \( y^{iL} \cdot \sum_{j<L} a_{iL+j} y^j \), where the inner sums use only scalar multiplications and additions (eq. (2), p. 8). The depth is \( \lceil \log((H - 1)L + 1) \rceil + 1 \), at most one more than computing a degree-\( B \) polynomial directly, and window powers sent by the receiver lower it further (§3.1, p. 9). For \( B = 81 \), the method needs 23 multiplications without partitioning against 80 for computing all powers (Example 1, p. 8).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: HE-PAPER-2012-FV and HE-PAPER-2012-BGV: the method is implemented over BFV in SEAL and over BGV in HElib (§2.3, p. 4; §5, p. 14). The Paterson-Stockmeyer algorithm (SIAM J. Computing 1973) has no record in any topic.

historical_context.narrative: To keep the circuit shallow, FHE-based PSI lets the client send several encrypted powers of each query value, from which the server builds all the powers it needs. The earlier protocols chose these powers by windowing, sending digits of a fixed base, which is simple but sends more ciphertexts than necessary. Cong and coauthors recognized the choice as the global postage-stamp problem from additive number theory: find few integers whose sums of at most \( h \) terms cover every value up to a bound. Sending powers at an extremal basis keeps the depth at the logarithm of \( h \) while needing fewer ciphertexts, for example three instead of five to reach the twenty-sixth power at depth two, and a scaled second basis serves the high powers of their polynomial evaluation.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Windowing, as in the earlier protocols, sends, for \( b \) the window base and \( B \) the bin size, the \( (b - 1)(\lfloor \log_b B \rfloor + 1) \) powers \( y^{i \cdot b^j} \) so that all powers up to \( B \) are reachable at depth \( \lceil \log(\lfloor \log_b B \rfloor + 1) \rceil \), with \( b \) derived from the target depth (§3.1, p. 9). The authors call it easy to use but far from optimal (§3.1, p. 10).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: In the \( B = 26 \) example the receiver sends three powers instead of five at the same depth (§3.1, p. 10). Combined with Paterson-Stockmeyer, the six powers {1, 5, 8, 27, 135, 216} support polynomials of degree 728 at depth three (§3.1, p. 11). The authors note that no efficient method for finding such bases is known and that bases with large h are hard to find (§3.1, pp. 10-11).
historical_context.technical_delta: Choosing which powers to send is cast as the global postage-stamp problem (Definition 1, p. 10). The sender iterates over the exponents and computes each missing power depth-optimally as a product of two lower ones (Figure 1, p. 10). Brute-forced bases for small instances are taken from the number-theory literature, one for the low powers and one scaled by L for the high powers of Paterson-Stockmeyer evaluation (§3.1, pp. 10-11).

limitations: bases with large \( h \) can be hard to find and may raise online computation because many powers are computed by non-scalar multiplication (§3.1, p. 11)
the paper reports no measurement isolating this change; the SEAL experiments combine it with the other optimizations (§5, p. 15)
qualifiers: the depth bound \( \lceil \log_2 h \rceil \), \( h \) the number of summands allowed, follows from computing each power as a product of two lower powers (§3.1, p. 10)
only small instances are used, for which extremal bases have been found by brute force in the literature (§3.1, p. 11)

source_locator.primary_source: §1.2 (p. 3); §3.1 Windowing (p. 9); §3.1 Extremal postage-stamp bases, Definition 1, and Figure 1 (pp. 10-11). IACR ePrint 2021/1116, PDF dated 2021-11-14.

metadata.statement: If the receiver sends encryptions of \( y^{a_1}, \ldots, y^{a_k} \) for an extremal postage-stamp basis \( \{a_1 = 1 < \cdots < a_k\} \), in which every integer up to \( r \) is a sum of at most \( h \) basis elements, the sender can compute all powers of y up to \( r \) within multiplicative depth \( \lceil \log_2 h \rceil \), \( h \) the number of summands allowed; this replaces the windowing of earlier FHE-based PSI, for example with three powers {1, 5, 8} instead of five {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} for all powers up to 26 at depth two, a 40% reduction of receiver-to-sender ciphertexts, and a second basis multiplied by L supplies the high powers of Paterson-Stockmeyer evaluation.
metadata.title: Fewer encrypted query powers at a fixed multiplicative depth in FHE-based unbalanced PSI, from extremal postage-stamp bases instead of windowing

sections.content: Extremal postage-stamp bases for the receiver's powers
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Definition 1 (p. 10) asks, for given \( h \) and \( k \), for \( k \) integers \( 1 = a_1 < \cdots < a_k \) such that every integer up to \( r \) is a sum of at most \( h \) of them, with \( r \) maximal. If the receiver sends encryptions of y at the basis exponents, the sender reaches all powers up to \( r \) in depth \( \lceil \log_2 h \rceil \). The basis {1, 5, 8} is the unique extremal basis for \( h = 4 \) and \( k = 3 \) (§3.1, p. 10). For Paterson-Stockmeyer evaluation one basis covers the low powers up to \( L - 1 \) and the same or another basis multiplied by \( L \) covers the high powers (§3.1, p. 11).

nodes.summary: If the receiver sends encryptions of \( y^{a_1}, \ldots, y^{a_k} \) for an extremal postage-stamp basis \( \{a_1 = 1 < \cdots < a_k\} \), in which every integer up to \( r \) is a sum of at most \( h \) basis elements, the sender can compute all powers of y up to \( r \) within multiplicative depth \( \lceil \log_2 h \rceil \), \( h \) the number of summands allowed; this replaces the windowing of earlier FHE-based PSI, for example with three powers {1, 5, 8} instead of five {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} for all powers up to 26 at depth two, a 40% reduction of receiver-to-sender ciphertexts, and a second basis multiplied by L supplies the high powers of Paterson-Stockmeyer evaluation.
nodes.title: Fewer encrypted query powers at a fixed multiplicative depth in FHE-based unbalanced PSI, from extremal postage-stamp bases instead of windowing

historical_context.narrative: The first labeled FHE-based PSI protocol handled long items by packing each hashed item into one slot over an extension field, which made every homomorphic operation slower, most painfully when long labels multiplied the work. Splitting an item across several small prime-field slots looks natural, but each slot value is short enough to guess, so partial matches would leak whenever the oblivious PRF step was skipped, as the earlier protocol allowed. Cong and coauthors made the PRF step mandatory, after which item chunks reveal nothing and prime fields suffice. For labels they encrypt each label under its item's PRF output, interpolate the ciphertext chunk by chunk, add a fresh nonce on updates, and move items whose chunks collide within a bin to another partition.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The earlier labeled-PSI protocol supported arbitrary-length items by hashing them into extension-field slots, which the authors say can be devastating for performance, especially with labels, and constrains parameter choices (§3.1, p. 7). It treated the OPRF step as optional, so small slot values could be guessed and partial matches would leak (§3.1, p. 7), and its label interpolation relied on extension fields, where non-zero values can be randomized and items never repeat (§4.1, p. 13; §4.2, p. 14).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors expect prime fields to be cheaper than extension fields, while interpolation remains \( O(B^2) \) field operations, \( B \) the bin size (§4.2, p. 13). With all their optimizations, for 288-byte labels, \( 2^{20} \) sender and 256 receiver items, they report 0.66 s sender online time on 16 threads and 11.2 MB, against 4.6 s and 17.6 MB for the earlier protocol (Table 3, p. 18). They also sketch the labeled-case security proof that the earlier paper left implicit (§4.2, p. 14).
historical_context.technical_delta: Hashed items are split into prime-field chunks and the OPRF is always applied, so chunks of non-matching items look random (§3.1, p. 7). Labels are encrypted under part of the OPRF output and interpolated chunk by chunk (§4.2, p. 13; Figure 2, p. 13). Appending a random nonce on each update avoids XOR leakage between label versions, and an item whose chunks collide in a partition goes to another or a new partition, since interpolation would otherwise be impossible (§4.2, pp. 13-14).

limitations: interpolation still costs \( O(B^2) \) field operations per bin, \( B \) the bin size, mitigated only by the updatability of the precomputation (§4.2, p. 13)
labeled PSI uses more partitions and fills them less than unlabeled PSI because of chunk collisions (§4.2, p. 14)
the labeled-case security is sketched as an extension of the earlier unlabeled proof, not proved in full (§4.2, p. 14)
qualifiers: relies on the OPRF of the earlier protocol, which gives security against a malicious receiver and privacy against a malicious sender in the random oracle model; the paper keeps those guarantees and proof (§3, p. 6)

labels longer than the item are split into item-length fragments, each with its own interpolation polynomial, so sender-to-receiver communication grows linearly in the number of fragments, \( O(\lceil \sigma_{\mathrm{L}}/\sigma \rceil) \) for \( \sigma_{\mathrm{L}} \)-bit labels (§4.2, p. 14; §5.3, p. 18)
the labeled protocol returns the intersection result together with the label results, so the receiver knows which labels hold valid data (§4.2, p. 14)

source_locator.primary_source: §1.2 (p. 3); §3 (pp. 5-6); §3.1 SIMD packing (p. 7); §4.1-4.2 and Figure 2 (pp. 12-14); §5.3 and Tables 3-4 (pp. 18-19). IACR ePrint 2021/1116, PDF dated 2021-11-14.

metadata.statement: If the OPRF step is always applied, each hashed item can be split across several consecutive prime-field SIMD slots, with the intersection polynomial evaluated on each part independently, instead of occupying one extension-field slot, because partial matches of OPRF outputs reveal nothing about the sender's items; for labeled PSI, each label is encrypted under a key derived from its item's OPRF output, with a fresh random nonce on every update, and the encrypted label is interpolated per slot-sized part, while the sender re-places any item whose parts collide with an existing item in the same bin and partition, at the cost of more partitions and a lower fill rate than unlabeled PSI.

sections.content: Prime-field slots for long items and labels
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: After the OPRF step, the receiver places each hashed item in a cuckoo bin and spreads it over several consecutive prime-field slots; the sender evaluates the intersection polynomial of each chunk position independently (§3.1, p. 7). For labels, the OPRF output is extended so that one part represents the item and another keys a symmetric cipher; the sender interpolates the encrypted label chunks (Figure 2, p. 13), and the receiver decrypts the label with the key derived from its own OPRF value (§4.2, p. 13). When inserting an item, the sender checks that none of its chunks already appears in the same positions of the target partition (§4.2, p. 14).

historical_context.narrative: The PaXoS encoding placed each item on an edge of a random graph, which keeps encoding linear but leaves more than half of the table slack, and in PaXoS-PSI every table position costs one oblivious transfer. Garimella and coauthors observed that hypergraphs with three positions per item stay peelable down to about \( 1.23n \) positions, so the same peel-and-back-substitute strategy works with a table little larger than the data. They kept the short random tail that absorbs the few unpeelable items and argued that, with current techniques, three positions per item is the right choice for peeling. Plugged into PaXoS-PSI, the smaller table cut communication by about forty percent, although the parameter \( 1.3n \) rested on experiments rather than a proven bound.
historical_context.prior_boundary: PaXoS used a cuckoo graph with two hash functions and about \( 2.4n \) positions, a heuristic choice with no proven failure probability, giving rate \( 0.4 - o(1) \) (§3, p. 9; Figure 1, p. 8); polynomial OKVS had rate 1 but \( O(n \log^2 n) \) encoding (§3, p. 7).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: Instantiating PaXoS-PSI with it, the authors report 1.61 times less communication than PaXoS-PSI with malicious security, because \( 1.3n \) OTs replace \( 2.4n \) (§8.2, p. 23; Table 1, p. 24), and an encoding of 20.80 MB against 38.40 MB for PaXoS at \( n = 2^{20} \) (Table 2, p. 29).
historical_context.technical_delta: The table moves from graphs to 3-hypergraphs, which are asymptotically peelable with at least about \( 1.23n \) nodes (§4.1, pp. 9-10), keeps the \( L \| R \) structure of PaXoS for the 2-core (§4.1, pp. 10-11), and is specified in Figure 2 (p. 12) with Lemma 6 (p. 11; proof sketch in Appendix A.1, p. 28). The implementation uses \( 1.3n \) nodes (§8.1, p. 23).

limitations: the authors call \( m = 1.3n \) an acceptable heuristic, and their table lists the error analysis of 3H-GCT as heuristic (§8.1, p. 23; Table 2, p. 29)
the rate 0.91 possible with Walzer's hypergraph construction takes effect only for very large \( n \) (Figure 1 caption, p. 8; §4.1, p. 10)
qualifiers: values are combined by XOR, so the OKVS is binary; the extra positions R are needed because small 2-cores often consist of two identical hyperedges (§4.1, p. 11, footnote 6)
Lemma 6 is conditional on a bound \( d(n) \) on the 2-core, which the paper does not derive concretely; known analyses do not give concrete parameters for failure \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (§4.1, p. 10)

source_locator.primary_source: Figure 1 (p. 8); §3, PaXoS (p. 9); §4.1 with footnotes 4-6 (pp. 9-11); Lemma 6 (p. 11); Figure 2 (p. 12); §8.1-8.2 (p. 23); Table 1 (p. 24); Appendix A.1 (p. 28); Table 2 (p. 29). IACR ePrint 2021/883, PDF dated 2021-11-30.

metadata.statement: Each key is mapped to a hyperedge of three distinct positions in a table L and to a random vector r(k) over \( d + \lambda \) extra positions R, with \( d = d(n) \). Encoding peels the hypergraph, solves the constraints of the remaining 2-core by Gaussian elimination in \( O((d + \lambda)^3) \) time, and fills the peeled positions in reverse order. If the 2-core exceeds \( d \) hyperedges with probability at most \( \varepsilon_1 \), the result is an OKVS with error \( \varepsilon_1 + 2^{-\lambda} \) (Lemma 6). The authors list its rate as \( 0.81 - o(1) \) with \( O(n\lambda) \) encoding and batch decoding, against \( 0.4 - o(1) \) for PaXoS.
metadata.title: Three-hash garbled cuckoo table: binary OKVS with about \( 1.3n \) main positions instead of the \( 2.4n \) of PaXoS, by peeling a random 3-hypergraph

sections.content: Three-hash garbled cuckoo table
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Each key k selects three distinct positions \( h_1(k), h_2(k), h_3(k) \) of L, and its value is the XOR of those positions and of the positions of R selected by r(k) (§4.1, pp. 9-11). Encoding repeatedly removes a hyperedge that touches a position used by no other remaining key, pushing it onto a stack; it then solves the system for the keys left in the 2-core, and finally pops the stack, setting for each key a position not yet defined so that the key decodes correctly (Figure 2, p. 12). Hyperedges of size three are used because larger hyperedges improve the orientability threshold but make linear-time peeling fail more often (footnote 5, p. 10). The construction improves the rate of the PaXoS table of PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-GARBLED-CUCKOO, and its failure probability is made concrete by the amplification of PSI-CONTRIB-2021-GPRTY-AMPLIFICATION. The PSI rows that use it are PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-GPRTY-MAL-3HGCT and, through the star architecture, PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-GPRTY-MAL-STAR.

historical_context.narrative: Cuckoo-style encodings are fast, but no one could say concretely how large they must be to fail with probability \( 2^{-40} \). The asymptotic analyses hide their constants, and confirming so small a probability by experiment needs more than \( 2^{40} \) trials. Garimella, Pinkas, Rosulek, Trieu, and Yanai turned the problem around. A failure rate near \( 2^{-30} \) can be measured on ordinary hardware, and a composite encoding whose central part repairs any single failed component fails only when two components fail, roughly squaring the probability. Splitting the keys among many small leaves keeps the total size close to that of one table. The security parameter then rests on a measured quantity and an exact combinatorial bound instead of extrapolation.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Randomized structures in PSI, such as cuckoo hashing, have asymptotic analyses with unclear constants, so parameters for failure \( 2^{-40} \) were set heuristically or, as by Pinkas, Schneider, and Zohner, extrapolated from experiments costing millions of core hours that could not validate such small probabilities (§1.2, p. 3; §5, p. 13, footnote 7).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors describe the star-architecture OKVS as the only construction in their comparison with an empirically proven error probability (Appendix A.2, p. 28; Table 2, p. 29); it is the encoding of their 'star arch.' PSI, which sends 1.43 times less than PaXoS-PSI with malicious security (§8.2, p. 23).
historical_context.technical_delta: Three architectures (§5.1-5.3, pp. 13-17) build a new OKVS from instances of an underlying OKVS with independent hash functions; the concrete instantiation (§5.4, pp. 17-18) validates \( \varepsilon \) for the three-hash table with \( 2^{33} \) runs at \( n' = 6600 \) and amplifies it with \( b = 10 \) or 160 leaves.

limitations: encoding calls the underlying encoder up to \( 2b + 1 \) times, \( b \) the number of leaves, and decoding calls it twice (§5.2, p. 16)
the failure probability of the instantiation depends on an empirical measurement, not a proof (§5.4, p. 17)
qualifiers: \( \varepsilon \) is an empirical upper bound at confidence 0.9999 from the Clopper-Pearson method, measured at \( n' = 6600 \) and assumed to hold for larger leaf loads (§5.4, p. 17; footnote 9, p. 18)
a failure of the underlying table is a 2-core larger than \( 0.5 \log n' \) after peeling (§5.4, p. 17)
the maximum leaf load \( n' \) is bounded by a balls-into-bins tail bound with probability \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (Eq. (5), p. 16)

source_locator.primary_source: Abstract (p. 1); §1.2 (p. 3); §5 with footnotes 7-8 (p. 13); §5.1-5.3 (pp. 13-17); Eq. (3)-(5) (pp. 15-16); §5.4 with footnote 9 (pp. 17-18); Appendix A.2 and Table 2 (pp. 28-29). IACR ePrint 2021/883, PDF dated 2021-11-30.

metadata.statement: From an OKVS that fails with probability \( \varepsilon \), replication with \( c \) copies fails with probability \( \varepsilon^c \) at \( c \) times the size. The star architecture hashes keys into \( b \) leaf OKVS and adds one central OKVS; a single failed component is set at random and corrected through the others, so the scheme fails only if two of the \( b + 1 \) components fail, about \( \binom{b + 1}{2} \cdot \varepsilon^2 \), at size \( (b + 1) \cdot \mathrm{size}(n') \) with \( n' \) the maximum leaf load. The generalized star replicates the central OKVS \( d \) times, \( d \) the replication factor, to tolerate \( d - 1 \) leaf failures, failing with probability \( O(\varepsilon^d) \). Over the three-hash table with an empirically measured \( \varepsilon = 2^{-29.355} \) at confidence 0.9999, the star gives failure \( 2^{-52.9} \) for \( n = 2^{16} \) and \( 2^{-45.05} \) for \( n = 2^{20} \) at about \( 1.3n \) size.
metadata.title: OKVS correctness amplification: replication and star architectures turn \( \varepsilon \), the empirically validated failure probability, into about \( \varepsilon^2 \), or \( O(\varepsilon^d) \) for \( d \) the replication factor of the central OKVS, at nearly the same size

sections.content: OKVS correctness amplification
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: All three architectures rely on two facts: whether an OKVS encoding fails depends only on its keys and hash functions, and a random vector of the right length is a valid encoding of random values (§5, p. 13). Replication tries a second instance whenever the first fails (§5.1, pp. 13-14). The star architecture decodes a key as the sum of its leaf's value and the central value; if one component fails, it is filled at random and the others are encoded to compensate (§5.2, pp. 14-16; failure probability in Eq. (3)-(4), p. 15). The generalized star replaces the central node by a \( d \)-fold replicated OKVS that can absorb up to \( d - 1 \) failed leaves (§5.3, pp. 16-17). In the concrete instantiation, each leaf is a three-hash table with \( 1.3n' + \lambda + 0.5 \log n' \) positions (PSI-CONTRIB-2021-GPRTY-3H-GCT), and the total size is about \( 1.3n \) (§5.4, pp. 17-18). The PSI row that uses it is PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-GPRTY-MAL-STAR.

historical_context.narrative: PaXoS-PSI took its correlated strings from a malicious OT extension, whose correlation mixes XOR with bitwise AND, and that mix is why it needed a binary encoding and a long error-correcting code. Garimella and coauthors observed that vector OLE supplies the same kind of correlation with a genuine field multiplication by the sender's secret. Any linear encoding then commutes with the correlation, and a hashed value with a nonzero offset already looks random without a code. They restated the PaXoS-PSI protocol for this setting, so that any linear OKVS can serve, including non-binary ones. At the time no malicious-secure vector OLE had been implemented, and the authors left open whether this route would beat the OT-extension version in practice.
historical_context.prior_boundary: PaXoS-PSI works only with a binary OKVS, because the bitwise AND in the OOS correlation is not a field operation, and it needs an error-correcting code of minimum distance \( \kappa \) so that \( C(d_i) \wedge s \) masks at least \( \kappa \) bits of s (§7.1, pp. 20-21).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The generalization admits non-binary OKVS and removes one source of overhead (§1.3, p. 4). The authors note that it requires a malicious-secure vOLE, none of which had been implemented, and leave to future work whether it is competitive with the OT-extension version (§7.1, p. 21).
historical_context.technical_delta: With the field correlation of vector OLE, \( \mathrm{Decode}(R, k) = \mathrm{Decode}(Q, k) \oplus \mathrm{Decode}(D, k) \cdot s \) holds for any linear OKVS, and \( H(a \oplus b \cdot s) \) looks random to the receiver for every nonzero b, so no code is needed (§7.1, p. 21); the protocol is Figure 3 (p. 22), adapted from PaXoS-PSI, with Theorem 7 (p. 21).

limitations: no implementation or concrete cost is given, and no malicious-secure vOLE had been implemented (§7.1, p. 21)
the proof is not written out; the paper states that it follows closely the proof of PaXoS-PSI (§7.1, p. 21)
qualifiers: malicious security in the vOLE-hybrid, random oracle model, with the hash lengths \( \ell_1, \ell_2 \) of PaXoS-PSI (Theorem 7, p. 21; Figure 3, p. 22)
the OKVS must be linear over \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{\ell_1}) \), and only the receiver learns the intersection (Figure 3, p. 22)
metadata.statement: The OOS correlation \( r_i = q_i \oplus C(d_i) \wedge s \) of PaXoS-PSI is replaced by the vector-OLE correlation \( q_i = r_i \oplus d_i \cdot s \) over \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{\ell_1}) \). The receiver's vOLE input is a linear OKVS D encoding the pairs \( (y, H_1(y)) \) for its set, and the sender sends \( H_2(x, \mathrm{Decode}(Q, x) \oplus H_1(x) \cdot s) \) for each of its items. For any linear OKVS and the hash lengths of PaXoS-PSI, the protocol realizes two-party PSI against malicious adversaries (Theorem 7).
metadata.title: Malicious two-party PSI from any linear OKVS and vector OLE, generalizing PaXoS-PSI and removing its error-correcting code

sections.content: PSI from a linear OKVS and vector OLE
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: In vector OLE the sender holds a secret s and a vector Q, and the receiver holds its chosen vector D and R with \( q_i = r_i \oplus d_i \cdot s \), where \( \cdot \) is multiplication in \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{\ell_1}) \) (Figure 3, step 1, p. 22). If D is a linear OKVS (PSI-CONTRIB-2021-GPRTY-OKVS) that decodes to \( H_1(y) \) on the receiver's set, decoding commutes with the correlation, so for such y the receiver's \( \mathrm{Decode}(R, y) \) equals the sender's \( \mathrm{Decode}(Q, y) \oplus H_1(y) \cdot s \), while for other x the two differ by a nonzero multiple of s (§7.1, pp. 20-21). The sender hashes its values with the item and sends them permuted; the receiver outputs the items whose hash appears (Figure 3, steps 2-3, p. 22). Compared with PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-MALICIOUS-PAXOS-PSI, the code that made the AND-based correlation hide s disappears, and any linear OKVS can be used (§7.1, p. 21). The paper also observes that the VOLE-based OPRF of Rindal and Schoppmann, PSI-CONTRIB-2021-RS-VOLE-OPRF, can use any OKVS in place of PaXoS (§6.2, p. 19). The complete row is PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-GPRTY-VOLE.

sections.content: MPC-PAPER-2019-PCG: the paper cites the pseudorandom correlation generators of Boyle et al. among the vector-OLE protocols that produce this correlation (§7.1, p. 21; reference [BCG+19], p. 24).

historical_context.narrative: Kolesnikov and coauthors had built multiparty PSI from two-party oblivious PRFs: each party masks its PRF outputs with shares of zero, and a central party sees the shares cancel only on items that everyone holds. Their most efficient variant was proven only against augmented semi-honest adversaries, in a model where the simulator may change corrupt inputs. Garimella and coauthors showed that after each PRF output is hashed together with the item through a random oracle, the same protocol is secure against malicious parties. Changing a corrupt party's input is harmless in that model, and the oracle lets a simulator read off the items an adversary encoded. Writing the protocol over any OKVS let it use the new fast encodings instead of polynomials.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Kolesnikov et al.'s most efficient multiparty PSI, built from an OPPRF that encodes zero shares with a polynomial or a garbled Bloom filter, had only augmented semi-honest security; other concretely efficient malicious multiparty PSI relied on garbled Bloom filters with cut-and-choose checks (§6.2, p. 19; §7.2, pp. 21-22; Appendix B.5, p. 35).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors call it the most efficient malicious multiparty PSI to date, at nearly the cost of the augmented semi-honest protocol (§1.3, p. 4; §7.2, p. 22), against garbled-Bloom-filter protocols that they report as about 10 and 2 times slower than that protocol (§7.2, p. 22; Table 4, p. 36).
historical_context.technical_delta: Figure 5 (p. 39) writes Kolesnikov et al.'s construction over an arbitrary OKVS and wraps each OPRF output in a random oracle so that the simulator can extract inputs (Appendix B.2, p. 30); Theorem 9 (p. 31) is proved in Appendix B.4 (pp. 30-35), with a compression argument bounding the extracted set by \( 2n \) (p. 34). Appendix B.6 (pp. 36-37) explains why the protocol is malicious-secure though not semi-honest-secure.

limitations: the protocol does not strictly enforce corrupt parties' advertised set sizes; restricting them to \( n \) items is left open (Appendix B.4, pp. 34-35; Appendix B.7, p. 37)
no implementation of the multiparty protocol is reported (§8, pp. 22-24)
qualifiers: secure in the \( F_{\mathrm{oprf}} \)-hybrid model with a malicious-secure two-party OPRF, for an exponentially large field F (Theorem 9, p. 31; Figure 5, p. 39)
star topology; only P0 receives output (Figure 5, p. 39)
all parties hold sets of the same size \( n \); with unequal sizes only a weaker functionality, in which corrupt parties may use the largest advertised size, is achieved (Appendix B.7, p. 37)
the \( 2n \) bound on corrupt parties' sets assumes \( |F| = 2^{2\kappa} \) and \( 2^{\kappa} \) oracle queries (Appendix B.4, p. 34)

sections.content: Malicious multiparty PSI from OPRF and OKVS
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Every pair of parties shares a PRF key, from which each party derives a share \( sh_i(h) \) of zero for any item h, with the shares of all parties summing to zero (Figure 5, step 1, p. 39). P0 learns \( \mathrm{PRF}_i(h) \) for its items from the OPRF with \( P_i \), and \( P_i \) sends an OKVS that decodes, on each of its items, to the oracle hash of the PRF value plus its zero share; P0 builds its own share in the same way and keeps the items on which all decoded values sum to zero (Figure 5, steps 2-4, p. 39). The only change from Kolesnikov et al.'s augmented semi-honest protocol is the oracle hash around the PRF value, which the simulator for a corrupt P0 or corrupt non-central parties uses to extract inputs (Appendix B.2, p. 30; B.4, pp. 31-33). Hazay and Lindell's example of a protocol that is malicious-secure but not semi-honest-secure explains the apparent paradox: the semi-honest simulator may not change a corrupt party's input, while the malicious one may (Appendix B.6, pp. 36-37). The paper compares communication \( O(\ell^2 \kappa + \ell n(\kappa + \lambda + \log n)) + o(\ell n) \) and four rounds with other multiparty protocols in Table 4 (p. 36). The complete row is PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-GPRTY-MULTIPARTY.

historical_context.narrative: Many PSI protocols hid a party's set by interpolating a polynomial through its items, which is compact but costs quasi-linear field operations, and PaXoS had shown that a sparse XOR-based encoding could do the same job faster in one protocol. Garimella, Pinkas, Rosulek, Trieu, and Yanai named the common requirement: an encoding of key-value pairs that decodes correctly on the encoded keys and reveals nothing about which keys were used when the values are random. They separated linear and binary variants and formalized the overfitting game that limits how many keys a malicious party can squeeze into an encoding. Polynomials, garbled Bloom filters, and PaXoS became instances, and protocols written against the interface could adopt any faster instance.
historical_context.prior_boundary: PSI and related protocols hid input sets by interpolating polynomials, as in OPPRF-based multiparty PSI, circuit PSI, and SpOT-light, at \( O(n \log^2 n) \) field operations (§1.1, pp. 2-3). PaXoS took a step toward an abstraction but covered only binary encodings (§1.1, p. 3), and its overfitting bound was proved for PaXoS (§2.4, p. 7).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: With one interface the authors argue that an OKVS can replace polynomials in sparse OT extension, OPPRF and its multiparty and circuit-PSI uses, PaXoS-PSI, and covert computation (§6, pp. 18-20), so that a better OKVS improves all of them (§1.3, p. 4).
historical_context.technical_delta: Definitions 1-3 (p. 5) define key-value stores, obliviousness, and linear OKVS; §2.3 (p. 6) identifies binary OKVS with PaXoS; Definition 4 (pp. 6-7) defines the overfitting game, and Lemma 5 (p. 7) restates the PaXoS bound for any key-value store. Section 3 and Figure 1 (pp. 7-9) place polynomials, random matrices, garbled Bloom filters, and PaXoS in one comparison of rate and encoding and decoding cost.

limitations: whether overfitting is computationally hard for polynomial-time adversaries, beyond the information-theoretic bound, is only conjectured (§2.4, p. 7)
qualifiers: obliviousness is required only when the encoded values are uniformly random (Definition 2, p. 5)
whether Encode fails depends only on the keys and the hash functions, not on the values (§2.1, p. 5)
the overfitting bound of Lemma 5 is information-theoretic and limits \( n' \) only beyond the size of the encoding (§2.4, p. 7)

metadata.statement: A key-value store is a pair of algorithms (Encode, Decode) such that \( \mathrm{Decode}(S, k) = v \) for every pair (k, v) used to create S, where Encode may fail with small probability depending only on the keys. It is oblivious if, when the values are uniformly random, encodings of any two key sets of the same size are computationally indistinguishable. It is linear over a field F if Decode(S, k) is the inner product of a key-dependent vector d(k) with S, and binary if d(k) is a 0/1 vector, which is a PaXoS. The \( (n, n') \)-overfitting game asks an adversary for an S that agrees with a random oracle on more than \( n' \) keys.
metadata.title: Oblivious key-value store (OKVS): key-value encodings that hide the keys when the values are random, with linear, binary, and overfitting notions

sections.content: Oblivious key-value store
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: An OKVS encodes a list of key-value pairs into a data structure S from which Decode recovers the value of any encoded key; Decode can be called on any key, and when the values are random, S reveals nothing about which keys were encoded (Definitions 1-2, p. 5). A linear OKVS over a field F stores a vector \( S \in F^m \) and decodes by an inner product with a key-dependent vector, so encoding solves a linear system, and choosing a uniform solution gives obliviousness automatically (Definition 3, p. 5; §2.2, p. 6). A binary OKVS restricts the key vectors to 0/1 entries; over \( \mathrm{GF}(2^{w}) \), \( w \) the value length, decoding is an XOR of positions and commutes with bitwise AND, and this is exactly the PaXoS of PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-PAXOS (§2.3, p. 6). For malicious protocols, the overfitting game measures how many pairs (k, H(k)) an adversary can fit into an encoding sized for \( n \) pairs (Definition 4, pp. 6-7); the information-theoretic bound of PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-RECEIVER-SET-SIZE-BOUND applies to any key-value store (Lemma 5, p. 7). The paper measures an OKVS by rate, encoding time, and single and batch decoding time (§2.5, p. 7).
