historical_context.narrative: Multiparty PSI protocols that tolerate malicious parties had paid for the worst case: they defended against all but one party colluding and made every party run interactive subprotocols built on oblivious transfer. Nevo, Trieu, and Yanai isolated the setting in which at most one party is corrupt. One party hands out fresh PRF keys and a key-value encoding that maps its items to combined PRF values; the others turn their items into PRF images, and only two designated parties still compare sets. That comparison can use server-aided two-party PSI, with a third party as the server that does not collude, so no oblivious transfer is needed at all. The paper also shows that a coalition of any two parties breaks the protocol, which marks the boundary of this setting.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Concretely efficient multiparty PSI protocols run OPPRFs on OT extension (Kolesnikov et al., Garimella et al.) or garbled Bloom filters with OT (Ben Efraim et al.), so every party runs interactive two-party subprotocols, and the malicious ones protect against \( n - 1 \) colluding parties even when fewer corruptions are expected (§1.1, pp. 1-3; §1.2, p. 4; Table 1, p. 2).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors state that, to their knowledge, this is the only multiparty PSI construction relying only on symmetric-key primitives (§1.2, p. 4). For three parties with \( 2^{20} \) items, server-aided two-party PSI lowers the running time from about 9 seconds with plain malicious PSI to about 4.8 seconds, and 32 parties with \( 2^{20} \) items finish in 10 seconds (§1.2, p. 4).
historical_context.technical_delta: With at most one corrupted party, PRF keys and OKVS encodings reduce \( \ell \)-party PSI to two-party PSI, either recursively with \( O(\ell) \) rounds (Protocol 3.1, p. 6; Theorem 3.2, p. 7) or between \( P_{\ell-1} \) and \( P_\ell \) in constant rounds (Protocol 3.3, p. 8; Theorem 3.4, p. 8). Items are concatenated with their PRF or OKVS values to stop a malicious P1 from forcing false matches (§3.1, p. 6; §3.2, p. 7), and the base case is server-aided two-party PSI with another party as server (§3.1.1, p. 6; Appendix A, pp. 13-14).

limitations: insecure as soon as two parties collude, since a party with both the key and the OKVS can test arbitrary inputs (§3.1.2, p. 6; §3.2.1, p. 8)
the computation of P1 and \( P_{\ell-1} \) grows as \( O(\ell n) \) (§3.2.2, p. 8)
qualifiers: at most one corrupted party; a collusion of two parties such as P1 and \( P_{\ell-1} \) breaks Protocol 3.3, which stays secure against any subset of \( P_2, \ldots, P_{\ell-2} \) together with one of P1, \( P_{\ell-1} \), \( P_\ell \) (§3.2.1, p. 8)

Theorem 3.2 is stated in the \( F_{\mathrm{psi}}^{\ell-1,1,n} \)-hybrid and random oracle model (p. 7); Theorem 3.4 is stated in the \( F_{\mathrm{psi}}^{2,1,n} \)-hybrid model (p. 8), and in the malicious case parties hash items with a random oracle H whose queries the simulator observes (Protocol 3.3, note a, p. 8; pp. 8-9)
the symmetric-key-only property depends on instantiating the two-party PSI with server-aided PSI, in which the server does not collude with either party (§1.2, p. 4; §3.1.1, p. 6)
the output goes to \( P_\ell \) only (Functionality 2.1, p. 4)
Protocol 3.3 has 4 rounds by the count in §3.2.2 (p. 8); Table 1 lists 5 (p. 2)

metadata.statement: Against a malicious adversary corrupting at most one of \( \ell \) parties, P1 sends PRF keys \( k_i \) to parties \( P_2, \ldots, P_{\ell-2} \) and sends \( P_\ell \) an OKVS mapping each of its items to the XOR of the PRF values under those keys; each \( P_i \) encodes its items under \( F(k_i, \cdot) \) in an OKVS sent to \( P_{\ell-1} \); \( P_{\ell-1} \) and \( P_\ell \) then run a two-party PSI on items concatenated with their decoded values, and \( P_\ell \) outputs the intersection. With an ideal two-party PSI functionality the protocol is secure, takes a constant number of rounds, and gives clients \( O(n \kappa) \) communication and computation; instantiating the two-party PSI with server-aided PSI, in which a party that does not collude acts as the server, removes oblivious transfer, so the protocol uses only symmetric-key primitives. A recursive variant reduces \( \ell \)-party to \( (\ell - 1) \)-party PSI with \( O(\ell) \) rounds.
metadata.title: Malicious multiparty PSI with at most one corrupted party from symmetric-key primitives only, by reducing \( \ell \)-party PSI to server-aided two-party PSI over OKVS encodings

sections.content: Malicious multiparty PSI without collusion
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: In Protocol 3.3 (p. 8), P1 picks keys \( k_2, \ldots, k_{\ell-2} \), gives \( k_i \) to \( P_i \), and sends \( P_\ell \) an OKVS that maps each of its items a to the XOR of \( F(k_i, a) \); each \( P_i \) with \( 2 \le i \le \ell - 2 \) sends \( P_{\ell-1} \) an OKVS mapping its items a to \( F(k_i, a) \). \( P_{\ell-1} \) XORs its decodings of these OKVSs and \( P_\ell \) decodes P1's OKVS; for an item in every set both obtain the same pseudorandom value. They append these values to their items and call a two-party PSI functionality, and \( P_\ell \) outputs the plain items of the result (Protocol 3.3, steps 4-6, p. 8). The round count is two rounds plus those of the two-party PSI, which the server-aided protocol of Kamara et al. completes in two (§3.2.2, p. 8). Section 3.2.1 shows why a direct variant in which every \( P_i \) sends its OKVS to \( P_\ell \) would leak more than the intersection (pp. 7-8).

historical_context.narrative: Malicious multiparty PSI against a dishonest majority had become concretely efficient through garbled Bloom filters and oblivious key-value stores, but those protocols cost the same whether one party or all but one might collude, and every party took part in the whole computation. Nevo, Trieu, and Yanai tied the cost to the collusion bound \( t_c \). Most parties act as light clients: each sends one PRF key per server and a single key-value encoding of its items to a pivot. The pivot and \( t_c \) servers then hold values that cancel only on items common to all sets, and a zero test built from programmable OPRFs and pseudorandom zero-sharing reveals those items. Against the largest coalition the protocol coincides with the earlier malicious one, and smaller bounds make it faster.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The augmented semi-honest protocol of Kolesnikov et al. and the malicious protocols of Ben Efraim et al. and Garimella et al. protect against \( \ell - 1 \) colluding parties at the same cost for every \( t_c \), and the semi-honest protocol of Chandran et al. tolerates fewer than \( \ell/2 \); the paper states that it was not known how to improve these protocols for smaller \( t_c \) (§1.1, pp. 1-3; §1.2, p. 4; Table 1, p. 2).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: Client communication is almost constant in \( \ell \) and in \( t_c \) below \( \ell - 1 \), and for \( (\ell, t_c) = (15, 7) \) with \( 2^{20} \) items a client needs 3.4 seconds on a LAN, which the authors report as 10-23 times less than the semi-honest protocols of Chandran et al. and Kolesnikov et al. (§5.1, p. 12; Table 3, p. 12). Total running time is 1.2-6.5 and 1.2-8.5 times lower than those protocols, and with \( t_c \) fixed the cost is nearly constant in \( \ell \) (§5.1-5.2, p. 12).
historical_context.technical_delta: Clients deliver a conditional zero-sharing of their items to the pivot and \( t_c \) servers through one OKVS and \( t_c \) PRF keys each (§4, p. 9; Protocol 4.4, p. 10). ZeroXOR outputs the keys common to all \( t_c + 1 \) parties whose values XOR to zero, using OPPRFs to \( P_\ell \) masked by unconditional zero-sharing so that values of non-matching keys stay hidden (Functionality 4.1, p. 9; Protocol 4.2 and Theorem 4.3, p. 10). Theorem 4.5 proves malicious security against \( t_c < \ell \) (p. 11), and at \( t_c = \ell - 1 \) the protocol coincides with that of Garimella et al. up to the OKVS instantiation (§1.2, p. 4).

limitations: at \( t_c = \ell - 1 \) there are no clients and the cost equals that of the augmented semi-honest protocol of Kolesnikov et al. (§5.1, p. 12)
comparisons with semi-honest protocols cross security models, and runtimes of Ben Efraim et al. are taken from their paper for \( \ell \in \{8, 12\} \) rather than rerun (§5.1, p. 11)
qualifiers: malicious adversary that statically corrupts any strict subset of the parties, \( t_c < \ell \) (abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 1; Theorem 4.5, p. 11)
Theorem 4.5 is in the ZeroXOR-hybrid and random oracle model with a proof sketch; Theorem 4.3 for ZeroXOR is in the zero-sharing and OPPRF hybrid model, and its proof is omitted (pp. 10-11)
the OPPRF is the malicious construction of Pinkas et al. (PaXoS), described in Appendix B (p. 14; §1.1.1, p. 2)
the output goes to \( P_\ell \) only (Functionality 2.1, p. 4)

the \( t_c + 1 \) parties that process the intersection can be chosen, and only a collusion of exactly that set reveals information, whereas any \( t_c + 1 \) parties can do so in the protocol of Chandran et al. (§1.1.2, p. 2)

the implementation uses PaXoS with expansion 2.5 as the OKVS and the table-based OPPRF code of Kolesnikov et al., which footnote 2 says is semi-honest secure and about three times slower than the malicious PaXoS-based OPPRF (§5, p. 11)

metadata.statement: For \( \ell \) parties with \( n \) items each and at most \( t_c < \ell \) corrupted and colluding, the parties split into \( \ell - t_c - 1 \) clients, one pivot, and \( t_c \) servers. Each client sends a PRF key to each server and one OKVS to the pivot that maps its items to the XOR of the PRF values under those keys; the pivot and the \( t_c \) servers then hold values that XOR to zero exactly on items in every set, and a ZeroXOR protocol among these \( t_c + 1 \) parties, built from OPPRFs and unconditional zero-sharing, outputs those items to \( P_\ell \). In the ZeroXOR-hybrid and random oracle model the protocol is secure against a malicious adversary corrupting \( t_c < \ell \) parties and runs in 4 rounds; a client sends \( O(n \kappa) \) bits and computes \( O(n t_c \kappa) \), the leader communicates \( O(n \kappa \max\{t_c, \ell - t_c\}) \) and computes \( O(n \kappa (\ell - t_c)) \), and at \( t_c = \ell - 1 \) the protocol reduces to ZeroXOR among all parties.
metadata.title: Malicious multiparty PSI against \( t_c < \ell \) colluding parties whose cost decreases with \( t_c \), with client communication \( O(n \kappa) \), from OKVS encodings and a ZeroXOR test over OPPRFs

sections.content: Malicious multiparty PSI calibrated to the collusion bound
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Let \( v = \ell - t_c \). Clients \( P_1, \ldots, P_{v-1} \) send key \( k_i^j \) to each server \( P_j \), \( j > v \), and send the pivot \( P_v \) an OKVS \( S_i \) mapping each item to the XOR over servers of \( F(k_i^j, \text{item}) \) (Protocol 4.4, steps 2-3, p. 10). The pivot pairs each of its items with the XOR of its decodings, and each server pairs each of its items with the XOR of \( F(k_i^j, \text{item}) \) over clients (steps 4-5). For an item in every set the \( t_c + 1 \) values XOR to zero, otherwise to a pseudorandom value, and ZeroXOR among \( P_v, \ldots, P_\ell \) finds the items with zero XOR (step 6; §4.2, p. 10). In ZeroXOR every party except \( P_\ell \) programs an OPPRF to \( P_\ell \) with its value masked by its unconditional zero-share, and \( P_\ell \) keeps the keys whose outputs and own value XOR to zero (Protocol 4.2, p. 10). A client communicates only its OKVS and keys, so its load depends on \( n \) alone (§4.2.1, p. 10).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: None. The OPPRF, OKVS, and zero-sharing building blocks are PSI mechanisms.

historical_context.narrative: Circuit-PSI hides even the intersection: the parties end with secret shares that a later computation can consume. The leading linear-communication protocol hashed the receiver's items into a cuckoo table and used an oblivious programmable PRF, built from polynomial interpolation, so that each bin yields equal strings exactly when its item is shared, before a small comparison circuit. Rindal and Schoppmann kept that structure and replaced the programmable PRF with one built from their VOLE-based OPRF and a sparse encoding of the sender's corrections. Because the PaXoS encoder sets some positions to zero, which could leak the sender's keys, they randomized every free position so that the encoding is uniform whenever its values are.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The linear-communication circuit-PSI of Pinkas, Schneider, Tkachenko, and Yanai combined an OPPRF based on polynomial interpolation with a small GMW circuit (§1.4, p. 6); the PaXoS encoder sets some positions to zero, so its output can depend on the encoded keys (§1.3, p. 5; §2, p. 10).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors report circuit-PSI up to 3 times faster than the previous protocol (abstract, p. 1), for example 23.3 s against 72.0 s at 5 Gbps for \( 2^{20} \) items with IKNP-based GMW, and 277 MB with SilentOT against an estimated 2,540 MB (Table 4, p. 29).
historical_context.technical_delta: XoPaXoS (Figure 1, p. 7) assigns random values to the free positions of the 2-core system and to one vertex per tree, making the encoding uniform for uniform values (§2, pp. 10-11); the OPPRF is Figure 8 (p. 38) with Theorem 5.1 (p. 21), and the circuit-PSI protocol is Figure 10 (pp. 38-39), whose proof the authors defer to the earlier work (§6, pp. 22-24).

limitations: the communication figures for the earlier protocol in Table 4 are computed from its theoretical costs, not measured (Table 4 caption, p. 29)
no malicious security is claimed for circuit-PSI (abstract, p. 1)
qualifiers: semi-honest security; the circuit-PSI proof is deferred to Pinkas, Schneider, Tkachenko, and Yanai, and the OPPRF is proved in the \( F_{\mathrm{oprf}} \)-hybrid model (§6, p. 23; Theorem 5.1, p. 21)
cuckoo hashing with expansion 1.27 and three hash functions, following the earlier protocol; the authors note disagreement in the literature about these parameters (§7.2, pp. 29-30)
the final comparison uses generic two-party computation, implemented with GMW whose OTs come from IKNP or SilentOT (§7.2, p. 30)

sections.content: Circuit-PSI from a VOLE-based OPPRF
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The OPPRF lets the sender program values \( z_i \) at points \( y_i \): the parties run an OPRF on the receiver's points, and the sender sends an XoPaXoS encoding P with \( \mathrm{Decode}(P, y_i) = z_i - F_k(y_i) \), so the receiver's output \( F_k(x) + \mathrm{Decode}(P, x) \) equals \( z_i \) at \( x = y_i \) and is random elsewhere (§5, p. 21; Figure 8, p. 38). Security against the receiver needs P to reveal nothing about the sender's points outside the intersection, which plain PaXoS does not guarantee because it fixes some positions to zero; XoPaXoS samples those positions at random (§2, pp. 10-11; Theorem 5.1 proof, pp. 21-22). In the circuit-PSI protocol the sender programs, for every bin and every item y hashed there with function j, the point \( H(y, j) \) to a random bin value \( r_i \); the receiver queries the item in its cuckoo bin and obtains \( r_i \) exactly when that item is in the sender's set, and a two-party circuit then outputs shares of the equality bit and of the associated values (§6, pp. 23-24; Figure 10, pp. 38-39). The OPRF underneath is PSI-CONTRIB-2021-RS-VOLE-OPRF. The complete row is PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-RS-CIRCUIT.
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-COMP-EVAL-GMW: the comparison circuit is evaluated with the GMW implementation of libOTe (§7.2, pp. 26 and 30). MPC-CONTRIB-2003-IKNP-OTEXT: one variant generates the GMW offline OTs with IKNP OT extension (§7.2, p. 30). MPC-CONTRIB-2019-PCG-SILENT: the other variant uses SilentOT, cited to Boyle et al., CCS 2019 (§7.2, p. 30; Table 4, p. 29); that CCS paper is distinct from the CRYPTO 2019 paper MPC-PAPER-2019-PCG and has no record of its own.

historical_context.narrative: Turning an oblivious PRF into malicious PSI is simple: the sender evaluates the function on its items and sends the results. The difficulty lies in the proof, where a simulator must identify the sender's items from these values. The standard argument asked for outputs long enough that no two of the sender's queries ever collide, which doubles their length to \( 2\kappa \) bits. Rindal and Schoppmann pointed out that collisions among the sender's own queries are harmless unless they land on the receiver's set, which is fixed before the function is chosen. Extracting only queries without collisions keeps the simulation sound with \( \kappa \)-bit outputs, so the sender's message shrinks by half.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The folklore analysis of the malicious OPRF-to-PSI transformation, as used by De Cristofaro, Kim, and Tsudik and by PaXoS-PSI, extracts every queried y whose output appears in the sender's message and therefore needs \( 2\kappa \)-bit outputs so that collisions among the sender's queries are negligible (§1.3, p. 5; §4, p. 19).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It halves the sender's message in the malicious protocol; the authors list it, with the shorter encoding, as a reason their malicious protocol sends less than PaXoS-PSI, whose analysis states \( 2\kappa \)-bit values (§7.1, p. 26).
historical_context.technical_delta: The new simulator discards colliding queries; a collision matters only if it hits the receiver's set, which is fixed before F is sampled, so for \( \kappa = 128 \) and \( n_Y = 2^{30} \) the sender would need about \( 2^{98} \) queries to distinguish, against \( 2^{49} \) under the folklore analysis (§4, pp. 19-20; Theorem 4.1, p. 20; Figure 6, p. 37).

limitations: the saving concerns the sender's message only; the cost of the OPRF itself is unchanged (§4, p. 19)
the paper's percentages differ by passage: about 33%, up to 50% (§1.3, p. 5), and 20% to 50% (§4, p. 19)
qualifiers: malicious security in the \( F_{\mathrm{oprf}} \)-hybrid model, in which F is a truly random function (Theorem 4.1, p. 20; §4, p. 19, footnote 3)
semi-honest instantiations use outputs of \( \lambda + \log_2(n_Y) + \log_2(n_X) \) bits (Figure 6, p. 37)
metadata.statement: In the transformation where the receiver learns F(x) for its set from a batched OPRF and the sender sends {F(y)} for its set, a simulator for a malicious sender that extracts only those queried y whose output collides with no other query suffices. Hence OPRF outputs of \( \kappa \) bits, instead of the \( 2\kappa \) bits required by the earlier analysis, give malicious security in the \( F_{\mathrm{oprf}} \)-hybrid model (Theorem 4.1). The authors estimate the saving at 20% to 50% of total communication, the larger figure when the sender's set is much larger than the receiver's.
metadata.title: Malicious OPRF-to-PSI transformation with \( \kappa \)-bit instead of \( 2\kappa \)-bit sender messages, by extracting only non-colliding OPRF queries

sections.content: \( \kappa \)-bit OPRF outputs for malicious PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The transformation is the standard one (Figure 6, p. 37): the receiver queries the OPRF on its set, the sender evaluates it on its own items and sends the values in random order, and the receiver outputs the items whose values appear. For a malicious sender, the simulator records the set \( Y^* \) of the sender's OPRF queries, keeps only queries whose outputs are distinct from those of all other queries, and extracts those whose outputs appear in the message (Theorem 4.1 proof, p. 20). A colliding pair can cause a wrong extraction only if one of its outputs equals the output of a receiver item, an event bounded by a target preimage probability of \( O(2^{-\kappa}) \) per item because the receiver's set is fixed before the function is sampled (§4, pp. 19-20). This analysis is applied to the OPRF of PSI-CONTRIB-2021-RS-VOLE-OPRF in PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-RS-MAL.

historical_context.narrative: Oblivious PRFs built on OT extension paid several \( \kappa \)-bit strings for every position of the receiver's encoded set, and the malicious PaXoS protocol paid more, because its correlation required a long error-correcting code. Rindal and Schoppmann observed that new vector-OLE generators, which expand a short correlated seed into a long correlation, give a correlation over a field at a cost that grows sublinearly in its length, \( o(m) \) for \( m \) the correlation length. The receiver solves a sparse linear system so that its encoding decodes to a hash of each of its items, then sends the encoding masked by its VOLE share. Linearity lets both parties derive the same value on common items, and hashing with a fresh random offset turns that value into an oblivious PRF.
historical_context.prior_boundary: OPRF-based PSI from OT extension, including PaXoS-PSI and SpOT-light, sent about \( 3.5\kappa \) bits per encoded position; malicious PaXoS-PSI needed \( 5\kappa \) bits per position because of its error-correcting code, an encoding of \( 11.8\kappa n \) bits (§7.1, pp. 25-26; Table 1, p. 25).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: With the PSI transformation, the authors report under 450 bits per element for \( n = 2^{20} \) with malicious security, which they call the lowest for any published PSI protocol (abstract, p. 1), and 57.86 MB against 247.6 MB for PaXoS-PSI at \( n = 2^{20} \) (Table 3, p. 29).
historical_context.technical_delta: Vector OLE with sublinear communication, from LPN-based generators that expand a short seed correlation (§3.1, pp. 13-14), replaces OT extension: the encoding P is sent masked by a VOLE vector, so each position costs \( \kappa \) bits, and linearity of decoding makes both parties' values agree on the receiver's set (§1.3, pp. 3-4; §3.2, pp. 14-15; Figure 4, p. 36). Lemmas 3.2-3.3 (pp. 16-18) prove security, with a malicious receiver's effective set bounded by the PaXoS size bound.

limitations: the 2024 revision states that the earlier version did not correctly address extraction of a malicious receiver's effective input (§2, p. 13)
the rate-1 variant with polynomial interpolation is analyzed in theory only (§7.1, p. 24; Table 1, p. 25)
qualifiers: random oracle and \( F_{\mathrm{vole}} \)-hybrid model; the simulators program the random oracle H (Theorem 3.1, p. 16; Lemmas 3.2-3.3, pp. 16-18)

a malicious receiver's effective input may have \( n' = O(n_Y) \) elements by the PaXoS size bound, \( n_Y \) its declared set size, and \( n' = m \), \( m \) the PaXoS size, under the authors' Strong OKVS Extraction Conjecture (§2, pp. 11-12; Lemma 3.3, p. 18)
the implementation instantiates VOLE from LPN with regular noise, with iterative bootstrapping and a consistency check for malicious security (§3.1, p. 14; §7.2, p. 26)
the implemented VOLE costs about \( 2^{17} \kappa n_Y^{0.05} \) bits, which dominates for small sets: 27,800 bits per element at \( n_Y = 2^{10} \) against 38 at \( n_Y = 2^{20} \) (§7.1, pp. 24-25)

metadata.statement: The receiver solves for P with \( \langle \mathrm{row}(x), P \rangle = H_F(x) \) for every x in its set using a PaXoS solver, and sends \( A = P + A' \), where the receiver's \( (A', C) \) and the sender's \( (\Delta, B) \) form a random VOLE correlation \( C = A'\Delta + B \) of length m. The sender sets \( K = B + A\Delta \); after a coin-tossed offset w, the sender's function is \( F(x) = H(\mathrm{Decode}(K, x) - \Delta H_F(x) + w, x) \), which the receiver computes as \( H(\mathrm{Decode}(C, x) + w, x) \) for its own inputs. The protocol realizes a batched OPRF against malicious adversaries in the random oracle, \( F_{\mathrm{vole}} \)-hybrid model (Theorem 3.1); the encoding costs \( \rho\kappa \) bits per input, with \( \rho \) about 2.4 for PaXoS, plus a VOLE whose communication is sublinear in its length.
metadata.title: Batched OPRF from vector OLE and a PaXoS encoding, malicious-secure in the random oracle and VOLE-hybrid model, sending about \( \rho\kappa \) bits per input plus a sublinear VOLE

sections.content: Batched OPRF from vector OLE
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The random VOLE functionality gives the sender \( \Delta \) and B and the receiver \( A' \) and \( C = A'\Delta + B \) (Figure 2, p. 14). The receiver encodes its set with the PaXoS solver so that the encoding P decodes to \( H_F(x) \) on its items (§3.2, p. 14), and derandomizes the VOLE by sending \( A = P + A' \) (Figure 4, steps 2-4, p. 36). For x in the receiver's set, linearity gives \( \mathrm{Decode}(K, x) - \Delta H_F(x) = \mathrm{Decode}(C, x) \); for other x the difference is a nonzero multiple of the uniform \( \Delta \), so the value is unpredictable to the receiver (§3.2, p. 15; Lemma 3.3, Hybrid 4, p. 18). The sender commits to its half of the offset w before the receiver's message (Figure 4, steps 1 and 5, p. 36), and x is hashed together with the value to extract a malicious sender's queries (§3.2, p. 15). The PaXoS solver is the one of PSI-CONTRIB-2020-PRTY-GARBLED-CUCKOO with \( 2.4n_Y \) main positions (§2, p. 9). With the transformation of PSI-CONTRIB-2021-RS-SHORT-OPRF-OUTPUTS this gives the PSI rows PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-RS-SH and PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2021-RS-MAL.
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: MPC-COMP-CORR-PCG: the VOLE generators used are pseudorandom correlations that expand a short seed correlation into a long one; the implementation extends Schoppmann et al.'s primal VOLE with the iterative bootstrapping of Yang et al. (§3.1, pp. 13-14; §7.2, p. 26). These VOLE papers have no record in any topic yet.

historical_context.narrative: Diffie-Hellman PSI was the cheapest option in communication, but making it secure against malicious parties had cost several times more messages and exponentiations. Cho, Dachman-Soled, and Jarecki had shown that protocol messages can be hidden by placing them as values of a polynomial at the parties' items, though they embedded full equality tests and needed an ideal cipher. Rosulek and Trieu kept the polynomial but placed in it only responses of an ordinary key agreement, let the other party send a single opening message, and replaced the ideal cipher by an ideal permutation, with random oracles giving the simulator a way to extract inputs. Using elliptic curves, the result costs about one group element per item, and on sets of a few hundred items it ran faster than any protocol in their comparison.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Cho, Dachman-Soled, and Jarecki embedded the messages of \( n \) malicious-secure string equality tests in polynomials, using an ideal cipher (§1.2, p. 5). The most efficient malicious Diffie-Hellman PSI, by De Cristofaro, Kim, and Tsudik, sends \( 6n \) group elements plus \( n \) hashes and computes \( 2n \) fixed-base and \( 4n \) variable-base exponentiations (§1.2, p. 6); Jarecki and Liu's protocol relaxes input independence (§1, p. 1).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors report the malicious protocol over 30 times faster than De Cristofaro-Kim-Tsudik with 80% less communication (§1.2, p. 6), and, for \( n = 256 \), 18-30% faster with 10% less communication than the next best protocol, which is semi-honest (§1.2, p. 5); for sets of at most 512 items they find it best in both communication and computation (§5.2, p. 20).
historical_context.technical_delta: Plain two-round key agreement replaces string equality tests, the sender sends a single key-agreement message instead of a polynomial, and an ideal permutation replaces the ideal cipher (§1.2, p. 5); random oracles H1 and H2 let the simulator extract inputs (§4, p. 10; Lemmas 5-6, pp. 10-12). A corrupt receiver's effective set size is bounded unconditionally through a polynomial overfitting game (§4.1, pp. 15-16).

limitations: the receiver's set-size slack is not removed; a tighter bound would follow from a conjecture that the authors state without proof (§4.1, p. 16)
computation is linear in exponentiations; on 10 Gbps networks OT-extension protocols overtake it between 500 and 1,000 items (§1, p. 2) and from \( n = 2^{10} \) in the LAN experiments (§5.2, p. 20)
the optimizations of Appendix B are not proved; the paper leaves their security to the reader (p. 28)
qualifiers: UC security against a malicious sender (Lemma 5, p. 10) and a malicious receiver (Lemma 6, p. 12), in the ideal permutation plus random oracle model (abstract, p. 1)
only the receiver learns the intersection (Figure 2, p. 6)

a corrupt sender's set is enforced to size \( n \); a corrupt receiver may input up to \( n' \) items, for example fewer than \( 8n + 4 \) for \( n = 2^{10} \) or \( 2^{20} \) and \( |F| = 2^{256} \), by an unconditional bound (§4.1, Lemma 10, pp. 15-16)
for a one-round key agreement such as Diffie-Hellman, the sender's two messages combine into a two-round protocol (§4, p. 15)
the implementation instantiates \( \Pi \) with fixed-key Rijndael-256 and the random oracles with SHA2 over Curve25519 with elligator encoding (§5.1, pp. 16-18)

metadata.statement: The sender sends one key-agreement message m; for each item \( y_i \) the receiver computes a fresh response \( m'_i \) and sends the polynomial P with \( P(H_1(y_i)) = \Pi^{-1}(m'_i) \); the sender computes \( k_i = \mathrm{KA.key1}(a, \Pi(P(H_1(x_i)))) \) for each item and sends the shuffled values \( H_2(x_i, k_i) \); the receiver outputs the items whose own key yields a value in that set. The protocol is UC-secure against a malicious sender if the key agreement has pseudorandom second messages, and against a malicious receiver if it is non-malleable with at least \( 2^{\kappa} \) keys, with \( \Pi \) an ideal permutation and H1, H2 random oracles. Instantiated with hashed elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman and elligator encoding, non-malleability is the oracle Diffie-Hellman assumption, and communication is one group element, \( n \) field elements, and \( n \) strings of \( 2\kappa \) bits.

sections.content: Key agreement to malicious PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Figure 4 (p. 11) needs a key agreement whose second-message space is a field F with pseudorandom messages, an ideal permutation \( \Pi \) on F, and random oracles \( H_1: \{0,1\}^* \to F \) and \( H_2: \{0,1\}^* \times F \to \{0,1\}^{2\kappa} \). The simulator against a corrupt sender programs \( \Pi \) so that every output is a key-agreement message with known randomness and extracts from H2 queries (Lemma 5, p. 10); against a corrupt receiver it extracts the items y with an H1 query whose \( P(H_1(y)) \) was obtained from \( \Pi^{-1} \) (Lemma 6, p. 12), relying on non-malleability to replace the other keys by random ones (Lemma 7, p. 14). Costs: one key-agreement message and \( n \) keys for the sender, \( n \) responses and \( n \) keys for the receiver, plus interpolation and multi-point evaluation of a degree-\( n \) polynomial in \( O(n \log^2 n) \) field operations (§4, p. 15).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: PKE-RESULT-1976-DH-INTERACTIVE-PUBLIC-CHANNEL-KEY-AGREEMENT: the key agreement used in the instantiation, in its hashed variant with elligator encoding (§3.2, pp. 8-9). Cho-Dachman-Soled-Jarecki (CT-RSA 2016), the stated starting point (§1.2, p. 5), the ideal permutation model, elligator encodings, and the oracle Diffie-Hellman assumption have no record in any topic.

historical_context.narrative: The two-message Diffie-Hellman intersection protocol from the late 1990s remained the reference point for low communication, and later work had trimmed only its computation. Rosulek and Trieu observed that in their key agreement construction one party needs to send only a single opening message, while the other packs one response per item into a polynomial. For honest-but-curious parties the hashing used to extract inputs can be dropped and the returned keys shortened to a statistical length. Two variants result: one relies on an ideal permutation and the computational Diffie-Hellman assumption, the other avoids the permutation at the cost of one extra field element and a stronger oracle assumption. Both send about one group element per item in total, which the authors present as the first communication gain over the classic protocol.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The classic semi-honest Diffie-Hellman PSI of Huberman, Franklin, and Hogg, as the paper describes it, sends \( 2n \) group elements plus \( n \) hashes and computes \( 4n \) variable-base exponentiations (§1.2, pp. 5-6); the only improvement the authors know, due to Jarecki and Liu, lowers computation by about 5-15% (§1, p. 2).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors call this the first improvement in the communication of Diffie-Hellman PSI in over 20 years, by over 40% (§1, p. 2), with 45% less communication than the next best protocol for \( n = 256 \) (§1.2, p. 5); for \( n_X = 2^{16} \) and \( n_Y = 2^{20} \) it sends 12.58 MB against 46.14 MB (§5.2, p. 19).
historical_context.technical_delta: One party sends a single key-agreement message and the other encodes its \( n \) responses in one polynomial, so the total is \( n + 1 \) group elements plus \( n \) hashes, with \( 3n \) fixed-base and \( 2n \) variable-base exponentiations and two degree-\( n \) interpolation or evaluation steps (§1.2, p. 6; Appendix A.1, Figure 5, p. 24; Appendix A.2, Figure 6, p. 26).

limitations: the hardness assumptions in Table 1 do not list the random oracle or the ideal permutation (Table 1, p. 4)
computation remains one or two exponentiations per item, so OT-extension protocols are faster on large sets in the LAN setting (§5.2, p. 20)

the comparison with classic Diffie-Hellman PSI uses the paper's own description of that protocol, with \( n \) hashes in place of \( n \) group elements in one direction (§1.2, pp. 5-6; Table 1, p. 4)
qualifiers: variant 1: secure against a semi-honest sender if the key agreement has pseudorandom messages and \( \Pi \) is an ideal permutation (Lemma 11, p. 24), and against a semi-honest receiver if the key agreement is secure against eavesdroppers (Lemma 12, p. 25)
variant 2: no ideal permutation; secure against a semi-honest receiver if the key agreement is non-malleable with pseudorandom second messages (Lemma 13, p. 27)
hashed Diffie-Hellman key agreement is secure against eavesdroppers under CDH in the random oracle model (§3.2, p. 8)
only the receiver learns the intersection (Figure 5, step 7, p. 24)
the October 2021 revision repaired a bug in the original semi-honest proof and added variant 2 (§1.3, p. 6)

metadata.statement: Dropping the random oracles used only for extraction, the receiver interpolates P with \( \Pi(P(y_i)) = m'_i \) and the sender returns its keys shortened to \( \lambda + 2 \log n \) bits (variant 1), which is secure against semi-honest parties if the key agreement is secure against eavesdroppers with pseudorandom second messages and \( \Pi \) is an ideal permutation; variant 2 drops the ideal permutation by fixing P(0) to a random value, at one extra field element, and needs a non-malleable key agreement. sections.content: Variant 1 (Figure 5, p. 24): the sender sends \( m = \mathrm{KA.msg1}(a) \); the receiver sends P interpolated on \( (y_i, \Pi^{-1}(\mathrm{KA.msg2}(b_i, m))) \); the sender sends the shuffled keys \( k_i = \mathrm{KA.key1}(a, \Pi(P(x_i))) \) of length \( \lambda + 2 \log n \); the receiver outputs \( y_i \) with \( \mathrm{KA.key2}(b_i, m) \) in the set. Variant 2 (Figure 6, p. 26): \( P(y_i) \) is the key-agreement message itself and \( P(0) = R \) for a random R, which lets the simulator program one evaluation point at a time (Appendix A.2, p. 26). Correctness fails with probability at most about \( n^2/|\mathrm{KA.K}| \) (Appendix A.1, p. 24).

historical_context.narrative: In VOLE-based PSI the receiver sends its encoded set masked by a VOLE vector, so every encoded position costs one field element, and the field had to be as large as the computational security parameter. Raghuraman and Rindal separated the two roles of that field. The sender's secret multiplier must be hard to guess, but the encoded values only need to avoid accidental collisions among all pairs of items, which takes about \( \lambda + \log n \) bits. Subfield VOLE, in which one vector lies in a small base field and everything else in a large extension, provides exactly this split. The receiver's message shrinks to statistical-parameter size per position, and communication no longer grows with \( \kappa \) times the set size.
historical_context.prior_boundary: VOLE-PSI performed all VOLE arithmetic over a field of about \( 2^{\kappa} \) elements, so derandomizing the correlation cost about \( \kappa \) bits per OKVS position, and its communication scaled with \( \kappa \) times the set size (abstract, p. 1; §1.2, p. 4).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors call it the first PSI with communication \( O(n\lambda + n \log n) \), not scaling with \( \kappa n \) (abstract, p. 1), and report \( 180n \) bits for \( n = 2^{20} \) against \( 426n \) for VOLE-PSI (§1.1, p. 3; Table 2, p. 25).
historical_context.technical_delta: Only \( \Delta \) must come from a large field for security; the encoded values need only be long enough to avoid spurious matches among the \( n_X n_Y \) pairs, so the OKVS lives in the base field of a subfield VOLE (§1.2, p. 4; §4, pp. 21-22; Figure 9, p. 23; Figure 12, p. 32); the proof is Theorem 3 (pp. 33-35).

limitations: the abstract reports \( 187n \) bits for \( n = 2^{20} \), while §1.1 (p. 3) and Table 2 (p. 25) give \( 180n \)
the low-communication instantiation is slower than the fast one: 1,353 ms against 369 ms for \( n = 2^{20} \) on one thread (Table 2, p. 25)
the malicious protocol of the paper does not use subfield VOLE (§4, p. 23)
qualifiers: semi-honest security only, in the \( F_{\text{sub-vole}} \)-hybrid model with random oracles \( H_{\mathbb{B}} \) and \( H_o \) (Theorem 3, p. 33)
requires a base field of size \( |\mathbb{B}| \ge 2^{\lambda + \log_2(n_Y) + \log_2(n_X)} \) and an extension field of size \( |\mathbb{F}| \ge 2^{\kappa} \) (Theorem 3, p. 33)
the low-communication instantiation uses the OKVS without clustering, \( m = 1.23n \) (§4, p. 22)

metadata.statement: In semi-honest VOLE-based PSI, a subfield VOLE \( C = A\Delta + B \), with \( A \) over a small base field \( \mathbb{B} \) and \( \Delta, B, C \) over an extension \( \mathbb{F} \) of size at least \( 2^{\kappa} \), lets the receiver derandomize the correlation by sending \( A - P \), where P is an OKVS over \( \mathbb{B} \) that decodes to \( H_{\mathbb{B}}(x) \) on its items. If \( |\mathbb{B}| \ge 2^{\lambda + \log_2(n_X n_Y)} \), the protocol realizes PSI against semi-honest adversaries in the \( F_{\text{sub-vole}} \)-hybrid model (Theorem 3). The receiver's message is \( m \cdot \log_2 |\mathbb{B}| \) bits, \( m \) the OKVS size, and total communication is \( O(n\lambda + n \log n) \).
metadata.title: Subfield VOLE in VOLE-based PSI: OKVS entries in a base field of about \( \lambda + \log(n_X n_Y) \) bits, giving \( O(n\lambda + n \log n) \) communication, semi-honest

sections.content: Subfield VOLE in VOLE-based PSI
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The receiver encodes \( L = \{(x, H_{\mathbb{B}}(x, r'))\} \) with the OKVS of PSI-CONTRIB-2022-RR-TRIANGULATION-OKVS over the base field \( \mathbb{B} \), obtains a random subfield VOLE with A over \( \mathbb{B} \) and \( \Delta, B, C \) over \( \mathbb{F} \), and sends \( A' = A - P \), which costs \( m \cdot \log_2 |\mathbb{B}| \) bits, \( m \) the OKVS size, (Figure 9, steps 1-3, p. 23; §4, p. 22). The sender's \( B' = B + A'\Delta \) satisfies \( C - B' = \Delta P \), so by linearity \( \mathrm{Decode}(C, x) = \mathrm{Decode}(B', x) + \Delta H_{\mathbb{B}}(x) \) for each x in the receiver's set; both parties hash these values with \( H_o \), and the sender sends its hashed values for its own set (§4, p. 22; Figure 9, steps 4-5, p. 23). Because \( \Delta \) is uniform in a field of size at least \( 2^{\kappa} \), the receiver cannot predict the sender's values outside the intersection (Theorem 3 proof, Hybrid 6, p. 34). The protocol is the semi-honest OPRF-based PSI of PSI-CONTRIB-2021-RS-VOLE-OPRF with the VOLE moved to a subfield. The complete row is PSI-CONSTRUCTION-2022-RR-SD.

historical_context.narrative: Sparse encodings such as the three-hash garbled cuckoo table were fast in principle, but their concrete parameters were shaky. The unpeelable core was solved wholesale with many dense columns, and a failure bound of \( 2^{-40} \) was reached only through an amplification that doubled the work. Raghuraman and Rindal recast encoding as triangulating a sparse matrix. A greedy pass finds the rows that back-substitution can handle and leaves a gap of a few rows, which a handful of dense columns over a large field resolve. They proved the greedy pass optimal in several cases and measured how the gap behaves around the known phase transition of random hypergraphs, which let them choose the expansion directly for a target security level.
historical_context.prior_boundary: The three-hash table of Garimella et al. solved its whole 2-core with \( \lambda + |\text{2-core}| \) dense columns, needed two graph traversals, and reached failure \( 2^{-40} \) only through the star amplification, at expansion 1.32 for \( n = 2^{20} \); its 2-core bound came from an experiment (§1, p. 3; §5.1, p. 24).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The authors report encoding \( 2^{20} \) items in 653 ms and decoding them in 54 ms, 13 and 64 times faster than the three-hash table, and 143 ms with clustering against 4,912 ms for the star construction (§5.1, p. 23; Table 1, p. 25); with this OKVS their PSI runs in 369 ms for \( n = 2^{20} \) on one thread, against 2,073 ms for KKRT on the same laptop (Table 2, p. 25).
historical_context.technical_delta: Figure 1 (p. 7) triangulates by repeatedly selecting the sparse column of minimum nonzero weight, so only the rows left in the gap need dense columns (§2, pp. 5-8; Lemmas 1-2, p. 8); clustering confines rows to blocks of about \( 2^{14} \) columns for memory locality and threads (§2.1, pp. 9-10). Section 3 proves optimality for \( w = 2 \) (Lemma 4, p. 12), for \( g = 0 \) (Lemma 9, p. 19), and for duplicate rows (§3.3, p. 20), and derives parameters from Equations (1)-(3) (pp. 14-19; §3.4, p. 21).

limitations: for \( w > 2 \) optimal triangulation is argued to be hard in general, and in the worst case the greedy gap can be as large as the 2-core minus one (§3.2, p. 15; §3.3, p. 20)
the fitted bound of Equation (3) is stated for \( 3 \le w \le 20 \) and becomes an upper bound outside that range (§3.2, p. 19)
qualifiers: concrete security levels come from empirical curves fitted for \( 30 \le \lambda \le 128 \), \( 3 \le w \le 10 \), and \( 2^6 \le n \le 2^{30} \), and the line through a common point is a conjectured trend (§3.1, p. 14; §3.2, pp. 17-19)
with dense columns over a large field the values must be field elements; the binary dense variant encodes arbitrary strings (§2, p. 9)
a doubly oblivious variant, used for circuit PSI, appends random rows so that the output is uniform (Figure 1, step 5, p. 7; Theorem 2, p. 31)

metadata.statement: Each key's row has \( w \) ones among \( m' = en \) sparse positions plus a short dense part, either random bits or powers of a hashed element of a large field. The encoder permutes rows and columns into approximately lower-triangular form, leaving a gap of g rows that it solves with the dense columns in \( O(g^2) \) time, and back-substitutes the rest, for \( O(m + g^2) \) time in total, \( m \) the OKVS size. The greedy triangulation is optimal for \( w = 2 \), where \( g = O(\log n) \) at \( e = 2 \), and finds a gap of zero whenever one exists; for \( w \ge 3 \) the authors fit empirical curves around the 2-core phase transition into a formula giving the statistical security from \( n \), \( w \), and \( e \). For \( w = 3 \) they use \( e = 1.23 \) without clustering and \( e = 1.28 \) with clusters of about \( 2^{14} \) columns.
metadata.title: OKVS by sparse triangulation with a small gap: about \( 1.23n \) positions for row weight 3, linear-time encoding, and concrete failure-probability bounds

sections.content: Triangulation OKVS
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: The encoder builds the matrix H whose rows are \( \mathrm{row}(k_i) \) and looks for row and column permutations that put it in the form \( \begin{bmatrix} A & B & C \\ D & E & F \end{bmatrix} \), with F a large lower-triangular sparse block and B, E the dense columns (§2, pp. 5-6). After eliminating C, only a \( g \)-row system on the dense columns remains; if it has full row rank, which holds with probability \( 1 - 2^{-\lambda} \) for \( \lambda \) extra binary columns (Lemma 1, p. 8) or with overwhelming probability for Vandermonde-style columns over a large field (Lemma 2, p. 8), the solution follows by back-substitution (§2, p. 6). For \( w = 2 \) the rows that can be triangulated form the independent sets of a graphic matroid, so the greedy choice minimizes the gap (Lemmas 3-4, pp. 11-12); duplicate rows, which occur with probability \( O(n^{2-w}) \), are the main failure mode and motivate \( w \ge 3 \) (Lemma 6, p. 13; §3.2, p. 16). An exhaustive variant searches subsets of the 2-core and is optimal when the gap is bounded (Figure 10, p. 30; Lemma 10, p. 20). The construction improves on PSI-CONTRIB-2021-GPRTY-3H-GCT and replaces the amplification of PSI-CONTRIB-2021-GPRTY-AMPLIFICATION by direct parameter choice; §5.1 (p. 24) argues that the empirical 2-core bound used there overstates security by a few bits (for example \( \lambda = 27 \) rather than 29).

historical_context.narrative: Threshold PSI among many parties had two kinds of protocols that avoid paying for the full sets: those built on fully homomorphic encryption, nearly linear in the threshold, and those built on additively homomorphic encryption, quadratic in it, \( O(\kappa \ell t^2 \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \). One protocol was nearly linear without fully homomorphic encryption, but only under a stricter condition that bounds all elements outside the intersection together. Ghosh and Simkin applied their bucketing compiler to the quadratic multiparty cardinality test of Branco, Döttling, and Pu, after rewriting it with generic secure computation, then reused their earlier step for computing a large intersection. The result releases the intersection when every set is close to it, communicates \( O(\lambda^2 \ell t \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \) bits, quasilinear in the threshold \( t \), and needs only oblivious transfer or additively homomorphic encryption.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Ghosh and Simkin gave \( O(\kappa t^2 \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \) for two parties from oblivious transfer and additively homomorphic encryption and \( O(\kappa t \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \) from FHE; Branco, Döttling, and Pu gave \( O(\kappa\ell t^2 \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \) for \( \ell \) parties from threshold additively homomorphic encryption; Badrinarayanan et al. gave \( O(\kappa\ell t \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \) when the union exceeds the intersection by at most \( t \), and FHE-based protocols matching \( \Omega(\ell t) \) up to polylog factors (abstract, p. 1; §1, pp. 1-2). The authors state that all three left asymptotically optimal multiparty protocols from assumptions other than FHE open (§1, p. 2).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: It gives multiparty threshold PSI for the large-intersection condition with quasilinear rather than quadratic dependence on \( t \) from simple assumptions, which the authors describe as a significant theoretical step (abstract, p. 1; §1.2, pp. 2-3).
historical_context.technical_delta: The compiler of the paper reduces the threshold handled by the inner multiparty cardinality test to \( O(\ln t\ell) \), so the quadratic inner protocol contributes only polylogarithmic factors (§4.1, p. 16; Corollary 5, p. 16); the intersection is then computed with the earlier Ghosh-Simkin protocol at \( \tilde O(\kappa\ell t) \) (§1.2, p. 2; Corollary 6, p. 16).

limitations: no round complexity is stated for the multiparty protocol (Corollaries 5-6, p. 16)
not claimed practical; concretely efficient protocols are left open (§1.2, p. 3)
the bound carries a \( \lambda^2 \) factor and \( \mathrm{polylog}(t) \) factors relative to the \( \Omega(\ell t) \) lower bound shown in the earlier works (§1, p. 2; abstract, p. 1)
qualifiers: passive security against a static adversary corrupting all but one party, with pairwise private channels and a unit-cost broadcast channel (§2.1, p. 4; Corollary 6, p. 16)
all sets have exactly \( n \) elements, and the output condition is an intersection of at least \( n - t \) elements (Figure 9, p. 11; abstract, p. 1)
the inner multiparty cardinality test of Branco, Döttling, and Pu is assumed adaptable to generic secure computation at \( O(\kappa\ell \,\mathrm{poly}(t)) \) (§4.1, p. 16)

\( \lambda/\kappa \) is in \( O(1) \), so the bound \( O(\lambda\kappa \ell t \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \) is \( O(\lambda^2 \ell t \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \) in the security parameter (§2, p. 4; abstract, p. 1)

historical_context.narrative: Threshold PSI protocols spend most of their effort on a single bit: are the parties' sets close enough that their intersection should be released? Known tests for that bit cost a polynomial in the threshold \( t \), quadratic in the best multiparty protocols that avoid fully homomorphic encryption. Ghosh and Simkin observed that random partitioning shrinks the threshold. After the elements are hashed into \( t \) buckets, each bucket of nearly identical sets differs in only \( O(\ln t\ell) \) elements, so an expensive test run per bucket with a logarithmic threshold costs only polylogarithmically much. Repeating the partition a security parameter's worth of times makes it likely that one partition works, and secret sharing lets the parties add bucket counts without revealing them. Any polynomial-cost test thus becomes quasilinear, \( O(\lambda^2 \ell t \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \).
historical_context.prior_boundary: Every threshold PSI protocol, following Ghosh and Simkin, first runs a cardinality test that outputs one bit and then computes the intersection; the second step already costs \( \tilde O(\kappa\ell t) \) from oblivious transfer or additively homomorphic encryption (abstract, p. 1; §1.2, p. 2). Multiparty cardinality tests from assumptions weaker than FHE, such as that of Branco, Döttling, and Pu, cost \( O(\kappa\ell t^2 \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \) (§1, p. 1).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The efficiency of the inner protocol only affects the constant in the \( \mathrm{polylog}(t) \) exponent, so multiparty cardinality tests with quasilinear dependence on \( t \) follow from effectively any assumption implying secure computation (§1.2, p. 2).
historical_context.technical_delta: Random partitioning into \( t \) buckets leaves each bucket, with constant probability per partition, at most \( O(\ln t\ell) \) elements outside its intersection (Lemma 2, p. 7; Theorem 5, p. 12); \( \lambda \) partitions make some partition good except with probability \( 2^{-\lambda} \) (Theorems 2 and 6, pp. 8, 14). Padding keeps bucket sizes equal so intersection sizes stay meaningful (Lemmas 3 and 5, pp. 11-14), and the exact bucket intersection size is assembled from cardinality tests at each small threshold (Figures 8 and 12; Theorems 4 and 8, pp. 10, 16).

limitations: the authors consider the results too inefficient for most real-world parameters (§1.2, p. 3)
the two-party instantiation does not improve asymptotically on the existing \( O(\kappa t \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \) (p. 4)
Theorems 3 and 7 are stated in hybrid models with ideal functionalities for the bucket counts and comparisons (pp. 9, 15)
qualifiers: static passive adversary corrupting all but one party; pairwise authenticated private channels and a broadcast channel of unit cost; standalone simulation-based security (§2.1, p. 4)
the input PICT must output secret shares, which the authors say all existing protocols can easily be adapted to do (§1.2, footnote 3, p. 2)
the partitions use public random functions; pseudorandom functions with a key known to all parties are said to work equally well (footnote 4, p. 3)
the statistical security parameter \( \lambda \) satisfies \( \lambda/\kappa \in O(1) \), and the field has at least \( 2^{\lambda} \) elements (§2, p. 4)
the multiparty version requires all sets to have exactly \( n \) elements (Figure 9, p. 11); the two-party version allows sets of at most \( n \) elements (Figure 1, p. 5)

metadata.statement: Against a static passive adversary corrupting all but one of \( \ell \) parties, any private intersection cardinality test (PICT) with secret-shared output and communication \( O(\kappa\ell \,\mathrm{poly}(t)) \) yields a PICT for threshold \( t \) with communication \( O(\lambda^2 \ell t \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \): the parties hash their sets \( \lambda \) times with public random functions into \( t \) buckets, pad every bucket to a common size, obtain for each bucket a secret sharing of its intersection size (or of a default value when the bucket's threshold \( \tilde t = O(\ln t\ell) \) is exceeded) by running the given PICT at each threshold up to \( \tilde t \), sum these per partition, and test with generic secure computation whether some partition's sum shows an intersection of at least \( n - t \); failure probability is at most \( 2^{-\lambda} \).
metadata.title: Compiler from any intersection cardinality test with secret-shared output and \( O(\kappa\ell \,\mathrm{poly}(t)) \) communication to one with \( O(\lambda^2 \ell t \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \), passive security

sections.content: Compiler for intersection cardinality tests
sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Two-party version (Figure 7, p. 9): for each of \( \lambda \) partitions and each of \( t \) buckets, the parties call \( F_{\triangle} \) with threshold \( \tilde t = 1 + 3 \ln 2t \) and default \( t + 1 \), add the shares per partition, and call \( F_{\text{vec-leq}} \) to test whether some sum is at most \( t \) (Theorem 3, p. 9). \( F_{\triangle} \) is realized from \( \tilde t \) cardinality tests at thresholds \( 1, \ldots, \tilde t \) (Figure 8, Theorem 4, p. 10). Multiparty version (Figure 11, p. 15): buckets are padded to size \( n + 1 \), \( F_{\ell\text{-}\cap} \) returns the bucket intersection size or the default \( n + 1 \), \( F_{\ell\text{-min}} \) removes the padding offset, and \( F_{\ell\text{-vec-intrvl}} \) tests whether some partition's total lies between \( n - t \) and \( n \) (Theorem 7, p. 15); \( F_{\ell\text{-}\cap} \) is realized from cardinality tests at each threshold (Figure 12, Theorem 8, p. 16).
sections.heading: Exact contribution

sections.content: None. Cramer and Damgård's constant-round secure linear algebra, used to instantiate the two-party inner test (p. 10), has no entry yet.

nodes.subtitle: Threshold Private Set Intersection with Better Communication Complexity
nodes.summary: Against a static passive adversary corrupting all but one of \( \ell \) parties, any private intersection cardinality test (PICT) with secret-shared output and communication \( O(\kappa\ell \,\mathrm{poly}(t)) \) yields a PICT for threshold \( t \) with communication \( O(\lambda^2 \ell t \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \): the parties hash their sets \( \lambda \) times with public random functions into \( t \) buckets, pad every bucket to a common size, obtain for each bucket a secret sharing of its intersection size (or of a default value when the bucket's threshold \( \tilde t = O(\ln t\ell) \) is exceeded) by running the given PICT at each threshold up to \( \tilde t \), sum these per partition, and test with generic secure computation whether some partition's sum shows an intersection of at least \( n - t \); failure probability is at most \( 2^{-\lambda} \).
nodes.title: Compiler from any intersection cardinality test with secret-shared output and \( O(\kappa\ell \,\mathrm{poly}(t)) \) communication to one with \( O(\lambda^2 \ell t \,\mathrm{polylog}\, t) \), passive security

historical_context.narrative: Each new multiparty PSI paper had compared itself with a few recent protocols, so older designs based on homomorphic encryption dropped out of view on the strength of measurements taken in other settings. Vos, Conti, and Erkin put the semi-honest, collusion-resistant protocols on one footing. They instantiate the homomorphic designs with elliptic-curve ElGamal and count curve multiplications per element, and they express the protocols built from two-party subprotocols in calls to oblivious transfer, programmable OPRFs, and oblivious linear evaluation. Counted this way, older homomorphic designs become competitive with recent proposals, and the cheapest choice changes with the collusion bound, the error an application tolerates, and the computing power of the assistants. The authors conclude that no single protocol is the state of the art.
historical_context.prior_boundary: Each new multiparty PSI paper compared itself with a small subset of earlier protocols, and older works received less attention because of performance comparisons that do not cover all points of comparison (abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2). The surveyed papers report experiments on different hardware, which the authors caution against comparing directly (§5.1.1, p. 10; §7, p. 12).
historical_context.significance_at_publication: The counts show that Hazay and Venkitasubramaniam is cheaper for weak assistants, Cheon et al. for equal computing power and small \( t_c \), and Vos et al. for \( t_c \) close to the number of parties \( \ell \) with a tolerated error (§7.1, p. 13), and the authors conclude that it is not possible to name one state-of-the-art protocol and that direct comparisons cannot be conclusive until realistic parameters are known (§8, p. 13; §9, p. 14).
historical_context.technical_delta: The authors derive or collect asymptotic communication, computation, and rounds for every protocol without known attacks (Table 2, p. 10; Appendix A, pp. 16-17), and worst-case counts of elliptic-curve multiplications for the PHE-based protocols of Sang and Shen, Cheon et al., Hazay and Venkitasubramaniam, and Vos et al., and of OT, OPPRF, or OLE calls for those of Inbar et al., Kolesnikov et al., Chandran et al., Kavousi et al., Nevo et al., Ghosh and Nilges, and Gordon et al. (§7.1-7.2, pp. 12-13; Table 3, p. 13; Appendix B, pp. 17-18), modifying some protocols so that only the leader receives the output.

limitations: counts of primitive operations, not measured running times or communication; no implementation is evaluated, which the meta-review lists as a concern (§7, p. 12; Appendix C.4, p. 19)
no count is given for Garimella et al., whose multiparty analysis was deferred to an unavailable full version (Table 3, p. 13; Appendix B.2, p. 18)
OT, OPPRF, and OLE counts are not converted into elliptic-curve operations, so the two families are compared separately (§7, p. 12)
qualifiers: semi-honest protocols with collusion resistance \( t_c \) and output to the leader only; server-aided protocols are excluded (§1, p. 2; Definition 1, p. 2)
PHE-based protocols are counted with elliptic-curve ElGamal, with precomputed multiplications taken as four times cheaper and homomorphic additions ignored (§7.1, pp. 12-13; Appendix B.1, p. 17)

2PC-based protocols are counted in sub-protocol calls, with one OPPRF as one OPRF and one OPRF as about 3.5 OTs; OLEs are counted separately, and setup such as base OTs is ignored (§7.2, p. 13; Appendix B.2, p. 18)
where possible, protocols are analyzed in the augmented semi-honest model (§7.2, p. 13)
some protocols are modified before counting, for example so that only the leader receives the output (Appendix B.1, pp. 17-18)

metadata.statement: For semi-honest multiparty PSI protocols that resist \( t_c \) colluding parties and give the output to a leader, the latest homomorphic-encryption-based protocols are instantiated with elliptic-curve ElGamal and costed in elliptic-curve multiplications per element, and protocols built from two-party subprotocols are costed in calls to OT, OPPRF (counted as 3.5 OTs), or OLE, for the leader, an assistant, and in total, in the worst case; derived asymptotic communication, computation, and round counts accompany them. On these counts the cheapest protocol changes with the assistants' computing power, the collusion bound \( t_c \), the tolerated error, and the number of parties, older homomorphic-encryption protocols instantiated with modern cryptosystems compete with recent proposals, and no single protocol is the state of the art.

sections.heading: Overview

sections.content: Table 3 (p. 13) gives, per element, the worst-case elliptic-curve multiplications of the leader, an assistant, and in total for four PHE-based protocols, and the OTs or OLEs for seven 2PC-based protocols; for example, Kolesnikov et al. need \( 7(\ell - 1)n \) OTs at the leader and \( 3.5(\ell + 1)(\ell - 1)n \) in total, and Nevo et al. \( 3.5t_c n \) at the leader (Table 3, p. 13; Appendix B.2, p. 18). Three use cases with assumed values of \( \ell \), \( t_c \), set size \( n \), and error (mutual customers, common IP addresses, consensus voting) are matched to protocols (§7.3, p. 13). The authors identify improvements in oblivious key-value stores and homomorphic cryptosystems as the most impactful technical advances (§8, p. 13).

introduced_in.citation: Pascal Paillier, Public-Key Cryptosystems Based on Composite Degree Residuosity Classes, EUROCRYPT 1999

metadata.name: Decisional composite residuosity (DCR)

references.citation: Pascal Paillier, Public-Key Cryptosystems Based on Composite Degree Residuosity Classes, EUROCRYPT 1999

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 no way to decide composite residuosity is known other than factoring the modulus; it is broken in quantum polynomial time by Shor's algorithm.

sections.content:
Let \( N = pq \) be an RSA modulus. An element \( z \in \mathbb{Z}_{N^2}^* \) is
an \( N \)-th residue if \( z = y^{N} \bmod N^2 \) for some
\( y \in \mathbb{Z}_{N^2}^* \). The decisional composite residuosity assumption
states that, given \( N \), no probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm
distinguishes a uniformly random \( N \)-th residue modulo \( N^2 \) from a
uniformly random element of \( \mathbb{Z}_{N^2}^* \) with non-negligible
advantage.
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
Factoring \( N \) breaks DCR, and no other attack is known. DCR gives
semantic security of Paillier encryption (`[Paillier99]`), which is
additively homomorphic, and is the encryption assumption in Paillier-based
two-party and threshold ECDSA (`[Lindell17]`, `[GG18]`,
`[CGGMP20]`) and in the LWE-to-Paillier compression of
`[ADK26]`.
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
DCR implies factoring; the converse is open. Paillier (1999)
also defines the computational composite residuosity class problem and shows it
is no harder than RSA with exponent \( N \). DCR and quadratic residuosity are not known to be related.
sections.heading: Relations

metadata.name: Decisional Diffie-Hellman (DDH)

references.citation: Dan Boneh, The Decision Diffie-Hellman Problem, ANTS-III 1998
Stefan Brands, An Efficient Off-line Electronic Cash System Based on the Representation Problem, CWI Technical Report CS-R9323, 1993
Antoine Joux and Kim Nguyen, Separating Decision Diffie-Hellman from Computational Diffie-Hellman in Cryptographic Groups, J. Cryptology 16, 2003
Alex Escala, Gottfried Herold, Eike Kiltz, Carla Ràfols, Jorge Villar, An Algebraic Framework for Diffie-Hellman Assumptions, CRYPTO 2013

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 DDH is believed hard in prime-order elliptic-curve groups without an efficient pairing and in prime-order subgroups of finite fields; it is false in groups with a symmetric pairing and in full groups \( \mathbb{Z}_p^* \), and it is broken in quantum polynomial time by Shor's algorithm.

sections.content:
Let \( \mathbb{G} = \langle g \rangle \) be a cyclic group of prime order
\( p \). The DDH assumption states that no probabilistic polynomial-time
algorithm distinguishes

\[
(g, g^{a}, g^{b}, g^{ab}) \quad \text{from} \quad (g, g^{a}, g^{b}, g^{c})
\]

for uniform \( a, b, c \in \mathbb{Z}_p \) with non-negligible advantage. In the
matrix Diffie-Hellman framework DDH is the case \( k = 1 \) of k-Lin.
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
DDH fails whenever a group has extra structure that tests the relation: in the
full group \( \mathbb{Z}_p^* \) the Legendre symbol leaks whether exponents are
even, so DDH is used in prime-order subgroups; in groups with an efficiently
computable symmetric pairing \( e(g^a, g^b) = e(g, g^{ab}) \) tests the tuple,
so DDH is easy while CDH may remain hard (Joux and Nguyen 2003). In
prime-order elliptic-curve groups without an efficient pairing, and in the
source groups of asymmetric (Type III) pairings, no attack better than
computing discrete logarithms is known. Boneh's 1998 survey credits Brands
(1993) with observing that earlier undeniable-signature proposals implicitly
relied on DDH.
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
DDH implies CDH and hence DL. It implies k-Lin for every \( k \ge 1 \)
in the same group, in particular DLIN; the converse fails
in groups with symmetric pairings, where DLIN is believed to hold but DDH does
not. SXDH is DDH in both source groups of an asymmetric pairing.
ElGamal (`[ElGamal85]`) and Cramer-Shoup (`[CS98]`)
encryption, TreePIR (`[LP23b]`) and the Glacius threshold
Schnorr signature (`[BDLR24]`) rely on DDH.
sections.heading: Relations

introduced_in.citation: Oded Regev, On Lattices, Learning with Errors, Random Linear Codes, and Cryptography, STOC 2005; J. ACM 56(6), 2009

metadata.name: Learning with errors (LWE)

references.citation: Oded Regev, On Lattices, Learning with Errors, Random Linear Codes, and Cryptography, J. ACM 56(6), 2009
Chris Peikert, Public-Key Cryptosystems from the Worst-Case Shortest Vector Problem, STOC 2009
Zvika Brakerski, Adeline Langlois, Chris Peikert, Oded Regev, Damien Stehlé, Classical Hardness of Learning with Errors, STOC 2013
Sanjeev Arora and Rong Ge, New Algorithms for Learning in Presence of Errors, ICALP 2011
Martin R. Albrecht, Rachel Player, Sam Scott, On the Concrete Hardness of Learning with Errors, J. Math. Cryptol. 9(3), 2015
Yilei Chen, Quantum Algorithms for Lattice Problems, IACR ePrint 2024/555 (claim withdrawn, April 2024)

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 no classical or quantum polynomial-time algorithm is known for LWE with the parameters covered by the worst-case reductions; a claimed polynomial-time quantum algorithm (Chen, April 2024) was withdrawn by its author after a bug was found.

sections.content:
Fix a dimension \( n \), a modulus \( q \), a number of samples \( m \), and an
error distribution \( \chi \) over \( \mathbb{Z} \), typically a discrete
Gaussian of width \( \alpha q \) with \( \alpha q > 2\sqrt{n} \). Sample
\( A \leftarrow \mathbb{Z}_q^{m \times n} \), a secret
\( s \leftarrow \mathbb{Z}_q^{n} \) (uniform, or from \( \chi^n \) in the
equivalent "normal form"), and \( e \leftarrow \chi^{m} \). Set

\[
b = A s + e \bmod q .
\]

Search LWE asks to recover \( s \) from \( (A, b) \). Decision LWE asks to
distinguish \( (A, b) \) from \( (A, u) \) with \( u \) uniform in
\( \mathbb{Z}_q^{m} \). For polynomial \( q \) the two versions are equivalent
up to polynomial factors.
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
Regev (2005) gave a quantum reduction from the worst-case approximate lattice
problems GapSVP and SIVP to LWE with approximation factor
\( \tilde O(n/\alpha) \). Peikert (2009) gave a classical reduction from
GapSVP for exponential modulus \( q \ge 2^{n/2} \), and Brakerski, Langlois,
Peikert, Regev and Stehlé (2013) extended classical hardness to polynomial
modulus by trading dimension for modulus.

The best known attacks are lattice reduction (primal and dual attacks with
BKZ), combinatorial BKW-type algorithms, and hybrid attacks; all take time
\( 2^{\Theta(n)} \) for the parameters used in practice. Concrete security is
estimated with the lattice estimator introduced by Albrecht, Player and Scott
(2015) and its later versions; the authors of that paper note that its cost
models have since been superseded. Arora and Ge (2011) solve LWE in time
\( 2^{\tilde O(n^{2\varepsilon})} \) when \( \alpha q = n^{\varepsilon} \) with
\( \varepsilon < 1/2 \), and in polynomial time when the error takes only a few
known values and many samples are available; this rules out very narrow or
few-valued error distributions, not the regime with \( \alpha q > 2\sqrt n \).

In April 2024 Chen posted a claimed polynomial-time quantum algorithm for LWE
with certain polynomial approximation factors (ePrint 2024/555); on 18 April
2024 the author reported a bug in a step of the algorithm and stated that the
claim does not hold.
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
Worst-case hardness of GapSVP and SIVP implies LWE hardness (quantumly in
general; classically for the moduli above). An algorithm for SIS on
the transpose of \( A \) with norm bound \( \beta \) such that
\( \beta \alpha q \ll q \) distinguishes LWE samples from uniform, so LWE with
matching parameters implies SIS.

Ring-LWE (ASM-RLWE) and Module-LWE are structured variants over
polynomial rings; LWE is the rank-\( n \), degree-1 case of Module-LWE.
Cheon and Stehlé (2015) reduce LWE to a variant of the approximate GCD problem. Succinct LWE gives the adversary extra trapdoor
information and therefore implies LWE. Evasive LWE is a
conditional assumption about LWE samples together with preimages and is not
implied by LWE.

introduced_in.citation: Oded Goldreich, Shafi Goldwasser, Silvio Micali, How to Construct Random Functions, J. ACM 33(4), 1986 (FOCS 1984)

metadata.name: Pseudorandom functions (PRF)

references.citation: Oded Goldreich, Shafi Goldwasser, Silvio Micali, How to Construct Random Functions, J. ACM 33(4), 1986
Johan Håstad, Russell Impagliazzo, Leonid A. Levin, Michael Luby, A Pseudorandom Generator from any One-way Function, SIAM J. Comput. 28(4), 1999
Mark Zhandry, How to Construct Quantum Random Functions, FOCS 2012; J. ACM 2021

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 PRFs exist if and only if one-way functions exist, the Goldreich-Goldwasser-Micali construction is secure against quantum queries, and practical instantiations (AES, ChaCha20, SHA-2/SHA-3-based PRFs) have no known attacks on full rounds.

sections.content:
A keyed function family \( F : \{0,1\}^{\lambda} \times \{0,1\}^{n} \to
\{0,1\}^{m} \) is a pseudorandom function if, for a uniformly random key
\( k \), no probabilistic polynomial-time adversary with oracle access to
\( F(k, \cdot) \) distinguishes it from a uniformly random function
\( \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}^m \) with non-negligible advantage. Quantum-secure
PRFs require indistinguishability even when the adversary queries the oracle
in superposition.

As used in topic results, the assumption is that some efficient PRF exists,
typically instantiated with a block cipher, a stream-cipher core, or a hash
function in a keyed mode.
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
Goldreich, Goldwasser and Micali (1984) built PRFs from any length-doubling
pseudorandom generator (ASM-PRG); with Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby
(1999) this shows PRFs exist if and only if one-way functions exist. Zhandry
(2012) proved the GGM construction secure against quantum superposition
queries when the underlying generator is quantum-secure. For concrete
instantiations, see AES and ChaCha20.
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
PRFs and PRGs imply each other. Concrete primitives modelled as PRFs (AES via
the PRP/PRF switching lemma, the ChaCha20 block function) imply that PRFs
exist. PRFs are the assumption behind client-preprocessing PIR such as
`[ZPSZ24]` and `[LP24]`, behind the
symmetric-key pseudorandom correlation functions of `[IKR26]`,
and behind the PRF and PRF_msg components of SPHINCS+ (`[HKB+19]`).

metadata.name: Pseudorandom generators (PRG)

references.citation: Manuel Blum and Silvio Micali, How to Generate Cryptographically Strong Sequences of Pseudo-Random Bits, SIAM J. Comput. 13(4), 1984
Andrew C. Yao, Theory and Application of Trapdoor Functions, FOCS 1982

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 PRGs exist if and only if one-way functions exist, and practical instantiations (block ciphers in counter mode, stream ciphers such as ChaCha20) have no known attacks on full rounds.

sections.content:
A deterministic polynomial-time function
\( G : \{0,1\}^{\lambda} \to \{0,1\}^{\ell(\lambda)} \) with
\( \ell(\lambda) > \lambda \) is a pseudorandom generator if, for a uniformly
random seed \( s \), no probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm distinguishes
\( G(s) \) from a uniformly random \( \ell(\lambda) \)-bit string with
non-negligible advantage.
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
Blum and Micali (1982) and Yao (1982) introduced the notion and built
generators from specific one-way permutations; Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and
Luby (1999) built a PRG from any one-way function. Practical instantiations
are block ciphers in counter mode and stream ciphers; their status is tracked
under AES as a pseudorandom permutation (AES PRP) and ChaCha20 block function as a PRF (ChaCha20).
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
A length-doubling PRG yields a PRF by the Goldreich-Goldwasser-Micali tree
construction, and a PRF yields a PRG by evaluation on distinct inputs, so the
two assumptions are equivalent as existence statements (ASM-PRF). Distributed
point functions, the basis of two-server PIR in `[GI14]`, are
built from any PRG.

metadata.name: Ring learning with errors (Ring-LWE)

references.citation: Vadim Lyubashevsky, Chris Peikert, Oded Regev, On Ideal Lattices and Learning with Errors over Rings, J. ACM 60(6), 2013
Damien Stehlé, Ron Steinfeld, Keisuke Tanaka, Keita Xagawa, Efficient Public Key Encryption Based on Ideal Lattices, ASIACRYPT 2009
Yara Elias, Kristin E. Lauter, Ekin Ozman, Katherine E. Stange, Provably Weak Instances of Ring-LWE, CRYPTO 2015
Chris Peikert, How (Not) to Instantiate Ring-LWE, SCN 2016
Ronald Cramer, Léo Ducas, Benjamin Wesolowski, Short Stickelberger Class Relations and Application to Ideal-SVP, EUROCRYPT 2017

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 no attack on Ring-LWE over cyclotomic rings with error distributions covered by the worst-case reduction is known to beat generic lattice reduction; known breaks apply only to non-standard rings or error distributions narrower than the reductions require.

sections.content:
Let \( K \) be a number field of degree \( n \) with ring of integers
\( R \) (the standard choice is the power-of-two cyclotomic ring
\( R = \mathbb{Z}[x]/(x^n + 1) \)), let \( q \) be a modulus and
\( R_q = R / qR \). Let \( \chi \) be an error distribution on \( R \) (a
discrete Gaussian in the canonical embedding, on \( R \) or on its dual
\( R^\vee \)). For a secret \( s \in R_q \), a sample is

\[
(a, \; b = a \cdot s + e) \in R_q \times R_q, \qquad a \leftarrow R_q,\; e \leftarrow \chi .
\]

Search Ring-LWE asks to recover \( s \) from polynomially many samples.
Decision Ring-LWE asks to distinguish such samples from uniform pairs in
\( R_q \times R_q \).
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
Lyubashevsky, Peikert and Regev (2010) gave a quantum reduction from the
worst-case approximate shortest vector problem on ideal lattices in \( K \) to search Ring-LWE, and a search-to-decision reduction for
cyclotomic rings and suitable moduli. Each sample gives \( n \) correlated LWE
samples, which is the source of the efficiency gain over plain LWE.

Elias, Lauter, Ozman and Stange (2015) broke decision Ring-LWE for explicit
families of non-cyclotomic fields; Peikert (2016) showed these weak instances
use spherical errors far narrower than the hardness theorems require, and that
instantiations meeting the worst-case reduction are immune to that attack.
Quantum algorithms for Ideal-SVP with approximation factor
\( 2^{\tilde O(\sqrt n)} \) in cyclotomic fields (Cramer, Ducas and Wesolowski
2017) do not reach the polynomial factors behind Ring-LWE, and that paper states
that Ring-LWE does not appear to be directly affected.
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
Worst-case Ideal-SVP hardness implies Ring-LWE by a quantum reduction. Ring-LWE
is the rank-1 case of Module-LWE. As with LWE and SIS, a Ring-SIS
solver with small enough norm distinguishes Ring-LWE samples, so
Ring-LWE with matching parameters implies Ring-SIS. Hardness of plain LWE
(ASM-LWE) is not known to imply Ring-LWE, and conversely.

Ran Canetti, Oded Goldreich, Shai Halevi, The Random Oracle Methodology, Revisited, STOC 1998; J. ACM 51(4), 2004
Dan Boneh, Özgür Dagdelen, Marc Fischlin, Anja Lehmann, Christian Schaffner, Mark Zhandry, Random Oracles in a Quantum World, ASIACRYPT 2011

metadata.status: As of 2026-10-10 the random oracle heuristic is not known to fail for any natural scheme in wide use, but there are artificial schemes that are secure in the ROM and insecure under every concrete hash function (Canetti, Goldreich, Halevi 1998).

sections.content:
A proof in the random oracle model gives every party, honest or adversarial,
oracle access to a uniformly random function
\( H : \{0,1\}^* \to \{0,1\}^{\ell} \) (or to a random function into a group or
another range). The reduction may observe the adversary's oracle queries and
choose the answers ("programming"), as long as the answers are distributed
uniformly. A scheme is then deployed with \( H \) replaced by a concrete hash
function such as SHA-2 or SHA-3. The model is a heuristic: it is not a
hardness assumption about any concrete function.

In the quantum random oracle model (QROM) the adversary may query \( H \) in
superposition, which is the appropriate model when the adversary is quantum
and \( H \) is a public hash function.
sections.heading: Definition

sections.content:
Canetti, Goldreich and Halevi constructed signature and encryption schemes that
are secure in the random oracle model but insecure for every efficiently
computable instantiation of the oracle. Their schemes are artificial; no
comparable failure is known for natural schemes such as RSA-OAEP
(`[BR94]`), Fiat-Shamir signatures (`[FS86]`) or the
Fujisaki-Okamoto transform (`[FO99]`) when instantiated with
standard hash functions. Because the instantiation claim is not a
statement about a fixed computational problem, it is not falsifiable in the
usual sense.

Classical ROM proofs that rewind the adversary or inspect its queries do not
automatically carry over to quantum adversaries; Boneh et al. (2011)
introduced the QROM for that reason, and many Fiat-Shamir and
Fujisaki-Okamoto results have since been re-proved there.
sections.heading: Status

sections.content:
The ROM is often combined with a concrete assumption (for example RSA with
random oracles for OAEP, RSA assumption (RSA); or generic groups with random oracles,
Generic group model (GGM), including the generic bilinear group model). A security proof "in the ROM under assumption X" assumes both the
idealized hash function and the hardness of X; it says nothing about security
with a concrete hash function beyond the heuristic.
